Apple’s HomeView is a $299 smart home hub with a 7-inch touchscreen, A18 chip, AI-powered Siri, and personalized experiences for up to six users. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, it offers smart home controls, FaceTime, and voice and face recognition, but has limitations with apps, games, and video.
It was pretty much THE product in the spotlight at Apple’s recent Welcome Home event. The HomeView marked Apple’s debut in the smart home hub segment. Of course, it does what every smart hub is supposed to do – let you control different smart devices in the house – but hey, this is an Apple product, so some distinct, different (and odd) touches have been added to the regular mix. As we wait for the HomeView to arrive in India at $299/Rs 39,900 on November 13, here are fourteen things worth noting about Apple’s most high-profile entry into the smart home segment:
Table of Contents
Totally buttonless with clean, smooth sides
Yep, Apple has finally delivered a touchscreen device with zero physical buttons. Only it is not an iPhone, as many had been predicting. The HomeView has only a single Type-C port (for power requirements) and no physical buttons or switches at all. Even the Type-C port is on the back of the wall-mounted version and in the spherical base of the regular version, so the sides of the HomeView are totally plain. Minimalism unlocked!
Comes in regular (iMac G4) and wall-mounted versions…and they both cost the same!
The HomeView is fundamentally a 7-inch touchscreen tablet that gives one access to different smart devices in the house, as well as does some very cool things (more on that later). It comes in two models: the regular version, which comes attached to a spherical, dome-like base and flexible “arm”, making it look like a small iMac G4 (the Sunflower Mac, remember?) and is meant to be used on a table, and there is a “Wall Mounted” version, which is just a tablet that can be mounted on a wall. Both need a power outlet as they have no battery of their own. Rather remarkably, both versions come at the same price: USD 299 (Rs 39,900). This is kind of odd because they both have rather different components and requirements, as we shall see.
Want more for your bucks? Get the regular HomeView; the Wall Mounted one has a few things missing (and fewer colors)
They might have the same price tag, but the regular HomeView is much more value for money than the Wall Mounted one. The HomeView comes with two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer, and also has dual force-canceling radiators for spatial audio and better bass. The Wall Mounted variant, on the other hand, is more of a tablet. It has only the two full-range drivers, and no woofer or radiator. What’s more, the wall mount for it costs extra – USD 59.95 or USD 79.95 depending on the option you choose from Schneider Home (more options are expected to come shortly). The regular variant also comes with a 1.5 meter Type-C cable and a 30W power adapter, which the Wall Mounted variant lacks (the mounts give these options).
As if this were not enough, you even get more color options in the regular HomeView – it comes in Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Grey, while the Wall Mounted variant has just Silver and Space Grey! If money is (relatively) tight, the regular HomeView is a no-brainer. You get additional speakers, more color options, a charging cable, and a Mac-ish design for the same price! Those speakers and that Mac-ish design at the same price as the Wall Mounted option would do it for us. The presence of that base does add to the weight of the regular HomeView – it is 952 grams as compared to the 286 grams of the Wall Mounted one.
As bright as an iPad (with also the lowest nit count on an Apple product)
The HomeView is basically a 7-inch touchscreen tablet. It comes with a Liquid Retina True Tone LCD display which is totally square in shape, with a resolution of 1088 x 1088 and a pixel density of 220 ppi. Interestingly, while its other specs are inferior to those of the iPad and iPad Air range, the HomeView comes with the same level of brightness – 500 nits. This means that the HomeView will have the same exceptional brightness that the iPad and iPad Air offer. 500 nits is also the brightness level of the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air. Interestingly, the HomeView also comes with the lowest brightness of any Apple product ever – a stunning 0.3 nits.
There’s an iPhone 16/ MacBook Neo family chip inside it
The HomeView is powered by the A18 processor, which is similar to that seen on the iPhone 16, 16 Plus and 16e. In purely tablet terms, this makes the HomeView more powerful than the base iPad (11th generation), which runs on the A16 Bionic. Interestingly, even the MacBook Neo launched earlier this year was powered by a similar processor, the A18 Pro.
Runs on…anonymous (as of now) OS
Although it says that “Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI,” Apple has not yet released the name of the operating system on which HomeView runs. It is a blend of iOS and iPadOS, and is believed to have been codenamed HomeOS. What it will be finally called is anyone’s guess.
You cannot install apps on it
Rather surprisingly, given Apple’s stress on apps, the HomeView has no app store of its own at the time of writing. It comes with a number of preinstalled apps (on Built-In Apps, as Apple calls them), but there seems to be no provision for installing apps on it. The HomeView can, however, run some apps from the iPhone – Audiobooks, Classical Music, and Apple TV. Rather interestingly, there is no visible support for any maps app yet.
It can identify faces and voices too (but seemingly does not have Face ID)
The HomeView comes with face identification through a single camera, and Apple says that it also recognizes voices, and comes with special “Secure Exclaves” that process camera and microphone feeds in a secure zone where they cannot be accessed by other software on the device or even by Apple. Interestingly, there is no mention of Face ID in the tech specs of the HomeView, so we are assuming that the feature is not available on the HomeView and the face identification system on the device is a different one.
Can handle up to six users…but guests are allowed
A single HomeView can have up to six different users who can use all its features and functions. The device takes information from iPhones or iPads, such as contacts and calendar, from the iPhone or iPad of the user to customize experiences for them. However, every user’s information will be kept private and not shared with others. There can be guest users too, but they will be able to access only a limited number of functions, such as controlling smart home accessories, checking the weather, setting timers, and playing music.
The camera is only for calling, as of now – no photography!
The HomeView comes with a 12-megapixel camera with an f/2,4 aperture, but from what we can see so far, its function is limited to identifying the user and making FaceTime calls. It comes with Center Stage that keeps you in the center of the frame during FaceTime calls, but as of now, it cannot record video or take pictures.
And it can switch seamlessly and speedily between users
Perhaps the most spectacular feature of the HomeView is the fact that it literally transforms itself depending on who is in front of it. It works with the iPhone or iPad of each user and shows them the content when they use the device. Every user has their own customizations and information, which the others cannot see, and the HomeView literally presents each user with their own version every time they appear in front of it and are identified – and judging by what we have seen in the demos, it does so almost instantly, while maintaining the privacy of the previous user. That A18 chip and that 12-megapixel front-facing camera are incredibly fast!
A tab that does not do too many videos…yet
In spite of being relatively large in size, the HomeView does not come with a dedicated app for videos – as per the Apple website, it does not even come with Apple TV preinstalled. While HomeView does not have a dedicated Apple TV app preinstalled, Apple confirms support for Apple TV content and compatible third-party video apps. However, the range of supported services and how they work on HomeView remain worth checking.
No fun and games either…yet
Rather remarkably for a device that is designed to be used by the family, the HomeView does not come with any games at the time of writing. We are so hoping that changes and Apple adds some fun, turn-based, multiplayer games to the tablet. Imagine being able to play Ludo, Scrabble, Chess, or Monopoly on this!

Madhuri Dixit recently revisited her experience of working with Sachin Pilgaonkar on Prem Deewane during an appearance on Sony Marathi’s Kon Honar Crorepati. The actor asked Pilgaonkar, who directed the film, what prompted him to cast her as an inspector at a time when she was largely known for dance and romantic roles.
Kon Honar Crorepati: Sachin Pilgaonkar reveals Madhuri Dixit’s Abodh performance prompted him to cast her as an inspector in Prem Deewane: “If she can do that, she can pull this off too”
During their conversation, Madhuri recalled her role in the 1992 film and asked Pilgaonkar about his decision to cast her in a character that was different from her then-established screen image.
“Sachin ji, we worked together in a film that you directed. It was called Prem Deewane. You cast me as an inspector, but until then, my image was mostly associated with dance and romance. What made you think of casting me in a role like that?” Madhuri asked.
Sachin Pilgaonkar recalls Madhuri Dixit’s Abodh performance
In response, Sachin revealed that her performance in Abodh had convinced him that she could take on the role. “I had seen your film Abodh before that, and I absolutely loved your performance. I said, ‘No, I want Madhuri.’ When I was asked, ‘Why Madhuri for this role?’ I said, ‘If she can do that, she can pull this off too,’” he recalled.
Madhuri acknowledged Pilgaonkar’s faith in her and thanked him for allowing her to take on a different kind of character. “Thank you for showing so much confidence in me and giving me the opportunity to do something different,” she said.
Prem Deewane, released in 1992, featured Madhuri Dixit alongside Jackie Shroff and Vivek Mushran, with Sachin Pilgaonkar serving as the director. The conversation on Kon Honar Crorepati offered a glimpse into how Pilgaonkar’s earlier appreciation of Madhuri’s acting helped shape his casting decision.

Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
- Published
Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.
It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.
Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.
Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.
"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe the independent federal judiciary."
Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.
This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.
Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".
His legal team has filed a motion to dismiss the charges.
Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC that the case may have exceeded the 10-year statute of limitations, giving the motion to dismiss the charges "a very good chance of being granted".
Kirschner said it seemed like the charges against Comey were a "revenge-fueled attempt by Donald Trump to have his Department of Justice find something that might stick".
Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.
Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.
Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.
He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.
In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.
The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.
The latest charges against Comey were made public the same day a federal judge ruled the justice department illegally fired his daughter, Maurene Comey.
Maurene Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father and because of her perceived political affiliations.
The judge ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.

The Best Folding Phones Now Includes Apple's iPhone Duo
Featured in this article
You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now (even Apple is in on the action), so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades.
They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.
Check out our other mobile buying guides, including the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Samsung Phones, Best Google Pixel Phones, Best Motorola Phones, Best Phones With a Headphone Jack, and Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US.
Updated October 2026: We've added the Apple iPhone Duo, more on the Z Flip8 after testing, and updated prices.
Other Folding Phones to Consider
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: If you want something compact, the Galaxy Z Flip8 is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis, and it comes a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.
Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable, triple 50-MP camera. But, overall, we prefer Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!
Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.
Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.
Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.
Things to Know Before Buying
Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and iPhone Duo are IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.
Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.
There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.
They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.
Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?
Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.
Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy?
If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.
If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.
My Favorite Folding Features
Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.
Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone. —Julian Chokkattu

Panaji , Oct 27: Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri on Tuesday denied that India was under any pressure to stop buying Russian oil.
Indian refiners would purchase crude from suppliers offering the most competitive prices as the country prioritises energy security amid global market uncertainties, he said.
India was not particularly buying Russian oil at present, but the decisions in this regard were guided by commercial considerations rather than pressure from any country, he added.
"I have never any felt pressure," Puri said during an interaction at the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet which began here on Tuesday.
"At the point of negotiation, whoever is supplying a particular grade, we will buy from them. Prices come down sometimes," he said.
The minister's remarks come amid international scrutiny of India's purchases of Russian crude, and Western efforts to curb Moscow's oil revenues following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Referring to the restrictions imposed on two Russian entities, Rosneft and Lukoil, Puri said buyers could source oil from other suppliers, including those in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
India had diversified its energy investments and sourcing, he said, mentioning investments in Saudi Arabia and other locations.
India, as a major energy-consuming nation, could not compromise on its energy security amid geopolitical developments and volatility in international markets, the Union minister stressed.
Puri also pointed out the complexity of global oil and petroleum-product trade, saying procurement decisions involved several commercial and supply considerations.
India's approach was guided by the need to ensure reliable supplies while managing costs for consumers and the broader economy, he added.
Puri also questioned the logic of treating India's oil purchases as a matter of external pressure, reiterating that procurement decisions would depend on the terms offered by suppliers.

Evidence from photojournalists on the scene confirms Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of the new White House ballroom and saluting officials visible far behind and to the left side of the helicopter.
In mid-to-late October, a video spread purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump waving to and saluting nobody on the White House South Lawn prior to boarding his helicopter, Marine One.
For example, Democratic commentator Harry Sisson said the footage (archived) highlights how Trump is experiencing increasing "mental decline."
The clip shows Trump walking toward Marine One — the call sign officials use when a president flies on a special fleet of helicopters — waving toward his left, continuing to walk and then waving, saluting and waving again in a slightly different direction, also off to his left. At the end of the clip, he salutes a Marine and boards the aircraft.
Numerous social media users and other left-leaning commentators shared the video and iterations of the rumor, including former cable news hosts Don Lemon and Joy Reid, as well as fellow progressive voice Adam Mockler. All three have prominent presences on YouTube.
Similarly, The New Republic initially reported, "Trump, 80, Wanders Off While Waving and Saluting to No One." The publication displayed that headline as an image on social media.
In sum, while the clip is authentic, meaning it displays no signs of artificial-intelligence manipulation, evidence shows Trump was appearing to wave at people working on the construction of his new White House ballroom, which has replaced the demolished White House East Wing. He was also saluting and throwing smaller waves to other darkly-dressed officials positioned far behind and to the left side of the helicopter. Therefore, the above social media posts miscaptioned the video.
Fox News broadcast the same live moment leading up to the moment in question, helping to confirm the date this occurred, Oct. 19, as well as providing a clearer look at two or more darkly-dressed individuals standing next to a white fence whom the president appeared to salute (pictured below, to the left of Trump).
(Fox News)
Snopes contacted Lemon, Reid and Mockler to ask if they wished to address this matter but did not receive responses prior to publication. The New Republic declined to comment, but said it updated its report to include a new headline and other updated information. We also emailed the White House to ask if a spokesperson wished to respond to people sharing the false claim. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Reputable media-licensing website Getty Images hosts several photos with text captions providing more information about the moment in question. For example, a picture of Trump waving (shown at the top of this article) is captioned, "U.S. President Donald Trump waves to people working on building the new ballroom as he departs the White House on October 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C." Other photographs show the ballroom construction happening behind Trump and people working on the project both on the ground and up high.
(Brendan Smialowski via Getty Images)
One of Getty's captions says the picture below shows a construction worker giving Trump a thumbs-up sign as Marine One prepared for takeoff.
(Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images)
The Associated Press' image-licensing website also provides more data, including a photo of the ballroom construction from the White House South Lawn, a glimpse of both the White House and ballroom construction from the Washington Monument, a view of Marine One flying over the work zone on the same day, and Trump giving a similar acknowledgement to workers with a fist sign last week.
For further reading, we previously reported on whether Trump took a 2.5% contractor fee on the construction of the new ballroom.

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Mercedes spent millions on nurturing Antonelli after Ferrari said no
MEXICO CITY, Oct 27 : Ferrari fans can only imagine what might have been had local boy Kimi Antonelli signed for their team rather than Mercedes as a young go-karter.
Formula One's oldest and most successful team had the chance to secure the talent now set to become Italy's first champion in 73 years, and Formula One's youngest ever, but let it slip through their fingers.
Mercedes seized the opportunity instead in 2018, when Antonelli was 11.
"For Ferrari, Kimi was still too young whereas Mercedes could offer better guarantees regarding his future prospects," Antonelli's former manager Giovanni Minardi told the Gazzetta dello Sport newspaper earlier this year.
Former Ferrari president Luca di Montezemolo, who was no longer involved with the team at that point, saw a silver lining.
"I am a Ferrari man but I'm delighted to see what Antonelli is doing," he told Spanish newspaper AS last month. "What I do regret is that Ferrari had the chance to sign him. They didn't.
"A great opportunity vanished, but almost better for Antonelli. Such a young Italian driving a Ferrari... It would have been terrible pressure."
Mercedes team boss and co-owner Toto Wolff credited Gwen Lagrue, who is joining Red Bull next year to run their young driver programme, for bringing Antonelli, now 20, on board.
He said also that people did not appreciate the amount of work that has gone into nurturing the team's successor to seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton.
"I read an interview with Piero Ferrari last week where he said, 'What a talent. He reminds me of Niki Lauda'. And I'm thinking, 'People don't get that this is the work of nine years'," the Austrian told reporters after Antonelli won last Sunday's US Grand Prix in Austin, his ninth win of the season.
"The development of nine years, the hardship of nine years, the integration of the team, the working with the engineers, the 10 or more millions spent in the development of his career, of his ability, of his character together with his parents.
"It's just not that it landed like this."
Wolff recalled how others said Antonelli, after nine rounds without points last year, should not have been given the Mercedes seat.
He spoke of those at other teams who suggested the youngster should not even be in Formula One.
"All of that now is extremely satisfying, to see what he's able to deliver and how he's working with the team, with (race engineer Peter) Bono (Bonnington) and yielding the results. But it wasn't an easy road."

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability" initiative on Sept. 30.
Fox News reported the 90-day requirement on Oct. 25 and quotes department spokesperson Sean Parnell throughout the article. Though Parnell shared the report on X that day, he has not confirmed the 90-day requirement.
In October, a claim circulated online that the Pentagon had announced an initiative called FORTRESS that would require military bases in the U.S. to be able to operate for at least 90 days without relying on civilian power, fuel, water or supply lines.
For example, one Facebook user who made and posted a video about the alleged measure wrote (archived):
The Pentagon just Built a 90- Day Survival Plan.
Under FORTRESS (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability), every major U.S. military base is being ordered to operate for 90 days with no civilian power, fuel, water, or supply chains, using portable nuclear reactors, microgrids, and stockpiles. The military is hardening itself for a grid-down war. Civilians are on their own.
Snopes readers contacted us to ask about the initiative, while similar posts about FORTRESS and what it entails also circulated on Instagram and Reddit (archived, archived).
FORTRESS is a real Department of Defense initiative and social media posts detailing what it involves are broadly accurate. The acronym stands for "Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability." Though the measure itself is new, it also includes some energy and manufacturing-related programs that already exist within the DOD.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced FORTRESS during a speech in Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 30. His speech and a department memo released that day describe the initiative as an "insurance policy" for the United States.
On Oct. 25, Fox News reported more details about the measure (archived), mainly saying it would require U.S. military bases to "keep operating for at least 90 days without outside support."
Fox News reported Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell has led the initiative. Parnell is quoted throughout Fox's report, which he posted to X (archived) that day. His posting of the article, however, does not explicitly confirm the 90-day operating requirement. Therefore, we've rated this claim mostly true.
Snopes contacted the DOD for official confirmation of the 90-day requirement and any additional information it could provide about the FORTRESS initiative. We await a reply to our inquiry.
FORTRESS merges existing DOD programs
The Sept. 30 department memo says FORTRESS would focus on five pillars: "Energy independence; supply-chain and defense-industrial base resilience; a strategic defense reserve; installation hardening and cyber resilience; and resilience in space and spectrum."
Hegseth explained the changes the initiative would bring as follows (at 32:07):
Every major military installation in America is going to generate its own power independent of the civilian grid. If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage or by any means, our bases stay lit. Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark.
We're bringing our critical supply chains home: the rare earths, the specialty metals, the semiconductors, the propellants mined in America, refined in America, built in America by American workers.
We are building long-overdue strategic reserves deep enough to fight through disruption. Think munitions, fuel, medicine, blood. Deep enough that if the world's supply lines break, and in a real war they're going to break, America keeps fighting anyway.
We're hardening every installation on American soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones.
And we're securing the high ground and the airwaves, our satellites, our spectrum, our ability to see, to navigate and to talk to one another.
Fox News reported that a "central concern" that FORTRESS would address is the military's reliance on the civilian power grid. Under the first pillar of "energy independence," Fox News said the measure would see the U.S. military developing its own sources of power such as "portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids."
Around a month before the DOD made FORTRESS public, the department had already announced five vendors to build and operate nuclear microreactors at Fort Benning, Georgia; Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Campbell, Kentucky; and Fort Drum, New York; and Fort Hood, Texas, as part of the Janus Program.
That program aims to supply U.S. military bases with "the energy resilience necessary to project combat power globally, without relying on potentially vulnerable external grids," according to the DOD, and seeks to build at least 20 microreactors.
FORTRESS would reportedly also use another existing DOD program — the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network — to identify domestic factories that could switch to manufacturing for the military in a crisis even if normal supply chains are disrupted.
Hegseth said during his Sept. 30 speech that FORTRESS was not meant to spread concerns about war on American soil. Rather, he said (at 33:56):
We'll make certain that America cannot be starved out, shut down or cut off. A fortress is not a place where you hide from. It's a ground you stand on, the foundation you fight from, the strength that lets you reach anywhere in the world, precisely because you are fully prepared at home.
It is unclear how the initiative would affect civilian disaster preparedness. Writing in The Wall Street Journal on Oct. 9, Tim Echols, who has served on the Georgia Public Services Commission since 2011, suggested the initiative could benefit consumers. Echols wrote that "the learning curve for building nuclear is paid for by the government" through microreactors for U.S. bases, whose technology could also apply to civilian power grids.
Echols also suggested that lessening demand for electricity in cities that provide substantial power to military bases would allow those power companies to retire older units and replace them with more-efficient ones.
Conversely, the user who made and posted the aforementioned Facebook video suggested FORTRESS would leave civilians "on their own" by taking away investment from shared resources.
The U.S. government provides disaster preparedness advice for civilians on Ready.gov.

Rama Rao Malla, the son of a farmer from Anakapalli, went on to earn a B.Ed., an M.Sc. and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from Andhra University. During Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Prof. Malla, of the Department of Life Sciences at the Gandhi Institute of Technology and Management (GITAM) (Deemed to be University), is leading research to develop a blood test for one of the most aggressive forms of breast cancer.
The first graduate in his family, Prof. Malla has been a teacher for more than three decades. He joined GITAM early in his career in 2001 and, after completing postdoctoral work at the University of Illinois College of Medicine, returned to set up the university’s cancer research laboratory in 2011. He has guided 14 doctoral scholars and completed several projects on breast cancer, with four more under way, he says.
His current research focuses on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), which lacks the receptors for oestrogen, progesterone and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), the targets of certain cancer therapies. Patients are treated mainly with chemotherapy, to which many develop resistance. TNBC accounts for 10% to 15% of breast cancers, he says, and is increasingly being diagnosed in women in their mid-30s and 40s. Mammography may miss small tumours, particularly in younger women. “If we can identify this cancer at an early stage, we can successfully eliminate the tumours by surgery,” he says.
The project, titled “Exploring Serum Exosomal microRNAs as Minimally-Invasive Biomarkers for Early Diagnosis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer”, has been sanctioned under the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)’s “Follow-on Nischayak Anveshan” Extramural Grants programme, with Prof. Malla as the principal investigator. He says the project has an outlay of more than ₹2 crore over three years.
The study will examine exosomes, nanosized vesicles released by cells, including tumour cells. Their microRNA content can reflect that of the cells from which they originate. The researchers will compare serum samples from patients with early-stage TNBC, provided by the Mahatma Gandhi Cancer Hospital & Research Institute (MGCHRI) and the GITAM Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (GIMSR), with samples from healthy women. Sequencing and digital polymerase chain reaction (PCR) will be used to identify candidate microRNAs, and a machine-learning model will be trained to distinguish patients with early-stage TNBC from healthy individuals. The ultimate objective is to develop a kit-based test.
“We hope we can achieve something after three years that will be useful for society,” he says.
The co-investigators are P. Kiranmayi, P. Vasudevaraju, A. Krishna Chaitanya and M. Srivenkatesh of the GITAM School of Science; K. Viswa Kalyan of GIMSR; and V. Muralikrishna of MGCHRI.
The World Health Organization advises that any abnormal breast lump should be examined by a health professional, even if it is painless.

The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we only highlight deals on devices we have tested that we’d be comfortable recommending to friends and family. MADRID — A type of targeted chemotherapy developed by Merck and China’s Kelun-Biotech cut by one-third the risk of death in patients with advanced endometrial cancer, a common gynecological cancer, according to randomized Phase 3 study results presented Monday.
The drug, called sacituzumab tirumotecan, or sac-TMT, has already shown survival-extending benefits for patients across multiple cancer types in studies conducted by Kelun in China, where it’s approved.
Merck is conducting 18 global Phase 3 studies of sac-TMT, including 10 studies in women’s cancers, to support approvals in the U.S., Europe, and elsewhere outside China. The drug plays a crucial role in Merck’s efforts to replace revenue that will be lost when Keytruda, its blockbuster immunotherapy, loses patent protection in 2028.

Alberta bill would stop provincial entities from considering diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring
Justice legislation also aims to create new consequences for sextortion
New Alberta legislation seeks to stop the provincial government and other public entities from considering diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring decisions.
Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled legislation Tuesday that would prevent the provincial public service, provincial Crown corporations, publicly funded post-secondary institutions, school boards and municipalities from hiring employees based on “personal characteristics,” according to a government news release.
“Hiring decisions should be about who is best qualified for the job, and these changes will help ensure that fairness is at the heart of hiring,” Premier Danielle Smith is quoted as saying in the news release.
Amery’s statement in the release says public-sector hiring should be based on merit, qualifications and competence.
The legislation — the first bill of the fall sitting — proposes to do this by amending the Alberta Human Rights Act so that employers may not consider characteristics protected by the act — such as gender identity, race, religion or disability — in hiring and promotion decisions. However, the government could grant exemptions in regulations.
The amendments would also prevent provincial entities from requiring employees to participate in diversity, equity or inclusion training. Workplace training must be “ideologically neutral and focused on job-related duties and skills,” a briefing note about the proposed amendment says.
In a technical briefing, officials said the legislation would not prevent post-secondary institutions from tailoring programs for particular students, or reserving spots for those with unchangeable characteristics, such as training for Indigenous teachers, doctors or lawyers.
The law would also apply to some private or non-profit organizations that receive government funding. However, officials said it would be up to the Alberta Human Rights Commission to determine which organizations, and only after someone files a complaint.
Consequences for threatening sextortion
If passed, Bill 33, the Justice Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (No. 2), would also expand provincial legislation to give victims recourse when someone shares intimate content of them without their consent.
The bill would rename and expand the Victims of Non-consensual Distribution of Intimate Images Act to include victims of sextortion, which is when someone threatens to distribute intimate videos, images or other content to blackmail another person.
If passed by the legislature, the amended law would include digitally altered media, such as AI-generated content including deepfakes, and would allow a victim to sue anyone who shares or threatens to share the media without their consent.
It would allow a person to withdraw consent at any time, unless they have signed a legal consent agreement.
The legislation would create a new provincial offence carrying a fine of up to $10,000, up to two years of jail time, or both.
At the technical briefing, officials said the provincial law is intended to cover what they say are gaps in federal criminal law, and give victims more avenues of recourse. Officials said a provincial law allowing a victim to sue someone for threatening to share intimate content would be the first of its kind in Canada.
Federal law, which was updated in June, allows a prison sentence of up to 10 years for distributing or threatening to distribute intimate images, including non-consensual deepfakes, without consent.
The bill would also update the Education Act. For instance, principals have the ability now to suspend or expel a student who shares intimate images of another student without their permission. The amendment would allow them to discipline a student who only threatens to do so, and add sound, video or any other media to the list of possible content.
The bill also seeks to make other changes, many of which affect the legal profession, including:
- Reversing some of the United Conservative Party government’s previous changes to give the justice minister additional control over the Alberta Law Foundation.
- Changing the threshold for members of the Law Society of Alberta to call a special meeting to 2.5 per cent of the society’s members from a minimum of 50 members — a rule that dates back to 1966.
- Requiring that a lawyer must have been an active member of the law society for at least five years before government considers granting them a King’s Counsel designation, which recognizes those who have made a significant contribution to the legal profession or public life in the province.
- Allowing lawyers seeking King’s Counsel designations to include their time away from practice in their years of service, to avoid disadvantaging parents.
- Ensuring public bodies disclose all income paid to public sector employees on so-called sunshine lists, when they move from one organization to another. The Public Sector Compensation Transparency Act requires the government to disclose pay, benefits and perks for public service workers earning more than $130,000 in compensation in 2026.

Heavenly Creatures killer Pauline Parker dies in Orkney, aged 88
- Published
To her neighbours and friends, Hilary Nathan was a quiet, religious woman who ran a riding stable in the small Orcadian island of Burray.
But her death in an island care home last week at the age of 88 closes a chapter on an extraordinary life that began 70 years ago on the other side of the world with a sensational murder trial.
As a 16-year-old and under her birth name of Pauline Parker, she was convicted alongside her schoolfriend Juliet Hulme of the murder of her mother Honora Parker.
The case shocked New Zealand – and the rest of the world.
The court heard the girls had become inseparable at Christchurch Girls' High School. Fearing that they'd be separated following the divorce of Juliet's parents and a planned move to South Africa, they plotted to kill Mrs Parker, who they believed stood in their way.
They lured her to a park and bludgeoned her to death with a brick inside a stocking.
By the time filmmaker Sir Peter Jackson was born in 1961, both girls had served five years in prison, been released, given new identities, and left New Zealand for good.
"It was known for its tabloid sensational aspect. I know a lot of English tabloids flew to Christchurch, New Zealand, to cover the case of the 'evil schoolgirl killers'," he told the BBC's Late Show in 1995.
"Repeating that stuff would have been easy, but that's not what we wanted to do. We wanted to understand more about Pauline Parker and Juliet Hulme, and what made them become friends."
His film Heavenly Creatures starred Kate Winslet as Hulme and Melanie Lynskey as Parker. It showed how their intense friendship spilled over into a strange shared fantasy life which culminated in the brutal murder.
The defence argued insanity, but both girls were found guilty of murder and only avoided the death penalty because of their age.
In 1960, having served five years in separate prisons, they were given new identities and moved away from New Zealand.
The court ordered that they should never meet again, and yet they lived part of their lives about 80 miles (129km) apart.
When the film came out in 1995, Juliet was living in Portmahomack in Rosshire, where she'd become a crime writer living under her new name, Anne Perry.
She told the Late Show that she didn't plan to see the film.
"It would be too harrowing," she said. "What was close to the truth would be distressing and what was far from the truth would be even more distressing."
"It's a bit like being stripped naked in the High Street for everyone to come and look and pick and poke. I'd rather put my clothes on and go back home, thank you."
During filming, Kate Winslet said she had no idea where the two women were, and after Anne Perry's identity was revealed, the actress expressed the hope that Pauline Parker would be able to retain her anonymity.
"These are two women who, for the last 40 years, have had to overcome so much in order to get on with their lives and just survive," she said.
"I hope she is never found."
But in 2011, Parker was found by lawyer and true-crime author Peter Graham, who had written a book about the case called So Brilliantly Clever, its title taken from her diary, which was used as evidence in court.
She, like Juliet, had come to the UK, where she had settled in a small village in rural Kent and opened a riding school. By 2011, and now known as Hilary Nathan, she had moved to Orkney, running another stable.
For both women, religion and small tight-knit communities provided a haven. According to an interview her sister gave to the New Zealand Women's Weekly, Nathan was a devout Catholic who led a reclusive life.
Perry was a Mormon, enjoying the support of her own community when reporters began to arrive after Heavenly Creatures was released.
She said: "The media descended on Portmahomack. I was horrified, especially since my mother lived in the village. It's not just the people the film is about, it's all the people around them. I felt it might ruin my family."
Although her books were hugely successful in America, she never really found the fame she merited here in the UK, partly because of her reticence to do any promotion.
Prime Suspect creator Lynda La Plante expressed interest in a TV version of Perry's books, but the author vetoed the plan for the same reason.
In 2001, I visited Perry in Portmahomack for a rare interview for Newsnight Scotland. At that stage, she was a glamorous author, with a back catalogue which had sold 15 million copies around the world.
"I think after 51 years, you can let it go," she told me. "It's not who I am now. It's not who I have been for decades."
We didn't talk about the murder directly, but you don't have to look far in her books for insight into what happened and how her life had turned out. Her detective, the Victorian policeman William Monk, suffers from amnesia, and sometimes wonders exactly who he is.
"Monk sees himself as just himself but because of his memory loss, he has to deal with the fact that he may be someone else. That comes from my own sense that other people view me as a monster," she admitted.
"Of course it affects what I write. I have far more compassion and understanding for people who do wrong things than I'd ever have if I hadn't been in that position.
"The questions of right and wrong and compassion and forgiveness concern me in a way they wouldn't have, had I not had the life I had."
Anne Perry died in Los Angeles in 2023 at the age of 84.
Hilary Nathan's death last week brings their strange story to a close.
How they reinvented themselves out of the world's harshest headlines, and found redemption in the smallest of Scottish communities.
"I would say if you had something which harrowed you, or caused you to feel shame, you should never give up," Anne told me.
"There's more forgiveness, understanding and help out there than you might think."

A video (here & here) purportedly showing US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy is being shared on social media as a genuine video. Let’s verify the authenticity of this clip.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of US Senator Richard Blumenthal calling India a failed state with a collapsing economy.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage is from a September 2026 press conference where the Senator merely urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil, and he did not make any derogatory statements about India. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length footage (here & here) from 17 September 2026. The video shows a bipartisan press conference following a House vote on a Russia and Iran sanctions bill.
In this video, Senator Blumenthal urged India and China to stop buying Russian oil and to seek alternative sources. However, he did not make any of the comments heard in the viral video. We then analysed the viral clip using AI video detection tools (here & here), which confirmed that the footage had been digitally altered.
Furthermore, a PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the video is a deepfake and that the Senator made no such statement.
To sum it up, the viral video is an AI-generated deepfake, and Senator Blumenthal never made the derogatory remarks about India being a failed state.

They also serve science, who are not scientists. One of science’s most egregious instances of epistemic dominance, where a powerful institution overrode and exploited a marginalised individual - was Henrietta Lacks – donor of the famous, immortal HeLa cell line. Cells extracted from her, without permission, transformed medical research, but her story was ignored, erased and obscured for decades. The scientific world that generously used this unique cell line for successful research into virology, vaccines, genetics and even cancer care, but the erasure of the donor of those cells was historic in its completeness.
Lacks, an African American tobacco farmer from southern United States, sought treatment at the ‘coloured ward’ in Johns Hopkins Centre for cervical cancer, way back in 1951. While it was common for medical professionals, in those days, to take samples and cells without the express permission of the patient, particularly if it was an African American woman, these cells were different. Johns Hopkins used the cells from her tumour to culture a line of cells that was extraordinarily durable outside the body. Usually human cells die outside of the body. Anonymised by a laboratory acronymn, Lacks’ cells (HeLa) turned out to be the first human cells to successfully grow, divide, and survive indefinitely outside the human body.
HeLa was a miracle that scientists had chanced upon. With HeLa, they could mass produce human cells in a standard format that could be used for biomedical research, and would underpin several breakthrough discoveries, that would revolutionise medical care. No one knew, however, of the immense exploitation behind this miracle cell line, and the profound lack of consent in procuring the samples.
Lacks, who died at merely 31 years, and was buried in an unmarked grave, remained invisible, not even a footnote, completely uncredited and her family entirely in the dark about her contribution to the world of science. Henrietta Lacks’ family first learned about her cells in nearly quarter of a century later, when scientists reached out to them, requesting blood samples once they suspected that the HeLa cell line had contaminated other research samples. This came as a bolt on the family, who could not fathom how cells from their mother had survived this long outside of her, and how this strange situation had come to be. While the academic world and several sections of the corporate world benefited richly from the HeLa cell line, Lacks’ own family had remained entrenched in poverty and struggling to make ends meet. The struggle of the family to come to terms with this exploitation, and the battles they had to fight with the system and science itself is well curated by Rebecca Sloot in her best selling book The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.
In the 1950s, bioethical norms, particularly around informed consent were either non existent, or, at best, weak. But, in this particular case, Lacks was a black farmer from a rural unit, being treated in a segregated section in a large hospital. Consequently, an entrenched rascism, still alive in the southern United States in the 50s, and class bias contributed in good measure to the shabby treatment of this very valuable patient. Unhesitatingly and boldly, Sloot dragged this out into the open, through the book, knocking on the consciousness of the world and science, biomedical research, urging a discussion, a debate and at the end of it, a nod to what happened. It took years before these units would shamefully acknowledge the great injustice meted out to Lacks’ and her family.
The book, published in 2010, drew attention to the larger debate of patient rights and bodily autonomy. Sloot also underlined the fact that donors need to be acknowledged, heralding a new woke world of bio ethics, laboratory practices and the responsibilities of researchers. No longer could a moral failure be allowed to take patients for a ride, rules and regulations should replace the conscience and a situation like this would hopefully never happen again.
But this story does not end this way. After nearly 75 years of fighting this battle, the Lacks’ family finally found some closure. Reparation was finally achieved with the family settling with Johns Hopkins and other associated institutions in a landmark agreement that firstly acknowledged harm had been done, and also included measures to compensate the family and honour Lacks’ role in science. This included significant financial recompense, and involving the family into research using HeLa cells.
This agreement did reinforce the supremacy of informed consent practices, thus refining research ethics policy, but it also expanded the involvement of the patient and the community in research work. The Lacks’ family success is a milestone of sorts in biomedical research, with calls now being made to improve how institutions and labs credit how their biological materials, and also look at reparative action for families historically exploited by science.
Lacks’ story is a cautionary tale for science. It’s a reckoning with what has historically gone wrong, to set some wrongs right , and make sure the violations of the past are not repeated, but do inform the future, so that scientific progress can proceed without losing respect for human dignity. For this stupendous achievement, we have Henrietta Lacks to thank. From being denied even the footnote in history, she has created a brave new world in science.
