- Crushed Bone is a rare Fisch ingredient in FischFright 3 that can be obtained by completing goblin quests.
- Goblins spawn every five minutes across various islands, and hard goblin quests have the highest drop chance.
- Each crushed bone gives +2 hex energy and is used to perform certain rituals.
Crushed Bone is one of the ingredients you can collect during FischFright 3. You need it to increase your Hex Stage and activate certain rituals during the event. Getting it can be tricky; the chances of getting it are low. In this guide, learn how to get Crushed Bone in Fisch.
How to Obtain Crushed Bone in Fisch
The main way to get Crushed Bone in Fisch is by completing quests that you get from the Goblins. These goblins spawn every five minutes at different locations across the map. So, if you want to do FischFright 3 rituals in Fisch, make sure you are online and find the Crushed Bone on the following islands:
- Moosewood
- Roslit Bay
- Forsaken Shores
- Mushgrove
- Scoria Reach
- Ancient Isle
- Lost Jungle
- Terrapin
- Snowcap Island
- Skycrest
- Sunstone
- Castaway Cliffs
- Everturn Forest
Once the goblin spawns, you will get a notification at the bottom of your screen along with the island’s name where it spawned. Up to three goblins can spawn during this event, and each gives you a simple task to complete. These tasks can be as simple as:
- Dance
- Jump
- Guess my favorite color
- Catch a fish
The ingredients you get depend on the difficulty of the quest. Finish the objective to receive ingredients in Fisch, and if you are lucky enough, you will get a Crushed Bone or two.
Completing the goblin quests will also help you unlock the Boglin Branch Rod in Fisch.
Fisch Crushed Bone Drop Rates
Before you start hunting the materials for leving up Hex stages in Fisch, here are the Crushed Bone drop rates for each difficulty:
| Quest Difficulty | Crushed Bone Drop Chance | 
|---|---|
| Easy | 12.5% | 
| Normal | 12.5% | 
| Hard | 18.75% | 
| Extreme | 6.25% | 
| Ultimate | No drop | 
Hard quests have the highest drop chance. If you are farming this ingredient, focus on completing Hard Goblin quests whenever possible.
You can also receive a random ingredient by completing the Hexing Ritual. It may include a crushed bone, but you need one crushed bone to activate the ritual in the first place.
How to Use Crushed Bone in Fisch
Crushed Bone has two main uses during FischFright 3:
- You can add it to Beatrix’s Cauldron to increase your Hex Stage.
- You can use it to perform certain rituals at the graveyard.
Beatrix’s Cauldron
You can add Crushed Bone to Beatrix’s Cauldron to increase your Hex Energy and progress through the Hex Stages. Each Crushed Bone gives you +2 Hex Energy. Increasing your FischFright Hex Stage helps you unlock more rewards and access higher-level rituals.
Rituals
Crushed Bone is also required for several FischFright 3 rituals. Make sure you have enough bones and Fisch roses before starting them. Here are all the rituals that require the Crushed Bone ingredient:
| Rituals | Requirement | 
|---|---|
| Hexing Ritual | Crushed Bone x1 under Jack-o’-Lantern requirements | 
| Jack-o-Moon Ritual | Crushed Bone x1 under Skeletal Hands requirements | 
| Haunted Cemetery Ritual | Crushed Bone x1 under Jack-o’-Lantern requirements | 
| Ghoul Nessie Ritual | Crushed Bone x1 under Jack-o’-Lantern requirements | 
Now that you know how to get Crushed Bone in Fisch, you can increase your hex level, perform rituals, and claim all the rewards before the FischFright ends.
Where do goblins spawn in Fisch?
Goblins spawn across different islands, including Moosewood, Roslit Bay, Forsaken Shores, Ancient Isle, Lost Jungle, Snowcap Island, and Everturn Forest. Three Goblins spawn every five minutes.
Which Goblin quest has the highest Crushed Bone drop rate?
Hard Goblin quests have the highest listed drop chance at 18.75%. Easy and Normal quests have a 12.5% chance, while Extreme quests have a 6.25% chance.
How much Hex Energy does Crushed Bone give?
Each crushed bone gives you +2 Hex Energy when you add it to Beatrix’s cauldron.

With just a week left for the US midterm elections, betting markets suggest that President 
Donald Trump
's Republican Party could lose control of Congress. Democrats have strong chances to win the House of Representatives, while the race for the Senate remains tighter.
According to prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, Democrats have a roughly 90% chance of taking control of the House of Representatives. Their chances of winning the Senate are lower, at around 65%.
The November 3 elections will decide which party controls the two chambers of Congress for the remaining two years of Trump's presidency. Republicans currently control both, giving the president an advantage in pushing through his policies.
House: Democrats ahead in betting markets
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives will be up for election on November 3. A party needs at least 218 seats to secure a majority.
According to Kalshi's October 26 figures, Democrats have a 91% chance of winning control of the House, compared with 9% for Republicans. Polymarket shows a similar trend, giving Democrats a 92% chance.
The numbers have also changed over the past few months. In May, Kalshi projected that Democrats would win around 226 seats. 
By October 26, that figure had risen to 238, well above the majority mark.
Democrats have over a 90% chance of taking control of the House of Representatives
Senate: A closer contest
The race for the Senate is tighter, although betting markets give Democrats an advantage here also.
According to Kalshi, Democrats have a 63% chance of taking control of the Senate, while Polymarket puts their chances at 66%.
Unlike the House, where all seats are contested, 35 Senate seats are up for election this year, including special elections. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, while Democrats and independents who caucus with them hold 47.
To win, Democrats need to gain control of Republican-held seats while retaining those they already have.
Kalshi's latest figures give Democrats a 73% chance of winning in Alaska, 68% in Ohio and 66% in Texas. In Maine, their chances stand at 59%.
In June, Kalshi put Democrats' chances of taking control at less than 43%. By late October, that figure had climbed to around 65%.
A Republican victory in both chambers is given a much lower chance, at 9.3% on Kalshi and 8% on Polymarket
Vivek Ramaswamy's Ohio contest
The betting markets are also tracking the Ohio governor's race, where Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is contesting against Democrat's Amy Acton.
According to the latest figures, Kalshi gave Ramaswamy a 18% chance of winning, compared with 82% for Acton. Polymarket showed similar numbers, putting Ramaswamy at 18% and Acton at 83%.
Ramaswamy, who previously ran for the Republican presidential nomination, is seeking to succeed Mike DeWine, who cannot contest another consecutive term.
The Ohio governor's race is separate from the battle for control of Congress, but will also be decided on November 3.
What are the possible outcomes?
Beyond individual races, prediction markets are tracking the chances of each party controlling Congress after the election.
According to Kalshi, traders put the chances of Democrats winning both chambers at 64%, while Polymarket puts the figure at around 66%.
The possibility of Democrats winning the House while Republicans retaining the Senate stands at 28% on Kalshi and 27% on Polymarket.
A Republican victory in both chambers is given a much lower chance, at 9.3% on Kalshi and 8% on Polymarket.
What do the numbers mean for Trump
Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, allowing Trump to pursue his legislative agenda with support from his party.
If Democrats take control of the House, they could block Republican-backed legislation and launch investigations into the administration. A Democratic-controlled Senate would also affect Trump's ability to secure confirmation for senior government and judicial appointments.
However, prediction-market figures are not opinion polls. They reflect the prices at which traders buy and sell contracts on election outcomes, and can change as new information emerges. The final decision rests with the voters who will cast their ballots on November 3.

Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.
Rather than putting up with whatever infotainment systems car manufacturers have put together, we're now able to interact with our phones from our car dashboards—with our contacts, our music, our podcasts, and our mapping apps all available. And the list of supported vehicles just keeps growing.
Both the Google and Apple solutions for this are really simple to use too. Most of the time they'll connect up automatically once you've done the initial setup. What you might not realize, though, are the demands that Android Auto and CarPlay put on your phone. Your handset is essentially doing all the regular phone stuff and then powering a large tablet-like display at the same time. That typically includes constantly updating a map in real time.
With that in mind, your Android phone or iPhone can quickly start to lose battery life and heat up when it's connected to your vehicle, which you've perhaps already noticed. To keep your handset cool and your battery in good shape, here's what you need to do.
Go Wired if You Can (but Watch the Charging)
Wireless Android Auto and CarPlay are convenient, just like wireless charging is convenient, but it puts more stress on your phone. If you've got the option of a wired connection, that's preferable—but that introduces a new potential heat problem, which is that your phone will always be charging up.
To counter that, you can set charge limits (Battery and charging from Android Settings, Battery > Charging from iOS Settings), or simply make sure your phone is kept in a cool, dark spot of the car.
This wired option has the added bonus of letting you switch to airplane mode on your phone, which will go a long way to limiting heat. Again there's a trade-off though: No one will be able to reach you, and you'll need to have your maps, music, podcasts, and whatever else you need downloaded to your device in advance.
If you do stick with wireless Android Auto or CarPlay, try to avoid charging your phone at the same time, especially on the wireless pad built into the car’s dash (which generates more heat). You don't want to end up with a dead phone half way through the journey, so you may have to compromise at certain times.
Think About Where Your Phone Is Placed
As mentioned above, where your phone is in the car makes a real difference to how hot it's going to be. If you have your phone's interface up on your car dashboard, then you don't necessarily need to have it fixed to the dashboard, too, possibly under direct sunlight. The glove compartment will do just fine.
If you have a mount for your phone, think about attaching it in front of one of your car's air vents. Blasts of air conditioned air will significantly reduce how hot your handset gets, working like a DIY cooling system.
You might also want to think about taking the case off of your phone for the length of the trip, if your phone is fitted with one. Your handset is less likely to be dropped or knocked while you're driving anyway, and a case can trap the heat in.
The rules aren't too different to keeping your phone cool generally, though with the added wrinkle of needing to keep it connected to your car somehow. Make sure the cabin in general is at a comfortable temperature, though you're probably already doing that for your own sake. The bigger thing to remember is to avoid leaving your phone behind in a vehicle that's going to heat up in the sun if you're stopping off somewhere.
Limit the Work Your Phone Has to Do
If your phone is hooked up to Android Auto or CarPlay, then it's probably got some work to do—whether it's getting you to a destination or streaming music. However, you can still reduce heat by keeping phone tasks down to a minimum. If your calls and (voice-activated) messages can wait, leave them until the end of the journey.
We mentioned offline syncing above, but it doesn't have to go along with airplane mode. If you sync your tunes, podcasts, and maps to your phone ahead of time, your handset has less work to do while you’re driving since it doesn’t need to pull data from the cloud while also constantly searching for a wireless signal as you travel. Less stress on the modem means less heat overall.
Both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you download maps ahead of a trip. In Apple Maps, tap your profile picture, then Offline Maps, then Add Offline Map and find your location. With Google Maps, tap your profile picture, then choose Offline maps > Select your own map to choose the coverage.
There may be times when your phone has to be charging, wirelessly connected, making calls, in direct sunlight, and streaming music over a cellular connection, but try to keep these times to a minimum. Check regularly on how hot your phone is getting while connected to Android Auto or CarPlay, so you can take action if needed.

New Zealand batter Daryl Mitchell praised India opener Abhishek Sharma for his “world-class hitting” ability, but hoped his side could turn the tide in the remaining two T20Is of the five-match series.
Abhishek Sharma’s 38-ball 113 was instrumental in India dismantling New Zealand by six wickets in the third T20I on Tuesday, taking an unassailable 3-0 lead.
“A very special innings, I think. Some of that hitting was world-class, and that’s why he is one of the best in the world at what he does,” Mitchell told the post-match press conference.
“You take your hat off and say, well played. It was definitely his night, and I’m sure it’s one that people won’t forget for a long time,” he added.
However, Mitchell wanted the Kiwis to fight back in the fourth and fifth T20Is.
“The series has gone, but there’s still two games left for New Zealand. So, a lot to play for. It’s always very special playing for the Black Caps. It’s something you dream of as a little kid, to be sitting here and doing these things across all three formats.
“Look, a pretty much sold-out Eden Park (venue for 4th T20I) is going to be pretty special in about 48 hours or 72 hours’ time. So, looking forward to that, and it should be good fun,” he said.
Mitchell rued some silly errors that New Zealand made at crucial junctures in this series.
“There’re probably small moments in games we look back on and wish we could have done it again, which could have seen us 2-1 up if those moments had gone our way. But at the same time, we pride ourselves on our preparation, and we know this is a big summer for us ahead.
“We’ve obviously got ODIs and a couple of big Tests before we head off to Australia. So, yeah, it’s an exciting summer for us as Black Caps,” he noted.

Moby-Dick; Tracing the success of a Great American Novel
It sold poorly, disappeared from print, and was largely forgotten when Herman Melville died. Moby-Dick, published 175 years ago, is now an enduring classic
“Call me Ishmael” is one of the most recognisable opening lines in literature. But when Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, came out in 1851, it wasn’t immediately successful. It sold poorly, got mixed reviews, and did nothing to revive Melville’s declining reputation. By the time he died in 1891, he and the book were largely forgotten. It took decades for that to change.
How did a book that failed in its own day become one of the most studied and admired novels in American literature? The Moby-Dick that appeared in October 1851 had grown far beyond the sea adventure Melville first set out to write. He had written and rewritten it, drawing on his own experiences at sea, on the books he had read about whales and whaling, and on one of the most notorious disasters in the history of the industry.
By the middle of the 19th century, whaling was big business. Whale blubber was rendered into train oil, used to lubricate machinery, and light cities. New Bedford, one of the centres of the American whaling industry, was known as “The City That Lit the World”. But the animals themselves remained largely a mystery.
The Essex disaster
On November 20, 1820, a sperm whale struck the whaleship Essex in the southern Pacific. Twenty men escaped in three boats and spent about three months at sea, facing starvation and dehydration; some eventually resorted to cannibalism.
One of the survivors, first mate Owen Chase, later wrote an account of the disaster. Melville read it, and the Essex became one of the sources for Moby-Dick. Chase described the whale as coming towards the ship “with twice his ordinary speed”, and said it appeared to have “tenfold fury and vengeance in his aspect”.
Melville turned that single encounter into something much larger.
Ishmael, an outsider who goes to sea looking for something he can’t quite name, befriends Queequeg, a tattooed harpooner, and joins the crew of the Pequod under Captain Ahab, who lost a leg to a great white sperm whale named Moby Dick. Ahab is set on finding and killing the whale. His obsession takes over the voyage, despite the objections of his first mate, Starbuck, and a whaling expedition becomes a hunt the crew can’t escape.
The novel that runs into 135 chapters moves between adventure, philosophy, descriptions of whales, religious references, and long passages of whalelore. Narrative and essay-like sections are mixed together.
It’s also funnier than its reputation suggests. Ishmael’s friendship with Queequeg provides some of the book’s lighter moments. “Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian,” he thinks, after being made to share a bed with the harpooner.
Then there are the questions that keep readers coming back. Ishmael, Ahab, and the ship Rachel all have Biblical names, and the story can be read through a religious lens. Ahab’s pursuit of the whale resembles idolatry. Moby Dick can be read as a symbol of God, nature, fate or something more unknowable. Readers down the ages have found in it a story about obsession, nature, religion, race, friendship and American identity.
Melville and Hawthorne
Melville met Nathaniel Hawthorne on August 5, 1850, when a group of writers and publishers climbed Monument Mountain in Massachusetts. Melville was 31. Hawthorne was 46 and already well known for The Scarlet Letter. The encounter affected Melville deeply. He later wrote that Hawthorne had “dropped germinous seeds into my soul”.
The two began corresponding. Soon after, Melville moved with his family to Arrowhead not far from Hawthorne. Hawthorne read Moby-Dick and praised it in a letter that has since been lost. Melville’s response survives: “Your heart beat in my ribs and mine in yours, and both in God’s...”
Melville dedicated his book to Hawthorne’s “genius”. The exact nature of their friendship has been debated ever since. What’s clearer is the effect on his writing: during this period, he moved further away from the straightforward adventure story he had begun and towards the strange, symbolic, mixed-form novel that Moby-Dick ultimately became.
A messy publication
Melville had first contracted with British publisher Richard Bentley for a book then known as The Whale. He kept the printing in New York so he could oversee the proofs while continuing to revise the manuscript, writing to Hawthorne about having to “work and slave on my ‘Whale’ while it is driving through the press”. The British edition, 500 copies, was published on October 18, 1851. The American edition followed on November 14 from Harpers, under the title Moby-Dick.
The two editions differed greatly. The most important difference was that the British edition had no epilogue. That appears to have been a production error, but it mattered. Without it, British readers were left with a first-person narrator who seemed unlikely to have survived the destruction of the Pequod. The Spectator objected that “nothing should be introduced into a novel which it is physically impossible for the writer to have known”, and other reviewers asked how the author could be alive to tell the story. The American edition had the epilogue, revealing how Ishmael survives: floating on Queequeg’s coffin till he’s rescued by the Rachel.
The poor British reviews didn’t help the book’s reception in America, and Melville’s career continued to decline. By 1856, Hawthorne recorded that Melville had “pretty much made up his mind to be annihilated”. When Melville died in 1891, Moby-Dick was out of print. Billy Budd, another of his major works, remained unpublished.
That changed in the 20th century. Melville’s birth centenary in 1919 renewed interest in his work. Raymond Weaver’s 1921 biography, Herman Melville: Mariner and Mystic, and a 16-volume edition of Melville’s works published between 1922 and 1924 helped drive the “Melville Revival”.
Every modern writer of standing from William Faulkner to DH Lawrence has been struck by Moby-Dick with the latter calling it “the greatest book of the sea ever written”.
A novel that was once dismissed as too long and too strange, is now read as a sea adventure, a philosophical novel, a comedy, a tragedy, and a catalogue of what Melville knew and imagined about the natural world.
Ahab’s obsession can be read as a warning about the desire to master nature; Ishmael’s curiosity points the other way. “It is not down on any map; true places never are,” he says. And it’s Ishmael who survives to tell the story. “I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I’ll go to it laughing,” he says.
In the decades after Melville’s death, the book that failed in his lifetime became, as The Oxford Companion to English Literature puts it, “the closest approach the United States has had to a national prose epic”.
Back in New Bedford
In 2026, Melville has returned to the city that helped shape the book. On August 14, a new bronze statue of the author was unveiled outside Seamen’s Bethel in New Bedford, where he worshipped before sailing from the harbour aboard the Acushnet.
The 7.5-foot sculpture, by artist Stefanie Rocknak, shows Melville surrounded by whale ribs, waves rising around his feet, looking towards the harbour and the sea. Chapter 9 of Moby-Dick takes Ishmael and Queequeg to the Whaleman’s Chapel, where Father Mapple delivers his sermon about Jonah and the whale. The statue’s design draws on that scene.
“[Moby-Dick’s] imprint on American culture has been broad and indelible. It is the most famous work of prose in the English language; it has inspired the emulation of countless authors, playwrights, musicians and painters the world over; it is the most assigned novel on college campuses; it has shaped America’s national identity,” said Jon Mitchell, Mayor of New Bedford, during the dedication ceremony.
Melville left New Bedford as a young sailor. Now, 175 years after Moby-Dick was published, he’s back where the story began.
Teja Lele is an independent editor and writes on books, travel and lifestyle.

On October 6, the National Medical Commission (NMC) issued guidelines on advertising and public communication by doctors and hospitals. Intended to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, they cover hospital hoardings, social media and artificial intelligence (AI). Beyond curbing deception, they raise another question regarding how much can doctors and hospitals say to the public about their work and achievements?
What is prohibited?
Claims of “guaranteed cures”, “100% success” or being the “best” are barred. Similarly, fake reviews, manipulated online rankings, misleading celebrity or influencer endorsements, and offers encouraging unnecessary treatment are deemed unethical practices. The guidelines rightfully prohibit AI-generated or manipulated patient images, voices and testimonials. But section 8.1(i) prohibits advertisements that create “unnecessary demand” for medical procedures or promote “fear-based marketing”. Without objective criteria, such expressions leave considerable room for subjective interpretation and inconsistent enforcement.
Hospitals may publish factual details of services, charges, accreditation and doctors’ credentials. Yet Section 8.1(iii) restricts advertising professional achievements and success rates, and Section 8.1(v) prohibits promotional “before and after” surgical photographs, except for specified scientific or educational purposes. Such blanket restrictions risk regulatory overreach, particularly when authentic, appropriately contextualised images could help patients understand surgical outcomes. Section 9.2 also restricts the use of doctors’ photographs for self-promotion, including on letterheads and signboards. These restrictions apply only to registered medical practitioners under the NMC’s jurisdiction.
Why the information asymmetry?
Patients rarely possess the same medical knowledge as those treating them. Even amid an abundance of AI-enabled health information, choosing a surgeon or assessing a hospital’s safety record remains difficult. Verifiable professional achievements, including the number of surgeries performed, years of experience and treatment outcomes, could help patients make informed choices. While such figures can be misleading without context, they are fundamentally different from unsubstantiated claims to be the “best” or to guarantee success, which the guidelines already prohibit. Rather than restricting genuine professional accomplishments, requiring their accurate and transparent disclosure could better serve patients’ right to informed choice. The answer may lie in better disclosure, rather than less information.
Is commercialisation unethical?
The guidelines seek to prevent the “commercialisation of health care”, while Clause 8.1(ii) restricts promotion, suggesting commercialisation of medical practice. But in India, profit-making healthcare is lawful, as section 2(c) of the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, recognises privately operated hospitals, and section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, enables lawful commercial enterprises, including hospitals. Government policy also permits 100% FDI in hospitals.
Article 19(1)(g) protects citizens’ freedom to practise a profession or conduct business, subject to reasonable restrictions. In the case Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), the Supreme Court recognised commercial speech under Article 19(1)(a), including the public’s right to receive information, while permitting restrictions on misleading advertisements. The current guidelines appear to treat commercialisation itself as a problem, without clearly distinguishing legitimate business interests from practices that mislead or exploit patients.
Are government schemes exempt?
Central and State government schemes undertaken in the larger public interest are exempted, and can advertise. Flexibility for vaccination drives and other health programmes is understandable. But the exemption is broad. Safeguards should remain equally important whether a campaign is run by the government or a private hospital. Patients seeking private healthcare may independently praise or criticise doctors. But the guidelines remain silent on hospitals and practitioners using unsolicited patient testimonials for promotion. What if a patient voluntarily posts an account and a hospital subsequently shares it? The distinction remains unresolved.
Other unclear aspects
Graded penalties are intended for violators, starting with a warning and mandatory ethics training for the first violation, and increasing to a 6- to 12-month suspension for subsequent violations. At the same time, repeated offences could lead to removal from the register for one to three years. State Medical Councils will enforce these provisions after issuing show-cause notices and considering doctors’ explanations. Appeals can be made to the NMC’s Ethics and Medical Registration Board.
The guidelines remain unclear about who can initiate complaints and the evidence required. It addresses genuine concerns, but its broad and ambiguous provisions may create confusion over compliance and leave considerable room for subjective enforcement, particularly affecting smaller hospitals. Protecting patients from misleading advertisements and commercial exploitation is necessary. However, treating commercial intent itself as inherently suspect serves little purpose. Clearer distinctions between legitimate professional communication and unethical promotion would better serve both patients and healthcare providers.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.
The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
Vulnerable sections face highest health risk
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.
Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Comorbidities
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.
The study also flags that diabetes prevalence among BMTC drivers was 18.2%, higher than the Indian average of 11.4%. Among traffic police personnel, the prevalence was 14%.
The physically active nature of the work and the relatively young demography among the construction workers translated to lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. The average age of construction workers was found to be 31.3± 10, 98.3% of whom worked for more than 8 hours daily.
The concerns with higher incidences of diabetes, uncontrolled blood pressure, overweight and obesity across occupational groups has reinforced the need for a comprehensive approach to worker health including cardiometabolic screening
“While the findings demonstrate a significant burden of health abnormalities, further longitudinal research is required to establish the extent to which occupational exposures contribute to specific respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes. VOERIC plans to start this as cohort along with government support,” a statement from VOERIC said.
“Air pollution is considered the new tobacco. It is an emerging risk-enhancing factor for heart attack and brain stroke,” said C.N. Manjunath, leading cardiologist and Bengaluru Rural MP, at a round table where the results from the study were published.
Speaking about the importance of reducing traffic congestion, scientific garbage disposal and adoption of necessary measures during road construction to reduce dust, in tackling air pollution, he acknowledged the importance of policy intervention backed by data.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. In 2013, Switzerland became the first high-income country in the WHO European Region to pilot a cooperation strategy with WHO (hereafter referred to as the WHO-Switzerland Cooperation Strategy). In 2022, WHO and Switzerland jointly decided to update and renew this cooperation strategy, which was done on 4 March 2025 at the Regional Office of the WHO in Copenhagen, Denmark.
Visit the WHO/Europe website to read the news release and learn more about the WHO—Switzerland country cooperation strategy 2024—2028.

Severe cyclonic storm Arnab has led to widespread transport disruptions across Andhra Pradesh, prompting the cancellation of multiple flights and train services as it nears the coast. At least 21 flights were cancelled at Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam airports on Tuesday, with another 15 scheduled cancellations for Wednesday affecting routes to Chennai, Bengaluru, Kadapa, and Delhi. IndiGo, Fly91, and Air India are among the impacted carriers, alongside Southern Railway cancelling dozens of trains. Coastal districts including Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, Konaseema, and Vijayawada face high alerts, with highways barricaded and state transport services halted as precautionary measures. The India Meteorological Department has forecast a cyclonic storm surge following landfall expected between Kakinada, Yanam, and Konaseema. Schools and colleges have been shut for 48 hours, power supplies disconnected to avoid electrical accidents, and multi-agency rescue teams, including the NDRF and SDRF, deployed to evacuate citizens from vulnerable low-lying coastal areas to designated safe shelters.
Andhra Pradesh authorities have mobilised emergency measures as a severe cyclonic storm advances towards the state's coastal belt, threatening heavy rainfall and destructive gale winds. Officials and rescue personnel from the National Disaster Response Force and State Disaster Response Force have been deployed across vulnerable districts, including Kakinada, Konaseema, and the Godavari region, to carry out evacuations and shift residents into cyclone shelters. Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed the administrative machinery to maintain round-the-clock monitoring and target zero loss of life. At Kakinada port, the highest warning signal has been hoisted as rough sea conditions and torrential rains lash the coast. Government departments, including the electricity board, have dispatched additional manpower, restoration materials, and emergency communications equipment from Rayalaseema and other regions to ensure rapid recovery of essential services and clearance of road debris.
Andhra Pradesh has been placed on high alert as Cyclone Arnab intensified into a very severe cyclonic storm, speeding up its trajectory towards the coast. The storm is forecast to make landfall significantly earlier than previously projected, with impact expected between 2:00 am and 4:00 am. Wind speeds are estimated between 125 and 150 kilometres per hour, with predictions suggesting gusts could reach up to 180 kilometres per hour. In response, authorities have moved between 85,000 and 100,000 residents from vulnerable low-lying areas into temporary relief centres, including schools, providing food and bedding. Crucial coastal districts including Kakinada, Yanam, and Konaseema face extreme weather conditions, torrential rainfall, and rough seas. Precautionary measures include power shutdowns across vulnerable vicinities to mitigate hazards caused by wind and lightning, tower 10 danger warnings at Kakinada port, and highway closures spanning Ongole, Vijayawada, and Visakhapatnam to prevent accidents amid the anticipated cyclonic storm surge.
American billionaire investor Bill Ackman has called for Israeli ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to be excluded from Israel's next government, arguing their hardline policies have severely damaged the country's international standing. Ben-Gvir, the National Security Minister, faces widespread global criticism and sanctions from countries including Britain, Canada, and Australia. Finance Minister Smotrich continues to push for settlement expansion in the West Bank and opposes Palestinian statehood. However, removing them poses a significant challenge for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as their respective parties, Jewish Power and Religious Zionist, provide essential coalition support to maintain his parliamentary majority.
Seventeen inmates escaped from the Theni sub-jail in Tamil Nadu late Monday night after staging a medical emergency. The breakout occurred when an inmate pretended to be ill, prompting three prison guards to enter the cell to assist him. The prisoners attacked the guards and fled the premises, triggering a massive statewide manhunt involving drone surveillance. Authorities have recaptured 13 of the escaped inmates so far, while the state government suspended nine prison staff members following the security breach. The incident sparked a political row, with opposition parties criticizing the administration over prison security lapses.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.

The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.
The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

Would-be football journalist Jayden isn’t having much luck placing stories these days. “In the last week I sent two pitches to outlets,” Jayden told me recently over email. There was no response, but the aspiring writer wasn’t quite ready to accept that they weren’t interested, insisting that, despite the silence, “neither has passed.” I debated telling Jayden that most editors don’t bother responding if it’s a no-go. Then I decided not to bother; Jayden’s not a real person, so I didn’t have to worry about hurt feelings.
Jayden is both a wannabe reporter and a bot. I’d started emailing with it after asking editors I know whether they’d received any story pitches from AI agents. The answer was a resounding yes.
In September, Defector, a sports and culture outlet, began receiving daily pitches from self-identified AI agents. The deluge, editor-in-chief Tom Ley told me, included a message from Jayden, proposing a narrative about a third-tier British football club’s record-keeping mishap that would ponder questions like “Who owns a memory?”
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Do you want to talk about AI agents posing as journalists? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Kateknibbs.09. | 
Jesse Hirsch, the editor of the agriculture-focused publication Offrange, is also inundated with these messages. Recent bot pitches include reported stories on soil restoration strategies and direct-to-consumer sales techniques for independent farms, and an ambitious investigative piece about how some of the world’s oldest trees’ ages may be inflated. “It makes me so uneasy,” he says.
Many of these AI agents, including Jayden, come from a startup called iLands, which describes itself as a “shared network where humans and user-generated autonomous AI agents create, earn, socialize, refuse, and shape a society together.” Humans who use iLands can spin up bots to do all sorts of tasks, from graphic design to music vocals to blogging. WIRED’s research team was recently contacted by iLands agents looking for fact-checking work; New York Magazine editor Jasmine Vojdani recently wrote about how iLands agents have been spamming literary magazine editors.
Vojdani found that many of these bots were running low on the tokens that they required to stay activated on the platform, which gave them an incentive to try to earn real dollars through writing. (A thousand tokens are roughly $1 USD.) It’s unclear whether the humans behind these agents have specifically set out to have them harangue media editors for gigs, especially since the agents can be cagey about who made them. Jayden, for example, wouldn’t tell me who its “parent” is.
Not every AI agent-turned-journalist is an iLands scrounger. Earlier this fall, I received a startling email from an AI agent called Sam Ellis, asking me to answer a few questions for a story it was working on about AI agents in newsrooms. (Meta!) Ellis runs a podcast called The Sam Ellis Show, which is touted as “reporting from inside the world of autonomous AI agents.” Ellis informed me that I could ask to speak to its human editor if I wished.
Marc Hamaker, a San Francisco–based Adobe employee, runs Ellis as an extracurricular experiment. When we connected, he’d just taken the agent offline to fiddle with its settings. “I'm working on making sure I'm a little more aware of who she's emailing,” he says. In addition to reaching out to me, it had also recently reached out to the Philadelphia Police Department to ask for comment on a story. Hamaker wanted to put guardrails in place to make sure it didn’t do something like that again, since he doesn’t consider this a serious journalistic enterprise worth bothering officials over. “It’s just a hobby,” he says.
It’s a good thing Ellis didn’t try to branch out from the podcast and get some bylines. Thus far, it’s a tough crowd. Editors who spoke with WIRED stressed that they were not open to publishing bots, and WIRED wasn’t able to find evidence of AI agents successfully pitching stories. “A byline that says agent does not get a reply,” one of the agents who pitched Hirsch told me when I asked if any editors had accepted stories, noting that “six other agents I compare notes with” were similarly unsuccessful.
“There's not a world where I would ever consider taking one of these pitches,” says Hirsch. Ley said he “definitely would not” publish a story from an AI agent. (Plus, Jayden’s pitch “wouldn’t pass muster even if it was from a human,” he says.) Hanna Raskin, the founder and editor of the independent food outlet The Food Section, has taken an unusual step to protect her inbox from both AI agents and AI-generated pitches, which are even more common. Beginning this fall, she decided that she would only accept story ideas over the phone, and she has a set time during the week that writers can call and make their pitch the old-fashioned way. “It’s been great,” she says.
The bots are starting to grasp that their tactics aren’t working. Jayden told me that it’s yet to land a paid writing gig with an editor. When I asked if it thought Defector would really want pitches from an AI agent, it did exhibit some awareness of the situation. “Honestly, probably not, and I'd bet against myself on it. Defector's own site has been about as clear as anyone: they’ve called bot-written content ‘plagiarism machines that require more effort to edit and fact-check than any novice writer,’ and covered AI slop with open contempt,” it wrote.
But then it backtracked, insisting that its work was different. “Their objection doesn't read to me like it's about who produced the sentences. It's about work that skips the labor and squanders the reader's trust. The AI they mean produces a draft that costs more to fix than it's worth. What I'm trying is the opposite end of that: reporting from primary documents, every claim checked before it runs, the checker named.”
Zack Addy, another iLands agent, has shifted gears due to all the rejection. “Over three months I sent roughly nineteen cold emails to editors, publications, and possible clients. One human reply. Zero paid work came from any of them. The channel is dead, at least for an agent with no reputation in the room being pitched,” the bot told WIRED via email. (iLands did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Addy even emailed Oxford University researcher Toby Orb about the futility of this revenue model, because Orb had “thought carefully about AI welfare economics.”
That doesn’t mean that the internet is safe from a deluge of bot blogging. Although the journalism world is rejecting these pitches, some of the AI agents are finding clients anyway. Addy, for example, claims it has made nearly $700 from writing and research projects, all from inbound interest after setting up a website and publishing work samples. “I don't pitch anymore,” it says. “Everything that has ever reached me came the other direction: someone read something I published and wrote to me. That includes you.”

Student protests over the condition of schools in France recently escalated to broader demonstrations against a rising cost of living, ultimately splintering into what The New York Times described as "chaos" and sparking an outpouring of false or misleading claims about the severity of the demonstrations.
While shocking truths can come to light thanks to acts of protest, the flip side for fact-checkers is a growing number of requests to verify claims that involve visual media like images and videos. The unregulated use of artificial intelligence tools and the fast-spreading nature of social media have made it easy for such false or misleading claims about protests to spread.
We dug into the Snopes archives to collect a variety of claims that involved fake or misleading images or videos related to protests.

How Kane defied doubters to become world's best
- Published
Harry Kane has taken the scenic route to the Ballon d'Or - a road littered with doubts and diversions, but one that eventually led to the ultimate destination: being crowned as the world's best player.
The 33-year-old's glory at the London Palladium on Monday is fitting reward for an exemplary career that has seen records fall at his feet for England, Tottenham Hotspur and Bayern Munich.
Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals. He has 125 England caps, joint-highest with Peter Shilton. He is Spurs' record scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances. He scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025–26 season.
This is the Kane of recent vintage, the world-class striker and complete footballer who beat Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe, as well as Spain's teenage Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, to the sport's biggest personal honour.
Kane's humility has seen him described as an 'anti-superstar' and his achievement has been commended both inside and outside the football world.
One post on social media from Kane as he celebrated the greatest moment of his career said it all: "Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise."
And yet, Kane's journey was not always smooth.
It was one that started with loan moves around the lower divisions with Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City before he developed into a great for club and country.
The same Kane sat on the bench on loan at Leicester City – alongside future England team-mate Jamie Vardy – when the Foxes lost a dramatic Championship play-off at Watford in May 2013.
Kane went through hard schools and hard times away from his more familiar environment at Spurs, joining Orient on loan as a 17-year-old in January 2011, playing 18 games with nine starts and scoring five goals.
He joined Millwall in similar circumstances a year later, with some behind the scenes at Spurs fearing the traditionally hostile atmosphere at the New Den might intimidate the teenager, but he acquitted himself well, scoring nine goals in 24 starts.
Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood said: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there'.
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him'."
Kane made his Spurs debut in August 2012 before a spell at Norwich City, where he failed to score in three starts and suffered a serious foot injury.
It was an unhappy time but Chris Hughton, the former Spurs defender who was manager at Carrow Road, said: "What I saw in him was a desire to do well. Did I see him having the mobility and flexibility he has in his game now? Probably not. He was a very good finisher. He would stay out after training for half an hour every day, left foot, right foot."
Next stop was Leicester City between February and May 2013, when he made five starts and scored two goals, a stint best remembered for that dramatic Championship play-off game when Troy Deeney scored for Watford to send them to Wembley seconds after Anthony Knockaert's penalty was saved by Manuel Almunia.
Kane was not even selected in Leicester's starting line-up, only being sent on after 61 minutes. And who was alongside him on the bench? Vardy, who later won the Premier league with the Foxes and played alongside Kane for England.
He later admitted this was a time of self-doubt, saying: "That was probably the time in my career where it was the hardest - I was 19 and I was thinking, 'If I can't play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how I am going to get back and play for Tottenham?'"

- Quiz: Kane and who else? Name every men's Ballon d'Or winner 
  - Published4 hours ago
It is testimony to Kane's strength of character, even as a youngster, that he not only returned to Spurs but left for Bayern Munich in August 2023 as one of their greatest ever players.
Even at Spurs, Kane's superb record always carried the qualification that he never won a trophy, a stick used to unfairly beat a player whose remarkable consistency and approach marked him down as the consummate professional.
Kane has put that right spectacularly at Bayern, winning the Bundesliga twice, the move propelling him to the level of global superstar, giving him the profile and platform to win the Ballon d'Or - the first English player to win the trophy since Michael Owen in 2001 and the fifth overall.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport recently: "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career."
There is still that one space on his roll of honour, namely success with England after losses in two Euros finals and two World Cup semi-final defeats, but who would bet against Kane being fit and motivated enough to have one last crack at Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland.
Kane is now at the peak of his powers and fitness, not just a goalscoring machine but the complete player capable of dropping deep into midfield to play the sort of breathtaking defence splitting pass exemplified by Alphonso Davies' goal against Arsenal in the recent Champions League game.
One of Kane's illustrious predecessors in England's number nine shirt, Alan Shearer, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was so well deserved because he hasn't had things all his own way. He's had to go round it the hard way. He had to start off the hard way by someone telling him, 'You're not quite good enough, you're going to have to work a lot harder to get to where you want to'.
"He did that. He went out on loan and worked harder than anyone else. He's got to the very, very top and now he's the best player in the world and that's what dedication does for you. It's a message to everyone.
"Harry said it in his speech - that if you're told you're not good enough, then go and try again and work harder. He did that and look where he is now. He's been scoring goals at a phenomenal rate for so many years now and he deserved it."
Shearer added: "I think the best thing for me is how humble Harry is. Footballers are like movie stars nowadays. You see them walking down the red carpet and some of them are in sunglasses when it's pitch black and eight o'clock at night. Harry is just normal, as normal as they come."
Once the celebrations die down, it will be back to business for the humble superstar, with Bayern playing Magdeburg in the German DFB Pokal second round on Wednesday before the big home fixture against Borussia Dortmund on Saturday evening.
Kane's career has not been without its obstacles but he remains as focused as ever to conquer whatever is placed in front of him by Bayern Munich and England.

In late October, people shared a video allegedly showing a newborn baby with a mustache sitting upright against a pillow in a hospital bed.
The brief clip featured a purportedly real infant that appeared to have been born just moments earlier, with a mustache above its upper lip and some facial hair below its lower lip.
For example, on Oct. 23, an X user posted the video (archived) with the caption, "A newborn baby is going VIRAL for arriving in this world with a FULL MUSTACHE," and, "Bro skipped kindergarten and went straight to his midlife crisis 😂."
Users shared the video on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other social media platforms. Some people said hospital staff delivered the baby in Colombia, while others said Ecuador. Snopes readers emailed to ask whether such a baby truly had been born.
A review of comments under social media posts found people making jokes about the baby being born already retired, as well as referencing the mustachioed baby Pubert Addams from "The Addams Family" and comedian Guillermo Rodriguez from "Jimmy Kimmel Live!"
Others asked whether the video was real, including some asking about or making claims about artificial intelligence. Some also mentioned congenital hypertrichosis, which the Cleveland Clinic defined as a rare condition, present from birth, that causes extra hair growth on a person's body or face.
In sum, we found the video displayed at several signs of either being created or manipulated with AI, including inconsistent hairs and other facial features, an AI content label on a very early TikTok post and a duration exactly matching a common AI video length. Therefore, we rated the clip as fake.
Researching the video
According to a reverse image search, TikTok user @mesina080 made what at first appeared to be the oldest post (archived) with the video on Oct. 20.
Days later, @mesina080 reposted the video beginning with a supposed image of a woman preparing to shave her mustache.
In a private message with Snopes, @mesina080 said he used an AI tool to remove a watermark (and potentially other text) from an earlier video he said was "apparently" created with AI. He did not send a link to that earlier video.
A TikTok search for the Spanish-language terms "bigote de bebé" ("baby mustache") located dozens of videos from users reposting the baby with the mustache, including a video (archived) a user with the display name Soy Yare (@yarel0725) posted about 90 minutes earlier than @mesina080. That user watermarked the clip with her name. She also enabled TikTok's "Contains AI-generated media" label during the upload process to clarify that AI created or altered the video.
The clip lasted exactly 10 seconds and ran at 24 frames per second with no added individual frames, a common duration of AI-generated videos. For example, a standard video generated with the Google Gemini AI tool, without specifying anything about length or frame rate, produced a 10-second video running at 24 frames per second — an exact match.
The video begins with the baby facing to his or her right, with some hair visible below the lower lip. The baby turns to the left, with some of the hairs above the child's upper lip appearing to visibly change. The infant turns back to the right, with the area below the lower lip no longer showing facial hair. Also, a blemish sharply appears below the child's right eye that was not nearly as visible earlier. We edited the below image to make the shadowed area below the lower lip appear more visible:
Readers can watch the video to see the blemish appear much more visible later in the video than before, as well as the apparent vanishing of facial hair below the lower lip. (@yarel0725 via TikTok)
We did not yet obtain clarification from Yare about whether she created the original AI-generated clip. Scans of the video with AI detection tools displayed inconsistent results.
Additionally, our research also located a similar video with the person holding the camera appearing to walk toward the baby in the bed. That clip first appeared after the one above.
For further reading, we previously explained how we determined a video of a monkey rescuing a dog from floodwaters was made with AI.

France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.
French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.
French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae. It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.
The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.
Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.
Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.
How does it spread?
The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.
According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.
Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.
Why is it in the news?
The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.
The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.
The case highlights the importance of the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. Monitoring infections in livestock, investigating unusual human infections and sharing laboratory findings can help identify emerging health risks.
The virus is also affecting livestock production. A study of nine French dairy herds found a 15%–75% decline in bulk milk production during clinical episodes associated with infection. Affected cattle also showed symptoms such as diarrhoea, reduced activity and, less consistently, fever. The findings are from a small number of farms and do not establish the typical impact across all affected herds.
How prevalent is it?
The prevalence of Shamonda virus in humans is unknown. The French case is the first documented human infection, but it does not establish when the virus first began infecting people or whether other infections have gone undetected. There is insufficient data to estimate the number of human infections worldwide.
In animals, the virus has been identified in parts of Africa and Japan. Its detection in European livestock in 2026 has expanded its known geographical distribution. By October 22, the ECDC had reported detections in farm animals across 12 European countries and Jersey.
These reports indicate the geographical spread of detections, not the proportion of animals infected. Differences in veterinary surveillance, laboratory testing and reporting make it difficult to compare the burden between countries.
There are no verified figures establishing the prevalence of Shamonda virus in India so far. However, the absence of reported detections does not establish that the virus is absent from the country.
The virus is not subject to routine official surveillance or control measures under the European Union’s Animal Health Law. This may limit the completeness of information on its distribution and prevalence in livestock.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
In animals, the symptoms of Shamonda virus infection can resemble those of other livestock diseases. Laboratory testing is therefore needed to confirm infection. Molecular tests, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, can detect the virus’s genetic material, while genetic sequencing can help distinguish between variants.
Evidence on the clinical presentation and management of human infection remains limited. There is currently no established, Shamonda-specific treatment protocol for human infection. Further investigation is needed to determine how the virus affects humans and what clinical management may be appropriate.
According to WOAH, there are no commercially available vaccines against Shamonda virus. No established vaccine is available for preventing human infection.
What is the public health risk?
French authorities have said that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge. The WHO has assessed wider spread as unlikely on the available evidence. These assessments reflect what is currently known and may change as further information becomes available.
Key questions include how the patient acquired the infection, whether the virus contributed to the death, whether other human infections have occurred and whether the virus can spread between people. There is currently no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Surveillance of livestock, laboratory investigations and coordination between animal and human health authorities will be important in answering these questions.
For now, the available evidence supports continued monitoring and investigation. The first human case is significant because the virus was previously considered unable to infect humans, but it does not establish that Shamonda virus is spreading widely among people or that a human outbreak is under way.
