Israelis are voting in a crucial parliamentary election on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin 
Netanyahu
 facing a major test of his leadership amid unresolved conflicts, divisions over the country's future and growing international criticism of its conduct in Gaza.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to retain power against a group of parties hoping to unseat him, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
The election is the country's first national vote since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack that triggered the war in Gaza and related regional conflicts.
However, reports of missing, damaged and defaced ballot slips have raised concerns about election integrity, with Eisenkot's Yashar party filing a complaint with the Central Elections Committee.
1. Netanyahu faces a crucial test
The election is a test not only of Netanyahu's leadership but also of the direction Israel should take, with voters divided over security, military conscription, judicial independence and the country's international standing.
Netanyahu's supporters view him as an experienced leader who has guided Israel through multiple wars and defended its Jewish identity.
His critics accuse him of prolonging the war in Gaza and the hostage crisis for political reasons, undermining judicial independence and allowing ultra-Orthodox religious men to avoid compulsory military service.
“The present government is driving the country into the ground,” voter Angela Bengur said in Jerusalem, the Associated Press reported.
Eisenkot's supporters see him as a leader with strong security credentials who could improve Israel's international standing and strengthen democratic institutions. His personal losses during the Gaza war have also shaped his public image: his son and two nephews were killed while fighting in Gaza.
2. Voter turnout hits highest midday level since 1973
Voter turnout in Israel’s parliamentary election reached 31.5% by noon local time, the highest recorded at that hour since 1973, according to The Times of Israel, citing the Central Elections Committee.
The strong participation reflects intense voter engagement as Israelis cast their ballots at more than 12,000 polling stations across the country.
Turnout had already reached 16.68% by 10 am, with more than one million people having voted, the Central Elections Committee said. The figure was higher than the 15.9% recorded at the same time during the 2022 election.
The Times of Israel reported that the morning turnout was the highest at that hour since at least 1996, when Benjamin Netanyahu first became prime minister. Other reports described it as the highest since 1981.
Around 330,000 young Israelis are eligible to vote for the first time. Many are approaching compulsory military service as the country continues to grapple with the consequences of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and the wars that followed.
Turnout among Israel Defense Forces (IDF) personnel was also higher than in the previous election. The IDF said 30% of service members had voted by 10 am, compared with 25.7% at the same point in 2022.
3. Netanyahu warns of Arab-backed govt as Arab-led parties eye key role
Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers in Israel’s parliamentary election if rival political blocs fail to secure a majority, potentially playing a decisive role in government formation, according to AP reports.
Netanyahu urged Likud supporters to turn out in large numbers, warning that the country’s future was at stake.
“This is an emergency call to Likud voters! Today no one stays home. No sea, no barbecue. Making sure that the family, friends, and neighbors also get to the polling station,” he wrote on X, sharing a video.
“The future of our Jewish state is on the line: a strong right-wing government or a left-wing government supported by the Arab parties. Going out to vote with all our might!” he added.
In another post, Netanyahu said buses were heading to polling stations and long queues were being reported in Arab communities, while right-wing strongholds had yet to see a comparable turnout.
“If we don't go out to vote now, we'll find ourselves with a government of the Arab parties. We must not stay home. Every vote counts! Going out now to vote - Machal, Likud,” he wrote.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population, giving Arab-led parties the potential to influence government formation if the main political blocs fall short of a majority.
“Our vote will change the government,” Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra’am party, said after casting his vote. He added that he hoped turnout in Arab communities would exceed 70%.
However, cooperation with Arab-led parties remains a contentious issue among right-wing politicians.
Israel’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has faced criticism for his treatment of Palestinian detainees and remarks about Palestinians in Gaza, warned that “it will be Mansour Abbas’ government” if Netanyahu and his allies fail to secure a victory.
4. Yashar party alleges ballot tampering, files complaint
Eisenkot's Yashar party has filed a complaint with the Central Elections Committee over reports that ballot slips bearing its designated voting symbol, “Derech”, were missing, damaged or defaced at polling stations.
The party said it had received reports from several locations across the country about ballot slips being removed, marked with pens or turned over inside voting booths, potentially resulting in votes being disqualified.
“After Likud's fake news campaign, we received numerous complaints about our ballot slips being defaced or removed,” party chairman Yoaz Hendel said, The Jerusalem Post reported.
The party described the alleged incidents as a possible systematic attempt to disrupt its vote and undermine election integrity.
“Anyone who tries to steal ballot slips is trying to steal the election. This is a serious violation of election integrity and the fundamental right of Israeli citizens to vote,” the party said.
The allegations had not been independently established in the information available at the time of reporting.
5. Eisenkot visits October 7-hit community before voting
Eisenkot began election day by visiting Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the communities hardest hit by the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack.
He walked alongside former hostage Gadi Mozes towards his polling booth before leaving to cast his own vote elsewhere.
“I am proud and moved to begin this day with Gadi Mozes, a symbol of the Israeli spirit and strength, of Israelis’ commitment to one another and their commitment to the state. I pledge to do everything I can to ensure that we are worthy of the price you paid, the price the kibbutz paid and the price we all paid, and to bring healing and repair to all citizens of Israel,” Eisenkot told reporters.
Mozes endured 482 days in Hamas captivity and campaigned for Eisenkot, according to The Times of Israel.
Eisenkot also criticised the government for not beginning election day in communities attacked on October 7. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here in the Gaza envelope,” he said.
Netanyahu had not appeared in public in the first three hours after polling stations opened, according to the initial reports. In Tel Aviv, families of people killed during the October 7 attack and former hostages observed a moment of silence.
6. President Herzog calls election a 'holiday of democracy'
President Isaac Herzog visited the Central Elections Committee headquarters and urged Israelis to participate in the democratic process.
“It is a real holiday of democracy, and no one can be allowed to ruin it — quite the opposite, this is our opportunity, all of us, to influence our fate, the fate of our children, and the fate of our grandchildren. It is something that is deeply embedded inside of our spirit, as a very democratic nation,” The Times of Israel reported him as saying.
“We are putting different slips in the ballot, and we are expressing different opinions, in the end we have a common fate. A common fate in this land, a common fate in our beloved country, and this election process is another way to express our love for our country,” Herzog added.
7. Israel deploys 100,000 personnel for election day
Israel has mounted a large logistical operation for the parliamentary election, with around 100,000 personnel, including election officials and workers, deployed across the country.
Acting director general of the Central Elections Committee Dean Livne said around 50,000 election workers had received training at approximately 2,140 venues.
The committee has prepared 12,018 polling stations, 18,000 ballot boxes, 12 million voting envelopes and 250 tonnes of paper for ballot materials. It has also established 6,209 accessible polling stations.
Special voting arrangements have been made for more than 600,000 people who may be unable to vote at their designated polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats and hospitalised voters. These voters can use an outer-envelope system, with checks designed to prevent duplicate voting.
Authorities have also arranged free travel on 660 intercity public transport routes, including all Israel Railways services, to help voters reach polling stations. Around 690 million shekels, or approximately $223 million, has been allocated for the election.
The Central Elections Committee has deployed around 15,000 cameras for electoral integrity inspectors to monitor polling stations and document voting and counting. The system is intended to protect ballot secrecy and allow inspectors to identify attempts to pressure or influence voters.
8. How Israel's electoral system works
Israel is a parliamentary democracy in which voters elect lawmakers rather than directly choosing the prime minister. The government must retain the confidence of the Knesset to remain in power.
The country uses a proportional representation system. Voters choose a party list, and the 120 seats in the Knesset are distributed broadly in proportion to the votes received by parties that cross the electoral threshold.
Unlike many other parliamentary democracies, Israel treats the entire country as a single constituency rather than dividing it into geographic electoral districts. This allows smaller parties representing religious, political and ethnic communities to win parliamentary representation.
Parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter the Knesset. The system often produces fragmented parliaments in which no single party wins an outright majority, making coalition negotiations central to government formation.
9. What happens after the votes are counted?
After the results are finalised, President Herzog will consult the leaders of the elected parties before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
The person chosen does not necessarily have to lead the largest party; the key consideration is who appears most likely to assemble a coalition with sufficient parliamentary support.
The designated lawmaker will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. If the attempt fails, another party leader may be given 28 days to try.
If that effort also fails, at least 61 lawmakers can request that the president assign the task to a particular member of the Knesset within a further 21-day period.
A new government must win a confidence vote in parliament. A minority government may also take office if it receives more votes in favour than against, even without the backing of 61 lawmakers.
The process could take weeks, leaving the identity of Israel's next prime minister uncertain even after election results emerge. If all attempts to form a government fail, the country could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office.
10. Iran tensions remain in the background
The election is also taking place amid continuing tensions with Iran. Netanyahu intensified his warnings to Tehran ahead of the vote, saying it would face “a devastating blow” if it attacked Israel.
Israel's conduct in Gaza and the occupied West Bank has also drawn growing international criticism. Public support for Israel in the US has fallen, while some European and other partners have imposed sanctions.

Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation
- Published
The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.
The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.
Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027.
However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".
'Take a step back'
NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.
"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.
Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.
"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.
"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".
Bulgaria beckons
The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all bocotted the 2026 contest over Israel's participation, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.
Eurovision organisers have announced a number of changes in an attempt to address the divisions, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition, and changes to the voting.
As well as the Netherlands, Ireland will also not take part in 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.
The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.
Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year with the dance track Bangaranga.

Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
- Published
On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.
Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.
Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.
Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.
The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.
Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.
The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.
Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?
Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.
D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.
In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.
Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.
Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.
But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.
"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."
That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.
Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.
Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.
Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."
The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.
In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".
The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.
Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.
After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"
There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.
Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.
Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security.
"There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

Big wins, shocking losses, and goodbye to a 46-year mayor: what to know about Ontario's 400+ elections
2026 municipal elections included lots of turnover, but also some large cities where almost nothing changed
There were more than 400 municipal elections in Ontario Monday, so naturally the results were all over the map.
From an anti-incumbent wave that hit many politicians, including one of Canada's longest-serving mayors, to several big cities that brought back almost every incumbent, here are some of the key headlines and takeaways from last night.
Chow wins easily in Toronto
After polling had suggested a "statistical dead heat," Toronto's incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow defeated challenger Brad Bradford with relative ease.
Political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications, said the Chow campaign struck a nerve with Torontonians by going after Bradford's pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater. Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset and opening the door to privatization.
"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," Knox said.
Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.
- Analysis Olivia Chow romps to victory as head of progressive new Toronto council
- Who are Toronto's new city councillors?
Mississauga's first male mayor since 1978
Polling at only 12 per cent as recently as August, Alvin Tedjo climbed from those depths to the Mississauga mayor's chair, defeating incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.
Tedjo is just the fourth person to hold the job in nearly half a century, marking a significant generational shift in a city long led by political veterans. He's also the first man to hold the job since 1978.
Horwath out in Hamilton
Since amalgamation in 2000, Hamilton's incumbent mayors have lost their seats more often than they keep them, and that held true on Monday. Andrea Horwath, the former Ontario New Democratic Party leader and former Hamilton Centre MPP, was unable to secure a second term.
The new mayor is Keanin Loomis, former president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction and former head of Hamilton's Chamber of Commerce, who will be joined by eight new councillors in a strong vote for change in the city.
- Hamilton mayor-elect Keanin Loomis says he's ready to bring a new approach to city hall
- Hamilton Votes 2026 Find Hamilton's full 2026 municipal election results here
Milton's 46-year mayor ousted
At least two dozen incumbent mayors lost their seats Monday, including nine who had served their cities for more than a decade.
Gordon Krantz, Canada's longest-serving mayor of a major municipality, had been in charge of Milton council since 1980. He lost handily to councillor George Minakakis.
And in Sarnia, the area's Chamber of Commerce CEO Carrie McEachran defeated mayor Mike Bradley, who had held the chair since 1988.
Other long-time mayors who lost include Oakville's Rob Burton (20 years) and Niagara Falls' Jim Diodati (16 years).
- Carrie McEachran wins Sarnia mayoral race, ousting incumbent of nearly 4 decades
- Niagara Votes 2026 Shocker in Niagara Falls, incumbent mayors ousted in 2 other Niagara municipalities
Some larger cities stay the course
The winds of change did not sweep away everyone in Ontario.
Ottawa, Brampton, London and Kitchener were among the communities that kept their mayors and most of their councils.
Zack Taylor, an associate professor of political science at Western University in London, said limited information about candidates can make it harder for challengers to gain traction. Taylor described the London campaign as relatively quiet compared with some previous election cycles.
“It could just be that [London Mayor] Josh Morgan benefited from incumbency and also not really having any kind of scandals occur,” Taylor said.
- London voters stick with familiar faces, but the reasons may go beyond the status quo
- Ottawa Votes 2026 4 key takeaways from Ottawa's city election
Mark Sutcliffe gives a victory speech after being re-elected as mayor of Ottawa on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)
A good night for women
Niagara Falls, Port Colborne and North Bay each elected their first female mayors, Ottawa's council has more women than men for the first time since the 2001 amalgamation, and the community of Merrickville-Wolford elected an all-female council.
At her victory party, Niagara Falls mayor-elect Lori Lococo downplayed the accomplishment.
"I always hope that people vote for people based on their experience and skills, not because of their gender," she said.
Women made up 32 per cent of the candidates province-wide.

- Hamilton Votes 2026 'I’m not going to let them silence me:' women political candidates push back against growing hate
Taxes, homelessness were key issues
Taxes were a running theme across many municipalities.
Tedjo in Mississauga promised a two-year tax freeze; Loomis in Hamilton promised to get taxes "under control"; and Windsor's new mayor Fred Francis promised to hold the line on taxes.
Other popular discussion points during the campaign were homelessness, encampments and community safety. These were key issues in places like Windsor, Thunder Bay and Oshawa.
Thunder Bay councillor-elect Julie-Ann Colquhoun said she wants to "help build a community where people feel safe … and people experiencing homelessness are supported with an understanding of the complexities they face."

క్లెయిమ్: మక్కాలోని మసీదులో అసభ్యకరంగా ప్రవర్తించారనే ఆరోపణలతో అక్టోబర్ 2026లో సౌదీ అరేబియాలో ఉరితీయబడిన బంగ్లాదేశీ జంటను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ అవుతున్న దృశ్యాలు ఉరితీయబడిన బంగ్లాదేశీ జంటకు సంబంధించినవి కావు. మొదటి వీడియోలో ఉన్నది మక్కాలో కాబా వద్ద తమ గర్భధారణ గురించి ప్రకటించిన యూకేకు చెందిన దంపతులు (బిల్లీ రెహ్మాన్, ఖదీజా) కాగా, మొదటి ఫోటోలో ఉన్నది ఈజిప్ట్కు చెందిన ఇన్ఫ్లుయెన్సర్ దంపతులు (గెహాద్ ఎల్బానా, రామ్జీ మహమూద్). కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left the country for the United States, an ally told news agency Reuters on Tuesday, confirming an earlier media report.
His reported departure came after Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours as part of a money-laundering investigation, in which he denies wrongdoing. Brazilian authorities cancelled his passports on Tuesday after he missed the deadline.
The reported move has drawn comparisons with his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who travelled to the US after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil and was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup.
Flavio has yet to formally concede defeat, saying he would seek to annul the election result over alleged voter irregularities. His Liberal Party, however, acknowledged Lula's victory on Monday.
Lula secured more than 64 million votes, defeating Bolsonaro, who received just under 60 million, by nearly 4.4 million votes. 
The incumbent is expected to take office on January 5, 2027, for a fourth non-consecutive term.
A key factor in Lula’s comeback was the mobilisation of voters who had abstained in the first round or backed other candidates. An additional 14.1 million voters participated in the runoff, with analysts estimating that three-quarters of these votes went to Lula.
Central to the campaign was lawmaker André Janones’ WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army”, which attracted nearly 11 million people and encouraged supporters to campaign on social media.
Bolsonaro has pledged to organise opposition to Lula and seek to nullify the results. He said, “I am going to gather elected lawmakers and senators to organize our strategy and make the lower house and the Senate our fortress against barbaric acts that are set to happen in another four years of Lula.”
However, overturning the result would require evidence of fraud affecting Lula’s 4.4 million-vote margin and approval from Brazil’s eight-member electoral court before certification on December 18.
Benjamin Gedan, director of the Stimson Center’s Latin America programme, warned, “False claims of fraud are becoming commonplace, though that does not make them any less dangerous.”

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.
It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.
However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, Trailblazer, released in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.
The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’
The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.
Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’
At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.
As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.
It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.
But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.
Mary is part of a legacy of tall women in Indian health care that helped sculpt systems that are propping the nation up today, including Muthulakshmi Reddy, Kadambini Ganguly, and Anandi Joshi. They are the forebearers who chipped away at the glass ceilings that prevented them from rising, and cleared the ladder for women who came after them, though history has not given them their due space.
But it is now time for reparation, it is time to say their name loud. Say her name: Say Mary Poonen Lukose, so every one can hear, and celebrate.

The onslaught of tech gear being delivered for WIRED Reviews, combined with the samples I receive constantly for my side hustle at Drinkhacker, means that delivery trucks are a constant occurrence on my suburban street. UPS and FedEx both make drops at my house nearly every day, and that’s not to mention occasional deliveries from the likes of DHL and, of course, Amazon and its ilk. But it’s usually not a problem. I work from home, so picking up packages left on the doorstep is just part of the scenery.
What is a problem is that I can’t be home 24 hours a day, and even though I have a very kind neighbor across the way who keeps an eye out for boxes on my front steps when I’m traveling, he isn’t always at home either. Package hold requests aren’t consistently honored by either of the major carriers—and earlier this year, FedEx seemingly discontinued its vacation hold option without bothering to tell anyone, the modern epidemic of porch piracy be damned. (A rep has since confirmed this with me, though no formal announcement has ever been made.)
Having packages held at shipping centers or access points usually costs money, typically about $5 per package and often more depending on the length of the hold, and that involves a trip after I get home to collect what’s arrived. If I’m gone for a week, that can mean fetching a dozen boxes or more.
All of that is a time-consuming pain, for which a startup called Hyve has come along to offer an assuagement: A smart lockbox that lets delivery drivers drop off packages in a secure location, notifying the homeowner whenever it’s been accessed. While the growing pains were significant, after weeks of testing, I found it a useful device that—just maybe—may earn a permanent home on my front porch.
Locking and Loading
Parcel lockboxes aren’t exactly a new concept. They operate basically like a standard post office mailbox, with a cantilevered hatch up top that allows deliveries to drop into a secure storage area below, where they can only be accessed through a keyed door. Delivery folks can put packages in through the hatch, but only you can get them out.
The Hyve Smart Package Locker is a play on this idea, forgoing the two-chamber design in favor of an electronic hatch accessed via 4-digit PINs. The box itself measures 32 inches high, 20 inches wide, and 20 inches deep, with interior dimensions about 4 inches shorter in each direction. That makes for a total of 7.4 cubic feet, which Hyve says will fit 80 percent of Amazon package sizes (though obviously this depends on the specifics of your ordering habits). For me, that math worked out: Deliveries of three-pack bottles of wine fit fine, but anything larger was typically left out by the courier.
It’s built from a combination of plastic and steel, and while the side panels seem a little flimsy, there’s enough reinforcement behind them that I never worried that the unit would be easily damaged by a would-be package thief without power tools. Units are available in gray or white; I requested the latter to match my home’s color, but alas received a gray one.

Seven out of ten women in West Bengal are anaemic, according to the last figures available. The National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) showed the rate to be 71.4% among women aged 15 to 49, the highest in India’s major states, as compared with 39% among men. However, when NFHS-6 released its fact sheets this year, the section on anaemia was omitted. For the first time since the late 1990s, India has a national health survey that does not include an estimate of anaemia, so it is now impossible to tell whether the situation for women in West Bengal has improved or gotten worse.
This more than a minor omission: anaemia in India is a major public health concern, of greater significance in women, since the difference between men and women when it comes to rates of anaemia is generally attributed to biology. This, however, isn’t entirely accurate.
A burden that kept rising
From 2015 to 2016, the rate of anaemia among women of reproductive age increased nationally from 53% to 57%. In West Bengal, the figure rose by approximately 9 percentage points, and for children between 6 months and 5 years, it rose from 54% to 69%. The gap appears early on: nationally, 59.1% of adolescent girls were anaemic as compared with 31.1% of boys, and this difference becomes greater as people go through their reproductive years. Within the State, the severity of anaemia is linked to disadvantage, so that in districts like Purulia and Uttar Dinajpur almost four out of five women were anaemic.
Anaemia prevalence, NFHS-5 (2019–21)
| Anaemia prevalence NFHS-5 (2019–21) | West Bengal | India | 
| Women 15–49 | 71.4% | 57.0% | 
| Men 15–49 | ~39% | 25.0% | 
| Children 6–59 months | 69.0% | 67.1% | 
Source: IIPS & ICF, NFHS-5 (2021). NFHS-6 (2026) did not report anaemia.
Not just biology
The usual explanation given in textbooks is that women lose more iron because they menstruate, carry pregnancies, and breastfeed; this is correct, but it does not explain a 30-point gap or why this gap changes so markedly across districts, castes, and wealth levels. The answer may lie in examining gender rather than biology alone.
It takes four factors to accomplish this. The first of these is time: since women’s duties, both at home and in agriculture, are mostly unpaid, they have little time for rest, for preparing iron-containing meals, or for visiting a health centre. The second is the meal pattern: in many households, food is given to men and children before it is offered to women, so that the women end up eating last and the least of the food from the kitchens that they manage. The third is social norms: it is considered a woman’s responsibility to look after people, and their own health is of secondary importance, and anaemia is regarded as a ‘women’s ailment.’ That stigma has a double effect in that about four out of every five men in West Bengal are anaemic as well, but they are almost never checked or treated. The fourth is money: women who rely financially on others are often unable to act on what they already know about diet.
An anaemia programme that ignores the gender dimension and merely distributes free iron tablets encounters all four of these obstacles and fails to alter any of them. Fieldwork carried out in Bankura in 2025 illustrates exactly what happens in practice. Pregnant and breastfeeding women discarded the fortified (with iron) rice kernels they were given, since they ‘looked like plastic’. They skipped the iron-folic acid tablets, which they did not like, and forgot their doses because of household chores no one else took on. Husbands, who are mostly engaged as migrant labourers, played almost no role in household nutrition. An improved supply chain would not remedy any of this.
The present scenario
The government has, this year, restructured the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme. In June, the previous 6×6×6 arrangement (six target beneficiary groups, six interventions and six institutional mechanisms) was replaced by a 7×7×7 scheme which includes testing and treatment, a digital ‘T4’ tracking system and a new national centre of excellence for anaemia. On paper, these steps are the correct ones. A digital tracking system broken down by sex could finally show the problem affecting men, a factor kept out of sight because previous messaging had focused only on women.
Yet, in this same year, the country lost its standard for measurement. The official stance is that that anaemia has been omitted from NFHS-6 since blood samples taken from finger pricks are not fully reliable and may have inflated the figures, and also because India had been following the World Health Organization’s cut-offs for anaemia, which may not be suited to the local context. Instead, venous blood sampling was recommended.
All of these are valid concerns, and there is merit in them. The government had also justified dropping the anaemia reading in the NFHS-6 by stating that it would be surveyed more scientifically in the Diet and Biomarkers Survey in India (since renamed the SAMPADA survey), spearheaded by the ICMR-National Institute on Nutrition, and launched in December 2022. Venous blood samples were collected from residents across 183 districts. The problem is, that SAMPADA has not yet released any of its results, despite the survey being completed in November 2025. Until it does, there is no up-to-date national or State figure against which to assess the new programme. It is therefore impossible to verify or alter West Bengal’s status as the most severely affected of the major States, and nobody can tell whether the new framework is having the desired effect.
At present, reform and measurement have become detached from each other, even though they should be closely linked. A programme which is not measurable cannot be held responsible for its actions.
What should follow
There are three issues. The first is that the government ought to make available SAMPADA’s findings on a specific date, breaking the findings down by sex, age and State, and it should ensure that the methods used are sufficiently similar to those employed in the NFHS so that the new figures can be compared with the old ones rather than simply replacing them. An improved measure must not cause the trend to disappear.
The second point is that the new tracking system should regularly provide data by sex, and supplementation for men should be carried out in exactly the same way as it is for women. The third is that counselling and outreach activities must treat anaemia as a problem that affects the entire household, not merely as a problem of women; it is therefore necessary to reach mothers-in-law, since they are often in a position to decide who eats what, and migrant husbands should also be targeted since they are never present in the room.
India is now carrying out a more ambitious programme than before to combat anaemia, and has no current figures with which to evaluate it. Until the data is available, we are facing a problem for which records have been discontinued, and the women who are affected most may be the last to find out whether or not any change has taken place.
(Anurag Telang is a researcher in public health. dranurag225@gmail.com; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of Economics at XLRI, Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking after blaming rapes on 'hookup culture'

Three brothers convicted of exploiting their wealth and access to luxury real estate to drug and rape dozens of women were sentenced Tuesday to 30 years in prison.
U.S. District Judge Valerie E. Caproni announced the punishment for Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — known collectively as the Alexander Brothers — after 11 accusers spoke in court. Some of the women choked up as they described how the assaults stole their innocence and left them haunted by nightmares and fearing men.
“It took one night, only a few hours, one invitation to completely wreck the girl I once was,” one woman, using a pseudonym to protect her identity, said as she stood at a lectern just feet from the brothers in a Manhattan courtroom.
Twins Oren and Alon, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40, were convicted in March of sex trafficking.
The brothers speak for themselves
None of the brothers testified during the trial, but each spoke Tuesday before they were sentenced.
Oren Alexander addressed the packed courtroom first, saying, “I am not here to discount what they have said,” referring to the women.
He said he and his brothers came of age at the height of hookup culture and, looking back and now as a father, he regrets many of the things he said about women at that time. However, he insisted that they never broke the law.
“My brothers and I have never drugged or raped anyone. We never trafficked anyone for sex and we never conspired to hurt anyone,” he said.
Tal Alexander also denied that he drugged or raped anyone. He asked the judge to be assign him to same prison as his brothers; saying their parents, both 70 years old, hope to visit them every weekend, which might be difficult if they’re at different lockups.
Alon Alexander said he, too, has evolved from his regrettable past, noting that not a single woman has accused him of wrongdoing in the eight years he’s been committed to his wife: “Over time, that became my life: work, home, children, parents, community.”
Victims describe a lasting dread
The accusers who spoke in court — and another whose statement was read by a prosecutor — were among at least 70 women who prosecutors say were assaulted by one or more of the brothers over the last two decades in posh locales including the Hamptons on Long Island and in Aspen, a Colorado.
Lindsey Acree, an artist and gallery owner, testified that she was raped by Tal Alexander and another man at a Hamptons home in 2011 after taking a drink that she said left her feeling paralyzed. Scrapping her prepared remarks, she told Caproni that a life sentence, wouldn’t begin to do justice for the women whose lives were irreparably harmed.
“This has wasted my damn time. It’s wasted your time. It’s wasted everyone in this room’s time,” Acree told the judge. Turning to the brothers, she said: “For why? For you. Because you did some really messed up stuff.”
“The biggest thing is why? Why did you do this?” Acree asked. “I don’t understand the cruelty. I don’t understand the hatred towards women.”
Another woman who testified that Tal Alexander raped her in August 2014 said she carried “a quiet funeral in me for the person I might have become had this not happened to me.”
“Every second that Tal raped me in that shower felt like an eternity of terror,” said the woman, who used a pseudonym.
Another woman speaking about her rape in the Hamptons, said: “What looked like a beautiful place became for me a mansion of horror, a mansion of dark secrets.”
Prosecutors had sought life prison sentences while the brothers’ lawyers had requested the 15-year mandatory minimum.
Stars of the New York real estate scene
Oren and Tal Alexander were once nicknamed real estate’s “A Team” for their ultra high-end sales and celebrity clientele.After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, the brothers started their own firm. Alon Alexander ran their family’s private security company.
The brothers projected an exclusive lifestyle of yachts, private jets and waterfront mansions in Miami, but prosecutors said they began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school, and over time developed a pattern of drugging and raping women who they enticed to join them on luxury getaways.
In remarks before the sentence was announced, Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa told the judge that the brothers’ “callousness, carelessness, cruelty” in repeatedly drugging and raping women over many years warranted a life prison term, especially since all their victims would be serving life sentences of pain.
“Women overcame all the forces telling them this was their fault, they should stay quiet, that no one would believe them,” the prosecutor said. “Despite that pain, so many came forward and 11 women testified at trial.”
Alon Alexander’s lawyer, Howard Srebnick, called a life sentence a “death in prison sentence.”
In court papers, defense lawyers said the brothers apologize to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times.” They also maintained their innocence.
The trio were arrested in 2024 and have been held without bail ever since.
The judge, Caproni, has said she believes the brothers should not be incarcerated at the same prison because they were a bad influence on one another. The brothers’ lawyers plan to argue that they belong together, even behind bars.

Social gaming platform Matiks has raised $10 Mn (₹95.1 Cr) in its Pre-Series A funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from upGrad founder Ronnie Screwvala as well as existing backers such as Info Edge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners and Untitled Ventures. In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its global footprint and invest in new games and social experiences. The fresh funding will also be used to deepen investments in engineering, AI, product, design and growth. A chunk of the capital will also be utilised to build an AI-powered engine, which will enable users to build and publish their own social games without writing code. Going forward, it has also set its eyes on scaling creator partnerships, global distribution and player community. “... We started Matiks with a simple belief: using your brain can be just as fun and addictive as any other form of entertainment. Our ambition is to make mind sports as culturally relevant as physical sports and esports - giving mental athletes, puzzlers, and competitive players the visibility, communities, and recognition they deserve…,” said Matiks cofounder and CEO Sudhanshu Bhatia. Founded in 2024 by Bhatia, Mohan Kumar and Sushant Timmapur, Matiks is an esports platform that allows users to play social games spanning mathematics, memory, logic and puzzles. It also allows users to compete with each other. The startup claims that more than 22 Lakh players had played 4.8 Cr games on its platform as of September 2026. Matiks also claimed that its daily active users currently hover around 3 Lakh, with early engagement also emerging from international markets such as Japan, the US and South Korea. The startup last raised $3.14 Mn in its pre-Series A round led by Tanglin Ventures in August last year. Going forward, the startup plans to initially prioritise expansion in the US before entering more tier I markets. Its future roadmap also includes building its AI-powered game creation engine, which the startup believes will foster adoption and create new experiences. The fundraise comes as India’s gaming market is expanding beyond the usual battle royale and casual games. Buoyed by 51 Cr gamers, the ban on real-money games last year, the rise of AI and regulatory push for social games, the homegrown gaming arena is seeing renewed traction and interest from investors. Earlier this month, mobile gaming studio Spill Games raised $10.5 Mn in its Series A round led by Elevation Capital. In April this year, another gaming studio LightFury Games also bagged $11 Mn in its pre-Series A funding round from Blume Ventures and others. In August, cricketer Rohit Sharma also joined LightFury Games as an investor, alongside MS Dhoni, Jasprit Bumrah, and Hardik Pandya, among others. At the heart of all this is the Indian gaming market, which is projected to become a $9.9 Bn opportunity by 2031.

The video ended with head coach Zaheer Khan responding to a question from CSK mascot Leo about the potential trade. “This much is enough for now,” Zaheer said.
No official trade has been confirmed, but several IPL franchises have been linked to rumoured trade talks involving Mumbai Indians (MI) for Hardik Pandya ahead of the IPL 2027 retention and trade windows.
