Consider a kurta priced at ₹799 sold directly on Flipkart by a fashion brand such as Globus Fashion. Since July, Flipkart stopped charging a commission on fashion products, so on paper the seller keeps more of each sale than it did a year ago. But under Flipkart's new penalty structure, effective August 23, the seller is penalised ₹30 the moment the kurta misses its dispatch-by date. If the order is then cancelled, the seller is penalised another ₹60. Flipkart now also counts three missed deadlines as a cancellation. But the flat penalty (a total of ₹90) means that sellers face a greater burden to clear low-value orders. This is one example of how selling online has become costlier this festive season, and penalties are just one part of it. Besides this, there are fee surcharges that apply to every order, whether or not it is delayed or cancelled. And the cost of production and fulfilment have also gone up due to issues ranging from a crunch in raw material supply as well as high fuel prices due to the instability in West Asia. No matter the seller, whether it is a brand or an Amazon-specific seller, these charges and surcharges are making it harder and costlier to sellers on ecommerce at a time when business is at its peak. Third-party sellers usually operate on thinner margins than brands and have no control over the price listed on Amazon India, according to industry sources we spoke to. Some brands take up the operations themselves, depending on the marketplace. Globus Fashion, for instance, sells directly on Flipkart but through Cocoblu Retail on Amazon. Another brand, Ruhe India, which sells smart kitchen and smart home products, holds its own seller account and sells directly on the marketplaces. The approach is different but the charges will remain. The changes coincide with the peak festive season sales on Amazon India and Flipkart. According to Redseer projections, festive ecommerce GMV will reach $15–16 Bn in 2026, up about 25% from roughly $12.5 Bn in 2025, with online festive shoppers rising to 180–185 Mn from 160 Mn. But these estimates do not account for the higher cost that customers and sellers will have to pay for using the ecommerce platform. And that’s before we even account for the potential slowdown due to the merchant discount rate or MDR coming up in merchant UPI payments. The New Penalty Structure On August 17, months before its main festive season shopping window, Amazon changed how it charges cancellation fees for sellers on Easy Ship and Self Ship. Under Easy Ship, Amazon picks up the order from the seller and delivers it; under Self Ship, the seller delivers it through its own courier. The fee, earlier tied to flat category-based referral charges, is now a percentage of the order value, according to Amazon's communication to sellers. Amazon now charges 10% of the order value on orders up to ₹10,000, 8% between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, 5% between ₹50,001 and ₹1 lakh, and 2% above that, plus 18% GST. A cancelled ₹30,000 order can end up costing the seller about ₹2,832 including the GST which is applicable on cancellation fee. Sellers of electronics, appliances and other big-ticket goods carry the most exposure per order. "This fee is conditional and only applies in the rare event of a seller-initiated cancellation, which accounts for less than 1% of orders on Amazon.in. We have appropriate measures in place to ensure sellers are protected when cancellations are due to circumstances beyond their control," Amazon told Inc42 in an emailed statement. Electronics sellers are already under pressure due to expectations that the 2026 winter season will result in slower sales than 2025. This is largely due to the rising prices of mobile devices and electronics this year, but the extra charges will also play a role in whether sellers even offer some products for sale. Flipkart did not respond to Inc42's queries. People familiar with the company's operations said the penalties follow its zero-commission push, which has nearly doubled seller onboarding year-on-year. In July, Flipkart dropped commissions across its fashion catalogue, removing an earlier ₹1,000 price ceiling for the waiver. Whose Fault Is A Delay? The platforms' position is that penalties apply only when sellers fail. Sellers, however, claim the line is not always clear. Responding to Amazon's notices on its seller forum, some sellers said cancellations were sometimes caused by delivery personnel failing to turn up for scheduled pickups, and asked why the fee should apply in such cases. A founder of a snacking brand, who wished to be anonymous, told us when a logistics-side delay gets billed to the seller instead of the carrier, this becomes a source of friction and can disrupt many smaller sellers. “We have contested such cases with evidence of timely dispatch, but found the process cumbersome," the founder added. Kapil Gupta, founder of Ruhe India, whose catalogue runs from sub-₹500 to ₹3,000-plus, told Inc42 that Flipkart's flat ₹90 penalty would land hardest on the brand's value-tier catalogue. Vinod Kumar, trustee of the Forum for Internet Resellers, Sellers and Traders (FIRST INDIA), said online sellers accept the need for timely fulfilment, but the increase in fees and penalties just before the festive season is a concern for MSMEs already dealing with thin margins and rising costs this year. Unlike the penalties, these charges apply regardless of seller performance, which seems like a blanket rule meant to punish even those who have a very low proportion of cancellations or delays. Deliveries Turn Costlier Too What makes matters worse is that delivery fees and logistics costs have gone up across the industry, meaning no brand or seller is immune to this. From September 7, Amazon raised its closing fee, a flat per-item charge separate from the commission, by ₹1 on products priced up to ₹500 and by ₹3 or higher-priced items. Amazon's seller fee page attributes the increase to higher fuel and logistics costs. Similarly, Flipkart's logistics arm is mulling a revision in fulfillment fees for sellers, according to sources. Logistics platform Delhivery added a surcharge on D2C shipments of ₹4 per express shipment and ₹2 per surface shipment, on top of contracted rates from September 1,. The company has reportedly attributed it to higher aviation turbine fuel prices, ground-staff costs and inflation across its network. The new pricing structure affects a specific group: brands shipping orders from their own websites. Delhivery declined to comment to Inc42 related to queries on increase in the pricings. Ruhe India's Gupta said the surcharge would be a challenge for brands building native website sales, which rely on third-party logistics players such as Delhivery. Globus Fashion, which sells directly and through marketplace sellers, said that logistics or fulfillment costs "can be renegotiated between the brand and marketplace", but others say that this is not a standardised process. The fashion brand expects festive logistics spending to rise with demand, but does not expect a big impact on revenue, because inventory placement and warehouse use have already been allocated ahead of time. Large enterprises stock regional warehouses months in advance to lock in contracted freight rates and accept the holding costs. Other brands may not have these pieces in place. But, freight operators see more and more brands responding to the festive rush ahead of time. Geetali Sunil Khare, founder of Rachana Speed Logistics, said brands and wholesalers are building inventory ahead of the rush rather than cutting order sizes to protect margins, to avoid stockouts and supply disruptions at peak demand. In categories such as electronics and apparel, sellers need to retain minimal stock to avoid post-festive inventory risk, and absorb higher, fragmented spot freight costs instead. Truck rental rates in September held above year-ago levels, but month-on-month increases across most corridors have been relatively modest, Khare added. The bigger festive challenge, she said, is meeting tighter service expectations with higher shipment volumes and heavier consignments. “On the logistics side it is mostly the truck movement to warehouses that makes up for substantial expenses operation wise. With the deliveries now expanding to regional markets , it makes it harder to to fill vehicles on the way out and leaving return legs empty or under-used,” Aman Mahlawat, founder of Mahlawat Logistics, added. On local runs, Mahlawat said, highway transit is smooth, but city entry restrictions and long queues at distribution hub docks cause major delays. Quick commerce, according to the industry players we spoke to, has also added to the cost-strain. High-frequency replenishment of dark store inventory is changing how stock moves upstream from warehouses to the distribution endpoints. Mahlawat said dark stores and retailers now prefer frequent, smaller drops to monthly bulk dispatches, which splits loads into smaller vehicles and leaves trucks spending more hours waiting at congested unloading docks than moving on the road. These frequent, fragmented dispatches need constant vehicle availability, squeezing truck turnaround times and load consolidation. "More predictability, enough lead time on fee and policy changes to plan for them, rather than absorbing them mid-season is the only way sellers or brands can work around these changes,” Ruhe India's Gupta added.’ Can Commission Cuts Offset Rising Costs? While Flipkart, Amazon India and others have cut commissions for sellers this year, the rising logistics costs, the extra charges this year, and the growing dependency on advertising spending on marketplaces have eaten into the margins of sellers. Amazon waived referral fees on products under ₹1,000 in March, and Flipkart extended zero commission to all fashion categories in July. Those cuts cover specific categories and price bands while closing fees, shipping charges and penalties apply across categories Sellers are bemoaning the lack of clarity on when new charges are introduced or why they are applicable to all sellers regardless of their past performance. What sellers are asking for is more predictability from marketplaces and platforms, especially around the peak festive season.

Healthtech startup Cent, launched by Practo cofounder Shashank ND earlier this year, announced the raise of $15 Mn (about ₹143 Cr) in a Series A round led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons (SPC), with participation from individual investors including former Vodafone CEO Arun Sarin and former OpenAI B2B CTO Srinivas Narayanan, among others. The fresh capital will be deployed to strengthen the preventive healthcare startup’s R&D function. Besides, the startup also intends to expand its AI, engineering and clinical teams. Apart from the fundraise, Cent also announced the acquisition of Medsee, an AI-powered radiology reporting workflow platform, to help it deliver faster and more consistent reporting as scan volumes increase. Cent was launched by Shashank, along with ex-Ola Electric CMO Anshul Khandelwal and former Lenskart product head Arpit Garg earlier this year. It last raised a $5 Mn seed funding round back then from OneFlow Holdings and South Park Commons. Bidding to build a positioning of helping users live a hundred years, Cent combines precision radiology, AI, and biomarkers to screen asymptomatic patients for over 300 conditions like cardiac disease, cancer, and neurological disorders. Its flagship offering, Cent Check, combines full-body MRI, low-dose CT, DEXA scans, ECG, echocardiography in a single visit lasting around two hours. Its proprietary CCNM protocol is designed to assess cancer, cardiac, neurological and metabolic health risks. It uses AI to consolidate findings from different diagnostic modalities and generate organ-level risk assessments, while AI-assisted imaging helps reduce MRI scan times, with an aim to identify serious conditions before symptoms begin to surface. Its comprehensive health screening package is priced at ₹27,500, positioning itself as an alternative to conventional preventive health checkups that largely rely on blood tests and limited imaging. The startup said it has completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi NCR since inception. It aims to scale this to 1 Cr scans by 2035. Cent plans to use the data generated through its scans to establish health baselines for asymptomatic Indians, train models to identify disease risks earlier and support clinical research.

On Monday, Microsoft said it will offer voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees, or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout.
Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company’s employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels.fyi, levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected “based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs.”
The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. In July, the Xbox division laid off 3,200 employees, or about 20 percent of its entire gaming division. As reported by CNBC, about 30 percent of eligible employees accepted the retirement offer, lessening the impact of the planned layoffs, according to Coleman. While the offer in April went out to long-tenured employees who might be nearing the end of their career, the VEO expands the effort to a much larger potential pool.

- Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6 adds Snow Bricks that can be crafted using 4 Snow Blocks, and they can produce slab, stair, and wall variants.
- There's a new Cold Sulfur Cube archetype that can be obtained when the Cube absorbs a Blue Ice block.
- With the Cold Sulfur Cube archetype active, the mob creates Frosted Ice beneath itself while moving across water in specific conditions.
The Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6 is out with new building blocks and a frosty addition to the Sulfur Cube family. Snow Bricks are the new decorative blocks alongside the Cold Sulfur Cube archetype that makes the mob capable of creating frosted ice as it moves across water. In addition to that, there are several gameplay tweaks and technical improvements for the upcoming Minecraft 26.4 winter update.
Minecraft Gets a New Set of Snow Brick Building Blocks
One of the biggest highlights of Snapshot 6 is the addition of Snow Bricks that give builders another option to create their best house ideas in Minecraft.
Crafting the Snow Bricks is quite easy and similar to the recipe for Packed Ice Bricks in Minecraft. Open up your Crafting Table UI and place 4 Snow Blocks arranged in a 2×2 pattern to get the Snow Bricks in the output slot.
However, unlike other building blocks and bricks, there’s no use of a Minecraft Stonecutter in crafting or shaping the variants of a Snow Brick block. If you want to create Snow Brick Slabs, Stairs, and Walls, you must use the same Crafting Table again.
Furthermore, you must also use a shovel to mine the Snow Bricks if you want to collect and place them elsewhere. Coming to the aspect of Minecraft Sulfur Cube archetypes, you can feed them a Snow Brick to get the Fast Sliding hockey puck type.
Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6 Introduces a New Cold Sulfur Cube Archetype
The second major addition to the Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6 is the special Cold Sulfur Cube Archetype. To get this, a Minecraft Sulfur Cube must absorb a Blue Ice Block, or you could simply feed it as well.
The Cold Sulfur Cube archetype shares the same properties as the Fast Sliding variant, with the only difference that the Cube floats on water and replaces it with a disk of Frosted Ice.
Well, the trick may look similar to the Frost Walker armor enchantment in Minecraft, but it only works if the Sulfur Cube begins moving from the ground. Moreover, there must be air blocks present above the water surface for the Frosted Ice to appear.
The rest of the changes in the Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6 include smaller adjustments, such as the Packed Ice Brick variants must now be mined using a pickaxe to drop themselves. The Brittle Ice blocks in Minecraft no longer break when a Stray stands on them. And the Ice Crystals occasionally produce ambient sounds when a Packed Ice block sits beneath them.
The game’s default JVM options are also updated, and Minecraft will now automatically allocate Java heap memory based on the system’s available RAM. It will use up to 25% of it and cap at 4GB.
That’s pretty much it for the changes brought about in the new Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 6. So, are you enjoying the Minecraft Ice Caves biomes and having fun with the Frostbite zombie mob? Tell us in the comments below.

Saudi Arabia has reportedly offered $1 billion to Yemen's Houthi group under an Iran-brokered arrangement aimed at securing a ceasefire and stopping attacks on the kingdom, Israeli media reported, citing diplomatic sources in the Gulf.
According to the reports, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman travelled to Tehran for talks on a possible ceasefire with the Houthis. The proposed arrangement reportedly involved transferring $1 billion to the group through Iran.
One diplomatic source claimed that the Saudi minister had even brought the money to Tehran aboard the Hercules military transport aircraft he arrived in. However, a Saudi official did not confirm that any money had been transferred, the reports said.
The talks reportedly brought together Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's army chief 
Asim Munir
, alongside Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary General Mohsen Rezaei and senior officials from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
According to the reports, Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis amid escalating attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, which have caused economic damage to the kingdom. 
Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have also disrupted oil exports from the Gulf, adding to regional instability.
The Saudi foreign ministry addressed the visit in an official statement, saying, "The visit to Tehran by Prince Khalid bin Salman, the defence minister, and representatives of the member states of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance comes as part of the 'Nato-style' alliance's ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan."
A Saudi official, speaking to Israeli media, did not confirm the reported financial transfer but said that part of the dispute with the Houthis centred on the implementation of understandings reached three years ago.
Under those understandings, Saudi Arabia was to provide direct financial assistance to the Houthis as part of efforts to reach a settlement. The funding was intended, among other purposes, to pay public-sector salaries in areas under Houthi control and rebuild civilian infrastructure. In return, the group was expected to maintain the ceasefire and stop attacks on Saudi Arabia, the reports said.
In recent months, the Houthis have sought to justify their "attacks" by alleging that Saudi Arabia reneged on the earlier understandings.
However, the Saudi position reportedly remains that the kingdom will not agree to a new ceasefire under "military blackmail". Israeli media reported that Riyadh also opposed transferring funds to the Houthis before they returned territory seized from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which Saudi Arabia backs.
The reported negotiations come amid wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Tehran has sought to strengthen its regional influence while promoting a security framework led by regional powers.
According to Israeli media, the Tehran meeting also marked the first official meeting between representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance and the Iranian leadership. The initiative reportedly took shape during the Pakistani army chief's visit to Tehran the previous week.
The reports said Iran was seeking to position itself as a regional diplomatic mediator while opposing US or Israeli military intervention in the region.
The reported $1 billion proposal, including the claim that the money was brought to Tehran aboard the Saudi minister's aircraft, has not been independently confirmed.

I understand the appeal of foldable phones—they let manufacturers keep expanding screen sizes while still producing devices that can reasonably fit in a pocket. In practice, though, every foldable Android phone I’ve seen in public has had a ridiculously visible seam between the two halves of the screen, often with what looks like delamination from the underlying surface, giving the display an ugly, bubbly appearance.
Back when Android phones began shipping with bigger and bigger screens and the iPhone was stuck at a miserly four inches, I was jealous. But I’ve never looked at anyone using a chunky, fragile-looking foldable phone in public and pined for Apple’s take on the idea.
Nevertheless, that take has arrived, in the form of the iPhone Duo. This $1,999-and-up foldable is the biggest change to the iPhone in years, with both hardware and software updates that dramatically change how you interact with the device.
Like most Apple products, it looks and feels solid, and Apple has managed to engineer its way around at least some of the problems that have bedeviled other foldables (in particular, it has wrangled the between-screen crease so close to invisibility that I rarely thought about it while using the phone unfolded).
But like most first-generation Apple products, it has some odd rough edges and costs more than most people will want to spend. Some aspects of its design feel like steps backward from the standard iPhone design, as exemplified by the current iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro.
The result is something that is technically impressive but not always enjoyable to use. As a little iPad, it’s surprisingly good. As an iPhone, though, I struggle to think of a single way I prefer it to a regular old iPhone.

The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone I’ve used in a long time that comes with a learning curve. It’s the first time since 2018’s iPhone X that a hardware update has fundamentally changed how you interact with the software.
For the first day or two, I found this pretty off-putting. I kept losing track of the iPad-style button-mounted Touch ID sensor and flipping the phone around with the camera upside down. When fully opened, the phone acts like an iPad: It’s orientation-agnostic, and it will work in portrait or landscape, regardless of which end is up. But in its folded one-handed mode, the Duo still has a right-side-up and an upside-down just like any iPhone, and it took a couple of days of retraining my muscle memory before I was consistently pulling it out of my pocket and looking at it the right way without thinking about it.
When folded up, the iPhone Duo has a more compact footprint than Apple’s other phones and a screen that’s both shorter and wider. The titanium frame looks and feels a lot like last year’s iPhone Air, which plenty of people (us included) pegged as a half-step toward a foldable design. The outer screen looks and feels like a typical glassy iPhone screen, and the “back” of the phone where the camera is (the only quadrant of the phone that isn’t a screen) uses familiar-looking and -feeling Ceramic Shield glass.
Despite having a familiar-looking camera cutout and Dynamic Island on the front screen, the Duo totally lacks a Face ID scanner, which is a pretty big behavioral change following years of face-scanning phones. The Touch ID button has been migrated to the power button, iPad-style, which is in the upper-right corner of the phone when it’s folded (when unfolded, the positioning depends on which direction is “up” because the phone flips its screen orientation no matter which way you’re holding it).
The outer screen of the iPhone Duo has a camera pinhole and Dynamic Island but no Face ID.

In general, the Duo’s button positioning is strange. The power button’s position is… fine. It’s the only placement that makes Touch ID authentication even remotely possible with one hand, even though I felt like I was about to drop the phone every time I tried. But the volume buttons are on the top of the phone in this mode. The left button is volume down and the right button is volume up in this orientation, like on a landscape iPad, even though the volume indicator itself is a tiny bar that lives in the Dynamic Island and travels up and down vertically.
The Duo’s other physical button is the Camera Control button. I would vastly prefer it be a customizable Action Button, which I use constantly on my iPhone 17 Pro. For a phone with this many acres of edge, it feels like the Action Button should have room to exist somewhere, but it doesn’t.
That shorter, wider screen leads to the biggest and most noticeable of the iPhone Duo’s software design changes, at least in folded-phone mode: Your dock moves to the right edge of the screen, and that’s where most app controls move, too. Controls for apps that normally appear on the top or the bottom of the screen are now generally relocated to the right side of the screen, which is still something I’m still getting used to, even after nearly a week of daily use.
These side-mounted controls feel like they’re swimming upstream against almost two decades of smartphone app design—and they don’t even really solve the “lack of vertical space” problem because as soon as the iOS keyboard pops up, the viewable area still shrinks to just a few lines of text.
This right-hand navigation area also feels weirdly underutilized, given the percentage of the front screen it takes up. Your dock is there, but Apple still limits it to four icons, leaving a ton of unused space above and below it. The nav area feels too wide, with too much negative space.
In the end, I only really liked the Duo in folded-down phone mode when it was sitting on a desk, couch, or table next to my laptop, serving as a separate compact notification screen—in other words, when I was not actively holding or touching it. And this isn’t something no other phone can do; it’s just a regular phone thing that the Duo doesn’t make worse.

While folded, the Duo is fundamentally designed for right-handed use. Controls throughout iOS and Duo-optimized apps have been scooted to the screen’s right edge to make up for the loss of vertical screen area. The screen is wide enough that any attempt by lefties to reach across with their thumbs to tab that part of the screen will be difficult to impossible, and I say this as someone with fairly large hands.
The Touch ID sensor—integrated, iPad-style, into the phone’s long, flat power button—is also mounted on the right side. Even if iOS did flip around the other way when you hold the Duo with the rounded edge on the left (and it doesn’t, to be clear), the camera would then be on the bottom of the phone, blocked by your fingers.
But even as a right-hander, I don’t find the Duo to be especially comfortable to use one-handed. Sure, I can reach everything, but the phone is so heavy and thick that the standard “rest the phone on my pinkie and use it with my thumb” move is fatiguing. A left-handed friend who held and tested the Duo found it extremely uncomfortable, particularly the stretch you need to do to hit any app icon in the side-mounted dock.

As frustrating as the Duo is when it’s folded, I genuinely enjoy it when it’s unfolded. Think of an iPad Nano, and you’ll be pretty close to what the experience is.
To answer the biggest question first: Yes, you can see and feel the seam between the screens if you’re looking for it. But most of the time, if you’re just holding it and watching video or reading a webpage and using a thumb to scroll in the corner of the screen, you just don’t notice it. Apple has gotten very close to making it invisible.
Frankly, I’m much more bothered by the under-screen camera, which is visible pretty much constantly. The seam is visible from some angles if you go looking for them. The under-screen camera pinhole is only invisible from some angles if you go looking for it. It’s out of the way enough not to be experience-ruining, but I did find it distracting, and I don’t know that I find it to be a net improvement over the actual-pinhole-with-Dynamic-Island solution that Apple has used for the last few iPhone generations.
When unfolded, the Duo’s screen expands from a squat 5.4 inches to a more comfortable 7.6 inches, which isn’t so far off from the new iPad mini’s 8.5-inch screen. The dock is still limited to four app icons, like a regular iPhone, but it moves back to a familiar place at the bottom of the screen, and apps have more room to breathe.
In landscape, apps usually retain the same side-mounted controls you see on the phone’s front screen, but when you pivot to portrait mode, they revert to more familiar positioning at the top and bottom of the screen—portrait mode looks pretty much like an iPad, while landscape mode looks more like a pair of iPhone home screens next to each other (more on that in a minute).
The inner screen has a matte nano-texture finish, which shares a name with the technology used in some Macs and iPads. But Apple says that both the materials used and the actual nano-texture pattern are both different, changes that were necessitated by the fact that this is a foldable phone and not an inert glass slab. A slightly raised rim around the edge of the screen keeps it from resting directly on a table or desk and leaves room for tiny bits of dust or crud to get trapped without grinding into the screen. If the inner screen does get damaged, this cover layer can apparently be removed and replaced without too much trouble.

To enter split-screen multitasking, open an app and swipe up from the bottom of the screen, then drag the window to the areas that appear on the left and right of the screen. Once you’ve anchored an app in this way, the unused half of the screen simply becomes a standard iPhone home screen, with all your icons, widgets, and the side-mounted dock (which can appear on the left side of the screen when the phone is unfolded).
Launch another app from that home screen, and it will take up the other half of the screen. Both apps can be used and dismissed independently, as though you were using two separate iPhones next to each other; you can even launch the same app twice if you really want to.
The center of the screen, where the fold is, is mostly treated as a dead zone by default, but drag it one way or the other to resize one of the apps to full screen, and tap the divider to lock two apps together so they always appear and are dismissed in tandem. If you close the phone’s screen, what you were doing on the right half of the inner screen is preserved on the outer screen, giving the transition a seamless feel.
The hardware’s design makes sense when you look at multitasking mode. Half of an unfolded iPhone Duo is exactly the same as using the iPhone Duo in its folded-down phone mode. The side-nav is pinned to the left side of the screen instead of the right side, but it otherwise feels very similar to having a pair of iPhones you can use in tandem (I would say “two iPhones for the price of one,” but that doesn’t work when the base Duo model is even more expensive than buying two regular iPhones).
Third-party apps need to be updated in one way or another to support the Duo, with baseline support granted at least partly for “free” to apps that target the Xcode 27.1 SDK. Apps that haven’t been updated look mostly OK on the outer screen, since its strip of usable space is roughly the same width as a regular iPhone. Apps that haven’t been updated look like iPhone apps running on an iPad when the screen is unfolded, though: little phone-sized windows with black borders all around, with an option to expand them so they take up the entire screen.
I’ve been surprised how many apps have added Duo support in the few days since the device came out, given that Apple didn’t even make these tools available to developers until just a few weeks ago. But early adopters will run into tons of apps that don’t know what to make of the Duo’s larger inner screen, and I suspect it will be a while before you can assume that any given app will work properly on it.
The iPhone Duo in between

The Duo can be a phone. The Duo can be a tablet. But it also supports several liminal states that exist somewhere in between the two (nomenclature mine):
A “tent mode,” where the phone functions as its own stand and the outer screen shifts to one of several dedicated StandBy views.
A sort of “bent tablet” mode, where content scoots away from the middle of the screen and treats the hinge area as a dead zone.
A “laptop/clamshell” mode, with one half of the inner screen lying flat on a table and the other half sticking up. The device’s hinge will hold its position at almost any angle rather than opening to a few specific hinge points, so how you use it and the angle you choose is pretty much up to you.
Not all apps that support the Duo do different things in every one of its modes, but apps can treat them all as their own unique views if they want to. (I asked a developer from the New York Times Cooking team at an Apple-hosted developer showcase how many distinct views they needed to support to cover every possible position that an app can appear in on the Duo. “Seven. It’s seven,” he replied without hesitation.)

But we’ve already seen a few examples of developers doing things that wouldn’t be at home on a regular iPhone or an iPad. The Headroom app uses a remote desktop connection to connect to a remote Mac and simulate a tiny MacBook; the Delta emulator app has been updated with a Nintendo DS mode; and the Tiny Computers app will change it into arguably copyright-safe facsimiles of distinctive classic computers. I can’t vouch for the quality of any of these apps, and Headroom and Tiny Computers in particular have a distinct air of “quickly vibe-coded to catch the wave of early adopter interest” to them. But the ideas are interesting, and they wouldn’t work as well on different hardware.
About those cases
The iPhone Duo Folio case and its kickstand.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo Folio case and its kickstand.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
Along with the review unit, Apple included a $79 iPhone Duo Case and a $129 iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand. The case provides a basic level of protection without really changing anything about how the Duo works (though the fact that it sticks to the phone using adhesive raises concerns about its longevity).
The Folio is more interesting. It attaches with magnets, and it has a retractable strip between its two halves that stretches to cover the hinge when the phone is folded and retreats into the case when it’s opened. The kickstand that props the phone up in tablet mode is genuinely useful; in phone mode, it solves one problem while creating another.
Here’s the problem it solves: By default, if you’re using the Duo in tablet mode and you fold it closed, the phone transitions your current app to the outer screen rather than putting the phone to sleep. Flipping the Folio cover open and closed does put the phone to sleep and wake it up. It makes the question of “is my phone awake or isn’t it” easier to answer.
The problem it creates is that this cover is opaque, and when you fold it around to the back of the phone, it covers both the camera and the flashlight. These are two things I regularly need fast access to when I pull my phone out of my pocket, and the Folio case asks you to leave the cover flopping around, remove the case temporarily, or snap the phone open into tablet mode instead of using it in phone mode.
Internals and performance
The chip and the camera in the iPhone Duo are way less interesting than the brand-new hardware and software changes, so apologies if this section feels like an afterthought. But it kind of is.
The Apple A20 Pro is Apple’s first 2 nm phone chip, and its second 2 nm chip overall after the M6 that debuted in the new Mac mini. It still uses two large CPU cores and four efficiency cores, the same as the last few generations of A-series chips, but it’s the first phone chip to include “super” cores instead of performance cores. Unlike the M6, which ships all three kinds of cores, the A20 Pro just uses super and efficiency cores.
The A20 Pro does ship with 7 GPU cores, up from the 5-6 cores in the A19 Pro, plus Apple’s upgraded 32-core Neural Engine (Apple usually refers to this as a “dual Neural Engine” with 16 cores each). The A20 Pro still includes 12GB of RAM, the same as the A19 Pro (both upgraded from the 8GB of RAM in the A18 Pro—either chip would be a solid upgrade option for a future MacBook Neo).
In the benchmarks I ran, Apple’s performance promises for the A20 Pro end up in the ballpark of the figures Apple has published: around 20 to 30 percent better single- and multi-core CPU performance compared to A19 Pro, and between 40 and 50 percent faster GPU performance (the 73 percent performance improvement for the 3DMark Wild Life Extreme test is an outlier). If you own any iPhone made within the last three or four years, the chip isn’t the reason to buy the phone, but it’s a respectable upgrade.
Cameras
The iPhone Duo’s camera system is roughly equivalent to the one in the basic iPhone, not the Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo’s camera system is roughly equivalent to the one in the basic iPhone, not the Pro.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The Duo’s camera system is fine. Like the iPhone Air, this hardware is priced well into iPhone Pro territory while lacking the camera system that makes the Pro my default iPhone choice.
The Duo uses the same basic camera configuration as the basic iPhone. It has one 48 MP main sensor and one 48 MP ultrawide sensor, both of which enable a 2x optical zoom feature by cropping a 12 MP patch out of the middle. (Apple’s tech specs page also claims that the ultrawide lens can zoom out by 2x, giving it a “4x optical-quality zoom range,” which feels hand-wavy even if you accept “optical-quality zoom” as an accurate description of what Apple’s cameras are doing).
What keeps me away from the standard iPhone these days is that I find the ultrawide lens to be by far the least useful one Apple ships and the telephoto lens to be the most useful. The Duo’s camera asks you to make the same kind of downgrade from a Pro iPhone, though it at least improves on the one-camera setups Apple ships in the iPhone 17e and iPhone Air.
Once you get past the lack of a telephoto lens, the Duo’s camera system is perfectly competent. Apple’s year-to-year camera quality improvements generally happen around the margins—a little less noise here, a little better low-light performance there—and that’s what I observed while comparing it to my iPhone 17 Pro. To my eye, the differences between the 17 Pro and Duo in good lighting were minimal, but the Duo did capture marginally better detail in low light (see the cat pictures). Of course, when you try comparing the Duo’s digitally zoomed 4x and 8x photos to the 17 Pro’s telephoto lens, there’s zero contest.

The front cameras, like Face ID, are another casualty of the Duo’s design changes. There are technically two front-facing cameras: a typical-ish pinhole cutout on the front of the outer screen and the one hidden underneath the inner screen (as we discussed before, “hidden” is generous; the camera is almost always visible underneath whatever you’re looking at).
The outer camera is lower-resolution than most other iPhones (12 MP, down from 18 MP), but it’s in the ballpark when you’re on a FaceTime call or taking a selfie. The under-screen inner camera is noticeably worse, capturing noisier video and photos that look excessively digitally sharpened to try to cover for its reduced quality and lack of detail. Apple doesn’t list a resolution for the inner camera, but its 2432 x 1824 resolution works out to around 4.4 megapixels, just one-third the resolution of the outer camera.
That the inner camera is so much worse than the outer camera is made even more obvious by the fact that the inner screen is twice as large; when you fire up a FaceTime call, you’re looking at a lower-resolution image on a larger screen. This isn’t a dealbreaker; the bi-directional FaceTime call that shows the person on the other end of the line on both the outer and inner screens remains genuinely cool, even with the potato-esque quality of the inner camera. But it’s yet another place where the core/traditional iPhone experience is degraded to make room for the Duo’s hero features.
Wrapping folding things up
The iPhone Duo.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
The iPhone Duo.
Credit:
Andrew Cunningham
In some ways, foldable phones remind me of the PC industry’s push toward convertible tablet PCs in the early 2010s. In the wake of Apple’s original iPad, Microsoft and its partners clearly thought that they had to figure out tablets or get left behind, but even the designs with staying power (mainly Microsoft’s Surface and Lenovo’s Yoga) aren’t as good at being laptops as a purpose-built laptop or as good at being tablets as a purpose-built tablet.
For me, the iPhone Duo straddles a similar line between the iPhone and the iPad. As a regular one-handed iPhone, it feels deeply compromised—too thick and heavy to comfortably hold in one hand for long, no Face ID, no action button, and power/volume/camera button positioning that feels like it was dictated by “where the buttons can physically fit on the phone” rather than ergonomics. It costs nearly twice as much as the iPhone Pro but has an inferior camera system.
I do really like the Duo as a Kindle-sized iPad. But if that’s what I want, I can buy something like it for less money without saddling myself with a regular phone I don’t particularly like using.
I see the promise of the Duo. It feels well-built—some users have had problems with screen breakage, but it’s not something we ran into. Its hardware and software are cleverly designed. It mostly solves the visible-seam problem that most Android foldables come with. An updated version of the Duo with Face ID support would be just about the best possible version of this form factor, given the limits of battery technology and physics. But for me personally—and for many happy iPhone users—it requires too many compromises to enable features I don’t want badly enough.
The good
A premium look and feel with a satisfying hinge. We didn’t encounter any issues with screen breakage.
Seam between screens is functionally invisible most of the time, a big step up from most other foldables.
Thoughtfully designed multitasking.
Comfortable to hold and use when unfolded.
Apps are being updated to support it reasonably quickly.
Characteristically competent camera system.
Characteristically excellent performance, thanks to the Apple A20 Pro chip.
The bad
$2,000 entry price. That’s more than a pair of iPhone 17s and the same price as the cheapest MacBook Pro.
Outer screen feels cramped.
Camera system isn’t as good as the iPhone Pro’s.
Visible pinhole camera on the inner screen is sometimes distracting.
Matte finish on inner screen shows smudges and makes black levels look less black.
Tacked-on Apple Pencil support.
Fundamentally right-aligned in a way that may be frustrating for lefties.
The ugly
The lack of Face ID and the awkward positioning of the Touch ID button is a small speed bump, but it’s one you’ll hit nearly every time you interact with the phone.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

In its latest gift to oil and gas companies, the Trump administration is expected to announce plans today to weaken rules that guard against methane leaks.
Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
The Environmental Protection Agency is lowering standards meant to keep methane from leaking from oil and gas infrastructure.
Methane is a smog-forming pollutant and a powerful greenhouse gas that’s up to 80 times as potent as carbon dioxide on a 20-year horizon. It’s the primary component of what the fossil fuel industry calls “natural gas” that routinely leaks from oil and gas wells and pipelines.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reversing course on its previous efforts to plug those leaks. As part of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory agenda, the EPA plans to undo Biden-era rules that were expected to cut methane emissions by 80 percent over 14 years.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming
The EPA teased the rule change earlier this month, saying in a press release that it was “days away” from making the proposal. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin says the rollbacks will save oil and gas companies $45 billion, while the previous rules would have incurred $18 billion in regulatory costs.
“This proposal takes on many of the problems American [oil and gas] producers and operators have raised with us,” Zeldin said in the October 7th press release. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.”
The agency is expected to step back standards for so-called “marginal wells” — old wells that produce little fuel but create an outsize amount of methane pollution from leaks. These wells are responsible for half of the industry’s methane emissions despite only producing 6 percent of US oil and gas, ProPublica reports. The EPA is also expected to end the Super Emitter Program that notified oil and gas infrastructure operators of large releases of methane reaching 100 kilograms per hour or more.
Trump plans to make the announcement from a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, today, Bloomberg reports. Not only is Texas the top oil- and gas-producing state in the US, it’s also the world’s biggest data center market. With more data center capacity under construction than any other state, Texas has become emblematic of the challenges energy-intensive AI models pose. In just five years, data centers could undo decades of air quality improvements in Texas, according to a recent report by the Houston Advanced Research Center.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming so far. But unlike carbon dioxide, which can linger in the atmosphere for hundreds or thousands of years, methane dissipates in a little over a decade. That makes eliminating methane emissions, particularly from unintentional leaks, one of the fastest and most straightforward ways to stop global temperatures from rising.
The EPA’s rollbacks quickly triggered furor from health and environmental advocates. “Any proposed rollback to the federal methane rule is a slap in the face to families who are exposed to oil and gas pollution where they live, work, and play,” Celerah Hewes, a senior manager for state field campaigns at Moms Clean Air Force, said in an email ahead of the expected announcement. “For over a decade, [our group] has been fighting for methane protections for our families—and we were making progress. Today’s announcement from EPA is a massive blow to the efforts to safeguard our children’s health and our climate.”
The Biden-era methane rules were estimated to bring in up to $98 billion in benefits by reducing climate risks and health costs from air pollution, even after factoring in the costs of compliance. Plugging leaks was supposed to lead to up to $13 billion worth of recovered natural gas.

Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.
Let’s start with iOS 27.2. This update is heavily focused on Siri AI. It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you. It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.
On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).
Other additions include context-aware suggestions within Messages (like turning a message inviting you to something into a calendar entry), SynthID watermarking support in Photos, and support for user profiles in the Apple TV app. There’s also the new Apple Music branding, plus the arrival of previously promised Apple Pencil support on the iPhone Duo foldable.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

Kerala passes bill aimed at protecting rights, dignity of senior citizens
Keralam becomes the first state in the country to adopt a comprehensive legislation for the protection and welfare of rights of senior citizens
The Keralam assembly on Monday unanimously passed a landmark legislation aimed at protecting the rights and dignity of elderly persons, shielding them from abuse and ensuring greater access to government and social services.
The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026 was passed by the House with the approval of both ruling and opposition MLAs with the government accepting the amendments moved by a few Left Democratic Front (LDF) legislators.
Keralam becomes the first state in the country to adopt a comprehensive legislation for the protection and welfare of rights of senior citizens.
“I view this bill as our first realisation of the reality that our world is changing. We must view with seriousness the changes taking place globally due to demographic shifts,” said VD Satheesan in the assembly during the discussion on the bill.

The CM stated that provisions guaranteeing the rights of senior citizens have not been included in past bills of similar nature passed by the state assembly or Parliament.
“This is a Special Act which will stand constitutionally. There is not a single provision in it that stands against the Central Act. Welfare is not the central tenet of this bill. Creating a silver economy is the principal aim. The population of senior citizens is rising as part of demographic changes. There are several schemes and projects in which they can play a key role. The goal is to enable them to provide leadership for it,” he added.
Home minister Ramesh Chennithala said numerous incidents of elderly persons being abandoned by family members at railway stations and other public places get reported regularly.
He spoke about the difficulties faced by elderly persons who remain in Keralam while their children live abroad.
“The state has today paved the way for a legislation that is extremely necessary,” said the home minister.
The consequential bill, moved earlier this month by the CM, had been sent to the expert subject committee for further discussions.
Also Read: Kerala Assembly unanimously approves state’s name change to ‘Keralam’
The bill states that the government will set up state-level and district-level senior citizen care protection units who will monitor schemes and policies for elderly persons, issue orders to redress complaints about senior citizen care centres and mobilise local organisations to carry out activities for the protection and care of senior citizens.
The bill fixes penalties for offences against senior citizens. A family member, legal heir or staff of a care centre causing physical or mental abuse or cruelty towards senior citizens can be imprisoned up to three years and fined ₹50,000. Those abandoning senior citizens without their consent can also be jailed up to three years and fined ₹50,000. The legislation also provides for mandatory registration of senior citizen care centres as well as training and certification of home caregivers.

Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.
Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities.
Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has cited investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year. Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure.
A “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before…creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.”
University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.
Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.
Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors. Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO. Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board.
Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run. For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious.
“Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.”
Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.
The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.
Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verge.
The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as reported by The San Francisco Standard.
All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge. “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.”
Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions.
“Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well. But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”
And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.
Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.
Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it. Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told The Verge. Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.
For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways. But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust. Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands. As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”

Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
- Published
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, their offices said. They said their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".
After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.
Tuesday's phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki.
"Finland and Norway border Russia," Stubb and Støre said. They said they had initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe".
"The war comes with enormous human and material costs," the Norwegian prime minister said. "The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
Tuesday's phone call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".
Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.
Stubb and Støre said they had taken the initiative to continue discussions held in the Norwegian capital on 20 October, after which Witkoff travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.
After the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.
After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on the upcoming trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi in November.
Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Vladimir Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue between her Nordic neighbours and Moscow.
"It hasn't been co-ordinated with any of the rest of us," she told Danish broadcaster DR.
Moscow regularly accuses European leaders of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.
While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.
“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.
The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.
Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”
The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.
Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”
You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”
Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.
Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.
