One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

The Calcutta High Court has ordered social media platforms, including YouTube, X and Meta-owned Instagram, to remove the 36-minute documentary, titled The Friendship Files: How Modi and Adani Stole India, and its specified reproductions. The court has also restrained Bhatia from disseminating the video, Bar and Bench reported. The interim injunction, issued by Justice Aryak Dutt, will remain in force until January 31, 2027, or until further orders. The case is expected to be heard again in January. Adani Enterprises alleged that the documentary contained false and defamatory claims and omitted material facts. The company told the court that the content had prompted inquiries from some investors. Bhatia, who is based in the US, has disputed the action against him. In a post on X, he said the lawsuit seeks ₹50 crore in damages and maintained that the documentary had struck a nerve. The dispute centres on the documentary The Friendship Files, which Bhatia uploaded on October 9 in collaboration with a channel called Shadow Citizens. The film uses archival footage to trace the relationship between Modi and Adani, both of whom hail from Gujarat. It also raises questions about Adani's successful bid for six airports in 2019 following a change in government rules. Critics have alleged that the change favoured the Adani Group, a charge similar to allegations raised by the opposition Congress party. The Adani Group has denied such allegations. The government has maintained that all regulations were followed and that there was no favouritism. In its legal challenge, Adani Enterprises argued that the documentary presented false allegations and created a narrative against the company by suppressing material facts. It also said its action was not intended to prevent legitimate criticism of government policy or business concentration. According to the court order, the company argued that the allegations had harmed its reputation and that continued circulation of the video could cause further damage. The court described the film as a dramatised narrative rather than a news report or an account of legal proceedings. "The impugned video is not a news report or an account of proceedings," the court said, according to Bar and Bench. Justice Aryak Dutt observed that allegations suggesting the Adani Group was complicit in, or shielded from accountability for, narcotics smuggling linked to terror funding or police violence against a farmer were not substantiated by any authority. The court also noted that the original video had already been disabled but was subsequently uploaded again by Bhatia. It said this prima facie indicated a lack of good faith. The court ordered the removal of the specified video, clips, excerpts and materially identical reproductions from the relevant accounts and platforms. It also directed social media platforms to disable access to the identified content and preserve relevant account and access records. However, the court clarified that its order does not prevent constructive criticism or fair reporting on the Adani Group or government policy, provided it is not disseminated through the disputed video, its reproductions or the specified defamatory statements. "Constructive criticism or truthful reporting on the petitioner or on Government policy, backed by evidence, is not barred. Online content spreads quickly through reposts and re-uploads, and the injury to reputation from continued republication cannot be adequately compensated in money. If the order is not passed now, its purpose will be defeated by further dissemination before the respondents [Bhatia and others] can be heard," the court said. The injunction is interim in nature. The court's observations at this stage do not amount to a final determination of the defamation allegations. Bhatia responded to the legal action through posts on X, challenging the damages sought by Adani Enterprises. On Tuesday, he wrote: “Adani is suing me for ₹50 crore, apparently valuing the damage to his reputation at that amount. I contend that wealth acquired through alleged wrongdoing does not confer credibility or reputation. My valuation of that reputation? ₹0. And if the reputational damage is zero, the compensation should be zero. ₹50 crore demanded. ₹0 deserved.” My valuation of that reputation? ₹0. ₹50 crore demanded. ₹0 deserved. In an earlier post, Bhatia wrote, "Truth is on my side". He also said: "I believe the documentary has rattled Adani Enterprises Limited and struck a nerve at the highest levels," he wrote. The company, meanwhile, has argued that the film contains false allegations and that its legal action is directed at the disputed content rather than legitimate criticism of its business or government policy. The documentary circulated across social media platforms and was shared by political opponents of Modi, who said it reflected allegations they had previously raised about the relationship between the prime minister and the industrialist, Reuters reported. Earlier, Maharashtra politician Raj Thackeray shared the film on his X account, where it garnered 4.8 million views, according to the Reuters report. He subsequently removed it, saying he had done so at the request of the Mumbai police commissioner. Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra also shared the documentary on October 11. On Monday night, she wrote on X: "I posted this on Oct 11th. It is still on my timeline so do watch it," she wrote on X on Monday night. Before the defamation suit, Maharashtra police issued a takedown notice to Bhatia on October 19, stating that the content "made serious unsubstantiated allegations". The interim order requires the specified content to be removed from the relevant platforms and prevents its further circulation by the respondents. The matter is expected to return to court on January 31, 2027, or as directed by the court. The case will examine the allegations made by Adani Enterprises and the responses of the defendants. The interim order does not constitute a final ruling on the merits of the defamation suit. The court has also made clear that its directions do not amount to a blanket ban on constructive criticism of the Adani Group or government policy, or on fair reporting supported by evidence. Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a morning briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.
Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.
“I'm kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.
Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.
“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. ”We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.
Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.
Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.
What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.
“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”
At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.
“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger-and-acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.
Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’s reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.
While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.
Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.
Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.
Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.
Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.
“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you're telling,” Shipper says. “And there's always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.
“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.
As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?
Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.
Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’s chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don't want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that's something that's already benefiting us.”
But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.
Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.
Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”
Murphy says that Axios’s starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.
“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn't the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn't really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It's AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”

Delhi Police has registered at least 40 First Information Reports (FIRs) in connection with the protests against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in the national capital since October 10, with teams analysing CCTV footage to identify those involved in the demonstrations, officials told The Hindu.
The cases have been registered under various charges, including violation of prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), vandalism and obstruction of public servants, among others. While the accused have not yet been named in these FIRs, the police are working to identify the protesters and those who “mobilised” them, officials said.
Police teams are examining CCTV footage as part of the investigations, and action will be initiated against those identified, officials said.
The FIRs were registered as protests continued over several days following a call by various youth outfits, including the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), on October 10, demanding the rollback of the SIR and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Demonstrations by student groups, youth organisations and women’s organisations followed, along with a rally by the INDIA bloc on October 12.
Officials said the police had been detaining protesters and registering cases on a daily basis for alleged violations during the demonstrations. Timely registration of FIRs was necessary to document the alleged offences and avoid delays that could be difficult to justify during court proceedings.
‘Car with sticks’
The police have also registered an FIR and arrested four occupants of a car allegedly seen carrying wooden sticks and batons near Connaught Place on October 11. The Uttar Pradesh-registered vehicle has been seized and remains in police custody.
The car triggered controversy after it was spotted near the protest site with a large number of wooden sticks inside. Journalists and protesters raised concerns about the vehicle, but police personnel initially allowed it to leave the area. The occupants were later seen near the demonstrations brandishing sticks and confronting protesters.
After videos of the incident circulated widely on social media, the Deputy Commissioner of Police (New Delhi) said on X that the vehicle had been taken to a police station for verification and that a search had found “nothing illegal or objectionable”. The occupants were also found to have no criminal records, the police had said.
However, the police have now registered an FIR and arrested the four occupants. Investigators said they are also identifying other people associated with the accused and involved in violence during the protests.
Separately, the Delhi Police have registered at least 10 FIRs after taking cognisance of social media posts alleging that right-wing activists assaulted protesters during the anti-SIR demonstrations. Investigations into those cases are under way.
Officials said the police had not received a call on the emergency helpline 112 regarding the alleged attacks on protesters. The police are also examining videos circulating on social media that purportedly show a vehicle carrying several khaki uniforms, along with footage of alleged assaults on demonstrators, to identify those involved and investigate the incidents.

British officials have begun discussions with the EU about a long-term relationship that could include a return to free movement, the business secretary has said while promising the British people “are the boss” when it comes to what the UK will accept.
Jonathan Reynolds said the focus for British negotiations was the EU summit in November to seal an agreement to ease some trading restrictions and a youth mobility deal. But he said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, had made it clear he wanted to see a long-term and stable relationship with the bloc.
“They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be. But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we’re going to make,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
He said the changes announced at the EU summit, including a food and drink deal and on emissions trading, would make a significant difference. But he added: “What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us, and we need to get as little uncertainty as possible.
“We need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be, and he is going to set that out after the summit. And he is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are.”
Reynolds said there had been “no assumptions made about the next stage after that. It’s the prime minister quite rightly saying he wants to set out to the British people what the options are to resolve some of the tensions that exist.”
He said no decision would be made without voters being given a say, without specifying whether this would be through a general election or a referendum. “No assumptions have been made on this. The British people are the people who will decide this. They’re the boss on this,” he said.
A number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.
The Labour MP for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes, Melanie Onn, was among those urging caution. “I am still not over the kind of very divisive debate that we had when we were leaving the EU post the referendum, and I don’t think that the scars have healed for many people around the country,” she told Today. “So I do think that this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the programme it would be “very, very poor indeed” to begin discussing freedom of movement. “Five months ago, Andy Burnham says to leave-voting Makerfield: ‘I’m not going to reopen these arguments.’ Two and a half years ago, a Labour government got a massive majority in parliament saying we will not be re-entering the single market, the customs union, or opening up the debate on the free movement of people,” he said.
“What I am saying is this: this prime minister has no mandate, and to hear that his officials are negotiating in Brussels already is really very, very poor indeed.”
Burnham made his plea for an “honest discussion” about freedom of movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.
Burnham also shared his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, if Labour put it in its manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.
The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

TL;DR: India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 monsoon, 12.6% below its long-period average. East and Northeast India recorded their lowest seasonal rainfall since 1901, while the South Peninsula received 24% less rain than normal. Although extremely heavy rainfall events rebounded to 388, southern reservoirs held 24.76 BCM against a ten-year average of 43.33 BCM. Historical records show repeated drought declarations in districts such as Ananthapuramu in Andhra Pradesh, while post-monsoon soil moisture remains below average in several states. Together, these indicators reveal an uneven monsoon impact and highlight areas requiring closer monitoring.
Context
India’s monsoon tells two stories this year. The country received 12.6% less rainfall than normal between June and September 2026, but the shortfall was far from uniform. Eastern and northeastern India received 26% less rain than average, while the southern peninsula recorded a 24% deficit.
The season began on a difficult note, with June rainfall nearly 40% below normal. July brought a brief recovery, with rainfall slightly above average, but the deficit returned in August and September. The rebound, in other words, did not erase the shortfall.
What does this mean for the land and the people who depend on the rain? The IMD had warned of a below-normal monsoon in May, when El Niño conditions were expected to develop. But the national rainfall deficit is only the starting point. To understand where drought risks are emerging, it is necessary to look beyond how much rain fell to where it fell, how long the dry spells lasted, and how much moisture remained in the soil.
Who compiles this data?
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) publishes rainfall data and monsoon forecasts, while the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (NCFC) monitors agricultural conditions using rainfall, soil moisture and satellite indicators. The India Drought Monitor, developed by IIT Gandhinagar’s Water and Climate Lab, tracks drought conditions using meteorological and satellite data.
Where can I download clean & structured data related to this?
Clean, structured datasets related to Indian rainfall, drought conditions, agriculture and water resources are available on Dataful.
Key Insights
India’s 2026 monsoon ranks among the weakest in decades, with sharp regional deficits
India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 southwest monsoon, just 87% of its long-period average (LPA). According to the IMD, this was the country’s fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901. The national shortfall, however, conceals sharper regional deficits.
East and Northeast India received 1,016.3 mm, or 74% of its regional LPA, making it the lowest seasonal rainfall for the region since 1901. The South Peninsula received 542 mm, or 76% of its LPA, ranking fourth-lowest since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001. Northwest India received 94.1% of its LPA, while Central India recorded 97%, within the normal range.
The shortfall also affected the monsoon core zone, which includes much of India’s rain-fed agricultural area. It received 779.9 mm, which is below the lower limit of the normal category (782.8 to 881.2). Across India’s 36 meteorological subdivisions, 17 (42% of the area) recorded deficient rainfall, 18 (53%) received normal rainfall, and one, in Odisha (5%), recorded excess rainfall. At the district level, 282 of 741 meteorological districts (38% of total area) recorded below-normal rainfall, while 34 (5% of total area) received significantly below-normal rainfall. Another 312 districts (42% of total area) recorded normal rainfall, 90 (12% of total area) received excess rainfall, and 16 (2% of total area) recorded substantially above-normal rainfall.
Extremely heavy rainfall events rebound in 2026, driven by a July spike
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies rainfall of 115.6–204.4 mm in 24 hours as very heavy and rainfall exceeding 204.4 mm as extremely heavy. During the June–September 2026 monsoon, India recorded 1,765 very heavy rainfall events and 388 extremely heavy events. Extremely heavy events rose from 296 in 2022 to 426 in 2023 and peaked at 473 in 2024, before declining to 303 in 2025 and increasing again in 2026. Very heavy rainfall events followed a different trend, rising from 1,875 in 2022 to a peak of 2,632 in 2024, before falling to 2,109 in 2025 and 1,765 in 2026. July 2026 alone recorded 269 extremely heavy events, the highest July count in since 2022, compared with 84 in 2025. These figures show that although the overall frequency of very heavy rainfall has declined since 2024, extremely heavy events rebounded in 2026.
Historical El Niño years show a recurring concern, but widely varying rainfall outcomes
Historical data in the IMD’s El Niño table show why the phenomenon matters when assessing India’s 2026 monsoon, but also why it cannot explain the season’s outcome on its own. Of the 17 El Niño years listed between 1951 and 2023, 12 recorded below-normal June–September rainfall, including seven with deficits exceeding 10%. Yet outcomes varied considerably: rainfall was 22.3% below normal in 1972 and 20.9% below normal in 2002, while 1994 recorded a 13.9% surplus and 1997 ended almost exactly at normal, despite being the only Strong El Niño among all.
Monthly figures reveal another important distinction. In 2002, July rainfall was 50.6% below normal, contributing to a seasonal deficit of 20.9%. In 2023, above-normal rainfall in July and September partly offset August’s 36.1% shortfall, leaving the season 5.3% below normal. A seasonal total can therefore conceal sharp monthly swings, just as a national average can mask regional rainfall deficits.
That distinction is relevant to the 2026 monsoon. India received 759.4 mm of rainfall, or 87% of its long-period average, with particularly large deficits in East and Northeast India and the South Peninsula. IMD reported that El Niño strengthened during the season, but the historical comparisons do not establish how much it contributed to this year’s shortfall. Nor does deficient seasonal rainfall alone establish the severity of agricultural drought.
Southern reservoirs fall to less than half their year-ago levels
The clearest concentration of pressure appears in the reservoir data. On 15 October, CWC’s 178 monitored reservoirs nationally held 68.58% of their live-storage capacity. Their storage was 16.44% below the corresponding ten-year average. Of the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission, on 15 October 2026, 105 held more than 80% of their ten-year average storage, while 73 were at or below that level. Of the latter, 31 had storage at or below 50% of normal.
The shortfall was concentrated in the South. Its 50 monitored reservoirs held 24.76 BCM, against a ten-year normal of 43.33 BCM, a deficit of 18.57 BCM. This accounts for approximately 74.5% of the net national storage shortfall of 24.93 BCM, including the effect of a small surplus in Central India.
State-level departures varied considerably. Storage was 61.50% below normal in Tamil Nadu, 59.33% in Andhra Pradesh and 51.63% in Telangana. Karnataka was 32.28% below normal, while Kerala was 17.67% below. These figures indicate a weaker reservoir position, but do not translate directly into equivalent reductions in water available to every user. Actual supply depends on the reservoirs serving an area, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems.
The timing is also important. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share of its rainfall during the October–December northeast monsoon, making subsequent rainfall and reservoir inflows important to watch. The 15 October 2026 figures are therefore a snapshot, not a final assessment of water availability for the coming months. Even so, the regional imbalance is clear: the national storage figure masks the depth of the shortfall in southern India.
District data show where rainfall deficiency meets underlying drought vulnerability
It is also important to look at districts apart from broad regions. IMD’s seasonal rainfall distribution records 282 districts with deficient rainfall and 34 with large-deficient rainfall. Together, that is 316 districts, or approximately 42.6% of the 741 districts listed. Further, 312 districts are recorded in the normal category, 90 with excess rainfall and 16 with large-excess rainfall. The distribution confirms that the deficient season was far from uniform. It also needs to be interpreted precisely: a rainfall-deficient district is not automatically a district officially declared drought-hit.
The agriculture ministry’s Crisis Management Plan (CMP) for drought provides a list of districts where state governments declared drought from 2011-12 to 2025-26. It has 472 districts declared drought over the years, and such declarations peaked in 2015-16 with 294 districts declared drought-affected, and in recent years, it declined: 71 in 2023-24 (Karnataka 31, Maharashtra 15, Rajasthan 12, Andhra Pradesh 13), and only 5 in 2024-25 and 4 in 2025-26, all in Andhra Pradesh. Ananthapuramu was declared drought-affected in 11 years, followed by Barmer, Jaisalmer, Bellari and 14 other districts with declarations in 10 years each.
A separate 2024 district risk assessment by the Department of Science and Technology identifies underlying vulnerability. It places 91 districts in the very high drought-risk category and 188 in the high category, 279 districts in total. More than 90% of districts in the Very High category (83 out of 91) are located in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra. These classifications combine hazard, exposure and vulnerability. They identify relative structural risk, rather than establishing that all these districts experience drought. The left image provides the Drought exposure Map, while the right image shows the current drought conditions as on 21st October, 2026, according to the India Drought Monitor.
Root-Zone Soil Moisture overlaps with low reservoir storage levels in Southern India
The NCFC’s report dated 19 October 2026 provides a more recent indicator of agricultural conditions. It compares root-zone soil moisture for 8–14 October with the average for the previous ten years.
The report finds that root-zone soil moisture was similar to or better than the ten-year average in parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, eastern and northern Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. In contrast, soil moisture was below the ten-year average in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and the Northeast region.
The comparison suggests that the effects of the monsoon deficit were not uniform across the country and that some areas entered the post-monsoon period with less soil moisture than their historical average. For agriculture, root-zone moisture is particularly relevant because it reflects water availability in the soil where plant roots draw moisture.
The overlap between below-average soil moisture and low reservoir storage in parts of southern India warrants particular attention. At the same time, soil moisture at or above the historical average in parts of eastern and central India shows why a national rainfall deficit cannot be used as a proxy for conditions in every district.
The coming weeks will bring further evidence about how these conditions develop. In Tamil Nadu, the northeast monsoon and associated reservoir inflows will be especially relevant. Elsewhere, changes in soil moisture and water storage will help clarify whether the seasonal rainfall deficit translates into continuing agricultural or water-supply pressure.
Why does it matter?
A national rainfall deficit reveals little about whether a farmer’s soil holds enough moisture or a household can count on its water supply. In 2026, 316 of 741 meteorological districts recorded deficient or large-deficient rainfall, while southern reservoirs held substantially less water than their ten-year average. The NCFC also reported below-average root-zone soil moisture across several states in October 2026. Together, these indicators point to pressure on water availability, although local supplies depend on reservoir storage, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems. Subsequent rainfall and reservoir replenishment will be particularly important for Tamil Nadu during its northeast monsoon season. Historical drought declarations and district-level risk assessments add another layer, helping distinguish the current rainfall shortfall from recurring drought exposure.
Key Numbers
- 13% below average: India received 759.4 mm of southwest monsoon rainfall in 2026, against a long-period average of 868.6 mm.
- 388 extremely heavy rainfall events: Up from 303 in 2025, an increase of approximately 28%, despite the deficient season.
- 316 of 741 districts: Recorded deficient or large-deficient seasonal rainfall, accounting for approximately 42.6% of the districts listed.
- 42.85% below average: Southern India’s monitored reservoirs held 24.760 BCM on 15 October, against a corresponding ten-year average of 43.327 BCM.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday criticised the Centre for failing to adequately justify steep markups on medicines, asking why it took years to cap trade margins on selected anti-cancer drugs and whether commercial considerations were being prioritised over patients’ lives. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta reserved its order in a public interest litigation (PIL) filed in 2023 by advocate and activist Kishan Chand Jain, seeking affordable medicines and reforms in drug pricing and medical regulation. The court also questioned hospitals’ pricing practices, asking why medicines were sold to patients at maximum retail prices (MRPs) that were far above their procurement costs. “The lives of people, Ms Bhati… don’t take it as commerce. Treat it as the life of the poorest citizen of this country,” the bench told additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre. “We have asked you no less than 30 times to tell us this justification,” it added. The hearing took place after the government capped trade margins at 30% of the MRP for selected non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines through a notification issued on 17 October. According to the Centre’s submission, the measure is expected to reduce retail prices by 20-70%. The bench also pulled up the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) over its delayed intervention and questioned whether the latest measure would meaningfully lower prices when the original MRP was itself substantially inflated. “Your body seems to be totally defunct, with due respect,” the bench remarked while questioning the authority’s record on addressing excessive markups. The court cited the case of a chemotherapy injection that a medical dealer said he could procure for ₹11,000 but for which a hospital charged ₹1.3 lakh. It asked the government to explain the disparity and why it had taken so long to intervene. The final ruling will determine the extent to which the Supreme Court can intervene to address excessive medicine mark-ups and whether broader price regulation is warranted. The decision will be closely watched by the pharmaceutical industry, hospitals and policymakers, given its potential implications for the Centre’s pricing policy and patients’ out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Bhati argued that the government’s policy sought to balance the availability of essential medicines at reasonable prices with innovation, competition, industry growth and employment. It favoured targeted interventions over comprehensive price controls, she submitted, cautioning that excessive regulation could affect investment and the availability of medicines. “Our policy is based on these four limbs,” she told the court, referring to the availability of essential medicines at reasonable prices, innovation, competition and industry growth, including employment and shared economic well-being. The bench, however, questioned the adequacy of the existing framework, asking why a medicine’s initial MRP could be set far above its supply price and then be allowed to rise annually. “You at the initial level fix the MRP right up to the moon. Then you increase by 10%,” the bench remarked. It also challenged the government’s reliance on market forces to regulate prices, saying patients had limited bargaining power and little information about the prices at which hospitals and retailers procured medicines. Senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for hospitals, argued that medicine margins helped private healthcare facilities meet the costs of maintaining operating theatres, catheterisation laboratories, MRI machines and round-the-clock medical staff. He said public hospitals were overstretched and private facilities needed adequate resources to provide healthcare. Rohatgi warned that restricting medicine margins could force hospitals to raise charges for other services. He also said listed hospitals typically operated on profit margins of around 10% and needed to invest thousands of crores of rupees in upgrading equipment. “These hospitals are listed companies… 10% is the profit of all these hospitals. I have to bring in thousands of crores every year to update machinery,” he told the bench. The bench suggested that medicine packaging display both the MRP and the price to retailer (PTR) to improve transparency. It also raised concerns about whether financial incentives arising from high medicine margins could encourage unnecessary procedures, though it clarified it was not making a definitive finding that such practices had occurred. An exciting new MacBook is rumored to be announced in just one week. If the reports end up being true, it'll be the most significant change to the lineup in many years, introducing a touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro. As exciting as it sounds, however, it's also the perfect opportunity to buy up the previous generation's M5 Max MacBook Pro at its lowest price ever.
That's especially significant considering the entire lineup got a price increase back in June. Right now, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with 36 GB of RAM and 2 TB of storage is $3,499, which is 20 percent off the retail price and $400 cheaper than it was just a few days ago. And historically, this is $150 cheaper than this configuration has ever sold for.
This absolutely stacked version of the MacBook Pro is one of the most powerful laptops you can buy. The M5 Max is a huge upgrade over both the M4 Max and the M5 Pro, offering GPU performance we've never seen on a MacBook before. For content creators, media professionals, engineers, and AI enthusiasts, this is nearly as good as it gets. It can even play AAA games smoother than any Mac (outside of the new Mac Studio). In my testing, Cyberpunk 2077 could average over 60 frame per second on the Ultra preset without relying on upscaling.
If you really want to get serious about AI performance, you'll want to upgrade to the 64-GB or 128-GB configurations—though third-party retailers like Amazon don't sell them. You'll have to buy directly from Apple for that, and the prices are exorbitant. But the 36-GB model that's on sale has plenty of juice for dipping your toe in the world of on-device AI, and it's a home run for video editors, designers, musicians, and engineers.
Beyond performance, it goes without saying that all MacBook Pros have the best speakers, displays, build quality, trackpads, and keyboards of just about any laptop. I test dozens of new laptops every year, and while some have come close (such as the Surface Laptop Ultra I just finished testing), none have taken the crown.
You might be wondering if waiting to see these new MacBooks next week is worth it. Maybe. I can't guarantee that this deal will stick around, and I don't know what these new MacBooks will be like. Rumors say that they will sport the same chip options as the current MacBook Pros, meaning we'd get an M5 Pro and M5 Max once again. If you were anything like me as a kid, trick-or-treating meant one, maybe two, pillowcases full of candy every Halloween.
Republicans are coming for your blue M&Ms
Why your Halloween candy might be a little less colorful this year.
And as fun as collecting all that candy could be, the real fun began when I got home and dumped my winnings onto my bedroom floor. That’s when the sorting began.
I had some very specific rules: The usual suspects — think Smarties, Tootsie Rolls, and Dum Dums — went into one pile. Fun-size chocolates, like Snickers, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, and Baby Ruths, went into another. And then there was my prized pile: Skittles, Warheads, Starbursts, and Sour Patch Kids. Those were meant to be eaten slowly throughout November. The rest was fair game.
The ways we sort and eat our Halloween candy are decided by some very particular, personal rules. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would like to add another distinction: Which candies are made with artificial dyes?
Kennedy’s ire for synthetic food dyes is years old, and they’ve become a major target of his Make America Healthy Again movement. Last year, he announced a plan to remove “petroleum-based synthetic dyes” from foods, arguing that companies “shouldn’t be feeding it to the rest of us.”
That plan has become a multimillion-dollar problem for Mars, the maker of M&Ms, which promised customers last year that they would create an all-natural version of their tasty chocolatey treats. As the Wall Street Journal reported this summer, however, its latest offering is missing one of the most iconic colored M&Ms — the blue M&M.
M&Ms aren’t the only snack food in Kennedy’s crosshairs: He has called out Doritos, Cheez-Its, Cap’n Crunch, and gummy bears, saying their ingredients include “a lot of poisons.” On Fox News, he described what children eat as “food-like substances” and also said that “some of it was made in petroleum refineries.”
In reality, the evidence is more complicated, because the Food and Drug Administration has long considered many of these approved synthetic dyes to be safe under its rules, while acknowledging that some children may be sensitive to them. Kennedy’s sweeping accusations go much further.
Still, pressure from Kennedy and those in the MAHA movement has led many companies to rethink the recipes of your favorite snacks. But producing those alternatives isn’t easy or cheap, as the story of the blue M&M illustrates.
Jesse Newman, a food reporter for the Wall Street Journal, went inside a Mars factory in Topeka, Kansas, to see the process for herself. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about why blue is so difficult to produce naturally, and what changing a candy’s color actually accomplishes.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
The Secretary of Health and Human Services, RFK Jr., has some issues with the blue M&M. What, what exactly happened? How did it draw his attention?
He is not a fan of any sort of chemical. He’s really concerned about toxins in our food. And Blue 1, which is the food dye that makes blue M&Ms blue, is a synthetic chemical.
He really takes issue with artificial dyes. He believes that they cause hyperactivity in kids, some neurological challenges. He thinks artificial dyes are linked to cancer.
As a member of the Trump administration, he formally set out to get them removed, didn’t he?
Oh yeah. He’s been putting a lot of pressure on the industry to strip artificial dyes from all kinds of products.
What do we know factually about artificial dyes? We hear that they’re bad for us. We hear that a lot of things are bad for us. We’re all still alive and kicking. Are artificial dyes really detrimental to our health?
The FDA for decades has said that there are nine artificial dyes approved for use in food. And they said that those artificial dyes are safe and have said so for years and years and years, as have other global bodies, so long as they’re used in accordance with some of the standards that the FDA laid out.
A California state agency has found that dyes are linked again to hyperactivity in children. And the FDA itself has said, ‘Okay, we think that these dyes are safe for the vast majority of kids, but some kids might be more sensitive to them than others.’
So I think the real issue is that it’s a chemical doing it. They’re purely cosmetic. They don’t do anything except color food. There is no nutritional benefit that you are getting from these dyes. And so do we need them? Absolutely not.
I think one of the issues is that if you’re looking at the ways our food contributes to health problems, artificial dyes are probably pretty low on the list.
You went inside a factory where they make M&Ms, and you looked at how they’re trying to make this happen. Tell me everything.
I went to this plant in Topeka, Kansas, to see how they were made. And it’s a massive industrial food plant, where they mix these colors and spray them onto these small chocolate orbs, which they refer to as lentils.
The M&Ms move through the plant, and they arrive at these massive [machines] that they call pans, but they look like big tumble dryers. And the M&Ms just tumble around in these pans, and the color is sprayed on. It’s a very, very industrial process, millions of M&Ms a day. And the challenge that Mars has now is making that happen with a natural dye instead of an artificial one.
A blue natural dye is the challenge. What are the problems?
They’ve been working on this for years. And they went with a product called spirulina, which is made from algae. But spirulina comes with a host of problems that they are now dealing with.
Blue 1, which is the artificial dye, arrives at the factories as a liquid. And they pour it into these mixers and they mix it up with this sugary syrup and it’s pretty easy to handle. Spirulina arrives as a powder. So now you’re mixing a powder into this same mixture, into the same recipe, and that is very different.
Because spirulina is a protein, the resulting mixture becomes a lot thicker. What they found was that the mixture containing spirulina would really clog up the piping. It was getting stuck. It moved less smoothly through the pipes.
Also because it is a protein, it was starting to coat and build up on the inside of the machinery. And when that happens, it’s a food safety hazard. It can mold; it can cause problems. For many reasons, it was a challenge to handle.
How much did this all cost?
I should say it’s not done. Mars wouldn’t give me an official figure for how much they spent. But they said that they are spending millions and millions of dollars.
They’re having to retrofit their plants, essentially. Mars said that they’re having to change about 300 types of machinery in their plants. It’s a real investment. And at the end of the day, it all comes down to cost.
What did they actually end up getting done? What was the outcome here?
Mars said what they committed to was that they were going to release a new version of their M&Ms and a few other of their products this year that were made with natural dyes instead of artificial dyes.
They didn’t come out and say we’re eliminating artificial dyes. And so folks should be really clear about that: Their artificially dyed M&Ms aren’t going anywhere. They are still on shelves.
What they said is that they’re going to come out with an option that is naturally dyed. So they tried to do that. And what they found was that they couldn’t do it at a cost that was acceptable to them. With the blue and with the spirulina, it would have been far too expensive to make it work at scale. We’re talking millions and millions and millions of M&Ms per day.
They had problems making the green, the blue, and the brown M&M because, if you go back to your elementary school color theory, they needed blue to make all of those M&Ms. Ultimately they said, “Okay, we can do green. There’s little enough spirulina in the green to make the green M&M.” But blue and brown, they are not able to get there yet due to the amount of spirulina that those colors require.
And so earlier this year, they launched their naturally dyed version of M&Ms with red, orange, yellow, and green M&Ms. And if you take a look at this bag, my colleague referred to these as autumnal. They look very autumnal.
They look sort of muted. 
You know, it really isn’t the same. It looks like a mature person’s M&M.
At the end of the day, what are the changes to the M&Ms? Let’s say I go online and get the natural dyed ones. What does that mean for my health? Am I now a healthy and virtuous person if I’m eating the autumnal M&Ms?
It means very little.
I would say you are, hopefully, still enjoying that sugary treat and the pick-me-up in the afternoon as you’re starting to tire. But you’re still eating candy; you’re still eating sugar. It really hasn’t changed very much.

Israel election 2026 results live: Exit polls suggest deadlock with Eisenkot’s bloc just ahead of Netanyahu
Neither prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot on track for a majority

Israel's election ended in an apparent deadlock on Tuesday, exit polls by major television networks showed, with neither prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot on track for a majority.
An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo after the country’s first national election since the October attack in 2023. The vote served as a referendum on Netanyahu’s wartime leadership.
Exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggest that neither Netanyahu’s political bloc nor that of his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Those polls indicated that Netanyahu's bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18. The strong showing by Arab-led parties could allow them to decide the next prime minister, but both blocs have until now refused to partner with them.
Netanyahu had been tipped for a stunning defeat in today’s legislative elections despite receiving a glowing endorsement from Donald Trump.
Before polls opened, the US president reiterated his “complete and total” support for Netanyahu, writing that he had been “strong, brave and brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition”.
Arab turnout has given their parties outsized influence
Benjamin Netanyahu had warned earlier that Arab parties that could make or break the election, saying they were receiving “truly massive support," and heading to the polls in "unprecedented numbers.”
In another sign of concern, Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party petitioned to extend voting hours past 10 p.m., but the election commission ruled against it, saying there was no justification.
Eisenkot had rejected the proposed extension and called on voters to ignore Netanyahu's “scare tactics.”
Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers — if other parties agree to join forces with them.
“Our vote will change the government,” said Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra’am party, while voting was still underway.
Arabs in Israel make up about 20% of the population.
Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are “not even people,” warned that “it will be Mansour Abbas’ government” if Netanyahu and his allies don’t win.
'Don't let anyone confuse you, this is a crushing defeat'- Yair Lapid
Current opposition head Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Highest turnout in decades
More than 74% of eligible voters had cast ballots by 8 pm, the highest turnout at that time in decades, and eight percentage points higher than in the last elections in 2022, according to the Central Elections Committee.
Over 7 million people are eligible to vote, and tens of thousands have reportedly arrived from overseas.
Israel’s president will be tasked with asking the party leader with the best prospect of forming a government, usually one with the most seats, to cobble together a coalition.
If none can, new elections could be held early next year.
Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate.
Netanyahu challenger Eisenkot says exit polls signal "lack of confidence" in Netanyahu
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the opposition bloc’s Yashar party, said the projections indicate “a total lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the ‘October 7th government’”.
In pictures: Israelis react to live results from today's election
Lack of majority could work in Netanyahu's favour
The stalemate in today’s election could work in Benjamin Netanyahu's favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers.
No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.
Knesset seat projections exit poll
According to Israel’s Channel 12 exit poll, the Knesset seat projections are as follows:
- Likud - 24
- Yashar - 22
- B’Yaschad - 12
- Joint List - 11
- The Democrats - 9
- Yisrael Beytenu - 9
- Shas - 8
- Ra’am - 7
- Otzma Yehudit - 6
- Religious Zionism - 6
- United Torah Judaism - 6
What have we learned from the exit polls?
Exit polls indicated that Netanyahu's bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18.
The strong showing by Arab-led parties could allow them to decide the next prime minister, but both blocs have until now refused to partner with them.
Netanyahu’s fate hangs in the balance
Exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggest that neither Netanyahu’s political bloc nor that of his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Like all surveys, exit polls are subject to potential error.
Preliminary results are expected in the coming hours.
Final results are expected in the coming days and may vary from the exit polls.

Marissa Mayer, former chief executive officer (CEO) of Yahoo and Google's first female engineer, is facing massive backlash for using an AI chatbot to describe her 10-year-old daughter's traits. According to the New York Post, ahead of Mayer's daughter's 10th birthday, her school asked Mayer to provide three bullet points describing the girl's personality. Mayer turned to Dazzle, an AI tool developed by her startup, for help, prompting criticism on social media. The 51-year-old said the chatbot described her daughter as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover” — a response she called "perfect". She initially said she had sought AI's help because she felt overwhelmed by the “range and complexity of potential answers”. Mayer revelation that she used the tool to come up with a three-adjective description has triggered widespread backlash online. Users on X mocked her for using the tool, openly acknowledging it and then featuring the incident in promotional material for her company. “Wow, I guess she doesn’t even know her own daughter if she thinks this is perfect,” one Reddit user wrote. “It describes a generic 10-year-old kid.” “I hope the kid doesn’t get to read this shxtty post about how her mom doesn’t give a shxt about her, bc I know my mom can write a whole essay about me,” said another. “Are you really this clueless and shallow? How embarrassing,” someone else wrote, while another simply said, “this is so bleak.” Mayer later took to X to clarify that she had not used the tool simply because she felt overwhelmed by the task. Instead, she wanted to test an early prototype developed by her team. “No, I was asked by my daughter's school to give 3 bullet points. Any parent knows that is impossible - I could write 80 pages. What was awesome about Dazzle was that it described her perfectly AND brought back examples of projects she had done in kindergarten (sandcat playground) to illustrate it. It just shows how much context is in your photos," she said. She explained that her daughter Marielle's fourth-grade teachers had emailed her about creating a slide celebrating Marielle and her twin sister, Sylvana, for their December 10 birthday. Mayer said she pasted the email into Dazzle to test its capabilities, expecting it to struggle because facial recognition technology often fails to distinguish identical twins. “So, when Marielle and her twin sister Sylvana’s 4th-grade teachers emailed asking for a slide celebrating each girl for their December 10th birthday, I pasted the email into Dazzle to test its limits. I fully expected it to struggle, since most facial recognition can’t even tell my identical twins apart. “Instead, Dazzle blew me away. AI-powered healthtech platform BioStack has raised $9.5 Mn (₹90.4 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Peak XV Partners, Afore Capital, DCVC, Emerson Collective, SV Angel, Verdict Capital, Streamlined Ventures, and Y Combinator. The startup plans to utilise the fresh capital to continue expanding its presence in the US and other international markets, including India, Brazil, and Argentina. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its tech stack and ramp up hiring across engineering and research teams. Founded in 2025 by Sanat Mishra and Parth Patwa, BioStack claims to be building the data infrastructure for the next generation of medical AI. It combines fragmented clinical information across systems such as electronic health records, medical imaging, clinical notes and medications. The startup then uses this data to create proprietary datasets for research, biotechnology, and the development and training of medical AI models. “We’re building the infrastructure that connects all of the clinical information and makes it useful, both for clinicians making decisions today and for the researchers and AI developers building the future of medicine,” said BioStack cofounder and CEO Mishra. BioStack currently works with multiple hospitals across the US, Brazil and Argentina. In India, it is also connecting cancer patients with an investigational cancer vaccine program. The startup also claims that it offers use cases such as AI model evaluation, disease modeling, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and treatment-response analysis. Besides offering custom workflows to protect patient privacy, the startup claims to have so far processed 10 Cr de-identified patient records, more than “several hundred thousand” fragmented X-Rays, MRIs and CT scans, and “several million” telehealth audio transcripts. For context, de-identified patient records are medical datasets that have had all personal and direct identifiers removed so that the individual cannot reasonably be linked to the data. The fundraise comes as India becomes a training ground to collect datasets for powering AI models and physical AI products. Startups are tapping India’s huge population to collect recordings of workers performing physical tasks, processing the footage, and selling the resulting datasets to frontier AI labs and robotics companies. For instance, the likes of Awign, Objectways and Human Archive are building pipelines to supply first-person footage of human activity to AI developers. Just a day ago, instant home services startup Pronto’s founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a US-based venture to collect data for physical AI systems. At the heart of all this is the Indian AI training dataset, which is projected to become a $1.3 Bn opportunity by 2033.

A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?
- Published
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.
He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.
South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.
With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.
The first task was to determine the species.
Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.
The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.
The shark had to return to sea.
A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.
They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.
Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.
As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.
Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".
People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.
Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.
City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.
A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.
Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.
Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.
More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.
The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.
"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."
But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.
As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.
Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.
At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.
But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.
On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.
At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.
The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.
It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.
With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.
On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".
When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"
"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."
Others thought it was time for her to return home.
"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."
People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.
"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."
Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.
"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."
Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.
On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.
This left her trapped between the two layers.
Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.
Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.
There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.
Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.
She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.
But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.
For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

On October 17, Saturday, even as 19 people were killed and several injured in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, a different scene of chaos unfolded a few kilometres away at Jadavpur.
A bulldozer was brought in by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Kolkata Police to demolish bookstalls of Left parties set up near 8B bus stand of Jadavpur. While locals and Left workers, including CPI(M) and AISA activists, protested through the night to thwart the attempted demolition, the authorities succeeded in bringing down certain bookstalls and damaging others.
Left book stalls have come under threat both from Right-wing fanatics and the administration after chief minister Suvendu Adhikari issued a warning. “You consider Sanatan Dharma to be merely cultural. You do not say Durga Puja; You call it ‘Sharadotsab’. I will tell all Durga Puja committees that if these so-called communists come to set up stalls and do not write Durga Puja, do not allow a single stall,” Adhikari had announced earlier.
Alt News has already reported on alleged attacks on book stalls by BJP workers in several parts of the state.
Same Stalls Set Up For Years
Left organisations, including the CPI(M), AISA, SUCI(C) and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), have historically set up bookstalls in and around the 8B bus stand area of Jadavpur. The CPI(M) has been setting up its bookstall there for over 40 years, while AISA’s stall has been set up for more than 10 years. The APDR has been setting up a bookstall for the past four to five years. This year, an RSS bookstall was set up right between the CPI(M) and AISA stalls.
Around 6 pm on Saturday, a joint team of Kolkata Police, Central Armed Police Force personnel and KMC arrived with a JCB earthmover to demolish the Left bookstalls. However, the RSS stall was left untouched.
According to the KMC personnel present at the spot, the Left stalls lacked the necessary permissions. Left parties, however, denied this allegation. Representatives of the Left parties argued that they had paid the required fees to the KMC to set up the stalls.
The administration, however, maintained that paying the fees did not necessarily mean that permission had been granted to set up the stalls. The Left parties, in turn, asked the authorities to show which documents they lacked, while also asking what documents the RSS stall possessed that made it legal. Their requests were repeatedly rejected, representatives told Alt News.
‘Authorities Passed the Buck’
“Police and the KMC workers were only passing the buck on each other. Police said the KMC had sought their help to demolish illegal structures. When confronted, KMC workers said that police had asked them to help demolish our stalls,” said DYFI Kolkata district committee member Sainik Sur.
“We asked police and KMC time and again to show the demolition order. But all they said was that there was immense pressure from higher levels to demolish all the Left stalls,” added Sur.
A similar claim was echoed by AISA state president Ritam Maji. “Police and the KMC made it very clear that the Left bookstalls were illegal, whereas the ‘Sanatani’ stall that came up this year for the first time was legal. We have paid the required fee to KMC and have the receipt of the same, yet they claimed that our stalls were illegal. When we asked them to show documents of the RSS-backed stall, to figure out what permissions we lacked, the police simply said that the top brass of the KMC had requested that the space be cleared,” said Maji.
Besides the earthmover, the administration had also brought a KMC dumper truck near the stalls, generally used to collect and dispose of garbage, allegedly to collect the debris from the stalls and the books, representatives of the Left said.
Hundreds Gather Around Bulldozer
After an APDR stall was partially demolished, nearly a hundred people — locals in the area and Left party workers — gathered near the bulldozer in the evening to prevent it from demolishing stalls. Armed with flags, books and posters, they formed human chains around the bookstalls, forcing the authorities to retreat. CPI(M) central committee member and former Jadavpur CPI(M) MLA Sujan Chakraborty also reached the spot to join the resistance.
Around 1 am on October 18, Sunday, personnel from Kolkata Police, CAPF and KMC workers started assembling near the bookstalls again. An hour later, they again started dismantling the APDR stall.
The SUCI(C) bookstall, set up near Gate 2 of Jadavpur University, was also demolished around this time. The area surrounding the stall was cordoned off by security personnel, and party workers could not prevent the demolition.
CPI(M) Kolkata district committee member Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the party’s bookstalls, documented the resistance against the demolition as scores of people stood in front of the JCB earthmover, through his Facebook Live.
After the SUCI(C) stall was brought down, the administration tried to demolish both the APDR and AISA stalls, which were interlocked in a single bamboo structure. Around 3 am, Left activists were again seen forming human chains around their stalls. A section of the activists sat inside the AISA stall as the police and central forces tried to demolish it, ultimately compelling police to retreat.
As the administration tried to bring down the APDR stall around 4:30 am, CPI(M), AISA and APDR workers tried to resist the advance in a unified manner. SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya was seen resisting the administrative forces, who tried to tear down the bamboo scaffolding of the APDR stall.
Subsequently, individuals identifying themselves as KMC workers used machetes to cut the ropes of the APDR stall and bring down the structure, despite the efforts of protesters.
After the APDR stall was demolished, protesters formed a human barricade in front of the CPI(M) stall. Actress Ushasie Chakraborty was among the protesters who held the barricade.
As the standoff continued, CRPF personnel wielded the baton briefly, but it failed to scatter the crowd. Around 5 am, the forces left the spot.
Although the CPI(M) stall was mostly left untouched, the AISA stall suffered extensive damage. AISA activists tore down a section of the stall and rebuilt it on Sunday morning. SUCI(C) and APDR also rebuilt their stalls, and books were sold through Sunday.
“The police informed us that if we dismantled our stall for repairs, they would not allow us to rebuild it. However, we repaired it nonetheless and carried on with our programme,” said Maji.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. “I have visited the 8B stall quite a few times in the past. Maybe this time I might have skipped coming here. But after what happened last night, I feel it is my duty to come here and show solidarity,” said Ghosh, with CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh standing by his side.
West Bengal Congress President Suvankar Sarkar also visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. So did CPI(M) state secretary Md Salim.
Chief Minister’s Warning
On September 10, Adhikari urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for bookstalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated his stance two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Following Adhikari’s warnings, on October 14, a division bench of the Calcutta High Court overturned the order of Justice Sougata Bhattacharya’s single bench and declined the CPI(M)’s plea to organise a bookstall in front of its party office in Bongaon in Jessore Road of North 24 Parganas district — a spot where a bookstall by the Hindu Jagran Manch had allegedly been set up.
