Finland's Stubb and Norway's Støre held 'frank and substantive' call with Putin on Ukraine
Oh, that’s interesting.
There were some rumours making rounds this morning that the Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the US-Ukrainian talks in Oslo last week, may have been active again.

Their call was “a follow-up” to the Oslo meeting, Stubb’s office said in a statement, as the Nordic pair wants to advance their diplomatic efforts to end the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine.
“Finland and Norway border Russia. They are firm supporters of Ukraine. The aim of the call was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin. The call was related to the upcoming meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi,” the statement read.
The trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi are expected in early November.
“Norway and Finland have always promoted peace and security in our region. The two countries have a shared interest in stability and predictability in the Baltic Sea region and the High North. This was highlighted in the call.”

Reacting after the call, Stubb called the discussions “frank and substantive,” saying that “ending the war requires direct discussions” with Russia.
“The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations. In the call we stressed the importance of de-escalation”, Norway’s Støre added.

New Delhi, Oct 27: Residents living within 20 km of a National Highway toll plaza can now obtain an annual concessional local FASTag pass starting November 1, 2026, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) said on Tuesday.
The annual fee for the concessional pass is Rs 1,500 for toll plazas outside municipal or local town limits, and Rs 3,000 for those within municipal limits, according to a notification by the ministry.
Under the new provision, eligible non-commercial vehicle owners with a valid and functional FASTag, residing within a 20 km range, can choose between the existing monthly pass and the concessional Local Pass for commuting through a specific fee plaza.
The pass will be valid only for that fee plaza and will not be transferable to any other plazas.
Currently, eligible residents can obtain a monthly pass for Rs 360, amounting to Rs 4,320 annually.
The ministry further said that no such concessional local pass shall be issued for commuting on a national highway or expressway on which a fee is levied based on the closed user fee collection system. It will also not be issued where a service road or alternative road is available for use by commuters.
"With over 13 crore FASTags issued across the country, the new provision aims to provide an option for eligible residents living near toll plazas to make travel more economical and enhance Ease of Commuting for local residents," MoRTH said.

Civil aviation ministry holds fog preparedness meeting for upcoming winter season
The civil aviation ministry reviewed winter fog preparedness for Dec 15-Feb 15, 2027, directing airlines and airports to ensure flight safety.
New Delhi: The civil aviation ministry held the first Fog Preparedness meeting for the upcoming winter season to review preparedness and coordination among stakeholders for the fog season.
The meeting was headed by civil aviation secretary Samir Kumar Sinha and attended by the director general of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) Vir Vikram Yadav, Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI) Puneet Kansal, senior officials from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), India Meteorological Department (IMD) along with representatives of Delhi airport and other fog-affected airports and airlines.
The IMD officials stated that the fog season is expected to run from December 15 this year to February 15, 2027.
"The meeting focused on ensuring smooth airport operations and minimising inconvenience to passengers during fog-related disruptions. Emphasis was laid on advance preparedness, timely communication, effective coordination among stakeholders and appropriate assistance to passengers in case of flight delays, cancellations and rescheduling," a release from the government stated.
It also said that the DGCA was emphasised to ensure regulatory oversight, compliance with applicable instructions, verification of aircraft and crew preparedness, and effective passenger facilitation measures by airlines.
Also read: DGCA to carry out final airline audits this week ahead of US aviation body checks
"The AAI and airport operators were directed to ensure the readiness of Instrument Landing Systems (ILS) and Runway Visual Range (RVR) systems, airside safety, adequate terminal capacity and effective coordination for airport operations during low-visibility conditions," it said.
The airlines, in the meeting, were directed to ensure the availability of qualified crew and compliant aircraft for low visibility operations, plan realistic flight schedules and take timely decisions regarding flight operations, the government stated.
"It was emphasised that passengers should receive timely updates through SMS, mobile applications and email regarding delays, cancellations and revised departure times, so that they don’t reach the airport without adequate information about their flights," the statement read.
It said that the IMD was also directed to ensure reliable weather forecasts, regular observations and timely dissemination of weather updates to facilitate operational planning.
"Air Traffic Control and air navigation service providers were instructed to ensure safe sequencing of air traffic, adherence to low-visibility procedures and coordinated traffic management during fog conditions," the government stated, adding that the role of BCAS and CISF in ensuring safe and orderly passenger movement, including terminal re-entry and re-boarding wherever required, was also discussed.
The government also directed airlines to ensure that their respective ground handlers maintain adequate staffing, ensure efficient baggage management and aircraft turnaround, and provide necessary assistance to passengers during operational disruptions.
"Particular emphasis was laid on passenger facilitation during prolonged delays and cancellations. Preparations to be made to ensure adequate staffing at check-in counters, airline helpdesks and customer care facilities. The Secretary emphasised that airlines need to ensure that their helpline desks at the airports are manned by informed and empowered personnel who can adequately address passenger queries," the government said in its statement.
It said that the collective objective is to minimise passenger inconvenience through advance preparedness, timely information, clear operational decisions and effective passenger assistance during the upcoming fog season.

A 48-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes developed persistent swelling in his left lower limb, followed by high fever and breathlessness. An ankle-joint sample was initially misidentified as Acinetobacter baumannii complex, while findings in his lungs raised suspicion of tuberculosis. Cultures from his blood and joint pus eventually identified Burkholderia pseudomallei -- the bacterium that causes melioidosis. His blood cultures cleared around the 21st day of treatment, and he recovered, according to a case report described by Atish Mohapatra, Assistant Professor, Department of Microbiology, Kalinga Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar.
In another report published in 2026, Dr.Mohapatra and colleagues described a 25-year-old patient living with sickle cell disease and type 1 diabetes who developed disseminated melioidosis involving the bones and lungs, with a splenic abscess and pulmonary embolism.
Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant, Infectious Diseases, Fortis Hospital, described a case involving a 54-year-old man living with diabetes and chronic liver disease. He had low-grade fever for about six weeks, followed by high fever over 15 days, and a persistent cough for three weeks. He also had swelling and pus discharge from his left foot. A CT scan showed extensive consolidation in the right lower lobe of his lung. Blood cultures and samples collected during bronchoscopy grew B. pseudomallei, confirming pulmonary melioidosis with bloodstream infection.
A study published in The Lancet Global Health, led by Nitin Gupta, Department of Infectious Diseases, Kasturba Medical College, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, assessed high-risk hospitalised adults at 15 Indian tertiary-care centres between January 2023 and December 2025. Culture-confirmed melioidosis was found in 262 of 2,953 patients (8.9%). Of those diagnosed, 50 (19.1%) died in hospital.
The infection and risks
B. pseudomallei is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions. Infection usually occurs when contaminated soil or water enters the body through cuts or wounds. Inhalation of contaminated dust or water droplets and, less commonly, ingestion of contaminated water can also transmit the bacterium. Human-to-human transmission is exceptionally rare.
Melioidosis can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate. Rarely, infection involves the nervous system. Severe disease can progress to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction.
Symptoms vary according to the organs affected. Patients may have persistent fever, cough, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, painful joint swelling, abdominal pain or localised skin infections. Some develop a slowly progressive illness resembling tuberculosis, while others deteriorate rapidly. The infection can also relapse if treatment is inadequate.
Diabetes is a major risk factor. Chronic kidney, lung and liver diseases, heavy alcohol use and reduced immunity can also increase vulnerability. Dr. Mohapatra says clinicians usually consider melioidosis in high-risk patients with unexplained sepsis, severe pneumonia, deep-seated abscesses or bone and joint infections, particularly when environmental exposure is plausible.
Why diagnosis is delayed
When it comes to diagnosis there are challenges at both the clinical and laboratory levels. Symptoms are often nonspecific, the disease can present in different ways and the incubation period can vary. Clinicians may not suspect melioidosis or send appropriate samples for culture, while microbiologists may struggle to identify the organism correctly.
Automated identification systems can help, but they are not infallible. Like in the above case, the bacterium was initially misidentified as A. baumannii complex. Dr.Mohapatra notes that even systems such as VITEK 2 can misidentify B. pseudomallei. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry can aid identification, but its cost and limited availability can be barriers. Validated molecular tests, including PCR, can support confirmation where accessible.
Culture of blood, pus, abscess aspirates, respiratory specimens or affected tissue remains central to diagnosis. Depending on the presentation, urine and other clinical samples may also be tested. Multiple specimens may be necessary because infection can involve several organs, and prior antibiotic use can make confirmation difficult. Imaging with ultrasound, CT or MRI can help locate deep-seated abscesses and identify organ involvement.
Madhumitha R., senior consultant, Infectious Diseases and Infection Control at MGM Healthcare, Chennai, says clinicians should consider blood cultures in patients with persistent fever, ideally before antibiotics when clinically appropriate. If melioidosis is suspected, the laboratory should be informed so that appropriate identification procedures can be followed. A history of contact with contaminated soil or water can also help guide testing.
Experts call for better communication between clinicians and microbiologists, training for laboratory personnel to recognise suspicious organisms, and referral pathways to facilities that can confirm difficult isolates. Standardised laboratory procedures and quality assurance are important, particularly where advanced identification methods are unavailable.
Treatment and surveillance
India’s National Centre for Disease Control provides technical guidance for melioidosis treatment in its 2025 manual on zoonotic diseases of public health importance. Treatment has two phases: an initial intensive phase with intravenous antibiotics, followed by prolonged oral eradication therapy to reduce the risk of relapse.
Ceftazidime is an established option for the intensive phase, while meropenem is preferred in severe illness, including septic shock and neurological involvement. Intravenous treatment may last two to eight weeks or longer, depending on severity and the organs affected. Bone and joint infections, neurological disease and deep-seated abscesses may require prolonged treatment. The oral eradication phase commonly uses trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for several months, with longer courses sometimes required for complicated infections.
Dr.Panda stresses that treatment must be individualised according to organ involvement, drug susceptibility, kidney and liver function, tolerability and clinical response. Drainage of accessible abscesses, control of underlying conditions such as diabetes, monitoring for adverse effects and follow-up after discharge are also important. Incomplete treatment can lead to relapse even after symptoms improve. There is currently no licensed vaccine.
The multicentre study found variation across participating centres, with the highest proportions in Odisha (26%), Madhya Pradesh (22.7%) and Karnataka (19.3%) – figures describe the selected hospital populations, not State-wide prevalence. The study also found associations with monsoon admission, outdoor high-risk occupations and groundwater as the main drinking-water source. These associations do not establish causation.
Earlier reviews have found confirmed cases in several Indian States, but differences in diagnosis, awareness and reporting may affect how many cases are recorded. Dr. Mohapatra says India should move beyond identifying melioidosis only when an unusual case appears. Experts recommend a phased surveillance system, beginning with hospitals and laboratories equipped to confirm infection and expanding as diagnostic capacity improves.
Such a system could track confirmed cases, geographical and environmental exposures, antimicrobial susceptibility, treatment regimens, deaths, complications and relapse. Better surveillance, alongside improved diagnostic access and clinical awareness, would help establish the disease burden and guide public-health responses.
Prevention is important especially for people who often come into contact with soil or water. Farmers and others at higher risk should use protective footwear, cover cuts and abrasions, and clean contaminated wounds promptly. Avoiding untreated surface water and informing a doctor about possible environmental exposure may also help reduce risk and guide timely testing.
Improving clinical awareness, access to reliable diagnostic testing and systematic surveillance will be essential to identifying more cases of melioidosis in India and reducing deaths from this potentially life-threatening infection.

SC questioned the Centre over pharma companies pricing medicines at over 1,000% of cost, saying the industry can't "run amok" in the name of free market.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday said the pharma industry cannot be allowed to “run amok” in the name of free market to fix the maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines at an exponentially high level, which in some cases happens to be over 1,000% of the price at which they are sold to retailers.Expressing anguish over the suffering of the common man who had to pay the price, a bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said the court is “pained by the loot” and repeatedly asked Centre to explain the rationale behind allowing a high MRP and who ultimately benefits from the policy. It reserved its order on plea to bring all non-patented medicines and medical consumables under price control mechanism like scheduled drugs.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati, who had to face a volley of questions from the bench, tried to convince the court that govt was aware of the problem and that was why it recently decided to cap the price of anti-cancer drugs. But the court responded that govt “woke up” only after it intervened and passed harsh observations on the prevailing system.She, however, said the deliberation was already on and SC’s intervention expedited it.
“People are living in a daydream that someday they will benefit from the drugs prices control order (DPCO)... The policy is only to give benefit to the corporate. We are thinking from the point of view of poor patients,” SC observed. Bhati, thereafter, submitted that medicine prices in India are among the lowest in the world due to free market and govt cannot take control of the entire pharma market, but the bench told her, “You are either not aware about the problem or not keen to solve the problem.
.. Why is the entire system working for the benefit of few people?”“Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. It is not that the govt has left the market unregulated but the complete control of the market is not feasible,” Bhati said, adding that the issue pertains to economic policy and commerce and the court should desist from interfering. Not convinced by this, the bench said, “Should they (pharma companies) be allowed to run amok? What is the justification for the difference in prices? You are not able to come with an answer. We have asked you 30 times. Do not talk about control... You are talking about economic policy and commerce. Is commerce more important than the life of citizens and be given precedence?”

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.
However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.
Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.
The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.
The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.
The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.
The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

The College of Magic turns ordinary kids into confident, top-hat wearing magicians
Dressed in a sharp black three-piece suit and a dapper yellow bow tie, Lubelo Mthenjana stands alone on a dark stage, taking in the last few seconds of quiet before the curtain opens. He takes a deep breath as his name is announced. Then he opens his arms wide and flashes a bright smile.
"Hello everyone! My name is Lubelo Mthenjana, and I will be performing for you … some magic!"
The audience of about 30 children and parents is spellbound. They laugh out loud as he makes a string of paper clips vanish into a plastic cup and gasp with surprise as the clips reappear inside a matchbox. Then comes his best trick: He conjures sweets out of thin air and tosses them into the crowd. The room erupts. As Lubelo takes his final bow to thunderous applause, his mom beams a proud smile at the 11-year-old apprentice magician.
On this cloudy Saturday morning in September, Cape Town's College of Magic is buzzing with energy as dozens of students are competing in the annual junior magic contest. Heading to their classrooms, children in top hats, crisp white shirts and ties dash up and down a staircase decorated with a riot of brightly colored posters. On every floor, display cabinets overflow with magic wands, sparkly hats, silk scarves, handcuffs, dice, Rubik's Cubes, toys, photographs and dozens of trophies earned by students in competitions all over the world.
Outside the old red-brick Victorian mansion, framed by palm trees, two teenage boys zip around the car park on unicycles. Balls, clubs and diabolos shoot up into the air as a handful of kids practice juggling on the porch.
The Hogwarts of Cape Town
Tucked away in a peaceful suburb, this extraordinary school is a real-world Hogwarts: Africa's only school for youthful stage magicians and illusionists. Every Saturday morning, about 190 starry-eyed students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in everything from puppetry, mime and clowning to juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. "All the skills that will make a good magician," sums up David Gore, the school's founder.
In 1980, Gore was studying law and paying his way by performing at private magic shows when he and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school.
"We walked into our local newspaper house with our top hats and tails, told our story about how we were starting the College of Magic, did magic for the journalists in the newsroom, and they published an article," he recalls. "From that article, we had 34 young people who started attending formal weekly classes studying magic."
At the time, South Africa was still in the grip of apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation that dictated almost every aspect of daily life. State schools were strictly segregated. Students of different races could not even share park benches, some building entrances or take the same public transport to school. Yet the College of Magic was multiracial from day one.
"When we started out, our organization was illegal," says Gore, referring to its no-segregation policy. "This was an opportunity for young people from all backgrounds to come together around a common interest in magic, to learn about each other and understand each other."
Nearly 50 years later, the school continues to stand out in a city still deeply divided along racial and economic lines.
"Many of our young people remain siloed in their socioeconomic groups, very often along either language or racial lines," Gore explains. "Some arrive in very fancy cars, others have taken an hour in a collective taxi to get here. But when they're here, they work with the same equipment, the same classes, the same stages and get the same food."
Though the six-year course costs a fee, about 80% of the students cannot afford to pay and are sponsored, mostly through private donations.
"Magic is such a wonderful companion for our young people here in South Africa," says Gore. "They're able to carry it in their pockets, into the communities and the marginalized areas where most of our students come from. It's an art form that can be performed without being wealthy or needing very expensive instruments."
Multiple studies have found that learning magic can help children develop self-esteem, curiosity, lateral thinking, fine motor skills and problem-solving abilities. A 2021 study conducted by researchers at the Universities of Hertfordshire and Edinburgh found that children who learned and performed a magic trick showed greater improvements in creative fluency and originality than those who completed a similar art activity.
Even watching a magic trick can challenge our assumptions about the world and stimulate more original thinking. In another study, researchers found that it stimulated areas of the brain associated with cognitive flexibility and processing unconventional information.
"Many of our graduates don't become performers or magicians. But one of the skills that this young generation is most going to need for their careers is creativity," adds Gore. "That is what's so fantastic about magic: Nothing's impossible for us."
A kid who's hooked on magic
For 11-year-old Lubelo, magic has "opened up a new world." After watching a family friend perform a trick, he was determined to join the College of Magic. He had to wait until he turned 10 to enroll. Now, he's hooked.
At home in Makhaza township, about 40 minutes from the college, Lubelo spends his free time watching magic shows online and practicing tricks on his brothers and parents. He keeps his props, tools and other secrets in a box hidden away in his room. He's even chosen a stage name: Spade Boy — after his favorite card suit.
"If my mom is cooking and asks me to pass the potatoes, I'll start juggling with them," he says mischievously.
Lubelo has also persuaded several friends to join the school, becoming something of an ambassador in a community where magic is often frowned upon and associated with witchcraft.
"Many people are afraid of magic. But at the College of Magic, we don't do dark magic," he explains. "We just do the kind of magic that makes somebody smile, makes them happy and takes the stress away."
Sometimes, he says, other children ask whether he can turn people into pigs. "Then I just say: 'Let me start with you!' and they run away," he laughs.
Lubelo's mother, Yandiswa, says the magic lessons have boosted her son's confidence. They have brought another kind of relief, too. "It keeps him occupied and away from this environment and everything that's happening outside," she says.
With nearly 60 murders per day, South Africa has one of the world's highest crime rates, and several of Cape Town's townships are among the areas hardest hit by violent crime. From his home in Makhaza, Lubelo often hears gunshots. He says boys his age are drawn into using and selling drugs.
The magic community hasn't been spared. Just a few weeks before our visit, the school held a memorial service for Duma Mgqoki, a promising young magician, former student and volunteer teacher who was killed in a shooting in July. He was 22.
"On a weekly basis, some of our young people come to us saying they've experienced crime on a firsthand basis," says David Gore. "These things need to change, and we're very hopeful that the younger generation of today are going to be the force of change to bring about the society which we all would like to live in."
Back at the college, after finishing his show, Lubelo steps off the stage to a chorus of fist bumps and backslaps from his excited friends.
"He was so good! We're swimming in happiness!" one teenager beams. Without skipping a beat, the boys run outside, pick up colorful leather balls and launch into a juggling competition.
Unicycles and prizes
By now, a light drizzle has set in, but the two unicyclists are still making their rounds in the car park, seemingly undeterred. "Even when the storm comes, even when the world ends, I'll never stop unicycling," declares 14-year-old Joshua Clyde as he whizzes past.
Inside the cafeteria, a wide-eyed crowd has gathered around a teacher showing off a magic trick. With a snap of his fingers and what seems like a touch of superhuman power, he makes a coin disappear from a student's closed fist. It reappears beneath the student's watch.
Others have opted for the puppeteering class, upstairs, where pairs of students are taught to bring their humanoid puppets to life.
Footsteps drum up and down the staircase as the remaining performers in this Saturday competition rehearse their routines, nerves and excitement mounting. "Why am I so nervous? I've got this!" says bubbly Kungentando Ndenetya, 12, repeating the mantra to herself.
Once every child has performed, the jury retires to a quiet office to deliberate. All four judges are former students or teachers at the College of Magic. Twenty-five-year-old Caitlin Hutchison, who comes from "a long line of magicians," says the school taught her "resilience training." Monica Nyakatya graduated in 2009 and now works in logistics but has remained close to the institution that, she says, "shaped" her.
The deliberations are strictly confidential. When the judges return, everyone gathers in the small theater. The young magicians hold hands, waiting anxiously as the results are announced. Then comes Lubelo's age group.
"In first place, Lubelo Mthenjana!"
Beaming, he strides onto the stage to shake each judge's hand — then runs into his mother's arms.
As soon as he gets home, he will practice his newest tricks.

Fintech startup Mochatrade, which offers US Stock tokens trading platform for Indian traders, announced the raise of $5.5 Mn (₹52.3 Cr) in a seed funding round led by CoinFund, with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Zero Knowledge Ventures, among others. The startup will use the fresh capital to bolster its trading engine and risk infrastructure and expand its reach among active Indian traders. Founded in 2026 by Utkarsh Sinha, Chetan Manda and Parth Maheshwari, Mochatrade is building a trading platform that allows Indian retail traders and global investors to trade perpetual futures and price-tracking contracts linked to US stocks, cryptocurrencies, commodities and major indices. Its waitlist has crossed 25,000 sign-ups, although it is yet to announce a public launch date. The platform is expected to allow users to fund their accounts through UPI and track balances, margins and profit and loss (P&L) in Indian rupees (INR). The platform's perpetual futures contracts will allow traders to take long or short positions based on their expectations of price movements, without owning the underlying assets. Unlike conventional futures contracts, these instruments have no fixed expiry date. Mochatrade will also offer leveraged trading, allowing users to take larger positions with less upfront capital. However, leverage can amplify losses as well as gains. The startup plans to earn revenue through trading fees and eventually introduce contracts linked to select pre-IPO companies, US stock options and social trading features, subject to regulatory approvals. “India traded $1.9 Tn in options premium turnover last year. The appetite to trade is already here. But when Indians want to trade the US market, the product still feels foreign,” said Sinha, CEO of Mochatrade. Sinha previously cofounded crypto wallet Martian in 2022, which recorded more than 2 Mn installs and $2 Bn in transaction volume. Martian raised $3.6 Mn from Race Capital, Superscrypt and Jump Crypto before being acquired by Lightspeed-backed Pontem. Manda became Sprinklr’s youngest director of product in 2025, while Maheshwari worked on Photoshop for the web at Adobe before leading payments and credit infrastructure at Navi. Mochatrade is entering the market as Indian investors increasingly look overseas for exposure to global assets, particularly US stocks. According to RBI data, Indian residents remitted $2.65 Bn overseas for equity and debt investments in FY26, up from $1.51 Bn in FY24. Remittances reached $1.4 Bn between April and July FY27, with July alone accounting for $344.6 Mn, a 121% year-on-year increase. These figures cover overseas equity and debt investments across markets, rather than US stocks alone. At the same time, regulatory changes are reshaping India's domestic trading market. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has tightened futures and options (F&O) rules to curb excessive speculation and protect retail investors. Measures include limiting weekly expiries to one benchmark index per exchange, increasing contract sizes and tightening margin requirements. The changes have weighed on trading activity and revenue at several brokerage platforms, including Zerodha and Groww, during FY26. Against this backdrop, Mochatrade is betting that demand for global market exposure will create an opportunity for a trading platform built around Indian users. Its ability to convert waitlist interest into active traders will depend on its product experience, risk controls and the regulatory framework governing the contracts it plans to offer.

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.
The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.
Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.
As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.
Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.
I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.
Trump the deal-maker
Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary. Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.
But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.
The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.
While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.
“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.
But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.
“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.
In a recent piece, Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.
As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.
The way forward
Despite these wins, in terms of future bilateral relations, “there are at least three reasons for caution,” warns Vaishnav. First, he points to the onslaught of US actions that have dented Indian interests. Trump had imposed a punitive 50% tariff on India in 2025, which was reduced to 18% earlier this year, but without a comprehensive trade deal being reached. Second, on immigration, the White House’s H-1B visa and green card restrictions have disproportionately affected Indian workers in Silicon Valley.
“This has created a real trust deficit on the Indian side, and with good reason,” says Vaishnav. The frustration was on display earlier this month, when New Delhi branded remarks made by the US vice-president, JD Vance, about Indian professionals as “deeply offensive”. Furthermore, Vaishnav argues that while governments and private sector firms might be great at making announcements, they’re not always a guarantee of delivery.
His final caution is how political tensions can have a chilling effect. The trade negotiations offer a telling example: in January, the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, blamed the lack of a trade deal on Modi’s failure to phone Trump, a characterisation that New Delhi has disputed. Vaishnav says: “Much of the progress we are seeing is the product of decisions made years ago. It is one thing to keep existing projects moving, but turbulence in the relationship could make new initiatives a heavier lift.”
If India is serious about making its ambition to be a global powerhouse a reality, Vaishnav thinks there’s a clearcut way to win. “I would argue that the most important investment is political – ensuring India remains a robust, inclusive, participatory democracy,” he says. “On the economic front, India has made massive new investments in physical and digital infrastructure. But the returns on those investments will be limited unless the government doubles down on reforms: more efficient dispute resolution, an impartial legal system, even-handed tax enforcementand regulatory certainty.”
Ultimately, neither side can afford to treat the other as expendable. The test now is whether strategic foundations can hold at a time of global political upheaval.

In a press statement, the venue said certain photos were “inconsistent” with its policy.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Film-maker Ritu Sarin, director of the annual Dharamshala international film festival, which runs from 29 October to 1 November, suggests a film from this year’s lineup:
“Shot over three years on real locations, Anmol Sidhu’s sophomore feature, Flowers of Acacia, follows wedding orchestra dancers in rural Punjab with a gaze that allows all the large brutalities and smaller intimacies to shine through. Sidhu’s confident, consummate grasp of the medium is on full display in terrifying scenes that stretch to the edge of what is palatable. The camera refuses to look away.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
7,633
That’s the number of trees Mumbai’s municipal authorities authorised to be felled over five months this year, to make way for development works, according to the Indian Express. Of these, about 3,500 will be permanently removed, while the rest will be replanted elsewhere.
Vibe check
Prarthna Singh has consistently placed the female identity at the heart of her artistic practice, documenting Indian women’s aspirations and acts of rebellion in male-dominated spaces. When commissioned to photograph rkivecity’s menswear line, made from discarded clothes reworked into new garments, she turned that same gaze outward. The setting was the acclaimed 151-year-old Mayo College boys’ school in Ajmer, Rajasthan – Singh attended the linked girls’ school, and credits it with shaping her rebellious spirit.
“I was thinking about how I could bring a sense of intimacy and camaraderie of boarding-school life to the images, because that exists,” she told me. One image shows a pair of hands holding another boy’s jacket, the faces left out of the frame, so the garment stands in for the familiarity they share. Seeing this work against the backdrop of students taking to the streets to fight for their rights lends the series a lasting significance. “This was just my way of showing all of this is connected. These worlds are not existing separately,” said Singh.

- Fortnite One Piece collab releases on November 1, 2026, after the downtime for Treasure Hunters Mini Season ends.
- The One Piece collab includes the Going Merry, numerous Fortnite skins, Mythics, and map changes.
- There are rumors of a Luffy Sprite coming to Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season as part of the collab.
The Fortnite One Piece collab is real, and it’s going to break the internet in more ways than one. What started as rumors in 2021, with the arrival of a glider that resembled Laboon, has finally culminated in a crossover that’s nothing short of historic. If you’re an anime fan, here’s everything you need to know about the Fortnite One Piece collab including its release date, skins, and more.
When Is One Piece Coming to Fortnite?
The One Piece Fortnite collab releases on November 1, 2026, once the Fortnite downtime ends for update 43.00. It is the main collab for the upcoming Treasure Hunters Mini Season, and the Straw Hat Pirates’ flagship, Going Merry, is going to replace the Fortnite Battle Bus.
This is a huge moment for fans, as they get to ‘walk the plank’ off of the Going Merry to dive towards the new Fortnite Island. It’s a change of pace from the regular Battle Bus, but don’t forget to thank the driver all the same.
Fortnite One Piece Collab Skins
In the newly released Fortnite Treasure Hunters trailer, we get to see quite a few characters from the One Piece franchise. The star of the show is undoubtedly Luffy, but there are many others such as Nami, Zoro, Usopp, Ace, and Buggy. Sanji has also been spotted in the background, which means Epic Games is trying their best to keep him as a surprise for fans.
A total of seven One Piece characters are being featured as skins in Fortnite Treasure Hunters, which is a huge deal. As seen from the official keyart, two of them, Buggy the Star Clown and Monkey D. Luffy, are even part of the Battle Pass. The rest will be listed in the Fortnite Item Shop.
Aside from skins, there is some speculation that Tony Tony Chopper, a very popular One Piece character, is going to feature as a Sidekick in Fortnite. He could also be part of the Treasure Hunters Battle Pass.
Fortnite One Piece Weapons and Items
Based on what could be seen in the Fortnite Treasure Hunters trailer, at least three Mythic weapons and one item will be part of the One Piece collab. Starting with the obvious, Luffy is getting his own Mythic, which will give players access to the Gum-Gum Rocket and Pistol ability.
We don’t know what Zoro’s Mythic is called, but we do know it functions as a melee weapon in Fortnite. Players can wield three swords, as seen in the trailer, and use them to fight. Lastly, we have Usopp’s Slingshot Mythic, which should function similarly to the Cobalt Slingshot from the Fortnite Reload Simpsons update.
Coming to Mythic items, we can see Nami carry a Tangerine. In One Piece’s lore, she grows them herself and is high in Vitamin C, which means it’s a healing item in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. This could be used by players to recover HP/Shields or get some buffs.
Fortnite One Piece Map Changes
A new island has been introduced as part of the One Piece collab for Fortnite Treasure Hunters, and is shaped in the form of a skull and bones. In the trailer for the upcoming Mini Season, we see three distinct locations related to the One Piece collab on this new island.
One of them is the One Piece Fortnite Treasure Chest that has been on the Battle Royale since Fortnite update 42.40 went live. The other two locations seem to be Arlong Park and Foosha Village. This can’t be confirmed just yet, but they resemble these locations rather closely.
Based on the size and layout of the island, there could be up to eight unique POIs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. We will get more in-depth information about these POIs later this week, hopefully during Fortnite downtime for update 43.00. Lord of the Coast could also be a Landmark on the map, but this can’t be confirmed at the moment.
That’s about everything we know about the One Piece collab in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. On an ending note, remember to enter any remaining Admin Panel Fortnite Lobby Hack Codes as they expire at the end of this month.
If you’ve completed your current Battle Pass and have nothing to do, head over to the Fortnite Chapter 7 Override Recap website to see how you performed this season.
Let us know if you are going to be ‘walking the plank’ on November 1, 2026, and joining in on the action in Fortnite Treasure Hunters.

Households in parts of Eastern district without water after pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan
Burst suspected to have been caused by construction work, with Hong Kong authorities conducting repairs and aiming to restore supply by midnight
Households in four areas of Hong Kong’s Eastern district have been left without fresh water after a pipe burst in Shau Kei Wan, with authorities expecting the water supply to resume before midnight.
A video circulating on social media on Tuesday showed water gushing from the ground at a worksite near a bus stop, with an excavator parked nearby.
The Water Supplies Department said on its website that the water supply was cut at 11am, affecting Sai Wan Ho, Shau Kei Wan, Aldrich Bay and the area from A Kung Ngam Road to Island Garden.
Eastern district councillor Wong Chi-chueng told the South China Morning Post that the burst pipe was outside 312 Shau Kei Wan Road and was suspected to have been caused by construction work carried out by a Highways Department contractor.

Luxury watch brand Rotoris has raised $8.5 Mn (₹80.9 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from 100Unicorns, Centricity, Diwakar Goel’s family office, Atul Singh’s family office, Adhiraj Burman’s family office, and Rannvijay Singha. The D2C startup said it would deploy the fresh capital towards research and development, expanding production capacity, and growing its Rotoris House retail footprint in India and overseas, including Mumbai and New York. Founded in 2025 by Bella Vita’s founder Aakash Anand, Wolfpack Labs’ founding partner Prerna Gupta, and Drink Free Advertising Media’s cofounders Anant Narula and Kunal Kapania, Rotoris aims to build “India’s first global watch brand”. It operates as a luxury watch brand, selling limited-edition watches through an invitation-only membership programme called the Rotoris Registry. Rotoris assembles and tests its watches at its Rotoris Atelier in Gurugram, using machinery sourced from Switzerland. The startup said its assembly processes were established with guidance from Swiss horologists with experience at watchmakers and luxury brands such as Patek Philippe, IWC and Tiffany & Co. “The design creates the desire, but the engineering, assembly and attention to detail earn the trust. We are building both sides of Rotoris with the same level of intention,” Gupta said. The startup launched its first collection of 2,100 numbered watches in February 2026, which it claims sold out within days. Since then, nearly 1 Lakh people have registered for access to its collections, with around 40% of demand coming from international markets, including the US, Dubai and Australia. Prior to this round, Rotoris bagged $3 Mn in a seed funding round co-led by Zerodha’s Nikhil Kamath, VC firms Venture Catalysts and 100Unicorns as well as actor Vivek Oberoi and content creator Tanmay Bhat, in December last year. The country's luxury watch market size is expected to grow at a 5.7% CAGR from $1.8 Bn in 2025 to $2.9 Bn by 2034. In this growing market, the analog watch segment holds the leading type share at 62.4% in 2025, while the men's segment leads end user demand at 48.9%. Rotoris bids to challenge the legacy luxury watch brands like Seiko, Tissot, Citizen, and Rado, who have established a strong foothold in the segment. Beside the Aakash Anand-led startup, Bangalore Watch Company and Jaipur Watch Company are also emerging contenders in the premium watch category.

Typhoon Champi was declared the strongest storm of the year so far after recording sustained winds of 185mph last week. From late Thursday to early Saturday, the typhoon battered Taiwan and Japan’s southern islands. Champi approached the east coast of Taiwan before the centre of the storm turned south along the Yilan County coastline, looping offshore and then tracking northwards away from the island. The storm brought gusts of up to 141mph and 48-hour rainfall totals of more than 620mm to parts of Yilan.
So far, the death toll remains at one, with 527 reported injured. There were widespread power outages, with more than 288,000 houses having no electricity at one point, although most had since been reconnected. Champi has been downgraded to a tropical storm as it rapidly weakens to the south-west of Japan’s mainland on Monday.
For the fourth time in October, parts of Greece are at risk of flooding. In the early part of this week, low pressure will bring severe thunderstorms and longer spells of heavy rain to much of the country, and this will be followed by a deep area of low pressure passing across southern areas.
The national meteorological agency issued warnings for Monday, with 30mm-60mm of rain forecast in a 12-hour period across central areas, and50mm-80mm in the north-east Aegean Islands. Forecast models indicate the potential for similar totals in a 12-hour period between Wednesday and Thursday, making further flooding possible.
A low-pressure system developed into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal this weekend. Cyclone Arnab is expected to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coast by Wednesday. The India meteorological department has alerts in place for extreme heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong surface winds across the eastern side of the country.
Models are forecasting gusts of up to 85mph, and six-hourly rainfall totals of up to 100mm, as the storm makes landfall, currently expected on Wednesday. From then, the system is set to drift to the north before gradually dying out over north-east India at the end of the week.

The global trailer of Gondhal, directed by Santosh Davakhar, has been released ahead of the film’s worldwide theatrical release on November 13, 2026. The psychological thriller, which is India’s official submission for the 99th Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category, will release in seven languages: Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada and English.
Gondhal trailer out: Santosh Davakhar’s Oscar-submitted film to release in seven languages on November 13, 2026
According to the makers, the multilingual release will cover markets including India, the US, the UK, Europe, Australia, Dubai and Africa. The film’s makers have described it as the first Marathi film to receive a seven-language global theatrical rollout.
Set against the cultural traditions of Maharashtra, Gondhal follows newlyweds Suman and Anandrao, whose lives take an unsettling turn as personal desires, marital responsibilities and devotion begin to intersect. The trailer offers glimpses of the couple’s strained circumstances and a series of mysterious events that form the basis of the psychological thriller.
Santosh Davakhar on bringing Gondhal to a global audience
Speaking about the film’s international reach, writer-director Santosh Davakhar said he wanted to introduce audiences to a lesser-seen aspect of Indian culture through the story.
“Global perceptions of Indian cinema are often shaped by narratives of poverty and caste conflict – important realities, but not the complete expression of India. Gondhal is not a film but generations of culture, people, traditions coming together. Getting the world to know about this tradition is something that makes me immensely happy,” he said.
View this post on Instagram
Davakhar also spoke about the role of international film platforms in bringing regional stories to audiences beyond their place of origin. “Global festivals like academy awards help filmmakers to bring forth the ethnicity of our very roots across continents and not only in India. To experience India in its truest form. I created this film to bring one such powerful tradition to the global screen through a culturally authentic and universal cinematic language,” he added.
Gondhal’s Oscar journey and cast
Gondhal has been selected as India’s official submission for the 99th Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category. The makers have also said the film is being considered in multiple categories, although further details about those submissions have not been specified.
Davakhar previously won the Silver Peacock for Best Director at the 56th International Film Festival of India (IFFI). The festival jury described Gondhal as “like a Shakespearean fable set in a real world.”
The film stars Ishita Deshmukh, Kishor Kadam, Yogesh Sohani and Nishad Bhoir. It is produced by Santosh Davakhar and Diksha Davakhar under the banner of Davakhar Films, with cinematography by Amalendu Chaudhary. The film opens with a 25-minute unbroken take, according to the makers.
Gondhal is scheduled to arrive in theatres worldwide on November 13, 2026.

Rangers manager Derek McInnes admits feeling "guilt" about leaving Hearts for Ibrox in the summer and accepts the rough reception that could come his way when he returns to Tynecastle on Wednesday.

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.
Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.
What makes it different
Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.
The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.
Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.
How was is developed
The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.
Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.
According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.
Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.
A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Cultivation factors
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.
At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.
On the other hand, at these locations, kufri manik yielded 31.52 tonnes per hectare and kufri neelkanth 36.61 tonnes per hectare. Further, kufri jamunia could moderately resist late blight, a disease caused by the water mould Phytophthera infestans, in laboratory conditions but has been reported as ‘susceptible’ in the field. Late blight is a devastator of potato crops and the CPRI team has already recommended that farmers apply fungicide.
Next, the multi-location trials also produced 29.19 tonnes of marketable potatoes per hectare, versus 33.48 tonnes for kufri neelkanth. So if the costs of cultivation were equal, kufri jamunia farmers could need a 15% premium on the selling price to attain the same gross revenue. (A study published by a CPRI in Indian Horticulture in 2020 estimated that, for regular potatoes, the seed material accounted for 40-50% of the production costs vis-a-vis regular potatoes, with a per-hectare seed cost of around ₹60,000-75,000 per hectare.)
Many unknowns
Taken together, there are many unknowns about kufri jamunia at this point to assess its overall cost-benefit ratio, including the cost of seeds and disease management, pricing, its uptake in the market, and how efficaciously it will deliver iron and zinc to the population. It would be premature as a result to deem kufri jamunia to be a proven solution to address India’s hidden hunger.

There is now proof for what we have suspected all along: What you eat will determine your quality of life. A new study that was conducted by Chennai-based Madras Diabetes Specialties Centre and the University of Reading, U.K., has found a link between quality of diet and the Asian Indian predisposition to high cholesterol. High and uncontrolled cholesterol levels are associated with a high cardiovascular disease profile.
The study, Low diet quality increases the genetic risk of high blood cholesterol levels in Asian Indian adults [CURES–165], was published last week in the international peer-reviewed journal PLOS ONE, and are considered to advance the understanding of how diet and genetic factors interact to influence cholesterol levels.
The researchers analysed data from 1,020 adults (25–80 years), comprising 452 men and 568 women, who participated in the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study (CURES). The study examined three genetic variants of two genes :TCF7L2 and FTO, with a known association with diabetes and other metabolic disorders.
Researchers found that a poor quality diet amplified the genetic susceptibility to high cholesterol. Study participants who already had a higher genetic risk and who consumed a poor-quality diet had significantly higher total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels. Conversely, researchers proved that among participants consuming medium- or high-quality diets, there were no significant differences in cholesterol levels between the high- and low-genetic-risk groups were not observed. Individuals with higher genetic risk had significantly higher fasting blood glucose and HbA1c levels.
Among the key messages is that genetic susceptibility alone does not necessarily translate into adverse cholesterol levels under all dietary conditions. Naturally, these findings support the role of sticking to healthy diets to counter cardiometabolic risk. This is particularly significant in India, witnessing a literal explosion of cases of diabetes, rising cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease. Researchers said there could be a role for precision nutrition, The findings also open up new possibilities for precision nutrition, where dietary advice is tailored to an individual’s genetic and metabolic characteristics.
Commenting on the results of the study, V. Mohan, Chairman, Madras Diabetes Research Foundation, who was also a co-author of the study, said the key message is that our genes alone “need not determine an individual’s metabolic destiny.” With adjusting of the diet, it is possible to lower the risk, even when the genetic load is present.

Amazon just issued new guidelines for software engineers in the AI era: Prioritize business outcomes over raw usage.
Terk Terkowitz, Amazon's vice president and distinguished engineer, said in a memo published Tuesday that AI is changing software development more quickly and fundamentally than earlier shifts such as cloud computing. But engineers should be judged by their impact on customers and the business, he wrote, not simply how much they use AI.
"We all need to embrace this change and take the time to learn, or we risk being left behind," Terkowitz said.
AI coding tools and agents are upending the software industry and changing what it means to be a coder. Amazon calls this the "era of the Renaissance Developer," where human judgement and machine intelligence combine to create new products and services faster and more efficiently.
"This is a time of change for our industry, and a time of change for what it means to be a software engineer," Terkowitz wrote in the memo.
The updated guidelines reflect Amazon's growing effort to make AI adoption part of how it assesses engineers and engineering managers. The company has tracked measures including AI usage, token consumption, and lines of code internally, and used leaderboards to rank teams by some of those metrics.
But the memo warns that using such measures as targets can produce bad outcomes, including "tokenmaxxing" rather than better software or customer experiences.
"Using these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes," Terkowitz wrote in the memo.
Amazon has been experimenting with ways to measure and encourage AI use across its engineering organization.
Earlier this year, the company was tracking engineers's use of internal AI tools and some teams used leaderboards tied to measures such as token consumption. The programs created friction among some employees, who worried that pressure to use AI could reward wasteful activity rather than productive work.
The new guidance offers Amazon's clearest public acknowledgment of that risk. Rather than lay out a detailed AI playbook that could quickly become obsolete, Amazon said its revised developer guidelines focus on long-term impact on customers and the business.
Still, the company said AI should be "at the center of software engineering practice" and urged engineers to incorporate the technology into their daily work.
Leaders are expected to use AI tools on production work themselves, understand where they help and where they fall short, and explain that judgment to their teams, according to the memo.
Terkowitz said Amazon has found that metrics such as token use, AI-tool adoption, and code reviews can correlate with the outcomes it values. But he said the measures must be used carefully. More token use can raise costs, while a focus on lines of code can create unnecessary complexity.
He also recommended that managers pay particular attention to teams at both ends of the AI adoption spectrum: those in the bottom 10%, to understand why they are not using AI effectively, and those in the top 10%, to determine whether heavier use is translating into faster delivery.
Terkowitz said Amazon's most AI-forward "frontier teams" have shown stronger productivity and delivery. He also said teams and individuals that are not adopting AI or increasing output metrics are falling behind.
But his memo left room for engineers whose work may not yet benefit from current AI tools. In those cases, he said, employees should document why and work toward a solution by sharing their findings with peers and managers.
"An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for," the memo said.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

United States GP: Martin Brundle's verdict on 'outstanding' Kimi Antonelli win in Austin and Oscar Piastri's struggles in 2026 F1 cars
Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle gives his verdict on Kimi Antonelli's "outstanding" performance which puts him on the brink of becoming F1's youngest world champion and the struggles for McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Mercedes' George Russell
Tuesday 27 October 2026 10:34, UK
Given that Red Bull and Ferrari, and from time to time McLaren, have undoubtedly closed down the pace advantage enjoyed by Mercedes in the first half of the season, it was looking possible that Kimi Antonelli might win the World Championship perhaps not fully in the style he would have wanted.
His Austin qualifying and race performances demolished that concern in the most comprehensive way.
From seemingly nowhere, he produced a stormer of an initial time in the third and final top-10 shootout to secure pole position and deny Max Verstappen's Red Bull and the two Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, all of whom had seemed likely to beat him. It was his seventh pole of the season but his first since Spa back in the summer eight races ago, and therefore very timely.
