Srinagar, Oct 27: Leader of Opposition Sunil Sharma on Tuesday criticised the Jammu and Kashmir cabinet expansion, alleging that the government had failed to maintain regional and cultural balance.
Speaking to reporters after the induction of four new ministers into the Omar Abdullah-led government, Sharma congratulated the newly inducted ministers but said governments must represent all regions and sections of society.
“Governments are formed not just to win elections. Governments have to take every section along. Every region, every area has to be taken along. Religious, regional and cultural balance has to be maintained. Today, that was not seen,” Sharma said.
Asked about the removal of the portfolio held by cabinet minister Satish Sharma, the BJP leader said it was too early to comment.
“Right now, it would not be appropriate to say anything,” he said, adding that he would first congratulate the new ministers.
On questions about discontent within the National Conference over the cabinet expansion, Sharma said the matter concerned the party internally and had nothing to do with him.
“Who is upset and who is happy with them is none of our concern. This is their organisation’s internal matter,” he said.
When reminded of his earlier remark that the National Conference would split on the day of the cabinet expansion, Sharma urged patience, saying only a few minutes had passed since the ceremony.
“Have some patience. Please be patient; you will get to know everything,” he said.

There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself. Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot. And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life.
When AI agents run your life
Muse, organize my life. Make no mistakes.
This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout. She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools. Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift. They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’”
Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload. They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet. But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents.
Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her. She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said. “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present. And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’”
Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do. But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology?
On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me, I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out. Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT.
“I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive. It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.”
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
What agents are out there right now?
At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse.
There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots. But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall.
You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote. How was that experience?
One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch. It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain. We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors. We have this specific budget. I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us.
One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace. There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me.
I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well. I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find. Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off.
Is that how this tech is typically used?
Most people are using this as part of a workflow. I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life. But people have been quite creative.
One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel. So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons.
I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me. I don’t love that concept.
That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies.
When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details. The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models.
I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize.
What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive.
Yes, especially because it’s all about automation. If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about.
There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account. And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see.
Oh no.
I would be mortified. So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make. If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing.
“You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.”
How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now. Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state. People are not loving it. How are they trying to sell this to the average person?
The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now. You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools. They’ve really, really leaned into cuteness and into adorable mascots.
Muse, if you haven’t seen its agent, looks like a mix between a Labubu and an Ewok. It’s very furry, very cuddly, very cute. OpenAI’s tools also have similar kinds of blobs with large eyes that might be a little endearing.
I feel like companies are hearing this kind of feedback that people aren’t trusting AI right now, or maybe they have moral or ethical reasons they don’t want to use these tools. You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.
Do you think AI agents are ultimately going to worm their way into our lives despite how unpopular AI companies are?
I do think so. I think in a couple months, maybe when I go home from Christmas, I would not be surprised if my mom had an agent on her phone because it does feel like it’s breaking through to average people in the way that ChatGPT had a moment a few years ago.
Even though there’s a lot of distrust for large companies like Meta, I think there are some appealing parts of this that will bring in millions of people. I do see this as the future of the internet.
When I think of the dream of the average person working in AI in Silicon Valley, it’s “We’re going to use AI. It’s going to free up the free time of so many people. Work is going to get done faster. You’re going to have more leisure time.”
Has that been the case for the people you’ve spoken with who are using this? Has it given them more free time to enjoy themselves or has it done something else?
You would think so, right? You would think that if people are automating these boring aspects of their life, that they would have more time to go touch grass, go see a movie, have some fun. But it does feel like that time just gets filled with other work, other productivity measures.
While agents may be able to take some more annoying or tedious things off of your plate, I am not as optimistic that it’s going to give us this utopia or freedom where I’m always at the beach.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a comeback after a first-round setback to win a fourth term in office, securing 51.8% of the vote against right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro. His victory followed an intensive runoff campaign that combined youth mobilisation, a revamped social media strategy, opposition to the Bolsonaro family and a series of popular economic and welfare measures.
The 80-year-old incumbent had described his first-round campaign as the most “disorganized” in decades. Ahead of the runoff, he changed his digital outreach, sought support from young influencer politicians and encouraged supporters to take their campaign both online and onto the streets.
Here are four factors that may have contributed to Lula's election victory.
Quick answers to key questions
Lula’s campaign mobilised young voters, expanded its social media outreach, framed the election around opposition to a Bolsonaro return, and highlighted welfare and workers’ rights measures. Persuading more voters to participate in the runoff also contributed.
The “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel grew from 60,000 followers to nearly 11 million in about three weeks. It gave supporters messages and tasks to share online, helping spread campaign content and encourage voter mobilisation.
Students and young people organised rallies in major cities and supported Lula’s social policies and promises to defend minority rights. Political scientist Eduardo Grin described their mobilisation as fundamental to the campaign.
Lula’s supporters presented the runoff as a choice between his agenda and the return of the Bolsonaro family. Concerns about democracy, social rights and the former government’s record helped give opponents of Bolsonaro a shared reason to mobilise.
The campaign highlighted a reform guaranteeing workers two days of rest per week, welfare payments rescheduled to arrive before the runoff, and debt relief for small-scale entrepreneurs. Lula also pledged increased Bolsa Família payments and broad debt relief for struggling households.
Youth mobilisation emerged as a key feature of Lula's runoff campaign after his first-round setback. Students and young people organised rallies in Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo and Belo Horizonte, chanting slogans such as “Bolsonaro never again” and expressing support for Lula's social policies and promises to defend minority rights.
“The mobilization of young people was fundamental,” Eduardo Grin, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV), told AFP.
Lula's Workers' Party (PT) had managed to reconnect with younger voters, Grin said. The president also compared the mobilisation to the 1984 movement that demanded elections during Brazil's military dictatorship.
The street demonstrations gave the campaign a visible grassroots presence at a critical stage of the Brazil election. They also helped supporters rally around concerns about social rights and the possibility of the Bolsonaro family returning to power.
Lula's campaign also sought to counter the political right's strong online influence by overhauling its social media strategy.
The incumbent enlisted young influencer politicians, bought his first cellphone and described himself as the “king of the selfie”. His supporters, meanwhile, spent hours sharing political content online and speaking to voters in person.
The scale of the digital push was reflected in the growth of the “Lula's Army” WhatsApp channel. It expanded from 60,000 followers to nearly 11 million in just three weeks, according to the report.
Publicist Taiza Mendonca, 36, told AFP that the effort demanded considerable time outside her regular working hours. Even older supporters, including her “60-year-old aunties”, learned to use hashtags, she said.
Oliver Stuenkel of the FGV also described the sustained activity of left-wing supporters, who spent hours posting content and engaging voters offline.
The campaign's digital outreach helped supporters circulate messages and mobilise voters beyond rallies and traditional campaign events.
Another factor was the effort to frame the election as a choice between Lula's agenda and a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, emerged as the right-wing candidate with the backing of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro. During the campaign, Flavio called his father his “compass” and promised to secure his release if elected.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence over an attempted coup following his 2022 election defeat, according to the supplied report.
Critics of the former president pointed to rising hunger, his administration's handling of the Covid-19 pandemic, violence against minorities and environmental policies that they said denied climate change.
Grin argued that street mobilisation and social media activity helped create concern about a return of the Bolsonaro family and the implications for democracy and social rights.
The strategy gave Lula's supporters a common message around which to mobilise. Rather than focusing exclusively on the incumbent's record, the campaign also sought to highlight the risks its supporters associated with a Bolsonaro return.
Lula's campaign was also accompanied by a series of measures aimed at workers, welfare recipients and small-scale entrepreneurs.
Congress approved a reform guaranteeing workers two days of rest per week, a key campaign pledge. The government also rescheduled October welfare payments so recipients would receive them before the runoff rather than afterwards.
These steps came alongside debt-forgiveness measures for small-scale entrepreneurs and other initiatives described in the report as popular with voters.
Defending the timing of the benefits, Lula said during a campaign interview: “I'm not going to stop granting a benefit I can grant just because there are elections.”
The measures allowed the incumbent to highlight policies with direct implications for household finances, working conditions and small businesses in the run-up to voting.
While the timing may have helped keep these issues in the campaign spotlight, the available information does not establish the independent electoral impact of each measure.

Artiva Biotherapeutics said Tuesday that it’s winding down after two patients died in a trial testing its cell therapy for autoimmune diseases, the latest in a series of safety events that emerged in a promising research field.
One participant in the Phase 2 study died from a neurological complication after receiving the treatment, an NK cell therapy. Researchers, however, determined the death was likely not related to the cell therapy itself, but to a chemotherapy that was given before the cell therapy, Artiva said. It’s standard to give patients chemotherapies before infusing cell therapies to lower the patients’ white blood cell count and make room for the new cells.
A second participant experienced sudden death about two months after treatment. Researchers determined that this was not related to any component of the treatment process, but the cause of death has not been determined, the San Diego-based company said.

Last year, Google DeepMind sent gaming stocks tumbling with the reveal of its Genie 3 world model. Since then, world models have become a major focus of AI labs around the world, but Google isn’t resting on its laurels. Researchers have been hard at work on an updated model that improves on Genie 3 in almost every way. And if you pay Google enough money, you might actually get to use Genie 4 before too long.
It’s easy to look at the output of Genie 4 and see a video game, which is why Genie 3 caused so much consternation in the gaming industry. DeepMind doesn’t think about it that way, though. According to Google, world models are a key element in the march toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). A world model creates a virtual world, but it doesn’t require pre-rendering environments or programming interactive elements. You simply tell the model what you want, and it generates the experience frame by frame in real time as you explore it.
DeepMind says this technology could create infinite training environments for physical robots or unlock new avenues of rapid prototyping for creative fields. Of course, that requires the model to accurately simulate what you want. Genie 4 has several improvements that make its simulations more useful, and that’s thanks in part to Google’s updated Gemini models.
When you prompt a world into existence in Genie 4, it leverages Gemini 3.8 Flash as a guiding agent to break down goals and evaluate each output frame. This helps keep the simulation on track, letting you move through varying environments without losing the original context. However, DeepMind notes that Genie 4 worlds still only remain consistent for a couple of minutes before they forget how things started.
Like Genie 3, the new version supports changing the parameters midstream. You can change the weather, add elements, or move the camera, and Gemini will help steer the simulation with each update. This is similar to the way reasoning models generate additional internal prompts to zero in on the right output tokens.

With a tactile dongle for on-the-fly customization and a metal chassis, the Wallhack M-001 is the most fun I've had reviewing a gaming mouse in a long time.
Magnesium shell. Hot-swappable, rechargeable batteries. 52-gram weight. Functional and innovative dongle. Satisfying tactile experience. Great styling and design language.
TIRED
High price point. Slightly outdated sensor. Only 2.4G wireless connectivity with dongle; no Bluetooth or USB-C connectivity on mouse.
Batteries. They're not typically thought of as a significant source of innovation. Most companies have spent the last few years removing mice in favor of more lightweight designs.
That's what's made the return of the replaceable and rechargeable battery surprising—something I once thought to be a lost technology from a bygone era. A few companies have recently realized that the ability to pop out and replace your battery in seconds is a great way to extend mouse life without needing to increase battery size or efficiency.
From the handful of mice I’ve tested with hot-swappable batteries so far, Wallhack does it best. The mouse is designed around the function’s ease-of-use, and everything else comes together to make a mouse that feels not only competitive for gaming, but also well thought-out and satisfying to use in everyday life.
Effective Shape
The M-001’s shape is a standard right-handed, symmetrical design. This means the mouse’s left and right sides are shaped identically, but only the left side has thumb buttons. There are two main buttons, two side buttons, a standard ratcheting scroll wheel, and a power switch on the underside.
With a length of 120 mm, the M-001 is slightly shorter than contemporaries like the Razer Viper V4 Pro (125 mm) and Logitech Pro Superstrike X2 (127 mm). The overall width and height are comparable, at 63.5-mm tall and a 39-mm wide. The largest difference is the profile of the mouse: The front end sits significantly lower than other mice, and the rear has a more significant hump, which creates a more angled shape overall. When using a palm grip, this puts your hand at a slightly more aggressive forwards angle, with your palm sitting higher and your fingers pointing more downwards. It’s a slight difference, but I found this angle to be better for quick movements compared to a more “flat” design. However, like most shape-related choices, this is ultimately down to individual preference. (To compare mouse sizes, I typically use a website like eloshapes)
The two main buttons are lightly sculpted, with subtle concavity for fingers to comfortably rest in. Similarly, there is a subtle taper at the bottom center of the mouse which makes lifting and moving easier. The side buttons use a simple, rounded shape placed just above the taper, making it easy to rock your thumb upwards to press them without getting in the way. They’re just elevated enough that the buttons don’t recess into the shell when pressed. The only shape-related issue I had was the scroll wheel, which is a good bit more elevated than other mice. This isn’t a huge issue, and I adapted to it after a few hours of use, but it’s something I could see being off-putting for users accustomed to a lower-profile scroll wheel.
(Not) Heavy Metal
The most important part of this mouse’s construction is the magnesium shell, which provides significantly more rigidity than the plastic shells used on most mice. Because of this, the mouse feels incredibly sturdy and solid. The metal shell also gives the mouse a cool, slick feeling underneath your fingertips, which I prefer to the matte plastic feeling that most mice have.
Despite using metal, it only weighs 53.6 grams, making the M-001 quite light by most standards, It still falls slightly behind the Viper V4 Pro’s 50.3 grams and lags way behind Corsair’s superlight, 36-gram Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight. But the M-001 is incredibly solid, with none of the flexibility or flimsiness that most plastic mice have. When compared to other magnesium mice like the AngryMiao Infinity .97 or Corsair’s magnesium-shelled Sabre, the M-001 has an entirely solid upper shell without any cutouts or holes, which feels much better for regular use with a multitude of grip styles (plus, it’s much less likely to have dust, dead skin, or anything else build up inside of it). While the full magnesium shell increases weight, it’s a worthwhile trade-off for a smooth and rigid shape.
It’s also worth noting that some of Wallhack’s promotional material depicts the mouse as being a solid black color, but this isn’t quite the case. The unit I received is much closer to a gunmetal color, with a significant amount of metallic flake across the finish. The color looks fantastic in person, but it's difficult to properly capture in images.
Flipping over this mouse reveals one of the more atypical design decisions being made: the lack of a bottom shell. Instead of an entire underside, there is a thin frame around the circumference of the mouse that holds six feet in place. Between them is a chasm that reveals the entire PCB and battery.
Of particular note is the PCB’s function inside the mouse: Instead of simply sitting inside of the shell, the PCB works as a primary structural component. Similar techniques have been used in designing supercars and sport bikes, with the Ferrari F50 using the engine block as a stressed member that provides rigidity to the entire car, a technology borrowed from Ferrari’s F1 team. This provides some obvious benefits to rigidity and weight-savings, but it’s also just undeniably cool to be able to flip over your mouse and see the entire circuit board.
Right behind the PCB is the star of the show, a hot-swappable battery. While I’ve tested quite a few mice with this technology, none of them have managed to make the battery-swapping so satisfying. Instead of being attached with magnets or a rotating locking mechanism, the batteries use a custom-made -spring-loaded ejector similar to an SD card or a Nintendo Switch cartridge. To insert the battery, simply press until you feel a click, and it will lock into place. To remove it, do the same: press until you feel a click, and it will pop out slightly. Of all the mice I’ve tested with removable batteries, this is by far my favorite mechanism to use: It’s intuitive, fun, and feels sturdy.
This battery system does come with a trade-off. Because hot-swappable batteries means an effectively-infinite battery life (as long as you remember to plug the old one into the dongle when you swap), Wallhack has decided to entirely remove the USB-C port on the mouse. This means it only functions as a 2.4G wireless mouse and cannot be plugged or charged in directly. This isn’t a huge issue (it never inconvenienced me, since there was always a fully charged battery ready to swap in), and it theoretically means the connection quality will be better, since there’s fewer components between the antenna and the receiver. But it is worth noting that, if a battery dies or your dongle craps out, there’s no other way to use this mouse.
The Perfect Dongle
In every high-polling mouse I’ve reviewed, the dongle has been a bit of a pain point. A high polling rate necessitates proximity, which in turn requires in a small thing sitting on your desk. In most cases, these things have only one or two functions: They connect to the mouse, and they maybe have a small number of LED indicators (between 1 and 3) that can display battery life, connection quality, or some other setting. Almost every time, they’re small and light enough to slide around on your desk and will inevitably end up falling behind it once or twice due to the weight of the cable pulling it back.
With the M-001, nearly all of these issues are resolved: The dongle is given purpose, function, and I’d even argue dignity. Instead of the small, existing-by-necessity designs that most manufacturers ship with their mice, Wallhack has managed to make a beautiful piece of industrial design. The dongle is a medium-sized metal wedge sporting a gunmetal gray finish identical to the mouse. It has two camera-like dials up front, a button, and a slot for a rechargeable battery. The DPI dial features numbering from 400 to 25,600, and the polling dial goes from 125 Hz to 8,000 Hz.
The dials both have LED indicators next to them, which illuminate alongside the mouse to indicate a setting being changed. When rotated, they both have a satisfying ratcheting mechanism that’s stiff enough to avoid accidental inputs, without being difficult to turn using a single finger.
While I loved these dials from the moment I saw them, I really didn’t expect to use them much. I’ve always been more of a set-and-forget type of person. But after testing this mouse for a while, I regularly found myself using both of the dials: On-the-fly DPI adjustments were great for games like Marvel Rivals. I tended to prefer, for example, a higher DPI for Thing and a lower for Thor. Polling adjustments, too, were useful in situations where older games (like Destiny 2) got grumpy when I was using a mouse above 1,000 Hz.
Performance and Software
Like many mice today, the M-001 uses an in-browser customization client. Wallhack’s web client, Wallhack Terminal, takes a unique stylistic approach, relying on a black-and-white, text-based system that resembles Command Prompt more than a typical gaming software. This is both a breath of fresh air stylistically, and much more straightforward than some of the software I’ve used in the past.
The configurator has an extensive feature set, including adjustments for mouse rotation, acceleration, and lift-off distance, which is adjustable by millimeters instead of the vague Low/Medium/High that some softwares use. The sensor can also be pushed to scan faster than the mouse’s 8,000 Hz polling rate, which can potentially improve the accuracy of the sensor, but limits battery life.
Along with adjusting DPI and polling with the dials on the dongle, switching them to the red “DPI” And “Hz” text allows for more granular adjustments within the configurator.
The sensor inside the mouse is a Pixart PAW3950. For anyone who doesn’t have an exhaustive list of mouse sensors floating around their head, this is the same type of sensor used in the 2022 Razer Viper V2 Pro (branded as the Razer Focus Pro 30k). That's four years old at this point. It’s not quite a cutting-edge sensor anymore. But unless you're in the top-tier of competitive play, the sensor will feel consistent and reliable enough, being able to easily track and manage direction changes during fast-paced shootouts. My personal daily driver is a Viper V2 Pro with the exact same sensor (I prefer the shape to the V3 and V4), and it’s still perfectly serviceable after four years of use.
The main buttons inside this mouse use Omron Optical switches, while the side buttons opt for low-profile Omron blue-dot mechanical switches. The scroll wheel’s encoder is a mechanical unit as well, which means it doesn’t have quite the same longevity as the optical units some mice are beginning to use. However, they are easier to replace or fix if something does go wrong.
The internal design of this mouse is impressively simple: There are six feet on the underside, and the outer four all have screws underneath. When you remove these four screws, the bottom half of the shell comes off cleanly (no flimsy plastic clips!), and a few more screws separate the internals from the top shell.
Mice Should Be Fun
I’ve said many times that, when it comes to peripherals, technical specs are only one part of the story. More than that, it’s important to have a device you enjoy using. Of all the mice I’ve tested, the M-001 is by far one of the most enjoyable. The shape is comfortable and natural for multiple grip styles, and the material ensures that the mouse feels rigid and stable despite its light weight. The dongle is a brilliant design that elevates itself from a sad desk tchotchke to a practical and functional device. And the battery mechanism is one of the most clever and fun designs I’ve seen in ages.
Everything about this mouse is deeply satisfying, and I found myself excited to use it every time I sat down. Of course, this mouse isn’t at the cutting edge of sensors or switches, and because of this, I can’t exactly recommend this mouse to someone looking for an ultra-cost-effective option with min-maxed specs. But in using the mouse on the daily, I didn't find that it mattered as much as you might think. 8,000 Hz polling and a 25,600 DPI sensor are enough for all but the pros. Instead, it uses tried-and-true internals that function perfectly well and, more importantly, have crisp and precise tactile responses.
Henri Robbins is a WIRED contributor specializing in mechanical keyboards and PC peripherals. He also reviewed hardware for Input and Inverse. He graduated from Miami University, where he studied journalism, media and communications, and photography. He resides in Cincinnati. ... Read More

The recent protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and helmed by Opposition parties, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have exposed a chink in journalists’ armour. The crackdown on journalists, especially freelancers and independent journalists, during the October 10 protests, has rekindled the debate on who has the right to be recognised as a journalist and about who decides who is a journalist.
One has seen how during the CJP protests, both in July over the NEET paper leak and in October over the demand for the CEC’s removal, freelancers and independent journalists, and content creators descended in hordes at the protest venue already bulging at the seams with reporters from registered media houses. However, during the second round of protests on October 10, phalanxes of riot police removed them from the protest site and sent them to detention centres. Only journalists with the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP) accreditation were allowed to cover the protests.
A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, while hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) which seeks the protection of the right to freedom of expression by freelance journalists and content creators, wondered whether the right to freedom of expression empowered every citizen of this country to be a journalist. “If everyone starts becoming a journalist, it will create problems for every other person,” the CJI said. During the hearing, senior advocate Indira Jaisingh said that there must be a national protocol for police not to obstruct the professional work of any journalist who has an identity card from the employer. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said that in the present era, any person with a mobile phone could claim to be an independent or freelance journalist when he/she would, in fact, be making reels only to garner popularity on social media to earn money by either presenting one-sided stories or sensationalising events.
Recognising journalists
These developments have put the focus back on the question of who recognises journalists. As per the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, a working journalist is a person whose principal avocation is journalism and who is employed in a newspaper, electronic media or digital media. This definition excludes people employed in a managerial or administrative capacity. Further, Central and State governments provide accreditation to working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Accreditation recognises working journalists and others and gives them access to designated official sources of information. For journalists in Delhi-NCR, accreditation is provided by the PIB for covering the Central government while the DIP accreditation gives them the right to cover the Delhi State government. Media accreditation guidelines of the PIB and DIP define the eligibility criteria for all those seeking accreditation. However, one of the major issues with government accreditation is that it has a quota depending upon circulation (for newspapers, periodicals and magazines), subscribers (for news agencies), licence under uplinking and downlinking guidelines (for private satellite TV channels), and unique visitors (for digital news publishers). Therefore, all journalists in recognised media organisations don’t get accreditation. This leads us to the question on how all working journalists can be recognised.
One solution could be a national media council or commission. Just like there is the Bar Council of India for lawyers and an Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for chartered accountants, the media council can recognise all working journalists, freelance journalists, camerapersons and technicians. Just like you need a law degree to practise law, a medical degree to become a doctor, the media council may mandate a degree or diploma in journalism and mass communication while applying for a licence.
A few years ago, the Press Club of India drafted a Media Transparency (and Accountability) Bill, which mandated the formation of a national media council, among other things. Recently, some other journalists’ bodies have also submitted a memorandum to the government with the same demand. As more and more people with a camera claim to be freelance journalists, it may be high time for the government to give some serious thought to the idea of such a council.
Rakesh Goswami is Professor of Journalism at Indian Institute of Mass Communication, New Delhi

On the eve of her debut at the Wrestling World Championships, Kajal Dhochak made a call from Astana, to her family back in India.
It was a big occasion and her uncle Krishan Malik, who has coached her for most of her career, admits he was jittery. This was the biggest tournament of the 18-year-old’s career. But even as he tried to hide his nerves, the voice on the other end of the line was as cheerful as if she only had a routine training session the next day.
“ Aap tension mat lo, belt le ke aa rahi hu! (You don’t worry about anything. I’m coming back with the winner’s belt),” she told him.
Kajal has all but walked her talk. The youngest contender in the women’s 76kg category, she’s one step away from becoming the first Indian woman and only the second overall to win gold at the world championships.
She’s come through a stacked division, beating Asian Champion Enkh Amaryn Davaarnsarn in the quarterfinals and then came back from a 1-7 deficit to beat two time World silver medallist Aiperi Medet Kyzy to reach the final. She faces two time European champion Anastasia Alpyeyeva for a place on the top of the podium.
It’s unlikely she’s going to worry about her opponent’s pedigree though.
“Her best quality as a wrestler is that she has no fear. She doesn’t think who is in front of her. As a coach you always think your wrestler is the best but even when I have doubts, she is full of confidence,” Krishan says.
As far as Krishan can recall, Kajal has always been this way. “She always had a lot of belief in herself,” he says.
Krishan was a former international wrestler for India himself, competing in the heavyweight Greco Roman category. When his career wound down due to injury, he began coaching his nephew – Kajal’s elder brother. He didn’t think then that she would be interested. Indeed, Kajal’s father, a farmer, had only moved his family to Sonepat city, a short way from the national capital of Delhi, from the village of Laath some 20km away since it was felt that it would make it easier for her to study.
But although Kajal was a good student, she decided as an 11-year-old she, too, wanted to wrestle.
“Every time I took her brother out for practise, Kajal would start crying. She kept saying she also wanted to come and wrestle. I told her that wrestling is something that girls didn’t do. But she would cry and tell me that she still wanted to wrestle and that she could do it. Finally I let her come with me,” he recalls.
Krishan says he thought that initial enthusiasm would fade away. But that never happened. “I never had to force her to wrestle,” he says.
For the first few years, her training wasn’t particularly strenuous. She was studying and only trained a few days a week. She didn’t go to an academy but exercised on a makeshift mitti (sand) pit her uncle had made in a plot of land he owned. Back then wrestling was mostly a fun activity. Even Kajal’s mother Babita, started to learn the sport. “I wanted her to train as a wrestler simply so she could understand what it was that her daughter was doing. But she ended up even competing in a state level competition,” Krishan recalls.
But it was Kajal who progressed far further than anyone expected. “When she was small and had just started wrestling, she would say ‘one day I’m going to win an Olympic medal’,” says Babita. “At that time there was no real expectation that she would reach where she has. But at her very first tournament she won a gold medal at the Haryana State Championships. That’s when I thought that maybe something big is written in her destiny.”
These days Kajal trains with former national coach Kuldeep Malik in Sonepat and has since progressed rapidly from the state, to national and then international levels. She competed and won gold at the U-15 Asian Championships in 2022, then followed up with the U-17 title the next year. In 2024, she won the world U-17 title. In the last two years, she won successive golds at the Junior Worlds.
She also made her senior debut at the Asian Championships, but although she lost her opening bout – a narrow 5-3 defeat to Kazakhstan’s Gulmaral Yekerbayeva, she’s only improved ever since.
But the competitive streak in her meant that setback rankled her as much as every loss does. “She absolutely hates losing. Even as a child she would try to compete with everyone. If someone did an exercise in a certain amount of time, she had to beat it somehow. It doesn’t matter to her if she’s competing with a senior and she’s still not reached that same age. She always thinks she can win,” according to Babita.
That confidence has been reinforced with every tournament and win.
The 76kg women’s freestyle category has become one of India’s most competitive field and Kajal has slowly cemented her hold on it. At the start of the year, Kajal beat two time junior world champion Priya Malik to earn a place at the Asian Championships. Although she lost out to the same wrestler in the selection trials for the Asian Games, she bounced back by claiming a spot in the Indian team. A week ago, she would also beat Reetika Hooda, a silver medallist at the 2024 Asian Championships, at an informal dangal competition.
But the worlds are a massive step up in quality and it’s in that rarefied environment that Kajal has shown she belongs.
“It’s very strange because someone like me knows just how big the World Championships are. I know how tough the competition is. But Kajal doesn’t seem to realise it. Maybe it’s just that she’s so young but when I was talking to her about the competition a few days ago, she was laughing about it,” he says.
This doesn’t mean that Kajal hasn’t been tested. After pinning Lithuania’s Kamile Gaucaite in her opening round and trouncing Mongolia’s Asian Champion Enkh Amaryn Davaarnsarn 9-2 in the quarter finals, the Indian was thrown and nearly pinned herself by Kyzy in the semifinal. Down 1-7 early in the match, she eventually fought back, scoring four unanswered take downs to turn the match around.
That lack of intimidation may yet serve her well in the final. For Kajal, the World Championships are not the ultimate destination but another step towards a much bigger ambition.
“The world championships is one of the biggest platforms for a wrestler but Kajal is already thinking beyond it. Her dream is to win a medal at the 2028 Olympics. From the time she started wrestling she would tell us that her goal was to do that. The world championships are just one step towards that goal,” Krishan says.
Whatever happens in the final, Kajal has already announced herself as a wrestler to watch over the coming years.
“She’s already believed that she belonged at this level. Now others know it as well,” he says.

NDA wrests Bengaluru Teachers' seat from Congress, Kumaraswamy calls it historic
JD(S)-BJP NDA candidate AP Ranganath defeated Congress's Puttanna by 908 votes to wrest the Bengaluru Teachers' Constituency in the Karnataka MLC polls.
The Janata Dal (Secular) on Tuesday wrested the Bengaluru Teachers' Constituency in the Karnataka Legislative Council elections from the ruling Congress, with the NDA candidate AP Ranganath defeating sitting Congress MLC Puttanna by 908 votes.
Ranganath secured 10,810 votes, while Puttanna, who was seeking re-election, received 9,902 votes, according to a press release. The victory came as a test of coordination between the BJP and JD(S), which contested the election as allies.
The JD(S) and BJP celebrated the result, with JD(S) leader HD Kumaraswamy calling the victory historic and linking it to the 2028 Karnataka Assembly elections.
In a post on X, the JD(S) congratulated Ranganath, describing the result as a "resounding victory to the voice of teachers". The party thanked teachers and professors in the constituency for placing their trust in the candidate and supporting what it described as the welfare of teachers and the upliftment of the education sector.
The party also expressed gratitude to leaders, office-bearers and workers of both the BJP and JD(S), crediting their united campaign for the victory.
Kumaraswamy said the result marked the defeat of what he described as “lies, misgovernance, money power and muscle power”.
Congratulating Ranganath, the former Karnataka chief minister thanked workers of both alliance partners and teachers who, he alleged, had rejected inducements and the arrogance of power by casting their votes.
"This victory is historic," Kumaraswamy said, claiming that the result had demonstrated the strength of unity and alliance politics.
He also linked the outcome to the next Karnataka Assembly elections, saying it provided a clear political mandate for 2028. Kumaraswamy asserted that the alliance would bring about a change in the state, invoking the upcoming Deepavali festival in his message.
He expressed gratitude to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and former prime minister HD Deve Gowda, whom he described as the motivating forces behind the alliance.
Kumaraswamy also claimed that NDA candidates were certain to win the remaining three Legislative Council constituencies where counting was underway.
Nikhil Kumar, the party's young wing president, in a post on X, targeted Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over allegations concerning electoral processes, pointing out that the Bengaluru Teachers' Constituency election was conducted through paper ballots.
"No EVMs to blame, state machinery in your hands, and election conducted via paper ballots," he said, referring to the Congress government in Karnataka.
He questioned what explanation the Congress would offer for the outcome, asking whether the party's response would be "Paper Chori".
He also congratulated Ranganath and the leaders and workers of the BJP and JD(S) for the victory.
The Bengaluru contest was significant because Puttanna had switched from the JD(S) to the Congress before the previous Assembly elections. Both Puttanna and Ranganath belong to the Vokkaliga community.
The election was viewed as a test of whether the BJP and JD(S) could transfer their support to each other's candidates. The Congress, meanwhile, sought to retain its lone seat and make gains in the other constituencies.
Congress leader DK Shivakumar, Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee working president BK Hariprasad, ministers and senior party leaders had campaigned across the constituencies.

Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated, but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target.
A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it’s now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level.
The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.
Focusing on function
Some of the best protein design tools we have available right now work through a two-step process. First, you specify a set of constraints, such as the need to bind another molecule or to have a specific arrangement of amino acids. One AI tool then generates a protein shape that meets those constraints. Once that’s done, a separate tool populates that shape with a specific sequence of amino acids that can ensure the protein folds into the appropriate configuration to match the shape.
Obviously, doing that often requires a fair bit of technical knowledge. If you’re designing a catalyst, for example, then you not only need to know what amino acids are critical to get a chemical reaction to happen, but you have to know where they should be located within a 3D space. That, not surprisingly, requires a fairly sophisticated understanding of protein chemistry and the ability to express that understanding in whatever form that the protein design tools require.
The thing is, if two experts were talking to each other, they wouldn’t need to get that specific. If one said “serine protease,” for example, the other would know a lot of what was implied by that in terms of the specifics of the reaction mechanism. We need to get specific when communicating with an AI tool because, while our current generation of tools are great at working through the 3D arrangements of amino acids, they’re kind of stupid about the functions that those 3D arrangements enable.
In the work of the team behind the new tool, called Pinal, this doesn’t necessarily have to be the case. We have databases full of millions of protein sequences tagged with notes about the functions those proteins perform. With the proper training, the researchers reasoned, it should be possible to just use the same terminology in those tags to get a system that outputs a sequence that performs exactly like what you’re looking for.
Proteins plus language
Pinal, on some levels, works quite like the standard tools, following a two-step process of building a backbone for the protein and then filling in the details of the amino acids that populate that backbone through a separate process. But there are very significant differences—beginning with what you need to do to start the process.
Rather than specifying some details of a few amino acids in the design product, you simply tell the system what you want. “The first stage is handled by T2struct, a text-to-structure module that translates a natural language prompt into a structural blueprint,” as the system’s developers describe it. T2struct doesn’t output a 3D shape, either; it simply produces a linear array of tokens that correspond to the spatial relationship between each amino acid and its nearest neighbors and assign a probability to each.
That gets handed off to a system called SAProt-T, which uses a combination of the original text and the output to T2struct to construct the sequence of amino acids in the final protein design. Here, the probabilities generated earlier matter, since SAProt-T performs a global re-evaluation. According to the authors, this avoids the risk of “overlooking a slightly less probable structure that can accommodate a far superior functional sequence.”
How do you develop a system that can do all of this? The researchers decided the best way was to use massive amounts of data. For each set of tags that describe a protein’s function, they fed the tags into an LLM and had it provide a plain-language description and used both the tags and the description as part of the training. They used protein sequences from three different databases, paired with structural information predicted by AlphaFold; just one of these databases contained 800 million keyword–protein pairs.
It’s noteworthy that AlphaFold is not 100 percent accurate in its predictions, so if you’re trying to generate something related to a relatively obscure protein, this could be a problem. But many common proteins have structural data available, which presumably would ensure AlphaFold made informed predictions.
In any case, apparently enough of the structural data was right for the training to work.
Functional proteins
To test Pinal, the researchers asked it to design four very different proteins: a fluorescent one, two enzymes, and one that takes part in a large multi-protein complex. While the details vary a bit from case to case, there was a similar process for each; we’ll use the fluorescent protein as an example.
The classic example of a fluorescent protein, which won its discoverer a Nobel, is GFP, the green fluorescent protein. Pinal was asked to produce 50,000 proteins that could fluoresce like GFP. This massive list was then filtered down by a number of criteria. For starters, the researchers rejected anything with a sequence that looked like a known fluorescent protein. But they selected for a couple of key features found in GFP: the ability to form a barrel-like structure, and the presence of a key amino acid that can be chemically modified to enable fluorescence.
In short, they wanted it to be a bit like GFP in general, but not very similar in terms of the specific amino acid sequence. That filtering left them with a high-priority list of just 29 candidate proteins, all of which were made in E. coli. A grand total of one of them fluoresced.
All the other examples were done similarly: start with a massive list, narrow it down computationally, then test a few dozen designs, of which only a few would work.
It would be tempting to dismiss this as a horrifically low success rate. But remember that a lot of the suggestions that were most likely to work would look a lot like known GFP proteins, and so be weeded out. The researchers also didn’t even bother to test whether things that didn’t form a structure similar to GFP might work, so they may have rejected a huge range of alternative fluorescent proteins based on that.
Not just proteins
Last week also saw the introduction of something very similar but focused on DNA sequences. A collaboration of the AI company Hugging Face, the Zhongguancun Academy, and the University of Naples “Federico II” introduced what they’re calling Carbon X, an open-weight model that can run on local hardware. It is based on a human-language model called Qwen3-14B but was retrained using DNA, followed by reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.
The re-training (technically termed mid-training) required a careful balancing act: “A low learning rate preserves English but leaves DNA at chance, and a high one learns DNA but forgets English.” But the result is a single model that can speak both DNA and English and translate between them. So, like large genome models, you can prompt it with a DNA sequence, and it will attempt to predict sequences that might come after it in a typical genome. But you can also prompt it with a mix of DNA and natural language, asking it things like “what would the consequence of changing this G to an A be?”
While the team has not released a publication describing the behavior of the system, their internal performance suggests it’s quite good, being competitive with large, specialized commercial models like GPT-6.1 Sol. That said, it also includes a few cautions. The system is not especially good at noting specific positions, especially on longer sequences. It can also be prone to hallucinations if the prompt isn’t specific enough. So, the usual cautions when using an AI tool definitely apply.
Hugging Face points out two major reasons why Carbon X might be a better option than commercial models, even for tasks where the commercial models tend to perform a bit better, both of them related to the fact that Carbon X can be run locally. The first is simply cost; the company’s demonstration video was done using a MacBook, so it can be run repeatedly on relatively affordable hardware. The second is that there are many situations where, for proprietary or privacy reasons, people will not want to share the inquiries they’re making with a commercial entity.
Keeping it plain
It’s easy to think this is dumbing biology down so anyone with the slightest bit of knowledge can start making custom proteins and viruses. That’s not entirely accurate. They can easily get the sequences out of the tool. But they will then likely need to use a lot of specialized tools to screen through these in order to find sequences that are more likely to be functional. And then there’s the issue of testing them, which requires a well-equipped biology lab and trained specialists.
Biologists have clearly not been taken out of the equation.
In many cases, this may solve ongoing issues faced by experimental biologists. In the post-genome era, there have been lots of questions that are best answered via computers. But a lot of tools made to get these answers were made by bioinformaticians who did not go out of their way to make their tools approachable. Many biologists can understand a relatively English-ish phrase like “find me all the enhancers that control the expression of this gene.” But far fewer will know which combination of tools are needed to answer that question, much less how to configure them.
Giving those biologists a tool that can answer these questions without the need to consult multiple software manuals has potential to accelerate research. But it may take a few years before it becomes clear that biologists find this capability useful.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

Excellent controllers tailored for VR or “regular” gaming. Solid performance on supported VR games. Virtual Imax-scale 2D gaming. Doesn’t pretend to be for work or productivity.
TIRED
Pricey. Blink-and-miss-it battery life. Unpredictable performance for installed games. Problematic pairing for streaming games.
Valve has had a complicated relationship with virtual reality gaming. Its Steam client—the number one distribution platform for PC games—has long supported VR titles and works with headsets from other manufacturers. But the company's flagship VR headset, 2019’s Valve Index, never quite escaped its niche. It saw a huge sales spike in the run-up to the release of headline title Half-Life: Alyx, but by February 2025, it accounted for only 13.2 percent of VR headsets used on Steam.
Enter the Steam Frame, Valve’s second attempt at snatching the VR gaming crown. More than a hardware refresh, it promises to reimagine PC VR gaming, operating as a stand-alone headset like the Meta Quest 3, the current reigning champion, while letting users seamlessly stream games from a more powerful remote machine. It mostly succeeds—but a few issues hold it back.
All in Your Head
Specs-wise, the Steam Frame is one of the better VR headsets, though far from a powerhouse. It packs a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip—a slightly dated offering, having debuted in 2023—with 16 GB of RAM, and either 256 GB (at the $1,059 price) or 1 TB ($1,299) of storage, plus a microSD slot for expansion, allowing it to install and run games locally.
It’s aesthetically pleasing, with a sleek black shell and glossy front that have given it a futuristic look. More importantly, it’s comfortable to wear, weighing 440 grams—75 grams lighter than the Quest 3. Valve smartly moved the 21.6-watt-hour Lithium-ion battery to the rear of the head strap for better balance, and thanks to cozy padding, it doesn’t feel hot against your head, even when running demanding games. The cable linking the battery to the headset makes adjusting the elastic straps a little fiddly, though.
The only real comfort drawback is if you wear glasses. While the Steam Frame comes with a spacer to add more depth (which easily clips on magnetically between the inner headset and the padded face gasket), the internal dimensions were still too narrow for me to wear with any of my spectacles. Custom Zenni prescription lenses are available if contact lenses aren’t an option, but it’s a pricey add-on.
Once it’s on your head, dual speakers push audio down the arms directly to your ears, with physical volume controls easily accessible on the left side of the headset. The audio lacks bass but has good directionality, bringing those immersive VR experiences to life. Dual microphones let you use voice controls, while outward-facing cameras enable positional tracking and provide a pass-through view—albeit monochrome with everything looking bluish. A dial at the top lets you adjust lens spacing to your required interpupillary distance, and an inner switch locks it in place.
The lenses themselves are decent, but again not spectacular. Valve uses two LCD pancake lenses (though rumors already hint at a revised OLED model), with a per-eye resolution of 2160 x 2160. That means sharp visuals and legible text—I could easily read fine details on notepads in Half-Life: Alyx, for instance—but you can discern pixels if you peer closely. The real win comes with a 110-degree field of view, enabling wide spans of virtual real estate, and refresh rates ranging from 72 to 120 Hz, with an experimental mode boosting it up to 144 Hz. As a result, games can look incredibly smooth when running on the Steam Frame.
The controllers might be the best part of the package. The dual grips mimic the Quest 3 controllers but outdo them with a full controller layout spread across the pair. They boast the same highly precise Tunneling Magnetoresistance thumbsticks as the regular Steam Controller, along with a full D-pad on the left, four ABXY face buttons on the right, two shoulder triggers and an underside button on each—squeeze that in, and the grip switches from controller mode to laser pointer to make selections in VR.
Position detection is great, with full six-degrees-of-freedom tracking, while excellent haptics deliver solid rumble and per-finger capacitive sensing for nuanced, precise interactions with virtual objects. You can also pair a regular controller to the Frame via Bluetooth, but the included ones are so good you likely won’t ever feel the need to—these are now the pinnacle of multipurpose VR controllers.
What Will Play?
After setup—a now-familiar routine for VR gamers that includes running necessary updates and drawing safe boundaries so you don't knock into furniture—you’ll sign in to your Steam account directly on the Steam Frame. It runs SteamOS 3 just like the Steam Deck or Steam Machine, the familiar home screen now floating in a VR void. Navigate to your library, and you can install whatever you like directly onto the Frame.
Unfortunately, while there’s a filter for games officially categorized as compatible, it’s unclear what rubrics Valve uses, or how many games have even been tested. Of my 1,300-plus-strong Steam library, only a meager 18 were marked “Great on Frame.” The strangest absence from that list is the totemic Half-Life: Alyx (which comes free with every Steam Frame purchase), especially odd given it runs without issue. Other dedicated VR games are hit and miss when installed directly on the Frame—I tried Obduction (opened and crashed, repeatedly), Doctor Who: The Edge of Time (ran with juddery performance and could only move by clicking in on the thumbsticks), Dungeons of Eternity (fine, bar some aiming and tracking issues), and Surgeon Simulator VR (totally fine).
You’re not limited to VR games on Frame. You can install and play anything in your library as 2D on a vast virtual cinema screen. Don’t bother with demanding AAA games—the hardware isn’t up to running them—but indies and AA-tier games can look phenomenal like this. Playing Hades II blown up to Imax-scale was a fantastic experience. Again, performance is unreliable—gorgeously animated Metroidvania MIO: Memories in Orbit launched when installed locally, but couldn’t load its assets, leaving me standing on invisible platforms and with no way to navigate the world.
The Frame also seems to default 2D games to 720p resolution. You can override this, but it may drop performance. Frame rates for all of the above games hopped all over the place, though mostly hovering around the 72 or 90 fps benchmarks. It feels like Valve has a lot of updating work to do to ensure Steam Frame can reliably function as a gaming platform for VR or non-VR titles. Right now, running anything is a gamble.
Wi-Fi Woes
The most annoying thing is that the Steam Frame isn't designed solely as a stand-alone headset—pairing it with a more powerful desktop (or laptop) should, in theory, let the PC do the grunt work and stream the output to the Frame. The package includes a dedicated 6-GHz wireless adapter—plug it into any device with a USB-A 3.0 port running Steam, and it should provide a dedicated network for the Frame. The headset connects to both the adapter and your home network, creating a mesh that reduces latency by using whichever has the least network traffic.
In practice, I could barely get it working. I tested it on a Windows 11 PC, a Windows 10 PC, and a Steam Machine—in every case, the Frame could connect to the remote device through the home network, but the adapter appeared as connected but unpaired. When it detected and created that mesh network (on rare occasions), streaming was flawless, but when connected only through the home network, performance was laggy enough to irritate.
Whether playing natively or through streaming, battery life is poor—expect two hours at the high end for locally run games, and maybe three if you’re purely streaming. Such short playing time makes the inability to physically connect Steam Frame to a PC with a cable all the worse, which would also overcome the streaming issues.
Better Days to Come
The biggest hurdle for most VR gamers is likely price. Like all of Valve’s recent tech, the Steam Frame is a casualty of RAM and storage shortages across the electronics industry. Like the Steam Machine, it feels almost compromised, especially that three-year-old processor. It doesn’t feel like $1,000-plus worth of headset, especially when its overall performance only just about beats the significantly cheaper Quest 3.
Yet despite its many early hiccups, the Steam Frame is incredible fun. The VR titles that work without issue are brilliant to play here, and the cinema mode for 2D games is the best implementation of that feature I’ve experienced on a VR headset. Streaming shows potential if Valve can work the networking kinks. If it gets that polish over the coming months as Valve pushes out inevitable updates, it could really shine.
I especially love how it’s unapologetically a gaming platform. It’s not trying to claim VR is useful for productivity, or office tasks—that ship sank along with Apple’s Vision Pro—and mercifully, there’s not even a hint of a blighted “Metaverse” here. The Steam Frame is for gaming, end of story. If Valve can iron out its software issues and make sure more games run on it properly, it’ll be a great way to play.

Fast bowler Mitchell Starc did not know Australia’s premier batsman Steve Smith would not take part in the decisive third Test against South Africa at Newlands on Tuesday until he went to warm-up ahead of play.
Smith tested his neck injury in the nets on Tuesday morning but was still experiencing discomfort, captain Pat Cummins said at the toss.
“He wasn’t happy with how his neck was feeling, so we had to look elsewhere,” Cummins said.
Smith’s absence meant he would not feature at the ground where he was embroiled in the 2018 ball-tampering ‘Sandpapergate’ scandal, with much of the pre-match focus centred on how Australia’s most experienced batter would cope with the occasion.
“I did not know he was not playing until I went out to warm-up today,” Starc told reporters after the day’s play. “He has been battling that neck since last week.
“I don’t actually know what happened with that and I have not asked. He seems upbeat enough, but I don’t know what he has had done.”
After winning the toss, Cummins opted to bowl, a rare decision at Newlands that might have been taken with the reshuffle of the top six batsmen after Josh Inglis learnt just before the start he would replace Smith.
The move initially appeared to have backfired as South Africa made a strong start. However, Starc produced a masterful spell with the second new ball late in the day, finishing with figures of six for 72 as the host was dismissed for 329 on the stroke of stumps.
“I am not in that pay bracket,” Starc said when asked if he agreed with the decision to bowl first. “My opinion doesn’t matter. It is what it is. At one point it looked like we were bowling a fair bit tomorrow, so it was good to bowl them out today.
“There was clearly not as much swing and sideways movement as we thought might be on offer (early in the day). But we found different ways to be effective and if you delete that first session, I think the last two were back on what we expected.”
It was another see-saw day in a series that has already seen plenty of twists and turns.
“These are two very good cricket teams. At times it is going to get away from you, at times you will wrestle the momentum back, which we did in the second half of the day,” Starc said.
“I expect more swings through the test match as we now need to go and bat and they have a very good (bowling) attack.”

Mourinho keeps Clasico midas touch 13 years on as La Liga heats up
- Published
Jose Mourinho has done it again.
The Real Madrid manager celebrated Kylian Mbappe's late winner at Barcelona on Sunday with a trademark knee slide, as he maintained his midas touch over their bitter rivals.
Mourinho has become just the third Real boss to go six El Clasicos in a row without defeat - 13 years after he last led Los Blancos in this fixture.
Four wins and two draws in his past six matches in charge of Real Madrid against Barcelona put him up there with Miguel Munoz (1962 to 1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001 to 2003) as Real managers who have gone six in a row without defeat against the old enemy.
It was also just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona for Real, with the return of Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions
And more importantly for Mourinho, Mbappe's double in Real's 2-1 win ended Barcelona's nine-game unbeaten domestic run with a crucial Clasico victory at the Camp Nou.
A Real defeat would have allowed Barcelona to establish a commanding nine-point advantage but the result has transformed the top of La Liga, bringing Mourinho's side to within three points of their rivals.
"In my view, Real Madrid do not play to win at the Camp Nou, Real Madrid play to win La Liga," he said.
"We could win with luck, but we won with calmness and with all merit," he said. "It's a very strong group. Everyone works very hard. Everyone was ready to win.
"The credit goes to the players. When you win, the credit goes to the players. But when you lose, the blame falls on you. And that's why we see coaches being sacked from their positions every week."
The Portuguese, who returned to Real 13 years after his first stint in charge this summer, has now won six and lost six El Clasicos.
He said: "I've learned that I have an extraordinary group, with the quality and mindset to play.
"In midfield, having a mix of talents gives us more than just having two players with similar characteristics. This mix of talents gives us balance when defending and quality when we go on the attack.
"We've beaten several teams by four or more goals, but this is Barca, and the players put on a great performance. We need to continue like this and don't go over the moon after this win."
Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said he didn't want to give excuses for the defeat but admitted his team lacked fresh legs after a demanding few weeks.
"We missed the freshness," he said. "It's not easy for our players. We have to recover well, train well and we have to respond from this defeat.
"In big games, small things are important and they decide the games and today, it wasn't on our side.
"I can see that today we were not fresh and this is what we have to change."

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”

The BCA Stadium in Kotambi is a special venue for Pratika Rawal. It is where she was introduced to international cricket two years ago against the West Indies.
She made quite the first impression with 134 runs in her first three games. It was a sign of things to come as she went about piling on the runs from one series to the next. Even in a tough World Cup campaign, which ultimately ended with a major injury to her ankle, she ground out some valuable runs, including a century against New Zealand.
But the volume of runs was never the issue with Pratika. It was the rate at which they came in.
Back in Vadodara for an ODI series against Zimbabwe, Pratika’s ODI game looks visibly different. While she was scoring at a strike rate of 84 in 2025 and managed just 79 runs in three games against Australia earlier this year at an even lower rate of 75.96, in Vadodara, she leads the scoring charts in the ongoing series against the Lady Chevrons with 161 runs in two games at a much-improved 98.77. Her century in the first game even came at a sprightly 104.16.
“The more matches I have played over the years, the more I am understanding the game. So, it’s basically an adaptation of that game, adaptation of my batting and adaptation to how the bowlers are bowling to me,” she told reporters ahead of the third ODI here.
There is a marked change in her approach, particularly in the PowerPlay. After being the steady hand that allowed Smriti Mandhana to unlock her quickscoring ways, Pratika is focusing on her own boundary hitting skills.
“I have worked on that as well, to be able to find more boundaries in the PowerPlay because there are only two fielders outside. You can actually get an advantage and hit a lot of boundaries. When you see Smriti batting at the other end, you feel there’s a lot to learn. So I try to replicate what she does when she is in her best version. Hopefully, I will get there as well.”
The numbers are telling. Before the Zimbabwe series, her PowerPlay strike rate was around 77. In the first two ODIs against the Women in Red, not only is Pratika unbeaten in the first 10 overs, but she’s also striking at 104.
Role clarity goes a long way in securing a batter’s focus firmly on their process. With Shafali Verma’s explosive quality, particularly in the PowerPlay, available for the team to utilise, Pratika needed to buck up. But it helps that the murmurs about batting position and shuffling are not ones the dressing room has in its space.
“There were no conversations inside the dressing room about the batting order to be very honest,” she explained.
