“Smriti and I knew that we were going in as openers and I think Shafali knew as well that she was going in one down. That’s the same batting order that we followed in the Australia tour as well. I went with a clear mindset that I’m opening for the Indian team. There were no doubts about that.”
That clarity was important given she was fresh from an initiation to T20Is that did not go as smoothly as she would have wanted. Handed a debut in the Asia Cup, the 26-year-old returned scores of 22,10, 4 and 20.
She didn’t make the cut for the T20Is in the Zimbabwe series, and had time to gear up for the One-Dayers.
“The first thing I did after going home was to bat for a longer duration because it’s a longer format. To be able to have that patience even when they bowl a flighted ball, to just stay there and push it for a single and try to build your inning — these were some points I worked on back home. Honestly, when you bat for a longer duration, you get that sense of confidence. You get that feeling that you are timing the ball well and everything else just works out your way.”
Her century came on the first anniversary of another ton, an important one, against New Zealand in the 2025 ODI World Cup.
“It wasn’t a perfect innings, and as a batter you have to learn from that. But it was one of those days when the ball went where I wanted it to. Luckily, it turned out really good today,” she had said after that knock. She only leaned into that comfort with a commanding half century that dug India out of trouble when it was left stumped at 19 for 2.
While working on her strokeplay, taking it deep into the innings is another element Pratika would want to stay on top of, more so now when her opening partner navigates the added pressures of captaincy.
In 28 innings, Pratika has a cluster of dismissals in between the 19th to 30th over, with only two past the 42nd over (when the game goes that long). Should India bat first on Wednesday, the Women and Blue and the steady opening bat from New Delhi will have their chance.

SERUA ISLAND, FIJI – As the sun sets over Fiji’s tiny Serua Island, its climate-threatened inhabitants soak in one of the reasons they have rejected attempts to relocate their village — the “$100 million views.”
The island looks like a utopia from the mainland, two steep palm-covered knolls sandwiching its low-lying center, flanked by coral reefs and rich fishing grounds.
But it is on the island itself that the risk from rising seas becomes clearer, with a concrete sea wall providing the only defense against waves that are already swamping homes.
“The stronger the air pressure, the higher the waves. So the waves wash through inside the village,” Serua Island resident Avenai Ranuku.
Dozens of homes are in harm’s way when cyclones hit Fiji, as are vegetable crops and graves.
Water laps at the feet of concrete piles where homes and a hospital once stood on the island’s eastern end, and two homes were also moved from the western side where land has been washed away.
Despite the risks, most residents say they would rather strengthen the island’s defenses than abandon their ancestral home.
Ranuku remembers when Category 5 Cyclone Winston hit as a child and the island’s population moved up one of the island’s peaks to take shelter.
“Terrifying,” Ranuku said of that night.
“All of the villagers, when the chief mention it, we go up. No one left behind. We help everyone, carry everything from the house, food. This is our evacuation plan.”
Safe on higher ground, Ranuku could hear “waves going around, and the roof of the houses being washed away.”
From that same haven on the hill, Ranuku explained why the threat of cyclones and sea level rise doesn’t deter people from living on the island.
“We love this island, you know. Fresh air, go out fishing every day, that’s why they don’t want to leave.
“Many people used to say, they go to that house on the hill to see the sunset, it’s a $100 million view.”
Serua Village worked with Habitat for Humanity in 2025 to write a detailed disaster risk reduction plan, as most of the population rejected calls for it to relocate.
Instead, residents wanted to protect their ancestral home and the culture linked to it.
The report found nearly 20% of homes on the island were in critical condition, and just three houses were strong enough to withstand a cyclone.
“Serua Island experiences more frequent seawall overtopping during high tides and king tides, saline intrusion affecting soil fertility, and standing water after rainfall, elevating health risks,” the report said.
“The assessment shows there is a lack of natural form of wave breakers on Serua Island, and it is constantly threatened by sea level rise and cyclones.
“More than 50% of houses have a combination of unstable foundations and roofs, and weak joints, walls, and bracing, making these homes most vulnerable to cyclones and severe weather events.”
On receiving the report, the village wasted no time in working to strengthen its resilience.
During a visit in October, dozens of workers were renovating homes along the northern coastline.
Flimsy walls and corrugated iron roofing were being removed and taken by boat to the mainland.
Some homes had already been raised to mitigate flood risk, and others would soon follow.
The report also recommended improving access to the island by building a more robust path.
During low tide, it is possible to walk the 750 meters to the island, guided by a string of power lines protruding from the sea floor.
But at high tide, the only access is by boat, and even then the report said work is needed to make docking on the island safer and easier.
It is work Ranuku said his village is committed to.
“Why would we want to leave?” he said, looking across the water to Fiji’s Coral Coast.
“We have $100 million views.”

A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.
The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.
"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion. "And yet, here we are."
Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.
"By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.
Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.
"We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.
In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.
Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."
"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.
Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.
That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."
"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."
The judge took aim at the government's contradictions
Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.
Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.
"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."
Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.
The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.
Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.
"To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."
She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."
She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.
"Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.
Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.
"The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."
What's next for East Potomac?
Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.
Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.
"It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character. "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."
Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.
That argument seems to hold water with Reyes, who said, the Interior Department likely violated the National Environmental Protection Act "by impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects."
Monday's ruling — and the administration's promised appeal — could slow that process even more. Trump said on social media that work "must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner."
But there are still many questions about the final product.
The rendering Trump shared earlier this month shows the park's three courses of varying ability levels combined into one that overtakes the entire peninsula, seemingly removing the perimeter road that runners and bikers use every day and raising questions about whether the historically affordable golf course could soon be less accessible.
Trump said Monday the redeveloped course will be able to host events like the PGA Championship and Ryder Cup, but will also be "open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C."
The project is one of many ways he's looking to make his mark on the nation's capital, from building the White House ballroom to adding his name to the Kennedy Center to pushing through plans for a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Tamil literature is replete with references to Siddha practitioners, traditional healers, and the faith, or lack of it, that people have in them. A segment of Tamil literature that has focused on class and caste hierarchies has also looked sharply and sensitively at the socio-economic determinants for access to health care. Among the pioneers of drawing technology and science into his writings in Tamil was the legendary, prescient novelist and screenwriter Sujatha. But in modern Tamil fiction, the employment of medicine and medical issues as the central theme and plot has been rather minimal.
While there might be only a few texts in popular, modern Tamil fiction that weave the story around a medical condition, these form a significant contribution to the genre. Muthumeenal’s Mul focuses on leprosy, and Sivakami’s Pazhayana Kazhithalum offers a health perspective couched in caste discrimination.
Among the Tamil writers who have formed a strong bond between their stories and health issues, Imayam stands tall, not merely through sheer numbers, but through depth of content. Many of his short stories and novels couch the essential human experience he portrays in medical conditions, each wrapped in the other, not distinct, but influencing and impacting each other.
Health in Tamil fiction
But before we dip into Imayam’s work, a full-length novel of note on a core health issue is Mul (thorn) by Muthumeenal, a deep and personalised account of living with leprosy. The narrator is a young girl whose life has been upended when she finds suspicious patches on her body. She moves into an institution where medical care is provided, around which the story is built, and the multiple angles, including stigma, politics, loneliness, and internal struggle, are woven into this autobiography. The public-health message is stigma-busting: that leprosy is treatable, and early therapy can cure it.
In retired IAS officer Sivakami’s work, a Dalit feminist treatise, Pazhayana Kazhithalum (The Grip of Change), the text deals strongly with the social determinants of health — caste violence, gender-based violence, bodily autonomy, and the mental and physical toll of bigotry.
In Imayam’s Ippothu Uyirodirukkiren (I’m Alive… For Now), the author artfully folds in the themes of both the above novels — crafting a social commentary within the nephrology ward of a government hospital where a teenager with end-stage kidney disease has been admitted. It follows his rapid decline, his transition onto dialysis, and organ donation. Reviewers have praised its ‘authentic’ portrayal of nephrology, the disease, and the treatment.
But this is an achievement across various novels that Imayam, a school teacher and politician, has penned. While known for his sharp critique of caste and gender hegemonies, Imayam has also built a strong subgenre of medical literature. Unlike authors who use disease as a generic plot device or a melodramatic tool to lead up to a crisis, he treats medical conditions with gripping sociological depth and clinical accuracy.
A Sahitya Akademi winner, Imayam attempts to explain the human condition through pain, suffering and debility, and as his longtime collaborator-translator Justice Prabha Sridevan says, “an astonishingly astute understanding of the feminine condition.” His recent novel, Noiputtru (disease), also talks of life derailed by leprous patches.
Set in a Tamil Nadu leprosarium in the 1960s, the novel documents the lived experiences of patients ostracised from their families and confined to State-run institutions, including detailed descriptions of the diagnostic and treatment processes. The descriptions of the impact of leprosy are merciless — thickening ears, flattened noses, and physical disfigurement — there’s no way to conceal this in the deliberate, yet sparse prose of the author.
Imayam’s world of illness
Very few novels in Tamil come with the searing commentary that he delivers in Sellatha Panam (A Woman Burnt). Unlike in the case of the protagonist of the above-mentioned novels, here, Revathi, an upper-caste woman who is forced to take the extreme move after her inter-caste marriage, is trapped in a liminal world and confined to bed. Around her, in the waiting corridors of the burns ward, social realities are exposed, the niceties ripped off, though his most effective literary tool is conversations between people. It is said Imayam spent time observing the JIPMER burns ward while researching the book.
Just launched, the English translation of Uppu Vandikaran (The Salt Vendor) harks back to the dark, panic-driven emergency of the pandemic lockdown. It’s not just about falling ill with COVID-19; instead, it exposes the lacunae and inadequacies in the medical system, as Chellamuthu goes from one hospital to the other, being rejected by each one of them since he cannot produce a certificate confirming his infection- a situation the world was familiar with during the first couple of years of the 2020s. Similarly, his short story Government Pinam (The Government Corpse) is situated in the pandemic, focusing on a boy quarantined with his sick father in a house sealed shut by government officials.
In Imayam’s debut novel Koveru Kazhudaigal (Mules), over three decades ago, a significant segment is about how the women of the Vannar community deliver through traditional midwifery practices, outside of medical institutions. He also broaches the subject of patient attendants, a subject gaining currency in a nation growing increasingly grey, and the care of the elderly comes into the spotlight. In Pinathuku Sondhakkari (Owner of the Corpse): Meenakshi, a live-in attendant, is left alone to handle her elderly employer Ramanan’s sudden death, his children away and slow to return.
Manamurivu (Divorce) deals with the gendered nature of infertility, dragging the reader through IVF clinics, menstrual cycles, hormone injections, and the inordinate stress to bear children on the woman in the relationship.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic drew science and medicine into drawing rooms and headlines, willy-nilly, it remains to be seen whether Tamil literature will now make room for more health-related content.

The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
- Published
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.
But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.
The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.
"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."
He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.
"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.
He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.
Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.
That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.
Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.
"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.
His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.
"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.
Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.
"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."
But his customers are getting more demanding.
"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.
"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."
And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.
Why is such data so important?
If you want robots to navigate the real world, they can't just be trained inside computer simulations, argues Manish Agarwal, the founder of Humyn Labs, which collects and processes human-generated data.
Most of that data comes from video, but sometimes collectors wear hardware on their hands and fingers to capture physical contact.
"Physical tasks require high-quality signals involving limb movements, fingers, wrists, elbows, shoulders and dynamic force application. For example: applying the correct grip force so a plastic bottle doesn't crumble versus a steel glass," he says.
And until recently, that data was not available.
"There is no existing internet archive of embodied human activity - no dataset of a kitchen being cleaned, or a car being assembled by hands that know exactly how much force to apply. That data has to be captured from scratch, in the real world, across diverse environments," says Agarwal, whose company has bases in Bangalore and San Francisco.
At the moment his firm has 96,000 data collectors across countries in Latin America and Southeast Asia.
Humyn Labs filters the thousands of hours of video supplied by those collectors, selecting the most useful content. It's then labelled so the AI knows what it is looking at and packaged in a format that can be used by clients.
"You need to source across a variety of factories, a variety of tasks, in different geographies because if you want to build deployment for US factories or US houses, you'd want environments that are a proxy for that. Residential houses in India may not be the right context for building a robotics use case for the US."
But are workers collecting data for machines that will one day do their jobs?
At the moment it's too early to tell says Bino Paul, senior professor at the School of Management and Labour Studies at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) in Mumbai.
For some workers AI might be a useful tool, but robots could automate other jobs, he says.
The problem is that, if machines do start to take over, there will be little workers can do about.
"By the time workers realise what they have participated in, things may have gone too far," he says.
Like many others, he wants governments to regulate AI.
"AI cannot be viewed merely as a technical system. We need to develop a socio-technical system in which ethics is upheld through human agency, ensuring that AI delivers beneficence rather than maleficence."
'This is survival'
Despite concerns over where AI is heading, money is still being poured into its development.
Some of that trickles down to workers in India, where there is no shortage of workers prepared to wear a camera for a few dollars a day.
Mohammed Arman has been working in the textiles industry in Bangalore for 10 years.
"Garments stitching and cutting. I know this work so well I could probably do it with my eyes closed. Cloth, thread, needle, machine after 10 years, your hands just know what to do before your mind even tells them," he says.
He has recently started wearing a head-mounted camera that records his work.
"For me, it's simple. This is survival. I have a family back home in Bihar, and every rupee I send back matters. If someone offers me extra money to wear a camera while I do the exact same work I've been doing for 10 years, I'm not going to say no.
"It doesn't cost me anything. I'm already doing the stitching, already doing the cutting. Now I just get paid a little more for it," he says.
While there is demand for such footage it will be collected somewhere.
"India's current role in this industry is largely as a supplier of raw material - people strap on cameras, record themselves doing ordinary tasks, and that footage gets shipped off to labs abroad," Agarwal says.
But he argues the value of that kind of work will quickly become eroded, as more companies compete for collection contracts.
"India can't afford to stay a footage supplier. It needs to move up the value chain: from recording raw video to owning the pipeline that turns that video into something usable - cleaning it, structuring it, validating it, and ultimately setting the standards for what counts as high-quality training data," he says.
For some people collecting data is attractive part time work.
Science teacher Jolly Arifur was looking for work she could do from home that would fit around her young son.
"For the past seven months, I strapped a rig-mounted camera on my head while doing my routine domestic work scrubbing, cooking, sweeping tile floors, and folding laundry."
Arifur, who lives in Guntakal, Anantapur, fits the recording work around her teaching.
"I get paid two to three dollars per hour. If I record three to five hours a day, that's a good amount in hand it's become an extra source of income for me, on top of teaching. I'm managing both honestly, fantastically."

I’m going to keep this short because I really want you to check out Jason Mast’s new story. I’ve got a bit of a teaser below, but the whole remarkable tale is worth your time. Stay well and thanks for reading.
A biotech company by and for Amish and Mennonite people
First, they saved the cow. Petunia was suffering from a bovine form of maple syrup urine disease, a life-threatening condition unusually prevalent in Pennsylvania’s Mennonite community.
At the local veterinary hospital, Petunia was given a novel gene therapy. Today, she is a healthy 5-year-old heifer.
The doctor behind this procedure wanted to save the calf, of course. But his mission was bigger — Kevin Strauss is building a biotech company by and for the people he treats inside a wooden, mortise-and-tenon frame medical center. The goal is to develop innovative gene therapies to treat the unique set of rare diseases that afflict Amish and Mennonite people.
Jason Mast has an inside look at the new company, including its effort to resurrect treatments abandoned by pharma or left to gather frost in an academic freezer, often because there are too few patients for a company to generate profit.
Our roundup of the big European cancer conference
My colleague Adam Feuerstein and I are leaving Madrid after a packed four days at the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual meeting. Selecting which readouts to cover is a form of triage given the massive amount of research being detailed (if you think we missed something game-changing, let us know), but one highlight in terms of outcomes didn’t come from some new drug. Rather, it was the combination of Amgen’s Imdelltra and AstraZeneca’s Imfinzi showing that it greatly extended survival in difficult-to-treat small cell lung cancer — and showing the potential of paired approaches.
Other highlights:
- Yes, the big readout was Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine, and yes, the wind got a bit taken out of the presentation’s sails with the embargo break. But it’s still a milestone in cancer research. Here’s our deep dive into what the results mean for melanoma care, and what they could mean for moving cancer vaccines into other tumor types. And don’t miss Adam chatting to Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel about the impact for the company, and where it goes from here. (We also got some early data from a vaccine designed to prevent tumors in an inherited condition that leaves people at much higher risk of cancer.)
- Scientists figuring out how to target KRAS led to a major advance in pancreatic cancer, as you’ve probably heard. Now more KRAS-targeting drugs are coming, often going after specific mutations. Roche unveiled strong data from divarasib in non-small cell lung cancer, and Incyte showed promising results from INCB161734 in pancreatic cancer.
- Three years ago at ESMO (coincidentally the last time the conference was in Madrid, so a real hardship assignment for me), I wrote about how antibody drug conjugates were all the rage. That continues to be the case, with important readouts from Merck, AstraZeneca, GSK, and beyond. One thing I’m thinking about going forward: These drugs in theory should be safer than the standard chemotherapies they’re designed to replace, but some of them carry quite serious side effects themselves. Too many emergency departments can’t handle child patients
A few years ago, parents rushed their baby to a small rural hospital. But the facility didn’t have pediatric specialists, pediatric nurses, or a children’s intensive care unit. As the little boy’s condition worsened, the hospital’s staff scrambled to identify a facility that could take him. But every children’s hospital in northern California was overwhelmed. No one had room for one more.
The baby died of RSV. And the problem has only gotten worse since then, write two pediatric care experts in a new First Opinion.
“In this new normal, community hospitals across the country are transferring children to dedicated pediatric centers not just because a child is critically ill, but increasingly because smaller hospitals have quietly lost the ability to manage even common conditions,” they write. “The nation’s relatively few children’s hospitals can’t accommodate every sick child, much as we would like to. We now routinely turn sick children away and hope one of our colleagues somewhere else will have a bed.”
What’s the solution? Read on.
The Washington news you need this week
Every week over in D.C. Diagnosis, STAT’s John Wilkerson highlights the most important news he’s watching. As midterms creep ever closer, here’s what’s on his mind:

A possible treatment for brain-eating amoebas, found in the sea
Brain-eating amoebas are the stuff of zombie novels and spooky season. They are also, unfortunately, real-world parasites found in warm freshwater. Infections caused by N. Fowleri are hard to treat and nearly always fatal. But researchers have isolated a compound that could help stop the disease.
The substance was taken from a marine bacterium, and has been able to kill multiple strains of N. Fowleri faster than the current treatment. There is much work to be done before this discovery can translate to medicine though. Researchers say their next focus will be studying whether the compound can cross the blood-brain barrier.

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

Leh, Oct 27: Amid public outcry over the rising number of wine shops and demands for a dry Ladakh, Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra on Tuesday called for wider consultations with religious and industry representatives to build consensus and find a middle path balancing public sentiment with the region's cultural and economic interests.
The chief secretary assured that the administration was flexible in its approach to public policy and would be amenable to a middle path solution in the matter.
Kundra was speaking at a meeting with women representatives of various religious organisations to discuss issues relating to excise policy. The meeting was attended by Excise Commissioner Romil Singh Donk and representatives of All Ladakh Gompa Association, Ladakh Buddhist Association, Anjuman Imamia, All Ladakh Hotel and Guest House Association (ALGAHA) and All Ladakh Tour Operators Association (ALTOA), an official spokesman said.
During the meeting, the women representatives put forth their views and concerns while demanding complete prohibition of liquor in the Union Territory (UT), highlighting the social and cultural considerations associated with the issue.
They expressed concern over the large number of bar licences issued.
The meeting was informed that in response to public sentiment, the Excise Policy 2026–27 had been rolled back and now the Excise Policy 2025–26 was in force, the spokesman said.
He said the participants were apprised of the status of liquor licences under the reinstated policy.
The meeting was informed that the number of retail liquor vends was two till last year but this year only one retail vend is functional. Similarly, the number of functional bars attached to restaurants offering retail sale of liquor, which was earlier 23, had increased by 17 newly issued licences, taking the total to 40, the spokesman said.
The chief secretary acknowledged the concerns expressed by the women representatives and emphasised the importance of giving due consideration to the views and sentiments of the people of Ladakh.
He observed that the demand for declaring Ladakh a completely dry UT is a significant matter that requires careful deliberation and consultation with all concerned stakeholders, to which all agreed.
The chief secretary cited the experience of other states like Bihar and Haryana where complete prohibition had led to serious consequences of spurious liquor and drugs being proliferated.
He suggested that this is also a cultural issue and the community needs careful consideration of the consequences of declaring Ladakh as a dry territory.
There are also issues of employment, tourism and economic activity and consultation with the hotel industry is also crucial in this regard, particularly given that tourism is the primary economic activity in the territory, Kundra said.
He said any decision on the matter would need to be taken through a broad-based consultative process involving religious organisations, hotel associations, tour and travel operators' associations and other relevant stakeholders, keeping in view the social, cultural and economic dimensions of the issue.
He suggested that in the first instance, the Ladakh Buddhist Association (LBA) should convene a wider consultation and build consensus on the way forward, with an endeavour to find a middle ground.
The chief secretary reiterated the importance of constructive dialogue and mutual understanding in addressing the concerns raised by the women representatives while ensuring that the perspectives of all affected stakeholders are duly considered.
The meeting provided an opportunity for the representatives to present their views and underscored the need for continued engagement and dialogue towards a balanced and informed consideration of the issue, the spokesman said.
The chief secretary said if required, another meeting with a larger set of stakeholders would be convened soon.

How much of Antonelli's success is down to his ability? - F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.
The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.
- Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet' 
  - Published1 day ago
This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian
The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.
In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.
Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.
He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.
But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.
The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.
As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.
On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.
Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.
"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.
"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.
"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."
Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.
However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.
The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.
So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.
With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam
Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.
"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.
"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."
Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.
Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".
The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.
Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.
Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.
As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.
Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.
First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.
Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year.
But Bearman has higher ambitions than staying at Haas for the rest of his career.
If Hamilton and Leclerc are going to be at Ferrari for the next four years, Bearman would have every right to be asking the team what that means for him.
If he isn't going to get into the senior team, what can they do to further his career? Do they let him go, so he can pursue his ambitions elsewhere, or do they allow him to do that while still maintaining links?
These questions become even more pressing for Bearman now Brazilian Rafael Camara - also a Ferrari young driver - is joining Haas for 2027.
Bearman needs to beat the Brazilian if he is not to face an existential threat to his future as a potential driver for a top team.
What's been happening with Alex Albon this season? Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz seems to have the better of him, and the car doesn't look to be in a good place. - David
Of the two Williams drivers, in a team that is struggling, Carlos Sainz has had the better season.
But it's not as stark as it perhaps appears just looking on the surface.
Sainz leads Albon by two points in the championship, and while the qualifying comparison is skewed heavily towards Sainz on a head-to-head basis at 13-5, the time gap between them is 0.115 seconds.
As if Albon was not already having a rough season, to top it he incurred the wrath of Fernando Alonso in Austin after the two collided on the first lap, leaving both with damaged cars.
Alonso said: "The quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex."
Williams are in such a state this year that comparing the drivers should be treated with a degree of qualification.
The car has been slow, and the team have struggled with consistency between parts, as well as quality and degradation.
In other words, two parts that should perform the same have not always done so, and some of them wear out and lose performance quicker than others.
Of course that works across both drivers but it does make comparisons difficult.
Albon was asked about the comparison with Sainz in qualifying in Monza last month.
He pointed out that the crash he had in Canada when he hit a groundhog had been costly because there was a new engine in the car that weekend, which was written off. That meant he had to run an old engine longer than ideal.
And he alluded to Williams suffering from the same issues with varying engine performance that happened in the early days of the new engine rules at Mercedes and McLaren.
"There's a few things," Albon said. "In the beginning of the year, it was very battery-dominated.
"If you think even just the George and Kimi situation, that's the manufacturer side of it having issues. So you can imagine it's not just them two that have had problems.
"There's been a few qualifying sessions where the corners have been good, but you don't see it in the lap time. It's on the stopwatch.
"And then we're also going through our own issues as a team. And that's not just on my side. There's also a side where to say that both cars are performing in the same way would not be true. We've been fighting some inconsistencies in the cars that's been there since the beginning of the year.
"We're much better now at getting on top of them. If you look at the last four or five weekends, we're actually very close in terms of performance. But it's taken a while to get there."
Do you foresee a world in which live F1 coverage ever returns to free-to-air telly in the UK or is it now stuck behind a paywall for eternity? I've now taken a different career path but becoming an engineer in F1 was my ultimate ambition when I was applying for university in the early 2010s, inspired by BBC's live coverage. - Ian
In the UK, the current situation is that Sky has exclusive rights to broadcast F1 behind a paywall, while Channel 4 has highlights on free-to-air television, with live coverage of the British Grand Prix.
Sky has the rights until the end of 2034, after it struck a new deal for a larger fee earlier this year.
That came in the wake of Apple buying the US rights starting from this season.
At the same time, the television market is in flux as streaming becomes increasingly prevalent as a means of consuming content.
In that context, as well as the wider sports broadcast situation, it's hard to imagine a situation where F1 could return fully to free-to-air television.
The wider picture is it is still on free-to-air in some countries - Brazil as an example.
But F1 would also argue free-to-air does not always mean more people getting sight of the sport, depending on how it's promoted in various ways, and viewing habits are not the same in all countries.
Social media output is also an important consideration. At the same time, F1 is a business that exists to make money.

The publication of her memoir is bound to create some “tamasha”, but it will allow her to set the record straight and tell her story, Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).
“There’s bound to be some tamasha when this book comes out. After all, others have spent decades telling my ‘story’, now it’s my turn,” Ms. Gandhi said in a post on X on Tuesday, sharing a video offering a glimpse of her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, scheduled for release on November 10.
In the 1.28-minute video, along with the post, Ms. Gandhi is seen going through the pages and reflecting on whether she should tell her entire story.
“I don’t know if I should tell the whole story,” she says, before recalling the time her late husband, former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, was asked to become Prime Minister. “When my husband was asked to become the Prime Minister, which I was totally against....,” she said, as the video moves on.
"People have different views; some people may change their views about me. Some people's views may become worse, but that is what it is, that is what happens when you write a book or when you are in public life. There is bound to be a 'tamasha' as you say it here," Ms. Gandhi says.
Her remarks in the video were interspersed with footage of key moments from her life — from her marriage to Rajiv to his assassination. There were also glimpses of Sonia Gandhi attending AICC meetings, as well as her photographs with Rajiv and her two children — Rahul and Priyanka.
In her debut post on X on Saturday (October 23), Ms. Gandhi described her late husband and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi as a very good-looking and gentle person. She shared her memories of their life as she made her debut on the social media platform X.
Ms. Gandhi made her Instagram debut last Thursday (October 22) with posts on her upcoming book, which she described as a "story of love, duty, loss and finding a place to belong".
This was Ms. Gandhi's first foray into social media. Over the years, she has been using the Congress' X handle to release her video statements or other messages and letters that she wished to make public.
Last month, HarperCollins India said it will publish Ms. Gandhi's 544-page memoir "Belonging: A Journey of Love" in India on November 10, ending the uncertainty over the book's domestic publication following an "impasse" between the author's representatives and Penguin Random House India (PRHI).
Exaggerated writings
“Well, I felt that since a lot had been written about me and a lot of it was not quite correct. It was either invented or exaggerated. So, it gave me a feel of being able to now put down my story and describe facts and things as they really were,” Ms. Gandhi added.
People have different views about her, and some of them may change after reading her book, while others may become worse, she said.
“...That is what happens when you write a book, or when you are in public life. There is bound to be a ‘tamasha’ as you say it here,” Ms. Gandhi said.
The video intersperses her remarks with photographs and footage from her life, including her marriage to Rajiv Gandhi, his assassination, Congress meetings and family moments with their children, Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.
Ms. Gandhi joined X last week, after years of using the Congress’s official account to issue video statements and release letters and messages.

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.
“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”
After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”
Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.
The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.
Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.
Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.
“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”
Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.
Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.
Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.
He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.
“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”
The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.
Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.
“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a high-anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.
According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”
The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 million in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.
While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump Administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply-chain risk.
“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.
In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.
The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.
The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”
“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”
The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.
Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.
Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.
“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”
A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”
Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.
In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.
Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.
Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.
Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.
“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

Kevin Bleyer, a writer who worked on “The Daily Show” and won four Primetime Emmy Awards, a Peabody Award and a Writers Guild Award, died Sunday in a car accident in Millrift, Pennsylvania. He was 54.
His family said the accident occurred on a rural road where he had a country home.
He spent nine years on “The Daily Show” and an additional eight years as a writer for “Politically Incorrect” with Bill Maher and Dennis Miller.
His other writing credits included Disney+’s “The Right Stuff,” Fox’s “Sleepy Hollow” and Bravo’s “Significant Others.”
Born in Bethesda, Maryland, Bleyer was raised in Seattle and had lived in New York City for the past 20 years.
He is survived by his wife, Nella Vera; his father Dtr. Archie Bleyer; and his brother Keith Bleyer, sister-in-law Kelly Schulz-Bleyer, nephew Evan Bleyer and niece Lauren Bleyer.

Pokémon Unite is shutting down
Its journey ends in March 2027.
Another live-service game bites the dust. Pokémon Unite, a five-on-five battle arena game in the vein of League of Legends, will shut down on March 23, 2027, at 00:00 UTC (8PM ET on March 22).
The multiplayer online battle arena game launched on Switch in July 2021 and landed on mobile a few months later. It supported cross-platform play between them. Players choose a Pokémon at the start of each match, and the monsters evolve and learn new abilities as the game progresses. Apparently, that was enough for a nearly six-year run in today's live-service climate.
In July, The Pokémon Company announced that the game wouldn't be part of the 2027 Pokémon World Championships, opting instead for a separate tournament in Tokyo. That event is still scheduled, with qualifier tournaments starting in December. But in hindsight, the game's split from the main event was a clue it was on its way out.
Built by Tencent's TiMi Studios, Pokémon Unite is free to play, relying on the unholy trinity of freemium monetization: battle passes, cosmetics and gems. Gem sales stopped today, along with new Unite Club memberships and auto-renewals. Gems already purchased will work until the shutdown, and existing Club members can keep their perks until their membership expires. On November 12, a final update will add a special farewell event.
The game will add a new Library feature that lets you keep viewing some of your in-game items after the end-of-service date. However, you'll need to log in before then to download the Library data — and since it's stored on your device, it "generally cannot be transferred" to a new one, according to The Pokémon Company. But hey, at least it's something.

Catit Pixi Smart Mouse Camera for $51: This cutie looks like a miniature mouse with oversized, magnetic feet that attach to a metal stand. The mouse legs hinge so you can adjust the camera’s height and angle. While adorable, it’s expensive for what it is: The lens doesn't move, and it requires a microSD card to capture video beyond a live feed. With the SD card, you can scroll through recorded video to see activity from past days, record live footage, and save photos and videos to your smartphone’s camera roll. Even with the SD card, though, it was hard to pinpoint the exact time when reviewing footage. The live video feed can be laggy, and there were connectivity issues a few times. It’s a tad expensive at this price point for its (lack of) capabilities.

The video feed was always clear, though the audio was a bit laggy and hard to hear. The treat portions were huge, dispensing a heaping handful of kibble even at the lowest setting. The dispensing alert was super jarring, and my pets were frightened by it—there was no way to silence it. Because of the kibble-dispensing hole's placement, the camera is angled low, making it hard to see the area I wanted. This is an okay pet camera, but its additional features become a burden rather than an asset.
How I Tested
To find the best pet cameras to test, I first looked for security cameras with extra pet-specific features. I set up each camera individually, noting any difficulties with initial setup, Wi-Fi configuration, and the camera feed's speed and reliability. I tested each camera for at least a week (most for much longer) in various spots around my house, and I rigorously tested the extra features available on most of the cameras, like scheduled feedings, food-dispensing, playtime, and scheduled recordings, noting any issues I experienced. Over the months of testing, I went out of town several times and completely relied on these cams to keep an eye on my two children—I mean, cats.
So, Is There Really a Difference Between Security Cameras and Pet Cameras? Sort Of
Security cameras let you keep an eye on your house (and pet) while you’re away, but pet cameras often include additional pet-specific features, such as the ability to dispense treats and interact with your furry friend via a two-way speaker. These cameras with special features can help ease common pet issues like separation anxiety or boredom. The Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion, for example, has attachments that let you remotely give your pet a treat or engage in “playtime.”
That's not to say you can’t use a security camera as a pet cam, but like any other smart home device that connects to Wi-Fi, it could be hacked and compromise your privacy. Make sure your Wi-Fi password is strong, and set up two-factor authentication in your camera’s app. It’s also a good idea to keep it turned off when you’re home, as an extra precaution.
