My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

Lancs treatment of Anderson 'disrespectful' - Broad
- Published
Lancashire have been "pretty disrespectful" in their treatment of legendary bowler James Anderson, says his long-time England bowler partner Stuart Broad.
Anderson, 44, was told last week he will not have his contract renewed by the Red Rose county, ending his 26-year professional career with the club.
Anderson took 50 wickets in the County Championship last season and served as captain, but incoming director of cricket Paul Farbrace has decided he wants to rebuild the struggling side, who finished second bottom in Division Two of the County Championship, for the future without England's all-time leading wicket-taker.
"I didn't like it from Lancashire," Broad said on the For The Love of Cricket podcast, external.
"It was not done in the right way. I think it was disrespectful.
"You give your icons or greats of the game a better send off than that."
Farbrace, who moved from Sussex at the end of the season, has not yet officially started in his new role at Lancashire but delivered the news to Anderson at a meeting last week alongside chief executive Richard Kenyon, who has also recently been appointed.
The news was first reported on Wednesday and Lancashire did not comment officially until Sunday. At a meeting with members on Monday, the club said they would look into arranging Anderson a farewell.
"It shows a lack of leadership at that club," said Broad, whose combined total of Test wickets with Anderson stands at a record 1,039 in 138 Tests.
"It shows a lack of doing it the right way.
"Paul Farbrace is new, but where is the chair? Where is the board demanding that this is done in a better way?"
Speaking publicly for the first time since the decision on Sunday, Anderson, who also had his England career cut short in 2024 in similar circumstances, expressed his sadness at the situation but stopped short of retiring.
Other counties are understood to be interested in signing the veteran.
"I get the thought process, 'we could probably get two half-decent cricketers for the one and losing that salary'," Broad added.
"It doesn't surprise me that some counties have already been on the phone and seeing what his interest levels are.
"I don't know what his next steps are. I think his statement was quite interesting.
"There will be a lot of counties that want him. He offers a huge amount, he's still one of the best bowlers in the country."

Quick Answer
To stop Google from using your Gmail, Drive, and Photos data for personalized ads, visit google.com/search-personalization, open Connected Content Apps, and disconnect Google Workspace and Photos. Then turn off personalized ads at myadcenter.google.com. You can also delete past activity at activity.google.com.
It’s not hyperbole to say AI agents are genuinely helpful. The big tech companies aren’t stupid to be investing billions of dollars to build these AI agents, but they need more than your money to help you – your data. Google is best placed to play this smart answers game considering it owns some of the most widely used services in the world – Search, Gmail, Chrome, Photos, and Android.
If you’ve let Google’s AI look at your Gmail or Google Photos for smarter answers, there’s a catch. As of October 16, 2026, Google’s privacy policy says data from those apps can also help personalize ads. Google is also testing ads in AI Mode for people who have connected their apps.
Here’s what changed, what it does and doesn’t mean, and how to turn it off.
Table of Contents
What changed
Since 2021, Google’s privacy policy has said that it doesn’t use your Gmail, Drive, or Photos content for personalized ads. According to Ars Technica and Google’s own archive, the old line read: “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos.”
The current policy, effective October 16, 2026, adds a condition:
We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos, unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.
A new passage in the same section spells out how this happens:
You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive… For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.
You “choose” this through Personal Intelligence, the opt-in feature that lets AI Mode and other Search tools draw on your Gmail, Calendar, and Photos. Calendar is US and English only for now, Photos isn’t available in every region, and Drive, though named in the policy, isn’t currently one of the apps you can connect to Search.
The ads side is already live as a test.
What it means for you
It’s easy to overstate this, so here’s what Google actually says.
What Google says won’t happen:
- In its Search help page, Google says: “Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or your Google Photos library.“
- Advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps, and Google doesn’t share your name or email with them.
- Google says it won’t personalize ads on sensitive categories such as race, religion, sexual orientation or health.
What can happen:
The same help page says Search “may reference summaries, excerpts and inferences” from your connected apps, and “that same info may be used to show you ads.” The policy gives an example of personalizing answers: ask Search about a recent hotel booking, and it may use booking details from an email. The ads link comes from the help page: that same kind of info may now be used to show you ads.
Search vs. Gemini:
The ad test is in AI Mode in Search. Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub says “Your Gemini Apps chats are not being used to show you ads.” The policy still lists “Gemini Apps” among services you can connect your data to.
Beyond AI Mode:
When you connect your apps, Google says all Search services can access them, including Search, Discover, Maps, Shopping, Flights, Hotels, Translate, and News. The same page says human reviewers may see some of that data.
Where this applies:
Connecting content apps to Search is available to adults in a long list of countries, including the US and India. The UK and EU countries don’t appear on that list. Personal Intelligence in Gemini is not available in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, Nigeria, or the UK. Google hasn’t said where the ads test is running, and the policy wording is global. What we think is, since Google doesn’t offer either feature in the UK yet, UK readers look largely unaffected for now.
How to opt out of Search Personalization
Disconnect Gmail and Photos from Search (web, Android, iPhone)
As per Google’s help pages, the steps are the same on the web, Android, and iPhone:
- Open your Google Account and go to Data & privacy > Personalization settings > Personalized Recommendations in Search services. Or you can click this if you are already signed in: google.com/search-personalization.
- Under Additional Personal Intelligence, open Connected Content Apps.
- Disconnect Google Workspace and Google Photos.
To go further, turn off Personalized Recommendations on the same page. Google says it’s updating these settings, so labels may differ.
Disconnect apps in Gemini
- Gemini mobile app (Android/iPhone): tap Menu > your profile picture > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
- Web (gemini.google.com): select Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps.
Turn off Google Workspace and Google Photos, plus any other apps you don’t want connected.
Turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center
Go to My Ad Center, select On or Off next to Personalized ads, choose Off, and confirm.
Google says it will then stop using your saved account info and activity for ads, and will show ads based on general factors like the topic you’re viewing. You’ll still see ads; they just won’t be tailored to you. This doesn’t stop connected-app data from being used for AI answers.
Clean up what’s already saved
Disconnecting doesn’t delete your Search Services History, which can still be used for product improvement. Review and delete it at activity.google.com. In Gemini, disconnecting doesn’t delete your Gemini Apps Activity either.
Should you disconnect?
Personal Intelligence is genuinely useful: asking about your trip without pasting in your booking is the whole point, and Google says advertisers don’t get access to your connected apps.
But helping you and choosing your ads are different uses, and the ads part was added after Personal Intelligence launched. If that bothers you, disconnect. A middle path is to keep Personal Intelligence on and turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center. Your data still feeds Google’s AI answers, and Search Services History can be used for product improvement, including AI model training.
The bottom line
While you’d see a lot of noise around these changes on social media, know that this change doesn’t touch everyone’s inbox, because it’s opt-in. But if you connected Gmail or Photos to its AI, what that AI learns can now help pick your ads, starting with a test in AI Mode. If that trade isn’t for you, the switches above take minutes.
FAQs about Search Personalization
1. Is Google reading my emails to target ads?
Not directly, according to Google. It says ads aren’t based “directly” on your inbox, but summaries, excerpts, and inferences Search draws from connected apps can be used for ads.
2. I never turned on Personal Intelligence. Am I affected?
As per the policy, Gmail, Drive, and Photos content isn’t used for ads unless you make it available to other services. It’s opt-in, but worth checking the settings above in case you connected and forgot.
3. Does this apply to Gemini chats?
Google says Gemini chats aren’t used to show you ads right now. The ad test is in AI Mode in Search.
4. Does disconnecting erase what Google already has?
No. Delete your Search Services History at activity.google.com and your Gemini Apps Activity separately, as we described earlier in this article.

Riaz, appealed to all and sundry not to undermine the government’s efforts to make the drug for SMA available to a larger number of patients.
According to him, the decision to provide SMA patients with a less expensive, generic version of the original molecule against SMA, in place of the imported original drug costing several lakhs of rupees for a single vial, had been taken by a technical committee comprising experts in the field.
The purchase procedures initiated during the previous government’s time were completed by the present government. The drug meets all regulatory requirements and quality norms, Dr. Riaz added.
‘Unfounded rumours’
Dr. Riaz appealed to all to stop spreading unfounded rumours about the generic SMA medicine and push patients and their families into an anxious state. He pointed out that the medicine had been available in the open market for nearly a year and was already being used by several SMA patients. To raise the argument that it was an experimental drug, just when the government begins to distribute it free of cost, was preposterous.

Financial assistance

It was common for agencies, companies and public-sector institutions providing CSR funds to hand them over and take photographs in the presence of the Health Minister or the Chief Minister, he added.
Instead of spreading baseless allegations, the efforts of the government and SAT Hospital to safeguard the welfare of patients with SMA should be given more support, Dr. Riaz said.

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

New Delhi, Oct 27: The two-day conclave of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum on Tuesday adopted a joint declaration strongly condemning the 2025 Pahalgam attack and all acts of terrorism as it pledged to combat the menace in all its forms and manifestations and also stressed on non-intervention in the internal affairs of any country.
The joint declaration, announced by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, also condemned the imposition of unilateral economic and secondary sanctions saying such coercive measures have far reaching negative implications on human rights, including the right to development, health and food security of people.
The BRICS Parliamentary Forum supported a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council, saying this reform should make it more just, equitable, democratic, representative, effective, and efficient, better reflecting contemporary realities and the needs of the international community.
"We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir (in Pahalgam) on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.
"We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens," the declaration read.
The Forum said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.
"We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. We emphasise the primary responsibility of States in combating terrorism and that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must fully comply with their obligations under international law, including the Charter of the UN...," it read.
The Forum said it looks forward to further deepening counter-terrorism cooperation and calls for an expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework and concerted actions against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.
"We reaffirm our adherence to the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, non-intervention in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes, as enshrined in the United Nations Charter, as essential foundations for global stability, peace and development," it said.
The Forum reaffirmed its unwavering support for the peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the two-state solution, with the two States living side by side, in peace and security, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.
It asserted the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and an independent, sovereign State.
The Forum expressed deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and, recalling the respective national positions, called for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.
It strongly condemned all violations of international humanitarian law, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, including in BRICS member states, as well as the denial or obstruction of humanitarian access and the targeting of humanitarian personnel.
Iran and United Arab Emirates, which are directly involved with the West Asia conflict, are members of the BRICS. Apart from India, other member nations of the BRICS are: Brazil, Russia, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia and South Africa.
The Forum underlined the need to address accountability for all violations of international humanitarian law.
"We recognise international efforts undertaken by BRICS members to promote respect for, adherence to, and effective implementation of international humanitarian law," it said.
Recognising the urgency of addressing climate change, the BRICS parliamentary body calls for intensifying efforts, through dialogue and international cooperation, to implement nationally determined contributions, strengthen mitigation and adaptation efforts, with a view to achieving the objectives of the UNFCCC and the goals of its Paris Agreement as applicable.
The Forum acknowledge the transformative potential of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and information and communication technologies (ICTs).
"We emphasise the necessity of ensuring the open, safe, secure, stable, equitably accessible, peaceful and interoperable use and development of ICTs environment while respecting sovereignty and national security of each country.
"In addition, promoting energy efficiency of AI systems, fostering AI science and innovation, leveraging AI for economic growth and social good and mitigating potential risks would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future of all countries, especially those of Global South," it said.

Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.
The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor partyroom came hours after senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”
MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats.
In the first Labor partyroom meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.
Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more”, and “more can and should be done”.
“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.
Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities of a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.
Home affairs minister Tony Burke also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.
Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a fulsome response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes like CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.
An ongoing review into Commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.
Opposition leader Angus Taylor told his MPs in a Coalition partyroom meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.
Payman speaks out
Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.
The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.
In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.
“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.
“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office? To me? For him to take our request seriously?”
Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.
Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.
“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan’s recent remarks questioning “unnecessary” angioplasty procedures have drawn objections from medical organisations concerned that it could undermine public confidence in doctors. But the Chief Minister’s remarks demand more than a reflex response; it requires a thoughtful, honest response built on up-to-date evidence based on clinical and research studies.
Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI), by balloon angioplasty and stent placement, has transformed cardiovascular care. During an acute heart attack caused by a suddenly blocked coronary artery, prompt angioplasty and stents can restore blood flow, save heart muscle and improve survival. There is no debate about this approach and second opinions are unnecessary as time is of essence in such an emergency. Stents also offer substantial relief to selected patients with persistent activity-limiting angina (chest pain caused by lack of oxygen-rich blood).
There is a crucial distinction between stenting as a life-saving measure in the above situations to medical treatment via stenting because a narrowing of blood vessels is seen on an angiogram. A coronary angiogram shows the anatomy of the arteries; it does not, by itself, establish that a narrowing requires intervention. The decision to intervene and how to intervene must take account of the patient’s symptoms, the severity of the blockage, its effect on blood flow, the overall pattern of coronary disease and the expected benefit of intervention.
The landmark ISCHEMIA trial, published in The New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, enrolled 5,179 patients at 320 sites in 37 countries with stable coronary artery disease and moderate to severe ischemia (restricted blood flow to the heart). The patients were assigned either to an initial invasive strategy — angiography followed by angioplasty or coronary bypass surgery — or to a conservative strategy of optimal medical treatment, with revascularisation reserved for those who had an acute event or angina. After a median follow-up of 3.2 years, there was no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcomes (cardiac arrests, hospitalisation for unstable angina or heart failure) and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were similar. After a follow-up of 5 years, there was still no significant difference between the two groups in composite outcome or mortality. The core lesson is that most patients with stable coronary artery disease with ischemia on optimal medical treatment would do as well as those who undergo stenting or bypass surgery.
Concerning scale
The growing scale of PCI in India deserves careful examination. National Interventional Council figures show that annual PCI procedures rose from approximately 1,13,000 in 2008 to more than 7,26,000 in 2024 — an increase of more than six-fold. In contrast, PCI procedures in the U.S. fell by about 40% between 2003 and 2016, reflecting progress in prevention and treatment.
These figures do not by themselves prove that stents are overused in India considering its large population, the substantial burden of premature coronary disease, the socio-economic progress in the past decades and the improved access to cardiac care centres. Nevertheless, the divergence in trends between the two countries raises an important question: how much of the increase in PCI is a reflection of fulfilling a genuine clinical need, and how much of it is a reflection of differences in practice patterns, financial incentives and gaps in knowledge on the efficacy of optimal medical treatment?
Optimal medical therapy, based on evidence-based guidelines, is the foundation of care for all coronary artery disease patients. The elements of optimal therapy include LDL-cholesterol lowering, appropriate anti-platelet treatment, blood-pressure control, evidence-based diabetes management and lifestyle changes. A coronary stent treats a specific narrowing; it does not cure the underlying disease of atherosclerosis or eliminate the risk of future heart attacks. Patients remain vulnerable to disease elsewhere in the coronary arteries and must continue preventive treatment.
The way forward is neither condemnation of cardiologists nor unquestioning acceptance of every recommendation for angioplasty. Most doctors strive to act in their patients’ best interests, but no profession is immune to inappropriate practice. The ultimate test of healthcare is not how many procedures are performed, but how many lives are saved and whether patients receive the right treatment at the right time at an affordable cost.
Dr. Enas A. Enas is Preventive Cardiologist and Physician-Scientist, Founding President of the CADI Research Foundation USA; Dr. Basil Varkey is Professor Emeritus of medicine

Shares of Ather Energy jumped as much as 8.1% to an intraday high of ₹1,702 on the BSE after HSBC and Nomura raised their price targets following the electric two-wheeler maker’s Q2 FY27 results. At 11:28 IST, the stock was trading 6.8% higher at ₹1,680.60, giving the company a market capitalisation of ₹66,672.4 Cr (about $6.9 Bn). The gains extended yesterday’s rally, when Ather shares closed 13.7% higher at ₹1,574 on the BSE after the company announced its Q2 FY27 results during market hours. Adding to the positive sentiment, HSBC and Nomura retained their ‘Buy’ ratings and raised their price targets, citing better-than-expected margins and stronger growth prospects following the launch of Ather’s Konarc scooter range. HSBC raised its price target to ₹1,800 from ₹1,600. The brokerage said Ather delivered a strong second quarter, with EBITDA breaking even ahead of expectations despite commodity cost pressures. Nomura increased its price target to ₹2,070 from ₹1,926. It said Ather’s EBITDA margin, excluding other income, stood at 0.8%, beating its estimate of negative 2.6% and the consensus estimate of negative 2.7%. Stronger bookings and improved growth visibility following the Konarc launch were other positives. Ather’s Maiden Profitable Quarter Ather reported a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against a loss of ₹154.1 Cr a year earlier, supported by stronger revenue growth, improving margins, and other income. It had posted a net loss of ₹51.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue rose 62.9% YoY and 20.3% QoQ to ₹1,464.2 Cr. Including other income, EBITDA stood at ₹74.2 Cr, with a margin of 4.9% as against -9.6% a year earlier and 0.8% in Q1 FY27. Total income rose to ₹1,527 Cr from ₹940.7 Cr a year earlier. However, operating revenue remained ₹61.5 Cr below total expenses of ₹1,525.7 Cr, underscoring other income’s contribution to net profitability. CEO Tarun Mehta said during the earnings call that Ather would prioritise capacity expansion and sales growth over near-term net profitability. He cautioned that some margin gains came from temporary measures, including changes to its product mix and reduced incentives, which offered limited scope for further support if commodity prices remained elevated. Ather To Expand Manufacturing Capacity Ather plans to invest ₹122 Cr to expand manufacturing capacity at its Hosur plant in Tamil Nadu and its upcoming Factory 3.0 in Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. The expansion is expected to add 2.25 Lakh units of annual capacity. At Hosur, the company plans to invest up to ₹58 Cr, including taxes, to add capacity for 75,000 units annually by December 2026. Ather has also earmarked ₹53 Cr for a new battery line, which is expected to be completed by Q3 FY28. At Factory 3.0, the company plans to invest ₹64 Cr to add 1.5 Lakh units of annual capacity to the planned 5 Lakh units. The expansion is expected to be completed by Q2 FY28. Ather will finance the investments through a combination of debt and internal accruals. During Q2 FY27, it also raised ₹1,300 Cr through a qualified institutions placement and ₹200 Cr through a preferential equity allotment. The expansion follows a sharp increase in customer interest. Enquiries rose 109% YoY to around 10 Lakh in Q2 FY27, while pre-orders more than doubled to 1.8 Lakh. Vehicle sales increased 42% to 93,211 units. Ather launched its sub-₹1 Lakh Konarc electric scooter range during the quarter, taking its portfolio to 15 variants across three product lines.

Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.
Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.
For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?
At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?
JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.
Before Parliament, I worked for the largest children's charity in the UK for three years on their policy and public affairs, trying to change legislation on behalf of the most vulnerable children in the country. Six years prior to that I worked for a domestic abuse charity called SafeLives where we did huge amounts of work to try and improve the situation for survivors of domestic abuse, particularly through the Domestic Abuse Act.
Those twin issues of women and children have become my focus in Parliament, and I’ve been very clear that my reason for being here, my mission really, is to be a voice for women and children.
Well, that’s a good entry point for us to start talking about this year. So in early 2026, there was widespread reporting on Grok, xAI’s chatbot, being used to create sexualized images of children and women, and those images being circulated on X. How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon of deepfakes being used in this way?
Very aware, and actually had been working with survivors who had experienced deepfakes for quite a number of years. Ever since the advent of AI this has been happening to women, and there’s also been developing risks of children both being put into child sexual abuse material and also children using nudification tools on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves because these tools are so easy to access and often free.
So I was already very alive to the huge harms being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children before Grok ever happened. It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools from other companies had already taken steps to stop them from being used to create this kind of content.
There are a number of tools where, if you type in “nudify,” or “take the clothes off this person,” the tool will refuse to do that. So into that environment came Grok.
Was there a particularly egregious example or incident prior to Grok when you became aware of deepfakes that really stuck with you?
There is a brilliant campaigner who goes by the name of Jodie. I think it was probably listening to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked, and it was such an affront to her that somebody would do this, and then she found out it was actually a friend. Such a betrayal of trust.
These things destroy not just the individual involved, but often families and everyone around them too.
For people who don’t know, who exactly was Jodie? Is this a constituent of yours or someone who came forward to you specifically?
No, no, no. She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue. That’s not her real name.
I know it sounds obvious, but what exactly is nudification?
It is where you ask an AI tool to take the image or video of a real person and use generative AI to make that person either nude, partially nude, or engaging in pornographic acts. This is something that, because of the photorealistic nature of AI images, it has become increasingly hard to see what is a fake image.
It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.
So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal earlier this year that made you want to raise this in the House of Commons?
It was the fact that we already knew that you could stop this from happening by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this.
This was completely avoidable. That’s why I spoke out, but also because I’d just spent a year and a half campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps, and here was an all-purpose AI tool becoming a nudification app.
It just felt to me as though we were making strides in the UK, and then the world’s richest man and his product decided to turn the clock back.
So what exactly did you stand up and say?
What I did was I talked about the need for the government to accelerate its ban on nudification apps, which it did. So the then secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, Liz Kendall, said that she was going to bring that ban into law through the Crime and Policing Act, which she did.
But I also said that it was very important that we went further than that, because, of course, Grok itself is not a sole-purpose nudification tool. It has a general use, and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots under the auspices of the Online Safety Act. That is also what eventually happened in the Crime and Policing Act, and we’re now waiting until that legislation comes into effect. There’s got to be a consultation, I understand, before it does.
So technically another Grok could happen in this period, but in the future there would be much stronger measures that we could take against tools like Grok creating nudification content.
So that’s a really positive outcome of your interjection in Parliament, but what else happened as a result of you standing up?
Well, one of the things that happened was that I posted on social media saying that Elon Musk should stop Grok from being able to do this.
And then, of course, I became a victim of the same trend. So Grok put this woman in a bikini. And most of the images were sort of pornified, I would say. They weren’t nude images, but they were me with inflated boobs in a bikini.
Then people tried to make it funny, I guess, by putting a swastika on me or hammer and sickles. Or making me pregnant with quintuplets and putting me in a kitchen. Because of course that’s the only use for women—birthing and making dinner. But the really disturbing one was a video of me being surrounded by a group of men, chloroformed over my mouth, and then I fall backwards onto a chair. Then my skirts are lifted up. So no nudity, but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault. So it was really distressing and disturbing.
That was the point at which a friend said, “You probably need to reach out to a lawyer.” Because each of these things we reported to X, and none of them contravened their terms and conditions. We just kept getting those sort of repeat emails coming back. “We’ve looked into this, and there’s nothing to see here.” So I did engage a lawyer, who sent a letter to X to ask for these to be removed, and they were.
But it was at that point that he said, “I think you might actually have a case. We think that xAI have broken the law.”
It’s impressive how you handled it, but it must have been really awful.
It was; it was awful. This is done to demean, to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces. From my perspective, I tend to use bad or difficult things that happen as a way of thinking about how we change this for the future.
My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell. She used to say to me, “How do we change this negative energy into something positive?” “How do we work our way out of this into a place where we actually feel that we’ve learnt from it?”
So I guess she instilled in me that sense that when something bad happens you’ve got a choice. You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it, or you can use it as a catalyst for change.
So I was quite trepidatious about the idea of taking on a legal action. Not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI, now SpaceXAI. [Eds. note: The company recently rebranded itself as SpaceXSI.] He’s the world’s richest man. But also because I didn’t want myself to necessarily be the story. Many, many women had things that were created of them through both Grok and other nudification tools that are much, much worse.
Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity to say that actually they’d broken the law, there was an important point of principle on behalf of all of the women and the children whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok, who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case. So I decided that I wanted to do this, because I wanted to be able to show that no one is bigger than the law.
Doesn’t matter how rich you are or how powerful you are or how big a reach you have in terms of your social media presence or who your friends might be at the top of various governments. If you break the law in our country, you need to feel the force of that. As an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator, it is important that we uphold our law where it has been broken.
So it’s also about giving control back, I think, to us as individuals, but also as a society. So many of these digital changes have been done without our consent or say, and I think there’s a feeling that there’s a sort of runaway train that we’re all on, whether we want to be or not, because we all need to use online spaces for our work, for connection.
And so my view is that we should be expecting companies to respect our law or at least make new laws to bring them more into line with what society really needs.
You said that you gave it some thought. In that moment of trying to decide how to respond, what are you weighing up? Who are you talking to? Are you going back and talking to your team or your family to work out how you should respond, knowing that it may invite further speculation and further attention?
My family mostly, my husband in particular. It’s one thing being a politician and arguing your case to change the law on behalf of women and children; it’s another having your own legal case.
So I was worried about the impact that that might have on my family, my children. I also know that this can bring danger to politicians. So I worried about the fact that I am obviously engaging and making the defendant somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media. However, I don’t like bullies. I very strongly believe that it’s important to fight on the field that you’ve got, and this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.
So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth having that kind of attention and potential danger, because there is a bigger issue here that we need to get right.
When you say you don’t like bullies, are you talking about, let’s face it, men who used Grok in this way in the first place, or are you talking about Elon Musk?
I’m talking about the men who use this as a form of trying to push women out of the online space. Actually it was quite clear in quite a lot of the comments that they were saying, “Well, if you don’t like this, then get off the platform.”
Either that or, “If this is too hot for you, get out the kitchen,” which I always find quite funny because they put me in a kitchen. I think it’s really interesting when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK, it’s highly weighted toward men. I think some of that’s down to the fact that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it. So I’m assuming, and correct me if I’m wrong, that the other side of the response to going public is that other women have come forward to you.
Absolutely. Actually, one of the heartening things has been people coming forward and saying, “Thank you, because this has now given me the license to actually accept that what happened to me wasn’t my fault. It’s not my shame.” So, in a way, what I’m hoping is that this has helped some victims to process what has happened to them and understand that this was not right.
I’ve also had emails from parents where they’ve said that this has happened to their daughter. It’s been done by boys at school. I’ve had teachers saying that boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them. And it’s something where we’ve just sort of let it happen and wash over us and accept that somehow this is now a part of the society we live in.
So yes quite a number of people have come forward. Obviously not all of their experiences have been through Grok, and I think one of the things is that often, when you see these films or images, you don’t know what platform they’ve been created on. I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok was because it was integrated with X, and you could see the commands that had been given by the users.
But much of the time, when this content is created, most victims don’t know by whom or on what platform. And so there’s really very little they can do about it. And I think it’s that sort of sense of helplessness that you have been violated, and that is the word that comes up so frequently from victims of this particular issue.
It’s not just that it’s nudified. Of course, much of my content wasn’t. It’s the lack of consent. And lots of people say, “Oh, but it’s fake. It’s just a laugh.” But what people don’t understand is that it is hyperrealistic, and it’s your face.
It’s a piece of your soul. It’s not just pixels on the internet. It is a person. And because obviously I’ve worked for a long time in violence against women and girls and spoken to many victims of sexual assault and to children who’ve been victims of child sexual abuse, it is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.
It can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma. And there have been a number of people I’ve met who have said that the world seems less safe to them because this has happened to them.
I think you’ve already touched on it, but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes that you would wish to dispel?
That it comes without any harm.
That it’s just a laugh.
There is clear harm, even when it’s not done to demean or degrade. So even if it’s done sometimes by friends, the fact is that you haven’t consented to that. There is something about the human psyche which is that when you see yourself so realistically created in a different situation or scenario, something that’s not something you would have done, I think it’s quite discombobulating.
I think your brain can’t quite process it because your brain knows it’s not true, but it looks very true. And I think psychologically we still don’t really understand how this content is going to change the way we think about our world, how we know what is true and what isn’t true.
Right.
Now, of course, you can do fantastic things with generative AI. All I’m calling for is that we respect people’s consent, and that’s why one of the things I’ve been working on since this happened is to look at whether we could create a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.
Could we create a greater right over our likeness online so that there’s a new social norm, which is that no, you can’t copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot and do whatever you want with it. That’s not yours. It’s not your data. It’s their data, and you’re breaching the law if you do that.
I think if we were to do that, we could have a wide range of applications. It wouldn’t just be in this space of the sexualization of women and children. But also with political disinformation. We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something that they didn’t, and then that leads to real-world harm. And so we’ve got to find a new social norm that says unless for public figures it’s parody or satire—and absolutely you’ve got to protect that—but in all other instances your picture, your voice, and your moving image is your personal data, and it’s not for anyone else to use.
So that’s interesting because you’re touching on new social norms and the possibility of new laws to keep up with this technology. But your lawsuit is specifically under a data law. Talk to me about that versus a law around consensual imagery or deepfakes specifically.
So, my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR, the data protection law, and it contends that Grok misused my data without my consent. It didn’t have consent to process my data, the data being my face and my likeness. But also under privacy laws that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy and that particularly the video of me being prepared for sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold and that nobody should be expected to be on the receiving end of.
Let’s remember, this is actually a product that has been designed by software engineers and developers, and that actually products should not lead to an invasion of privacy and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that, including distress and a sense that I was being harassed by this particular creation of this particular video.
So, it rests on good solid legal grounds, and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.
I don’t know how much you can say, legally, but what part of the process are you in? What happens next? What’s the timeline for a resolution to this case?
So like with a lot of legal cases, it’s very, very hard to pin down a timeline. But my understanding is that we should be receiving the response and the defense from SpaceXAI in the near future. But we don’t have a deadline or a particular time that I can put on it.
After that, my understanding is that the case will then be looked at, and if there is a case to answer, then it will go to a court hearing. But once again, no idea when that might be. And I think there’s lots of legal things that I don’t understand that need to be worked out in the meantime as well between my lawyers and their lawyers.
Have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself from Elon Musk or anyone at xAI about this case? Has he ever spoken publicly about it?
No.
Would you expect him to?
I don’t think so. They clearly want to challenge this case, and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case come through.
You were in New York recently to address the city council about your case. You didn’t get to speak to anyone directly at the company, is that right?
No. I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn’t turn up. Four of the other frontier AI companies did attend under subpoena. SpaceXAI didn’t, but they eventually did get their hearing with SpaceX in the city council. So, they have now had their opportunity to put questions and indeed did raise my case with them, I understand.
Was it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that where a company that you’re suing doesn't bother turning up?
I think it’s quite rude to the elected members of the New York City Council when you are a business that operates in New York. Indeed, I was told that they were just a few subway stops from City Hall. So I had traveled quite a long way from England to be there. And they couldn’t be bothered to turn up, which yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub, but they’ve now got there, so that’s a good thing.
Since you made the decision to take this to the courts, there have been a number of proposals in Parliament, notably there was a proposal for a kill switch bill at one point. Now I believe it’s dead or it’s not going very well. Is that right?
So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch. And my understanding is the government rejected that. There continues to be strong calls for regulation of particularly superintelligent AI. We’ve heard various theories, whether it’s 2 percent, 10 percent, 20 percent risk of human extinction from this sort of race to superintelligence, a recursive AI, and we wouldn’t allow those margins of risk in any other sphere.
We would not allow it in bridge building or airplane making. They didn’t even allow it when they were testing the nuclear bomb and the Trinity test. It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking is outside of democratic structures. It’s not with the public. It is being done by some incredibly, exceptionally wealthy companies and organizations who say they have the interests of the planet at heart.
But each time, actually, they’re asked about whether that is the future of humanity or whether they think that these risks could kill humanity, there’s a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, “We’ll just keep going because we want to make money,” I guess.
It has been reported in the British press that there are members of Parliament, some of whom are working on committees to do with technology, who still don’t really understand what AI is. And clearly you’re not one of them because you’re aware of the dangers of this issue. But do you feel working across parties that you’re still having to explain technology and its dangers and possibilities to people who are making laws, or should be making laws, to protect the public from AI?
Well, look, I don’t think that’s only the case about AI. We are humans after all, and we have to deal with every single subject that exists under the sun. We have to get our heads around things that we’ve never heard of before.
A bit like being a journalist actually.
That’s true. But you have to then make laws and decisions. So, I don’t want to be unfair to my colleagues.
You may be a specialist in housing policy and you then need to get your head around AI. But I would say that this is the most important issue in front of anybody in parliament or politics at the moment, and therefore, everyone needs to get their head around AI.
My background is in social policy for women and children. But because we did quite a lot of work on the Online Safety Act when I was working for a children’s charity, we campaigned to get the age verification ban for children in pornography into the OSA. And indeed, created quite a strong piece of legislation in respect of that.
We had to get our heads around online safety on the online space. The problem was, of course, that act didn’t include AI chatbots. There were a number of amendments that tried to get it in and we would’ve been in a much better place had we actually succeeded.
But you know, I’m still not a tech expert even though I had quite a while to try to understand these things. But my view is that this is definitely the new front line of where harms are occurring. We can see that hugely in the increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, which is absolutely exploding.
In the end it comes down to the people who create the products. And that’s why we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.
I’m very, very hopeful that the government is going to look at it really, really closely because there are always design choices that you can make and that can help to prevent these harms, these harms that are completely knowable. We can predict these harms, and so it should be easy to design them out from the start.
Companies can put in more safeguards. Why don’t they?
Profit. But also, let’s be honest, these are global tools and companies. So unless you have international agreement it is a bit like playing whack-a-mole, isn’t it?
The person who made that horrible video of me being chloroformed lives in the US, so the police aren’t gonna follow it up because they’re out of the country.
Do you know who did it?
I don’t know who they are, but the police did find who they were because it’s a criminal offense what they did. They just weren’t able to bring the charge.
We’ve spoken in the last 40 minutes about the full spectrum of human awfulness. I don’t think there’s any area of it that we haven’t …
Oh, sorry. Welcome to my life.
I’m really struck by how cheerful you are despite this. How do you remain so upbeat and hopeful while dealing with all of this?
Because you’ve always got to have hope for the future. I do have a really strong conviction that with the right group of people pushing toward a goal, you can achieve that. You don’t have to accept that things will always be like this. When people come together, when communities come together, you can act for change.
We’re just about to introduce our ban on strangulation in pornography, which is another thing that I’ve been campaigning for and introduced an amendment last year, which the government accepted.
There are always things that we can do to change. You just need to keep going. And also I would say that when you work with these terribly dark areas, yes, it can be quite vicariously traumatizing. But actually the people who work within the sectors are some of the most hopeful people, partly because if you lose hope, then it’s really bad. And we can’t because we’re talking about protecting vulnerable children, and we are fighting for women and our rights to be free of this harm.

The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
TIRED
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.
Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.
At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.
A Screen Has Its Perks
The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.
As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.
I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.
The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.
I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back
The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.
Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.
Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)
The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.
Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.
The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.
The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.

Age proved to be no barrier for Poona A Bamba, a retired Delhi High Court judge who took on an unexpected challenge in November 2024: trekking to Everest Base Camp with her husband, Anil Bamba, then 66, an experienced traveller and former bureaucrat.
What began as an unplanned decision turned into a 10-day trek spanning more than 65 kilometres across rugged mountain trails, dense forests, suspension bridges and freezing conditions.
The couple reached Everest Base Camp, located at an altitude of 5,364 metres.
“I thought to myself, if he can go at the age of 66, why can’t I?” Bamba recalled, as reported by The Indian Express.
Initially, she had not planned to join her husband. But when he struggled to find companions for the trip, she reconsidered and decided to take on the challenge herself.
Born on September 1, 1961, in Delhi, Poona A Bamba pursued her education in the capital. She graduated with honours in Botany from Hansraj College, University of Delhi, in 1980 before completing her LLB in 1983 and LLM in 1988 from the university's Faculty of Law.
She also earned a diploma in Administrative Law from the Indian Law Institute, New Delhi.
Bamba began her professional career as an advocate, practising in Delhi's district courts and the High Court from 1983 to 1987. She subsequently worked with Punjab National Bank and Central Bank of India as a law officer and deputy chief officer (Law), respectively, between 1987 and 1996.
From 1996 to 2002, she worked with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in Mumbai, serving as Division Chief (Legal) and Joint Legal Advisor.
During this period, she represented the institutions before courts across India and the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
In December 2002, she joined the Delhi Higher Judicial Service, beginning a judicial career that spanned nearly two decades before her elevation to the Delhi High Court.
During her tenure in the judiciary, Bamba presided over several jurisdictions, including matrimonial and family courts, land acquisition cases, appellate proceedings under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, and sessions courts.
She also served as a special judge handling cases investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) at Patiala House Courts.
Her administrative responsibilities included serving as District and Sessions Judge in different districts of Delhi. She held positions in South East District at Saket, New Delhi District at Patiala House Courts and South District at Saket Courts Complex.
Bamba was elevated as a permanent judge of the Delhi High Court on March 28, 2022. She retired on August 31, 2023.
She authored books on marriage, parenting and the justice system
Beyond her judicial responsibilities, Bamba has written four books exploring relationships, family disputes and the justice system.
Her works include Perfect Marriage — Not a Mirage, How to Save Your Marriage, Temple of Justice — A School of Life and Parents at War — Custody Battles in Indian Courts.
She has also published articles in journals associated with the Delhi Judicial Academy, the National Stock Exchange and the Central Bank of India.
Alongside her writing, she has served as a guest faculty member and resource person at institutions including the Delhi Judicial Academy, the UTI Institute of Capital Markets and training institutes associated with financial institutions.
These included programmes at Baruch College in New York and the US Securities and Exchange Commission in Washington.
Her interests, however, extend beyond law and finance. A sports enthusiast, she earned the title of Best Athlete at the University of Delhi's Faculty of Law in 1983.
She is also a bird watcher and nature enthusiast who has participated in initiatives involving micro-forests and tree adoption at district courts.
