Are Chelsea finally playing the brand of football Sonia Bompastor wants - and is it WSL title-worthy?
Digital journalist Laura Hunter returns for a second season with a WSL-dedicated column, analysing all the big talking points from across the weekend's action; this week's focus is on Chelsea's resurgence and Man Utd's swift development under Eva Olid
Tuesday 27 October 2026 12:48, UK
Sky Sports columnist Laura Hunter analyses the big talking points from the sixth round of Women's Super League matches, bringing you closer to the key stories at the heart of the women's game. Plus: Vote on the topics you want covered in the next few weeks.
Are Chelsea back in business?
It's been a long time since Chelsea entered a domestic campaign as underdogs. The bookies might have had them as favourites to win the WSL title before a ball was kicked but most hardened observers chose Man City as the more likely champions. The market appeared to be hedging their bets on history.
While I still believe Man City are the team to beat, Chelsea's start to the season cannot be ignored. After seven played they are top by virtue of goal difference, with a perfect record since their opening day draw with Aston Villa. City and Chelsea's results in a head-to-head count are actually identical - but of course the nip and tuck is more nuanced than that.
Chelsea's win from behind to beat Crystal Palace at the weekend, without Keira Walsh or Lauren James, was a deliberate show of strength. And an indication of Sonia Bompastor's intent to balance her squad between priorities. The Blues host Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Are they equipped to sustain such momentum? The numbers suggest they are well placed to compete with Man City. Chelsea are the league's top scorers, best chance creators and have conceded the fewest goals against. Dig a bit deeper into the data and their improved output presents the picture of a team revitalised.
It may have taken two years, but Bompastor has finally got her wish. The Frenchwoman always wanted her side to have greater technical control but was struggling to get the arrangement right, especially in midfield. At long last, Chelsea are a team with an identifiable attacking style, based on the principles of progressive, possession-orientated football.
The system relies heavily on high-advancing full-backs, who are dynamic enough to stretch the pitch in possession and make it more compact when the ball is lost. Ellie Carpenter and Katie McCabe are perfect for the role.
Carpenter is the WSL's best in class when it comes to two-way influence. She ranks as the league's highest-performing defender in terms of goals scored (3), shots taken (17), touches in the opposition box (49) and open-play crosses (40). She and McCabe have generated 17 chances for team-mates apiece.
In central areas, the introduction of Lexi Potter has encouraged a higher role for Keira Walsh and the combination has meant Chelsea are able to dictate tempo with greater success and variation. Aesthetically, Chelsea are a better watch, but crucially, with more reliable end product.
Melvine Malard was an inspired signing in the summer, boasting four WSL goals from four starts so far, matched by the consistency of James. Goals are coming from elsewhere, too, as the intensity of Chelsea's midfield press continues to generate high turnovers and therefore opportunities for lesser-known scorers. Walsh and Sjoeke Nusken have bagged four between them.
Such consistency of delivery is enough to excite even the most skeptical of spectators. And Bompastor must take credit too, making two changes at half-time against Palace to turn the result on its head.
No doubt Chelsea in a relentless rhythm spells danger for the competition. Only time will tell if such an uptick means they remain close chasers of Man City - or have in fact managed to overtake them.
Are Man Utd in better shape than first thought?
Man City won 3-0 home and away in the derby last season. It was the least competitive that fixture had been for some time. And there was plenty to suggest a similar pattern would repeat itself this term, given City's perfect start and United's patchy evolution under Eva Olid.
But Olid's side have turned a corner in recent weeks. Now on a four-game unbeaten streak, the Spaniard's possession-led approach is starting to take recognisable shape.
Against Charlton last Sunday, United completed 700 passes with an accuracy of 88.7 per cent. Both club record high figures in a WSL game. This week, they went toe-to-toe with the league's pass-masters and boasted an equal share of the ball, landing more accurate passes overall and a higher amount in the opposition half. Few sides are technically capable of doing that to City.
"If you want to see the progression of this United team, this is a great example of it," said Sky Sports' Izzy Christiansen on co-comms at Leigh Sports Village. United were breaking lines with the frequency of a side who had been modelled on this tactical plan for years.
Jess Park in particular was outstanding, involved prolifically in the build-up phase. She is the glue. The ball-carrier, but also the player with the cognitive ability to play in a way that accepts responsibility for being at the heart of every attack. Importance is placed on Ella Toone too.
Such numbers represent more than baby steps. It's evidence that United's squad, fairly modest in size, can produce the systematic style Olid prefers while also getting results. To be the first to take points off City is a triumph in itself. They have jumped into fourth in the table as reward.
Of course there are many more layers to this approach and Olid is relying on key contributors to make it work consistently. But major ground has been broken over the past six weeks. The manager is clearly enthused: "How this team has built in confidence from day one to now, in a short period of time, the progression has been massive."

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

వీడియోను నిశితంగా పరిశీలించినప్పుడు, అందులో కొన్ని అసమానతలు కనిపించి వైరల్ వీడియోను HIYA, Resemble AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్ ద్వారా ఇది డీప్ ఫేక్ ఆడియో అని నిర్ధారించాము.
పైగా, ప్రభుత్వానికి చెందిన PIB ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ కూడా వైరల్ వీడియో నకిలీదని స్పష్టం చేసింది.

Ranking England's Ballon d'Or winners - how does Kane compare?
- Published
English Ballon d'Or winners have been few and far between. Triumphs to be treasured, names never to be forgotten.
Harry Kane, England's great talisman and captain, is the first to claim football's grandest individual accolade in 25 years after a sensational campaign in Bayern Munich colours - and only the fifth Englishman to ever do so.
Before him Michael Owen, in 2001, was the first Three Lions star to take it since Kevin Keegan's successive triumphs 22 years earlier.
England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton did it in 1966, and that came after Stanley Matthews won the inaugural prize a decade earlier - handed what began life as the European Footballer of the Year award in 1956.
Others have come close - Billy Wright, Bobby Moore, Gary Lineker, David Beckham and Frank Lampard are all among the runners-up. Lucy Bronze, in 2019, and Beth Mead, 2022, also more recently finished second.
Of course, the award has gradually evolved into the global behemoth it is today.
The caveat with those earlier winners is that it was not a worldwide prize - until 1995 it was only open to European players, and only in 2007 did it expand to include all players from all clubs across the world.
However, that does not detract from the award-winning performances these stars produced - each enjoyed prize-worthy campaigns that caught voters' eyes across Europe and the world.
But who among the five to have held the coveted prize is England's greatest Ballon d'Or winner?
5. Michael Owen, Liverpool, 2001
We won't hold it against Michael Owen for suggesting he didn't know what the Ballon d'Or was when Gerard Houllier first rang to announce he'd won it.
And, in fairness, the then 22-year-old swotted up sufficiently by the time he received the award, reeling off a list of previous winners.
Owen in those days, even after his initial hamstring struggles, was explosive, electric - searing pace and acceleration complemented by the most ruthless of finishes. He became a renowned goalscorer in his teenage years and, by 2001, was one of the most sought-after youngsters in world football.
Owen's Ballon d'Or-winning year was one of iconic moments. He helped Liverpool to a treble, clinching the League Cup on penalties before beating Arsenal in the FA Cup final - Owen scored twice late on to turn the game in Liverpool's favour.
The leveller was an acrobatic and clinically taken strike inside the Arsenal box, the winner a devastating break in which the prolific striker darted away from Lee Dixon and Tony Adams before slotting past David Seaman with his left foot.
The forward then set up two of the goals as Houllier's side beat Alaves 5-4 in extra time in the Uefa Cup final, having earlier in the competition scored a famous double against Roma at the Stadio Olimpico that carried the Reds through.
He finished the season as Liverpool's top goalscorer with 24 in all competitions. Owen's most iconic performance that year, however, came for England against Germany, scoring a famous hat-trick in Munich.
Injuries meant Owen never maintained that peak for as long as he would have hoped. Indeed, only Brazilian great Ronaldo claimed a Ballon d'Or at a more tender age.
4. Stanley Matthews, Blackpool, 1956
Sir Stanley Matthews, first and oldest winner of the Ballon d'Or - a prize then decided by voters from 16 countries.
Twelve of the panel put the Blackpool winger on their ballot, with six placing him first - beating Alfredo di Stefano and Raymond Kopa, who competed in the inaugural European Cup final for Real Madrid and Reims, respectively. That alone shows how revered Matthews was.
Matthews, two months shy of his 42nd birthday when he received the award, led Blackpool to second in the English top flight. This was behind Manchester United's Busby Babes that season, though voters were likely influenced by his performance in the FA Cup final three years earlier. Then, the Tangerines beat Bolton 4-3 in a match dubbed the 'Matthews Final' and broadcast in cinemas.
In an era where following the game often came largely via radio and newspaper reports, Matthews' mythical status drew fans to stadiums in huge numbers, with curious onlookers keen for a glimpse of his magic whenever Blackpool came to town. He dazzled for England, too.
Matthews was born during the First World War and would remarkably continue playing for another nine years after his award, retiring aged 50. His longevity no doubt was a factor, but should not take away from his continued brilliance.
Matthews was famous the world over, lauded by fellow stars for his creativity and ingenuity at a time where greatness did not boil down to individual stats. A creator rather than a scorer.
He was innovative, too. Nicknamed 'The Wizard of the Dribble', he would perform stretching and breathing exercises, do extra training and take care of his diet - fasting and not drinking alcohol.
Most poignantly, he was one of football's great entertainers, described by Ballon d'Or founder Gabriel Hanot - who was thought to have preferred Di Stefano - as the sport's Charlie Chaplin.
Matthews was adored by a generation, an outside right who became an icon. He received the award in the modest surroundings of Blackpool Town Hall, a low-key affair but one that cemented his legacy.
3. Harry Kane, Bayern Munich, 2026
Now, Harry Kane has produced one of the most sensational individual campaigns on record. You could argue that should place him higher, but those above him on this list have done some heavy lifting, too.
Looking at his output from the beginning of the 2025-26 season to the end of this summer's World Cup, the evaluation period for this year's award, Kane has delivered the most goals for club and country by any player in Europe's top five leagues since Lionel Messi's astonishing 2011-12 return.
The England skipper netted 61 times in 51 outings across all competitions for Bayern, winning a German league and cup double while also becoming the fastest player to hit a century of Bundesliga goals.
He also scored 12 times for his country, with six of those coming during England's run to the World Cup semi-finals.
The argument, of course, is that Kane is playing for a dominant Bayern side in a league they are heavy favourites to win each year.
The counter is the 33-year-old has redefined the centre-forward role - his incredible passing range and hold-up play making him an all-round playmaker.
Kane has been developing and maturing into one of England's all-time greats ever since those early loan spells at Leyton Orient and Millwall. His Premier League output for Tottenham was phenomenal season upon season, gradually adding assists to a prolific goal output.
In Munich, especially last season, Kane has just taken that to another level.

2. Bobby Charlton, Manchester United, 1966
The question mark hanging over those winners pre-1995, when the award opened beyond European players, or even before 2007, when it became truly global, is whether there was a more worthy recipient sitting outside the current criteria.
Some may argue Igor Belanov was slightly upstaged by Diego Maradona in 1986, for example.
But 20 years earlier, few could dismiss the credentials of a man who pioneered the Three Lions' first and only World Cup triumph, Manchester United's Bobby Charlton.
A survivor of the Munich Air Disaster in 1958, Charlton and United went on to win the FA Cup in 1963 and English top flight two years later. By 1966, at the age of 28, Charlton was in his prime, heading into the World Cup on the back of 16 top-flight goals from midfield for United that season.
Not only was he at the heart of that United side, who reached the European Cup semi-finals, he was the man England boss Alf Ramsey decided to build his team around for a first World Cup on home soil.
After an opening goalless draw with Uruguay, Charlton gave England's campaign lift-off with a scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark strike from distance that was still rising when it crashed into the corner of the Wembley net.
Charlton helped carry the hosts to the semi-finals, where he scored twice as England knocked out Euesbio's Portugal, before he and West Germany's Franz Beckenbauer tussled in the final as England won 4-2 in extra time.
Benfica's Eusebio finished second to Charlton in the Ballon d'Or rankings that year and Bayern Munich's Beckenbauer was third, with Charlton's World Cup performances showcasing not only his knack for a goal, passing range and poise, but also his selflessness. A true team player.
It was a fruitful era for individual success at Old Trafford. Scotland's Denis Law won the Ballon d'Or two years earlier and Northern Ireland's George Best scooped the prize in 1968 as United won the European Cup.
Charlton finished second in successive years after his triumph. But his pivotal role in England's World Cup triumph earns him the runner-up spot on this list.

1. Kevin Keegan, Hamburg, 1978 & 1979
It had to be, really.
Kevin Keegan scored 20 times as Liverpool won the European Cup and English First Division in 1977, and were a whisker away from completing the Treble - losing the FA Cup final to Manchester United. He also finished as Ballon d'Or runner-up to Borussia Monchengladbach's Danish star Allan Simonsen.
Keegan followed Simonsen to Germany by the time the award was announced, joining Cup Winners' Cup holders Hamburg on a lucrative deal, though they were hammered by his former side in the European Super Cup - and Keegan endured a slow start to Bundesliga life that was not helped by an eight-week suspension for punching someone in a friendly during the winter break.
Keegan soon settled but his first season was nothing spectacular. Instead 'Mighty Mouse' made a flying start to the new campaign - one in which Hamburg would become Bundesliga champions for the first time.
He also produced some impressive individual displays for England, even though the Three Lions missed out on that summer's World Cup, scoring against Brazil in a friendly and twice against Denmark in September.
Keegan's form was timely. He arguably deserved to win the Ballon d'Or a year earlier, which perhaps lingered in voters' minds, making 22 of the 26 ballot papers and ranking top on nine to finish above Barcelona's Austrian star Hans Krankl.
Keegan continued to flourish after Christmas to finish with 17 top-flight goals, including 11 in 12 games during the run-in. But it was more than just the goals, with Keegan a scampering, relentlessly creative presence.
The fluid, attacking HSV were in the midst of storming their way to a European Cup final when Keegan was named Europe's best player for a second successive year on Christmas Day 1979, this time being named top by 18 of the 26 voters.
The permed Keegan was the continent's biggest star and a cultural icon, too.
Hamburg would lose the European Cup final to Nottingham Forest at the Bernabeu, Keegan's last game before leaving for Southampton.
But he stands alone as the only British player to win two Ballon d'Or awards - at the time, only Johan Cruyff had matched his feat of going back-to-back - and that, of course, makes him England's greatest recipient.

A successful alliance with the INDIA bloc hinges on the YSRCP and Congress aligning, which could be Jagan Mohan Reddy’s biggest challenge
NEW DELHI: Is YSRCP supremo YS Jagan Mohan Reddy signalling a drift towards the Congress-led INDIA bloc? Or is he trying to break free from the image of being soft on the BJP?The former Andhra Pradesh chief minister has provided issue-based support to the BJP-led NDA government on several key legislations in Parliament while he was in power in the state. However, he has stayed away from joining any alliance till now. So, when Jagan Reddy recently regretted his “mistake” of supporting the 2023 NDA legislation for selecting the Chief Election Commissioner, it fuelled speculation about his future political moves."We regret supporting the process under which the ruling party nominates the Chief Election Commissioner at the Centre. Neither the CEC nor the SEC should be appointed by the ruling party. The selection committee should comprise the Prime Minister, the leader of the opposition and the Chief Justice of India (CJI), with all three exercising their voting rights," the YSRCP chief said recently, calling the current selection system "flawed."The timing and context of Jagan’s remarks are significant. So, is he rethinking his “solo” politics? And if yes, will the Congress be ready to tango with him in Andhra Pradesh? After all, alliances with regional parties have been the Congress’s biggest Achilles heel across states.
Jagan’s support for NDA’s key Bills
Jagan Mohan Reddy’s MPs backed the Modi government several times between 2019 and 2024, both in Lok Sabha and in Rajya Sabha, on many important legislations. However, when it came to stitching an alliance for the 2024 elections, the BJP ignored Jagan’s help and joined hands with his arch-rival Chandrababu Naidu. Together, TDP and BJP swept the polls in Andhra Pradesh, winning 164 out of 175 seats in the assembly and 21 out of 25 seats in Lok Sabha. The YSRCP was reduced to 11 seats in the assembly and 4 in Lok Sabha.Despite being spurned by the BJP and his party’s shock defeat, Jagan Mohan Reddy remained confident about his BJP ties. After all, he still had 15 MPs (4 in Lok Sabha and 11 in Rajya Sabha) to provide the much-needed support to the BJP’s minority government at the Centre. Jagan even announced that his MPs would extend issue-based support to the NDA government in matters concerning national and state interest.But with the BJP heavily dependent on Chandrababu Naidu’s support for survival of its government at the Centre, there was little room for the saffron party to accommodate Jagan Reddy. Nearly two and a half years down the line, Reddy seems to have accepted this harsh reality and is perhaps gearing up to chart a new path for the next political challenge in 2029.
Jagan vs Congress
However, for any successful alliance with the INDIA bloc - the YSRCP and the Congress will have to be on the same page. And that perhaps would be the biggest challenge for Jagan Mohan Reddy.Jagan Mohan Reddy had a bitter parting from the Congress in 2010, a year after the death of his father YS Rajasekhara Reddy. YSR Reddy was in his second term as the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh when he died in a helicopter crash on September 2, 2009. Jagan’s supporters, who were many in number, lobbied hard with the Congress high command for the top post, but Sonia Gandhi did not budge and made K Rosaiah the chief minister. The Congress leadership did not approve of Jagan’s Odarpu Yatra, which was part of his announced plan to meet the families of many people who had sacrificed their lives after his father’s death.That set the stage for his eventual exit from the Congress, which he announced on November 29, 2010 in an open letter to Sonia Gandhi carefully written to ensure there was enough public sympathy for his second phase of political career.In the 2014 assembly elections, the YSRCP made an impressive debut and won 67 out of the 175 seats with a vote share of 44.46%, while the Congress could manage only a vote share of 2.8%. The Congress decision to bifurcate the state and create Telangana played a huge role in the party’s declining political fortunes in the state.On November 6, 2017, Jagan embarked on the Praja Sankalpa Yatra and covered 3,648 km in 341 days, crossing 134 assembly constituencies. The Yatra, from YSR Ghat at Idupulapaya to the northeastern tip of Ichchapuram, powered Jagan Mohan Reddy to a historic mandate of 151 seats in the 175-member assembly in the 2019 elections. The Congress’s vote share was reduced to less than 1%.The Congress, since then, has been making efforts to reclaim its lost political space in the state. It roped in Jagan Reddy’s sister Y S Sharmila as part of the party’s revival plan. Sharmila, who started her political career with her brother Jagan Mohan Reddy eventually drifted towards the Congress and was appointed president of Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee in January 2024.However, both Jagan Mohan Reddy and his sister Y S Sharmila failed to make an impact in the 2024 elections. The 2024 elections saw a dramatic collapse of Jagan’s electoral fortunes, and his party was reduced to only 11 seats. The Congress once again failed to make its presence felt.
The 2029 challenge
And that brings us to the 2029 elections - a do-or-die challenge for both Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress. Jagan’s remark on backing the CEC appointment Bill is his first open “regret” for backing the BJP.But does this “open regret” mean an olive branch for the Congress?Former Congress leader and senior political commentator Sanjay Jha strongly feels that Jagan and Congress should come together, though he admits that this may not be easy.“Politics is the art of the possible and I'm sure Jaganmohan Reddy is aware that Chandrababu Naidu has been an extremely close alliance partner of the Modi government. While the Congress doesn't have a base in Andhra like it used to have once upon a time. The support base of Jaganmohan Reddy is basically the Congress vote which moved away from the traditional Congress to the Congress that Jaganmohan Reddy, branded as the Congress of his father. So, if the merger were to happen, it would, frankly speaking, give them a huge advantage because then both the Central Congress and the Jaganmohan Congress could be on the same page,” Sanjay Jha says.However, he accepts that merger of the two parties could be a difficult process while stitching an alliance may be easier. “Once a political party becomes independent and has power, they don't like to give it up in a hurry. The TMC or the NCP are good examples. In which case it could be an alliance,” Sanjay Jha adds.The third option, according to Sanjay Jha, is for the Congress to resurrect itself on its own strongly in Andhra by capturing both the anti-incumbent votes against Chandrababu Naidu and winning back the loyalist voters of the Congress who had moved over to Jaganmohan Reddy.
This is easier said than done. The Congress has a poor track record when it comes to winning back states it has lost. We have seen several states across the country where the Congress has lost its government and eventually its support base but does little to reclaim it.In Andhra Pradesh, Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP are going all out to consolidate their position. Naidu’s call for greater cooperation and coordination among southern states at a recent conference is perhaps an effort to keep his importance and relevance intact. We saw DMK’s MK Stalin make similar moves before he lost power to Vijay’s TVK in the last assembly elections.Jagan Mohan Reddy and the Congress face an uphill electoral battle in 2029. It will be interesting to see if they can agree to an alliance to take on Chandrababu Naidu and the BJP.

Ayush Shetty has withdrawn from the Hylo Open 2026, a BWF Super 500 tournament, after retiring hurt at the French Open in Paris last week.

The silver made him the first Indian man in 61 years to reach the men’s singles final at the continental event. He rose to a career-high world ranking of 18 that month.

At the World Championships in New Delhi in August, he stunned defending champion and then world No. 1 Shi Yuqi 21-14, 13-21, 21-19 on his debut at the event. As the protests and hunger strike continues to unfold at Delhi’s Jamia Millia Islamia, students on October 27, Tuesday, reported a near-complete shutdown of normal university activities with the campus has being turned into a fortress surrounded by police personnel and tear gas vans deployed outside the main gate.
Additionally, Section 163 of the BNSS has been invoked, criminalising gatherings of more than four people. A warning sign erected by South-East District of Delhi Police mentions that unlawful gathering or assembly will be dispersed using physical force and legal action will be initiated.
Why are the Students Protesting?
On October 12, two students, Jasim Ali Khan and Ebin Basil, began an indefinite hunger strike to demand the resumption of the student union elections, which have not been held for two decades. The last elected union was dissolved in March 2006 amid allegations of campus violence and disruption. The university has not had a restored, university-wide elected Jamia Millia Islamia Student Union (JMI-SU) since then.
View this post on Instagram
Representatives from various student organisations submitted a memorandum to the vice-chancellor, demanding that necessary facilities, space, and support must be provided to students for their democratic right of free expression and protest. Within the next few days, six more students, Rehan Khan, Rehan Haider, Faizan Ali Khan, Rida Nausheen Khan, Ritik, Altaf, and Abuzar, joined the hunger strike and several students joined the sit-in demonstration around the Mirza Ghalib statue on campus. What followed is severe police crackdown, administrative retaliation, and a state-sanctioned attempt to curb what students described as a peaceful protest for their rights.
‘Students Beaten, Dragged & Detained’
Five days into the protest, around 5:30 am on October 17, Delhi Police personnel arrived in large numbers outside the university gate, and allegedly detained at least 10 students with the aid of the campus security guards. Students alleged that authorities turned off the lights, beat and dragged the protesters out of the campus in the break of dawn in the presence of the chief proctor of the university.
CPI(ML) Liberation alleged that Jamia Millia Islamia administration forcibly removed students on hunger strike from the campus around 5:30 am on Saturday while they were demanding the restoration of the students’ union. In a post on X, the party alleged that campus lights were switched off and students were beaten, manhandled and harassed before being handed over to Delhi Police. It said all detained students had since been released. The students are demanding the restoration of Jamia’s students’ union and the holding of union elections. CPI(ML) Liberation condemned the alleged action and urged the administration to stop what it called repression and restore the union.
— The Observer Post (@TheObserverPost) October 17, 2026
Footage surfacing on social media showed clashes between authorities and the students protesters on the morning of October 17, with videos showing police dragging and pulling students away from the campus.
View this post on Instagram
A video also showed Ebin Basil, writhing in pain, alleging that he had been brutally assaulted by the security guards.
Subsequently, as scenes of utter chaos kept emerging through the day, a large group of students were seen breaking the gate and storming inside the campus even as the police reportedly denied detaining anyone and only removing those attempting to break the gate.
View this post on Instagram
Admin Condemns Slogans, Shifts Classes Online
On October 18, a high-level committee comprising seven university professors was formed to mediate between protesting students, and to convince them to call the demonstration off. During this meeting certain slogans that were painted on walls by students also came under the administration’s scrutiny. These slogans included ‘Restore JMISU’, ‘Reclaim Jamia’, ‘Inquilab Ayega’, ‘Free Palestine’, ‘Free Sharjeel Imam’, and ‘RSS Se Azaadi’ among others.
In a press release published by the official handle of the university on X, the slogans were labelled “highly condemnable and detrimental to the nation’s integrity, security and sovereignty.” The release further stated that the administration has adopted two resolutions. First, to urge the protesters to vacate the protest site and call off their agitation, particularly at the Ghalib statue lawns, which they claimed had been “illegally occupied by the protesting students despite Gate No. 18 being the designated protest site at JMI”. Second, “to repaint the defaced walls and cover the slogans”.
The press release added that the administration had been compelled to issue a notification to shift all classes online allegedly due to the protesters’ resistance to call off the demonstration. “After two hours of efforts to persuade the students to call off the protest…the students continued chanting slogans, shouting that the faculty should “go back” and suddenly began pushing security guards, staff and teachers…even after their demands had been met earlier this week,” the release stated.
Further, the university administration took disciplinary action against Ebin and Jasim. Ebin was rusticated for one academic year and barred from campus while Jasim Khan was barred from campus for six months.
Following the administrative action, students held a press conference on October 18 and expanded their demands beyond the restoration of the JMI-SU — they demanded the withdrawal of disciplinary proceedings against protesting students and an end to further punitive measures. They also demanded the resignation of the chief proctor and security advisor.
Students Vow to Continue Strike, Clampdown Increases
Even as certain hunger strikers gave up due to declining health, the remaining students vowed to continue their hunger strike and sit-in protests. Solidarity for the protesting students poured in from within and beyond the campus, however, the police deployment outside the campus and administrative clampdown also intensified.
“The irony lies in the fact that the same administration that condemned unauthorised police clampdown on students during the CAA-NRC protests in 2019 is deploying that very body against its students in 2026 to suppress the constitutionally safeguarded right of free and independent expression,” Ateerah, a post-graduate student, told Alt News.
On October 23, Congress MP Imran Masood was detained by Delhi Police after he arrived at the university to express solidarity with protesting students.
Water, Electricity, Basic Amenities Cut Off
On October 24 — the 13th day of the hunger strike — through another notice the administration shifted all classes to online mode, shut its gates, suspended canteen services, and restricted access to the Central Library. In what students viewed as an attempt to discourage the protest, electricity and water supply were also cut off in the campus space, students told Alt News. “They have essentially converted our dissent into a question of law and order, to justify police action on a peaceful protest,” said Abdul, another student.
On the same day, a large number of Delhi Police personnel and paramilitary forces were stationed outside the university premises. The protesting students told Alt News that in the afternoon, the proctor’s team, along with university professors and non-teaching staff, had rounded up students who had gathered for a sit-in demonstration within Gate No. 7 of the university premises, at the Ghalib Lawn.
Students alleged use of force on both male and female protestors by the security guards. The protest site was allegedly dismantled, which compelled the protesting students to take shelter within the Political Science building and continue their hunger strike, they added.
View this post on Instagram
Mantasha, a post-graduate student, told Alt News, “The whole affair was an unpleasant reminder of what had transpired within the university premises in 2019. This time, our own professors joined in with the security guards. Some just watched, while others proceeded to manhandle us. Until our 13th day of protest, a solitary female washroom was kept open at night. However, after the protest site was dismantled in the afternoon of October 24, we found that it had been sealed off, leaving us no option but to share the male washroom.”
Students Reject Admin’s Notification
The next day, on October 25, the administration released a notification that said that a student election would be held after 15 days from the date of approval of the constitution of the JMI-SU.
It stated that show cause notices and suspension orders against students during the period of protest would be revoked, and a committee would be constituted to enquire into the actions of the security staff. It also added that students should issue a public apology for any defamatory statement, action, or posts made during the protest against the administration.
However, students expressed their apprehension regarding the notification, pointing out that the date of constitution of the union was unspecified. Those on hunger strike continued their fast, deeming the notification an incomplete victory as all of their demands had not yet been addressed.
They demanded an assurance on the resignation of the chief proctor and the security advisor, and the revocation of all disciplinary actions on protesting students, besides declining to issue a public apology. “The Constitution of the union is to be drafted by December 20, after which it is subject to approval from the V-C. This allows a lot of scope for administrative inaction and complacency, since the approval itself can be indefinitely stalled by the administration,” alleged Abdul.
On October 26, two gates — one in front of the Ibn-e-Sina reading library, and another which serves as a key access point to the campus for residents of the Boys Hostel — were sealed off by the administration, with the suspension of offline classes still effective.
A student protestor, speaking on terms of anonymity, told Alt News, “The gate provides access to facilities serving not only students and hostel residents but also members of the general public, including an Indian Post Office, a public sector bank, an Aadhaar centre, a university health centre and a dental hospital. Restricting access to such essential public services, including medical care for patients with scheduled appointments, warrants immediate reconsideration.”
Less than 24 hours after the administration released the notice, Delhi Police however went on to detain several students for merely attempting to enter the premises of their own university, students told Alt News. Video footage showed police personnel pushing students onto a detention bus.
Speaking to Alt News from the protest site, students alleged that they are not being able to leave the campus given the heavy police and paramilitary deployment in front of the gates. Food and water deliveries are allegedly being intercepted by security guards at the gates, cutting off the basic means of survival for students who have remained within the campus.
“We had earlier put out a message asking for people in solidarity to send in drinking water, but the guards would not let it through. Is this how a university treats its students?” a student, requesting anonymity, asked.

Mihir Ahuja is set to explore a different genre with Netflix’s upcoming film Dilwali Diwali after being part of the military drama Operation Safed Sagar. Produced by Terribly Tiny Tales (TTT), the film also stars Manoj Pahwa and Neelu Kohli and centres on family relationships and the emotions surrounding Diwali.
Mihir Ahuja says Dilwali Diwali allowed him to explore a different side of his acting after Operation Safed Sagar
Speaking about the shift between the two projects, Mihir said Dilwali Diwali allowed him to explore a different side of his acting. “As an actor, I’m always excited by the opportunity to step into a world that feels different from what I’ve done before. After being part of something as intense as Operation Safed Sagar, Dilwali Diwali gave me the chance to explore a completely different emotional space,” he said.
The actor added that stories about families and relationships appeal to him because of their relatability. He also spoke about the process of understanding his character and exploring aspects of his performance that audiences may not have seen before. “There’s something very special about stories rooted in family, relationships and the festive spirit because they are so relatable. What interested me was discovering the nuances of this character and finding a side of myself that audiences may not have seen before,” Mihir said.
Mihir Ahuja on connecting with audiences through Dilwali Diwali
Mihir said every role gives him an opportunity to learn more about the character he is playing as well as his own approach to acting. He hopes the film’s familiar situations and emotions will resonate with viewers. “For me, every character is an opportunity to discover something new, both about the person I’m portraying and about myself as an actor. What makes Dilwali Diwali exciting is the chance to connect with audiences through emotions and situations that feel familiar, yet still have their own surprises,” he said.
The actor also expressed hope that viewers would respond to his performance in the film. “I hope people enjoy seeing me in this different space and connect with the character in their own way,” he added.
With Manoj Pahwa and Neelu Kohli joining the cast, Dilwali Diwali brings together performers known for their work across film and television. The film’s family-oriented story marks a change in genre for Mihir following his involvement in Operation Safed Sagar.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

In the winter of 2022, two parents carried their sick, coughing baby boy into an emergency room deep in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. The small rural hospital had no pediatric specialists, no pediatric nurses, and no children’s intensive care unit. But it was hours closer than any hospital that did.
The doctor at that rural hospital recognized immediately that the baby’s condition was beyond their capacity to treat. They called regional children’s hospitals like ours for help. But the winter of 2022 was the peak of the “tripledemic” — Covid, influenza, and RSV striking children simultaneously — and every children’s hospital in northern California was overwhelmed. None of us had room for one more.
There was no single call the team at that hospital could make to locate a pediatric ICU bed. They worked a phone tree, hospital by hospital, asking for an opening. Meanwhile, the baby’s condition worsened. As the team tried to insert an infant-sized breathing tube, the baby died.
That patient’s death and others like it were galvanizing for those of us in on the other end of those desperate calls for help. Saying no to our colleagues and the patients they’re caring for feels horrible.
But the extraordinary crush of the tripledemic has continued. In 2026, the unprecedented pediatric patient crowding of 2022 has become a normal Tuesday.
In this new normal, community hospitals across the country are transferring children to dedicated pediatric centers not just because a child is critically ill, but increasingly because smaller hospitals have quietly lost the ability to manage even common conditions. A 1-year-old with an allergic reaction, a 6-year-old with an asthma attack, a teenager with gallstones — community hospitals once handled these patients locally. Now, as they degrade or eliminate pediatric care, that local safety net is disappearing. The nation’s relatively few children’s hospitals can’t accommodate every sick child, much as we would like to. We now routinely turn sick children away and hope one of our colleagues somewhere else will have a bed.
There is another story from that same winter of 2022. Two parents brought their sick baby girl to a small rural hospital in Washington state’s Northern Cascades. For 12 hours, doctors there tried to find a hospital that could take her. Again, no children’s hospitals had room.
Finally, the emergency physician called Washington’s Regional Medical Operations Coordination Center, or RMOCC — a kind of air traffic control for patient transfers that can match critically ill patients to available beds across a region. The RMOCC pediatrician who answered later recalled the terror in the calling doctor’s voice: “Don’t you know I feel like I am having a heart attack every moment I am caring for this tiny baby? It has been 12 hours. I am terrified she will die here. Why can’t anyone help?”
The RMOCC found a hospital willing to make an exception to its infection-control policies and accept the baby into a neonatal ICU. Unlike the California baby, she lived.
The Washington RMOCC closed last year after budget cuts. It is seeking renewed funding in this year’s budget.
There are many reasons for the collapse of pediatric capacity. Most are fundamentally financial. Hospital bottom lines require high reimbursement, high volume procedures, and expensive, complex treatments. Children’s care often reimburses below the cost of care, meaning that pediatric admissions for common childhood diseases lose money. Hospitals are incentivized to abandon pediatric care in favor of complex adult surgical programs and cancer treatments.
There are three changes in health care policy that could save and restore regional pediatric capacity.
First, Medicaid payments for pediatric care need to reflect the costs of that care. Hospitals can’t be asked to lose money on pediatric admissions and ED visits. Unfortunately, coming cuts to Medicaid seem likely to make reimbursement for children’s care worse rather than better. The incoming Congress must act to preserve and augment funding for pediatric care.
Second, regional RMOCCs like Washington state’s should be a standard part of regional disaster planning and a state and national funding priority. At least 19 states had regional or statewide MOCCs in 2023, though many were open only during surges, and some, like Washington’s, wound down with the end of the pandemic. When a sick child arrives at a rural emergency department, the hospital shouldn’t have to resort to a phone tree to find an accepting specialty facility. A single phone call to a regional air traffic control system for patient movement saves time and lives.
Finally, children’s hospitals need support to be regional resources to the smaller hospitals that depend on them for advanced pediatric care. Incentives for providing telehealth consultations, training, and quality improvement support for community hospitals are essential, as children’s hospitals face the same fiscal realities as their rural peers and cannot provide infinite unfunded support to their communities. Remote support from pediatric specialists can reduce the need for transfers and make local care safer, which could drive down pediatric care costs in the long term.
In pediatric medicine, we like to say that “children are not little adults.” Unfortunately, they are also not what health care executives call “priority populations.”
But children deserve to have quality care available in their own communities. They shouldn’t have to spend hours in waiting rooms and hallways awaiting transfer to overwhelmed regional centers. As pediatric physicians, we’ve gone from seeing the crisis coming to living the crisis every day. So far that crisis has been mostly hidden within the walls of our hospitals, but it’s time everyone know: Our children are out of room.
Jonathan E. Kohler, M.D., is a pediatric surgeon in Sacramento, Calif. Mary A. King, M.D., M.P.H., is a pediatric intensivist in Seattle.

India evacuates tens of thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears eastern coast
Indian authorities have evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state of Andhra Pradesh as a severe cyclone over the Bay of Bengal is expected to make landfall along the country’s east coast
HYDERABAD, India -- Indian authorities on Tuesday evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state of Andhra Pradesh as a severe cyclone over the Bay of Bengal was expected to make landfall along the country’s east coast, authorities said.
The India Meteorological Department, or IMD, said Cyclone Arnab strengthened into a “very severe” cyclonic storm and was expected to make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast by Wednesday morning with gusting winds and heavy rain.
Authorities stepped up preparations and began evacuating people from low-lying and flood-prone areas ahead of its expected landfall. They also canceled some train services as heavy rain and gusty winds had already started lashing parts of the Andhra Pradesh coast, officials said. At least 89,000 people have so far been evacuated in Andhra Pradesh, according to an official statement.
The state’s disaster management authority said more than 12 million people live along the cyclone’s expected path.
Prakhar Jain, a top disaster management official in Andhra Pradesh, said the cyclone was moving at about 20 kph (12 mph). “Extremely heavy rains and strong gusty winds” are likely in parts of the coastal region on Tuesday and Wednesday due to the impact of the cyclone, he said.
Authorities set up over 2,000 cyclone shelters across 20 districts, while emergency alerts were being sent to the mobile phones of millions of residents, Jain said, according to the Press Trust of India news agency. More than 30,000 fishing boats were secured along the coast, while nearly 1,100 medical teams were deployed across affected areas to provide emergency assistance, he added.
In neighboring Odisha, officials plan to evacuate about 48,000 people from areas likely to be affected by the storm.

Quick Answer
The best free alternatives to popular Microsoft apps include LibreOffice for Microsoft 365, ShareX for Snipping Tool, Files for File Explorer, Everything for Windows Search, System Informer for Task Manager, and ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos. These offer more features, better speed, and greater control.
Microsoft bundles plenty of apps with Windows, and you probably use a bunch of them on your PC — some out of personal preference, others because there aren’t enough good alternatives.
Now, there’s nothing wrong with using these apps if they serve you well. But if you find their functionality limited or want a free version, you don’t have to settle. Here are some of the best free alternatives to popular Windows apps that are worth checking out.
Table of Contents
LibreOffice for Microsoft 365
Microsoft 365 is a subscription service that gives you access to Office, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, alongside 1 TB of OneDrive storage. You can get Microsoft 365 for free, but you need a paid subscription for unrestricted access. However, if you don’t wish to go that route and want unrestricted access to the office suite, LibreOffice is a solid Microsoft 365 alternative worth checking out.
LibreOffice doesn’t require an account or subscription; you can download the app and get started right away. The suite includes three tools — Writer, Calc, and Impress, which are free equivalents to Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, respectively. You also get a vector graphics editor (Draw), a database management system (Base), and a mathematical formulas and equations editor (Math). The app works completely offline and stores all your data locally on the device. It doesn’t have any AI features either, so you have full control over what you do.
ShareX for Snipping Tool
Windows has a built-in screenshot tool called Snipping Tool to help you take screenshots and record the screen. Although Microsoft has updated it over the years to include OCR/text extraction and screen recording capabilities, its functionality is still largely limited compared to many third-party screenshot apps. ShareX is one such app, which is quite popular among power users.
ShareX offers plenty of screenshot modes, including scrolling capture, active monitor, custom, and auto-capture, as well as those you get with the Snipping Tool. Scrolling capture and auto-capture are two standout modes here. The former comes in handy when you want to capture content that extends beyond what’s visible on the screen. On the other hand, the latter lets you automatically take screenshots of a specified area at set intervals, which may be useful when you want to document the steps or monitor some process.
However, that’s not all; ShareX is better than Windows Snipping Tool at a bunch of other things. For example, it supports batch operations and automation capabilities. This allows you to apply edits to a bunch of screenshots at once. Then there are a few extra tools like Imagine Combiner to stitch multiple images, Ruler to measure dimensions, Color to extract color values from elements in your screenshots, and more.
Files for File Explorer
File Explorer is Microsoft’s own file manager for Windows. Although it has largely remained unchanged from Windows 10 to Windows 11, it did receive some noteworthy changes in appearance and functionality. Still, some of its elements, like the dialog box, look archaic. Not to mention, it lacks customizability and many features you otherwise find on its alternatives. This is where Files comes in.
Files is a popular File Explorer alternative that gives you everything you get with File Explorer, along with plenty of other useful features, while blending well with Windows 11 aesthetics. For starters, it supports Miller columns, which makes navigating nested folders easier. Likewise, it has a dual-pane mode for side-by-side file and folder comparisons.
Among other things, Files lets you add color-coded tags to files, view folder sizes at a glance, and preview a bunch of different file types like Markdown and SVG natively. It also offers Git integration for developers and a built-in FTP/SFTP client to manage files on remote servers. Last but not least, Files has a Command Palette, which is essentially a search box pop-up where you can search for files, change settings, and perform a bunch of other actions without digging through different menus.
Everything for Windows Search
Windows Search — the built-in search tool on your Windows PC, which lets you find apps, files, settings, and more- has come a long way over the years. It feels more integrated into the system and gives you options to control the kind of results that appear. Still, Search can feel quite slow, especially on relatively older hardware. It actively scans folders in the background, which increases resource usage. For this reason, it’s best to switch to Everything.
Everything is one of the popular file search tools for Windows. Its biggest highlights are speed and low resource usage. This is partly because of the way Everything indexes files and folders. Instead of crawling folders, it reads the NTFS Master File Table (MFT) — a type of database Windows uses to track files on the drive. This also enables Everything to instantly reflect any changes you make to files on your PC.
Among other things, Everything supports Regex and offers granular search options to help you find exactly what you’re looking for. It also has a handy batch renaming tool built in that lets you rename multiple files at once. Everything also has excellent keyboard-based navigation support, if you prefer that. You can even customize your most-used actions to your preferred keyboard shortcuts.
System Informer for Windows Task Manager
im is a powerful Windows app for monitoring and managing apps and background processes running on your computer. It comes in handy when you want to know what (and how much) resources an app or process is using, manage startup apps, and close frozen apps and system processes. However, it doesn’t support advanced task-management operations and isn’t quite effective at many supported tasks. Switching to System Informer thus makes sense.
System Informer provides low-level control over apps and processes, allowing you to manage them more effectively. It uses interactive graphs to show you all the processes hogging system resources. You can click on any data point for more information. This way, you can see all the past and dead processes to find the culprit. Similarly, the app makes it easier to view, start, and stop low-level system drivers, which is useful when you want to fix system crashes.
For times when you see an unknown background process eating up resources, System Informer lets you learn more about it without leaving the app. Last but not least, System Informer lets you find all processes using a particular file and kill them easily. This can be useful when you’re unable to edit or delete a file because some process is using it.
ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos
Microsoft Photos is the app that your PC launches whenever yoscru open a peenso in File Explorer. It lets you view photos and do basic edits (crop, repair, stylize, and enhance). There’s also cloud integration support to help you view and manage photos from your OneDrive or iCloud account right in the app, along with a bunch of AI features. Honestly, though, all of this feels like overkill for an app meant just to view photos. Not only does it make the interface look cluttered, but it also slows the app down significantly. Hence, the need for alternatives like ImageGlass.
ImageGlass is one of the popular Microsoft Photos alternatives after IrfanView. Although IrfanView is packed with advanced features, it feels dated in today’s time. Add to that the fact that Microsoft Photos is primarily a photo viewer, and ImageGlass starts looking like the better option. It’s fast, thanks to its use of hardware caching, which preloads adjacent images so they load instantly when you use the left or right arrow keys. And unlike Photos, it supports over 90 image formats, including WebP, JXL, and multiple RAW formats, natively. As such, you don’t need to download external plugins or extensions to open images.
Another reason to choose ImageGlass is the clean experience. It’s an entirely local-first image viewer that doesn’t integrate cloud services, nor does it push AI or other unrelated features. The app just lets you open images to view them. That said, you do get basic editing options (rotate, flip, crop, resize, etc.), along with a few other useful tools like a color picker and an EXIF metadata viewer. The app’s UI is customizable too, and you get plenty of themes, layouts, and other options to play with.
Those are some Microsoft apps I’ve replaced on my Windows PC with better alternatives. All of them are free to download and use, though some, such as Files and ImageGlass, offer a paid version that unlocks access to a few additional features. You can visit their website to learn more about these features, and if your workflow demands them, upgrade to their paid versions anytime.

Israel exit polls show election deadlock, with Netanyahu’s fate in balance
The vote saw record turnout as Israelis passed judgment on the PM after the October 7 attacks and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran
Israel’s election ended in an apparent deadlock on Tuesday, exit polls by major television networks showed, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot on track for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The stalemate could work in Netanyahu’s favour, allowing the long-serving prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition.
Final results could take days, and Israel’s fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

By the early 1880s, bacteriology was emerging as a rigorous science. Within the circle of German microbiologist Robert Koch in Berlin, investigators were attempting to isolate specific disease-causing organisms. The logic was to prove that a microbe caused disease, one had to grow it in pure culture, separate it from contaminants, and study its properties systematically. The available solidifying agent was gelatin. It provided a temporary structure to the nutrient broth, allowing colonies to form on the surface. But gelatin was fundamentally flawed: It liquefied at temperatures approaching 37 degrees Celsius, precisely the temperature required to culture many human pathogens. Even worse, several bacteria secreted enzymes that digested gelatin itself. The medium collapsed, colonies merged, and experimental clarity dissolved into formless fluid. For scientists attempting to establish causation of individual species in infectious disease, this was not a minor inconvenience: it was a structural limitation.
Who was Fanny Hesse?
Fanny Angelina Hesse was not formally appointed as a scientist. She assisted her husband, Walther Hesse, who worked in Koch’s laboratory. She prepared materials, maintained cultures, and drew meticulous illustrations of bacterial forms for publication. She was present, not as an investigator, but as a quiet labourer in daily experimental work. It was in that proximity that she repeatedly encountered the gelatin problem. Failed plates, melted surfaces, cultures lost at incubation temperatures. The frustration was practical and persistent. At home, however, she handled another substance entirely. Agar jellies prepared in her kitchen remained firm even in summer warmth. They did not soften as gelatin did. They did not seem to degrade. One evening, in what history records only briefly but imagination can render vividly, the domestic and the scientific converged. The problem of the laboratory and the memory of the kitchen overlapped. She suggested that if agar could withstand heat on the dining table, why would it not withstand incubation in the laboratory?
Before the laboratory
Agar is a complex polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls of certain red algae, mainly species of Gelidium and Gracilaria. Chemically, it consists primarily of two components: agarose and agaropectin. Agarose is a linear polymer made up of repeating units of galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose, and it is this fraction that gives agar its remarkable gelling property. Agaropectin contains sulfate groups and contributes to viscosity and charge characteristics. The word “agar” is believed to derive from the Malay term agar-agar, meaning jelly.
Long before bacteriologists struggled with melting cultures in Berlin, agar had already lived a quiet life in kitchens. Extracted from red seaweed and known in parts of Asia for nearly two centuries, it was used to set desserts into firm, translucent gels. Unlike gelatin derived from animal tissue, agar did not collapse in warm weather. It held its structure. It was stable. It obeyed heat differently. In the nineteenth century, European cooks encountered agar as an exotic culinary thickener. But in scientific circles, its potential was invisible. The laboratory and the kitchen were separate worlds, divided by sex, habit and hierarchy. No one imagined that a domestic ingredient could resolve a foundational problem in bacteriology.
Thus, Fanny Angelina Hesse’s suggestion to replace gelatin with agar, was out of the box.
Moment of trial
When agar was introduced into nutrient media in Koch’s laboratory, the transformation was immediate and decisive. The medium remained solid at incubation temperatures. It did not liquefy. Most bacteria lacked the enzymatic machinery to degrade it. Colonies appeared as discrete, visible units, each derived from a single organism. For the first time, bacteriologists possessed a surface that was chemically inert, thermally stable, and optically clear. The ability to isolate pure cultures became reliable rather than tentative. Within months, the method was embedded in the experimental practices that led to the identification of the tuberculosis bacillus and other pathogens in the decades to come.
To understand why agar transformed medicine, one must first grasp the idea of culture. A culture medium is an artificial nutrient environment that allows bacteria to grow outside the human body under controlled conditions and at a controlled temperature. Individual bacteria are invisible, but when placed on a suitable medium, such as agar, they form individual visible colonies. This enables laboratories to isolate the exact organism from samples like blood, urine, or sputum. Once identified, the bacteria are tested against different antibiotics to determine which drugs are effective and to detect resistance. Imagine culture is like switching on a floodlight in a dark room. Agar becomes the illuminated stage where hidden microbes step forward, enabling precise diagnosis and rational treatment.
The breakthrough was not dramatic in spectacle. It was a shift merely in material. Yet that shift altered the trajectory of microbiology.
Aftermath and recognition
The scientific practice and literature of the period absorbed agar rapidly, but credit did not travel with equal speed. The technique became standard practice. Petri dishes were designed to accommodate solid media. Textbooks described agar plates as routine apparatus. The name of Koch became synonymous with bacteriological rigour. Fanny Hesse’s contribution receded into footnotes. For decades, the laboratory bench carried her insight without carrying her name. Only later did historians of science begin to recover her role and situate it within the broader narrative of microbiology.
Agar today
More than a century later, agar remains foundational. In every microbiology laboratory, from district hospitals to advanced research institutes, agar plates are prepared daily. Blood agar to detect haemolysis, MacConkey agar to differentiate lactose fermenters, chocolate agar for fastidious organisms. Selective and differential media, all structured upon the same seaweed-derived matrix. Antibiotic susceptibility testing depends on agar diffusion methods. Colony counting for public health surveillance relies on agar surfaces. Molecular biology workflows begin with bacterial colonies grown on agar plates before plasmid extraction or genetic analysis. Even in the era of automated diagnostics and genomic sequencing, agar persists as the primary tool for culturing living microbes.
Today, major production occurs in countries such as Japan, Spain, Chile, China, Indonesia, and Morocco, where seaweed is cultivated or harvested. Beyond microbiology, agar is widely used in the food industry as a vegetarian gelling agent, in confectionery and desserts, in pharmaceuticals as a stabilizer and laxative, and in biotechnology for gel electrophoresis to separate DNA and RNA fragments.
Its properties remain unmatched. It melts at high temperatures but solidifies at lower temperatures, allowing sterile preparation and convenient pouring. It is largely resistant to microbial digestion. It forms a clear, stable gel that supports nutrient supplementation without chemical interference.
Firming up microbiology
Without that transition from gelatin to agar, the systematic isolation of pathogens would have been delayed. The architecture of modern microbiology would have developed more slowly, along a more convoluted path.
Fanny Angelina Hesse recognised continuity between her kitchen and her laboratory. Today, when a microbiologist streaks a plate and waits for colonies to appear, the act is routine. Yet beneath that routine lies the insight of Fanny Hesse. Without her intervention, the discipline might have remained uncertain at its foundation, its cultures unstable, its conclusions tentative.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)
