Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

Barcelona and Spanish striker Alexia Putellas reclaimed her crown when she won the 2026 Ballon d’Or Féminin at the Palladium Theatre in London, England, on Monday.
It was the third Ballon d’Or for Putellas, having won the trophy in 2021 and 2022. The 32-year-old has had a fantastic year with FC Barcelona, winning the Liga F, Copa de la Reina, Supercopa de España and the UEFA Women’s Champions League.
Spain continued its domination with her in the midfield, winning the UEFA Nations League and finishing runner-up in the UEFA Women’s Championship.
“I want to start by saying thank you teammates. I think anyone here could have fairly won this trophy and be giving this speech here right now. A great pleasure to play alongside each and every single one of you. Incredible experiences as a team, we overcome some difficulties, some injuries, some moments we weren’t expecting as a team and a great pride for me as captain,” Putellas said.
“All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn’t matter if you’re a boy or if you’re a girl. It doesn’t matter where you come from. Don’t listen if someone tells you, you can’t do it. Believe in yourself.”
The award is also more iconic because it was given in London, where Putellas currently plays. Having won 36 trophies at Barcelona, she left the Spanish club as its most decorated women’s player to join Women’s Super League side London City Lionesses this summer.
Putellas became the joint-most successful player to win the women’s Ballon d’Or, tied with her national teammate Aitana Bonmati, who had completed a hat-trick of the titles last year.

UK ‘set to miss’ heavily-reduced aid spending target of 0.3%
The UK needs to allocate additional funding in the upcoming Budget to meet it’s international aid targets, think tank says

The UK will need to allocate additional funding for international aid if it is to meet its target of 0.3 per cent of gross national income, with a current estimated shortfall of £410 million, according to a new report.
Forecasting by the Center for Global Development (CGD), a think tank focused on global development, shows planned spending is likely to undershoot the target and meet only 0.29 per cent of national income.
Its most conservative forecast estimated a £250m shortfall, while a gap of as much as £580m, leaving a spend of 0.28 per cent of national income, was “very plausible”.
It represents material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid, the CGD said in a blog post published on their website, with the extra money enough to halve cuts to Africa that “will cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de-facto exit from the south and east of the continent”.
It could also fund reform of the Green Climate Fund, which helps other countries’ ambitions on cutting emissions.
The UK chancellor, John Healey, is expected to outline new budget proposals on Wednesday amid speculation of potential tax rises or spending cuts to fill a growing black hole in the public finances.
The CGD has urged the new foreign secretary and international development minister to resist any artificial delay to aid spending and insist that the Treasury honors its commitment to 0.3 per cent.
It said the upcoming Budget “is a moment for the new government to put its stamp on how Britain is run”.
“The government made steep and damaging cuts and set a new target of 0.3 per cent for 2027 that would be a 25 year low. The very least it could do is ensure that target is fulfilled,” the CGD said.
The shortfall was attributed to higher forecasts for nominal national income, driven partly by inflation and rising energy prices following the conflict in Iran.
As aid spending is calculated as a proportion of gross national income, the higher forecast means the government must spend more in cash terms to meet its 0.3 per cent target.
The government announced in February 2025 that it would cut aid spending from 0.5 per cent to 0.3 per cent of gross national income by 2027 to fund higher defence spending. The reduction is expected to free up £6.5 billion for defence in 2027-28.
The new target is the lowest proportion of national income spent on aid since 1999.
The cuts come as aid budgets are under pressure internationally, with other major donors including the US, France, Germany and Japan also reducing spending.
A Foriegn, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”
Gideon Rabinowitz, Director of Policy and Advocacy at Bond, a UK network for organisations working in international development, said that the NGO has “repeatedly warned that the UK aid budget is at risk of falling below the targeted 0.3% of GNI”.
“Today's analysis further confirms our fears and risks leaving communities experiencing the impacts of conflict, crisis and climate change worldwide to pay an even higher price,” Rabinowitz said.
“With this injustice in mind, the Chancellor must use the Autumn Budget to honour Labour's manifesto commitments - by ruling out further cuts to the UK aid budget, and ensuring savings by other departments spending the UK aid budget are returned to the FCDO and that credible and transparent spending targets are set and maintained,” he added.

Very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ to trigger extremely heavy rain across 16 Andhra districts
Widespread rainfall is forecast across Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday and Wednesday, with extremely heavy rainfall likely in several districts.
Very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ began impacting coastal Andhra Pradesh early Tuesday, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall that are expected to intensify across the state’s northern coast over the next few hours, State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) managing director Prakhar Jain said.
According to the India Meteorological Department, the cyclone, which had moved with a speed of 22kmph during the previous 6 hours, was at 5:30am centered roughly 260 km from Visakhapatnam, 300 km from Kakinada, 390km from Machilipatnam, and 380 km from Gopalpur in Odisha.
It is projected to turn northwestward by Tuesday evening and make landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, near Yanam, by Wednesday morning. Wind speeds along the coast are expected to reach 90–100 kmph on Tuesday, and may increase to 115–125 kmph with gusts up to 140 kmph during landfall.
Deep Dive
Jain appealed to people to remain alert, avoid unnecessary travel and stay indoors in safe locations. He specifically warned people against standing near trees, large hoardings and dilapidated buildings, which could collapse or be uprooted in strong winds.
Widespread rainfall is forecast across Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday and Wednesday, with extremely heavy rainfall likely in several districts. The combination of intense rain and strong winds could cause damage to trees, electricity infrastructure, temporary structures and buildings in vulnerable areas.
He said extremely heavy rainfall was forecast in Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari and Eluru districts on Tuesday. Heavy to extremely heavy rainfall is likely at several places in Srikakulam, Manyam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Polavaram, Anakapalli, NTR, Krishna, Guntur and Bapatla districts.
Heavy rainfall is also likely in Palnadu, Prakasam, Markapuram and Nellore districts.
On Wednesday, extremely heavy rainfall is forecast in Visakhapatnam, Anakapalli, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Polavaram, Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari, Eluru, NTR and Krishna districts.
Officials said the rainfall intensity and the geographical spread of the impact would depend on the cyclone’s movement and the conditions prevailing during landfall.
Eight State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) teams and seven National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams have been kept ready in the cyclone-affected districts. An additional three SDRF teams and five NDRF teams are also available for deployment, if needed.
In addition, 115 teams have been prepared to remove fallen trees and rescue teams equipped with 13 boats have been prepped to respond to emergencies, including road blockages, flooding and the need to evacuate people from vulnerable locations.
The arrangements are intended to facilitate rapid response and minimise disruption to essential services during and after the cyclone’s passage.
The Andhra Pradesh government on Monday night released ₹27 crore for cyclone-related preparedness and relief operations.
Each of the seven districts in north coastal Andhra will receive ₹2 crore each, while 13 other districts will be provided ₹1 crore each, to fund precautionary measures and emergency-response activities in the affected areas.
Jain said people in vulnerable coastal and low-lying areas have been urged to take precautionary measures and remain in safe locations.
SDMA also said people could reach out to them through the Mana Mitra WhatsApp number: 9552300009.
Officials said Real Time Governance Society (RTGS) secretary Bhaskar Katamneni and chief executive officer Prakhar Jain were reviewing cyclone preparedness measures and coordinating with officials from various departments.
Chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu is being briefed on the precautionary measures implemented across the state.
Preliminary assessments indicate that 16 districts, spanning 2,460 revenue villages and 92 urban areas, were expected to face significant impact. Authorities have designated 1,763 cyclone shelters, set up 2,907 control rooms at mandal levels, and deployed 3,185 nodal officers.
Beaches have been closed, and traffic on coastal roads will be suspended from Tuesday afternoon.
All fishermen who had ventured into the sea have returned home, and 30,043 fishing boats secured at harbours to minimise the risk of damage.

Aerospace technology startup Parsec Aerospace, founded by former Pixxel engineer Effy John, is in talks to raise around $10 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners, sources told Inc42. The funding round is also expected to see participation from existing investors, including Lightspeed Venture Partners, the sources added. The Bengaluru-based startup is developing next-generation engines for aerospace applications and remains in stealth mode. Details about its engine technology, target customers, commercialisation plans, and proposed use of the fresh capital are not publicly available. Queries sent to Parsec Aerospace and Nexus Venture Partners did not elicit a response by the time of publication. John founded Parsec Aerospace after working at spacetech startup Pixxel, which develops hyperspectral imaging satellites and Earth-observation technology. Parsec Aerospace was incorporated in September 2025, according to publicly available corporate records. Rising Investor Interest In Deeptech The funding talks come amid increased capital deployment into India’s deeptech ecosystem, spanning aerospace, defence technology, robotics, and semiconductors. Indian deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals in Q3 2026 compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the corresponding quarter last year. Funding rose nearly 2.8X, although the number of deals edged lower. Among recent investments, metal additive manufacturing startup ThinkMetal raised ₹27 Cr in a round led by IAN Alpha Fund earlier this month. The startup builds industrial printing systems used to manufacture tools such as moulds, dies, jigs, and fixtures. In September, Aeron Systems raised ₹45 Cr in a pre-Series B round jointly led by Riverwalk Holdings and MGF-Kavachh. It develops inertial navigation and weather-monitoring systems for aerospace, defence, renewable energy, and other industrial applications. More directly in aerospace propulsion, D-Propulse Aerospace raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund earlier this year to develop propulsion systems for defence and aerospace applications.

- The claim that a Catholic priest in Ecuador stole $2 million in church funds then died when a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass is unfounded.
- The claim spread on social media following the Oct. 17 death of Father Patricio Sánchez Molinari. The original source of the theft allegation remains unclear.
- Although the priest's death was real, Snopes found no credible evidence supporting the alleged theft. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil told Snopes there was no evidence to support the accusation and that it didn't receive any complaints of financial mismanagement involving Sánchez or his parish. The Archdiocese also confirmed that Sánchez was responsible for the parish's finances.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the Redemptorist congregation, Our Lady of Perpetual Help Parish and Ecuador's Prosecutor General's Office and await their responses.
In October, social media users claimed that a Catholic priest in Guayaquil, Ecuador, who died after a large wooden crucifix fell on him during Mass had previously stolen $2 million in church donations.
For instance, one Threads post claimed, "Catholic Priest Killed by Giant Cross During Mass After Stealing $2 Million in Donations."
(Threads user @the_awaken1814)
"LET THIS TRAGEDY BE A WARNING TO ALL WHO THINK GOD ISN'T PRESENT IN THESE TIMES," the user wrote above a video showing the crucifix falling on the priest during livestreamed Mass.
The allegation also circulated on Facebook and Instagram, with some people suggesting the priest's violent death was a form of "divine punishment." Snopes readers also contacted us to ask whether the incident really happened and whether the accusations were true.
In short, the strange circumstances of the Rev. Patricio Sánchez's death were real and documented on video, but the allegation he stole $2 million in donations beforehand wasn't supported by credible evidence. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil rejected the allegation in statements to Snopes.
What happened to Sánchez?
On Oct. 17, 2026, Sánchez was celebrating Mass at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church when a large wooden crucifix mounted behind the altar detached from the wall and struck him. The Associated Press reported on the incident, citing confirmation from the Archdiocese.
The incident was captured during a livestream of the Mass, a recording of which remains available on Facebook (archived):
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced a memorial Mass for Sánchez on Instagram, scheduled for Oct. 18:
Sánchez was 52 years old and belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, commonly known as the Redemptorists. According to an obituary published by the congregation, Sánchez served Catholic communities in several Ecuadorian cities before becoming parish priest at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church in Guayaquil.
In an Oct. 21 article, Spanish newspaper El País interviewed parishioners who recalled Sánchez's work in the community, including activities supporting children and young people.
The exact reason the crucifix fell wasn't clear in the immediate aftermath of the incident. On Oct. 19, Metro Ecuador reported that the cause had not yet been officially established. On Oct. 20, Ecuadorian newspaper El Comercio reported that Sánchez's relatives wanted authorities to investigate the circumstances of his death.
What did the Archdiocese say?
Snopes contacted the Archdiocese of Guayaquil to ask if it was aware of the theft allegation, whether there was evidence supporting it and if whether the archidiocese had ever received complaints about financial misconduct involving the priest.
In a message to Snopes, communications manager Steven Pincay said:
There is no evidence to support the claims made in this video. The Archdiocese of Guayaquil has not received any accusations or complaints of mismanagement of funds within the Perpetual Help Parish or by Fr. Patricio Sánchez, CSsR., who was the administrator and responsible for the finances of said parish.
In a separate message, the Archdiocese said it did not endorse the allegation, which it claimed was "maliciously disseminated by a YouTuber to gain views, regarding the death of Fr. Patricio Sánchez, CSsR." The Archdiocese didn't identify the YouTuber and we have reached out for more information.
Where did the theft allegation come from?
The exact origin of the $2 million theft allegation remains unclear. It was circulating online by Oct. 18, one day after Sánchez's death. We found no evidence it had circulated before his death.
On Oct. 18, Christian News & Investigative Reports published an article addressing the rumor, saying it found the accusation on social media. The following day, Kenyan news outlet K24 Digital reported the allegation was spreading online but remained unsupported by credible evidence.
On Oct. 20, a more elaborate version of the story appeared on a website called Cross Message. In addition to claiming Sánchez stole $2 million, the article alleged "some people also pointed out that church members had previously seen him driving expensive luxury cars and living in a mansion, raising serious questions about where his wealth came from." It also claimed a wooden cross he held during an earlier Mass developed cracks, which some believers supposedly interpreted as a warning from God.
The article didn't identify the sources of these allegations or provide evidence to substantiate them.

On September 29, 2015, a memo went out from Swasthya Bhawan, the West Bengal Health Department’s headquarters in Salt Lake, to every medical college principal and every district’s chief medical officer of health. Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.
The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.
At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.
Why the concern
A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.
The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate, the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.
The opening of the gap
The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.
The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.
The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.
The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.
Prevalence of C-section delivery, West Bengal
| Survey Round | West Bengal (%) | India (%) | Difference (% points) | Change in WB (% points)) | Change in India (% points) | 
| NFHS-1 (1992–93) | 3.3 | 2.5 | +0.8 | — | — | 
| NFHS-2 (1998–99) | 10.3 | 7.1 | +3.2 | +7.0 | +4.6 | 
| NFHS-3 (2005–06) | 10.2 | 8.5 | +1.7 | −0.1 | +1.4 | 
| NFHS-4 (2015–16) | 23.8 | 17.2 | +6.6 | +13.6 | +8.7 | 
| NFHS-5 (2019–21) | 32.6 | 21.5 | +11.1 | +8.8 | +4.3 | 
| NFHS-6 (2023–24) | 44.5 | 27.2 | +17.3 | +11.9 | +5.7 | 
Source: NFHS reports
Private vs. government
Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.
While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.
The move to private care
Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.
These private facilities now perform almost 6 in 10 of the State’s Caesareans (57%). Had births stayed where they were at NFHS-5, the same arithmetic would give a rate of about 38%. The move into private care accounts for more than half of the 11.9-point rise, about 6.6 points, and higher rates in government facilities for most of the rest, about 4.1 points.
The pattern holds outside cities as well. In rural West Bengal, 88.1% of births in private facilities are Caesareans, slightly more than the urban figure of 86.8%.
A belt around Kolkata
On a district map, the highest rates form one contiguous belt in the south of the State. Kolkata and North 24 Parganas are at 67.5% each, Hooghly at 66.6%, Nadia at 62.9%, Purba Medinipur at 59.1% and Howrah at 58.5%.
Urbanisation alone does not account for the belt. Purba Medinipur, a coastal district where 11.6% of people lived in towns at the 2011 Census, has a higher rate than industrial Paschim Bardhaman (48.1%), where 81.6% did.
Purulia, on the Chota Nagpur plateau in the West, has the State’s lowest rate at 21.6%, followed by Jhargram (27.4%), South 24 Parganas (28.5%), Maldah (29.9%) and Bankura (30.1%). Every district except Purulia is above the national average of 27.2%.
A low district average, however, can also obfuscate women in remote blocks who need an emergency Caesarean and cannot get one. Almost every birth in the two districts with the lowest C-section rates now takes place in a health facility (95.7% in Purulia and 97.7% in Jhargram, against 94.9% for the State), so what matters here, is whether those facilities can perform a Caesarean when one is needed. Block-level hospital records would show how often they do.
Behind the rise
Explanations for the rise need records the survey does not hold. The first concerns money.
Swasthya Sathi, the State’s health insurance scheme, was launched in 2016 and opened to every resident on December 1, 2020. It covers up to ₹5 lakh per family a year in government and empanelled private hospitals. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, the share of households with at least one member covered by a health insurance or financing scheme rose from 33.7% to 88.2%.
The timing matches the shift to private care. West Bengal was surveyed for NFHS-5 before the scheme became universal, and the births counted in NFHS-6 straddle the change. A scheme that pays for care in private hospitals would be expected to move births into them. The same years brought the COVID-19 pandemic. By May 2020 the State had set aside 69 hospitals for COVID-19 patients, 16 government-run and 53 privates. The disruption fell on both sectors, and the survey cannot separate its effect from the scheme’s.
Whether the scheme’s payments also tilt private hospitals towards surgery is a question its claims records could settle. They would show what share of delivery claims are Caesareans and how package rates for normal and Caesarean births compare.
Another explanation feeds on itself. A woman with a previous Caesarean can safely try labour only where an emergency operation can follow at once, which most district hospitals in India cannot promise. Each first operation therefore tends to bring a second, and the rate keeps rising over years.
Additionally, more women of childbearing age today are overweight or obese (34.6%, up from 22.7%), and more have 10 or more years of schooling (40%, up from 32.9%). An analysis of NFHS-5 data links both to higher odds of a Caesarean.
What the memo asked for
The 2015 memo already proposed periodic audits by the officials who license private clinics. The WHO statement it enclosed put forward a common method for such audits, the Robson classification. It sorts women into 10 groups by details such as how labour began and the baby’s position, so that hospitals can be compared fairly.
Published for each hospital, including every private hospital empanelled under Swasthya Sathi, the results would show where Caesareans are common among low-risk women, the group most likely to have unnecessary operations.
Fewer unneeded operations also require labour wards that can manage a normal birth safely at any hour, and protocols that let suitable women attempt a vaginal birth after a Caesarean. In Purulia and Jhargram the task would have to run the other way, to keep emergency surgery within reach.
What is needed now
The first step is for the State to say whether the audits suggested in 2015 were ever carried out, and what they found. Caesarean audits must then become routine in government and private hospitals alike, under the health department’s supervision. Swasthya Sathi can check each Caesarean claim against the medical reason recorded for it and devise methods to ensure hospitals are given no reason to prefer surgery.
Every woman who needs a Caesarean should get one without delay, and no woman should have one when there is no compelling medical reason behind it.
(Dr. Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher with the MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

Barcelona handed €602 fine over Alvarez approach
MADRID, Oct 27 : Barcelona's pursuit of Julian Alvarez came at a modest cost on Tuesday after the Spanish FA fined the club €602 ($672) following a complaint by Atletico Madrid over contact with the striker.
Atletico accused Barcelona of approaching the Argentine, whose contract runs until June 2030, without first notifying them in writing.
The sanction falls under Article 133 of the federation's regulations. Atletico also complained to FIFA, which declared it had no jurisdiction over the case.
For Alvarez, the repair work has been rather more public.
The striker scored Atletico's winner against Deportivo La Coruna on Saturday, finding the net for a second successive match as his side moved within two points of LaLiga leaders Barcelona, before apologising for expressing his desire to join their rivals.
"It was a mistake. I understand why the fans are angry. If I were a fan, I'd be angry too. Especially given how they've supported me since I arrived," Alvarez said referring to an interview during the 2026 World Cup in which he said that he "wanted to fulfil his dream" of playing for Barcelona, triggering a transfer dispute that stretched through the summer transfer window.
Frequently booed by the home fans this season, Alvarez received a standing ovation from sections of the crowd after scoring on Saturday, a sign of a thawing relationship with the Metropolitano faithful.

Ghanaian twin brothers and US woman plead guilty to $9m romance scam
- Published
Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.
The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.
The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.
Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (£6.7m).
While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.
As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.
The three accused go by several names:
- Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement
- Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster
- Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman
In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.
Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.
In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (£5.9m).
He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.
The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

Flexible workspace provider WeWork India reported a 219% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹20.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 from ₹6.4 Cr in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year, as revenue growth outpaced the rise in expenses. The company returned to profitability sequentially, compared with a net loss of ₹4.1 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 33.6% to ₹767.8 Cr from ₹574.7 Cr a year earlier. Sequentially, it increased 12.3% from ₹683.8 Cr. Including other income and finance income, total income stood at ₹786.4 Cr. Total expenses increased 32.4% to ₹766.9 Cr from ₹579 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Separately, WeWork India reported an IGAAP-equivalent net profit of ₹65.8 Cr, up 67.4% from ₹39.3 Cr a year earlier. Total revenue on this basis increased 31.6% to ₹768.7 Cr. The company’s IGAAP-equivalent presentation adjusts the treatment of leases and certain other items under Ind AS. These figures differ from its statutory financial results. On the same basis, EBITDA increased 37.6% to ₹162.9 Cr, with its margin expanding to 21.2% from 20.3% a year earlier. Sequentially, EBITDA grew 17.8%. Record Desk Additions WeWork India added 11,700 desks during the quarter, its largest quarterly addition to date, taking operational capacity to 145,300 desks across 85 centres in eight cities. Capacity increased 26.9% from a year earlier. The company added 18,400 desks in the first half of FY27, with another approximately 4,500 desks becoming operational in the first week of October. In his letter to shareholders, MD and CEO Karan Virwani said the bulk of the company’s ongoing capital expenditure cycle was now operational. He expects these centres to support operating leverage as they mature. WeWork India’s expansion pipeline comprises more than 9,000 desks under signed leases and over 38,000 desks covered by letters of intent (LOIs). Including these, the company pegged its total planned capacity at 1,90,000-1,95,000 desks. Its member base increased 32.5% to 1,21,700, outpacing capacity growth. Portfolio occupancy stood at 83.7%, up 357 basis points (bps) from a year earlier. However, occupancy declined 114 bps sequentially, which the company attributed to newly added capacity that was still being filled. Global capability centres contributed 40.8% of core revenue during the quarter. Services Outpace Core Growth Beyond its core private office and managed office offerings, WeWork India earns revenue from value-added services (VAS), including events, food and beverages, office customisation, and technology services. Its digital offerings include on-demand workspace access and virtual offices. On an IGAAP-equivalent basis, combined VAS and digital revenue grew 38% to ₹108.8 Cr, outpacing the 31.7% increase in core revenue to ₹657.7 Cr. VAS revenue rose 35.2% to ₹79.6 Cr, while digital revenue increased 45.6% to ₹29.2 Cr. The company’s contracted core revenue stood at ₹3,843 Cr, up 66% from a year earlier, against corresponding committed rent of ₹1,421 Cr. WeWork India reported a net cash position of ₹23.1 Cr at the end of September as against a net debt of ₹310.5 Cr a year earlier.

Cyclone Arnab starts landfall process along Andhra Pradesh coast, triggers heavy rain and strong winds
Authorities remain on high alert as rescue and relief teams continue to take precautionary measures to minimise the impact of the severe cyclonic storm.
Cyclone Arnab's landfall process started along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday around 1:10am, bringing strong winds and heavy rainfall to several areas, the Indian Meteorological Department said.
In its bulletin issued at 1.10am on October 28, the IMD said Arnab’ was moving westwards over the west central Bay of Bengal, close to the Andhra Pradesh coast and Yanam, at a speed of 10 kmph.
IMD estimated the storm’s intensity at 125-135 kmph, with gusts reaching 150 kmph.
The storm is expected to cross the coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, south of Yanam, between 2 am and 4 am. Winds are likely to gradually weaken after landfall.
Track live updates on Cyclone Arnab
Authorities remain on high alert as rescue and relief teams continue to monitor the situation and take precautionary measures to minimise the impact of the severe cyclonic storm.
Andhra Pradesh and Odisha had stepped up preparations on Tuesday ahead of the expected landfall of very severe cyclonic storm Arnab, with thousands of people moved to safety, nearly 4,000 cyclone shelters readied and at least 50 trains cancelled across the region.
Air travel impacted
Air travel was also affected, with at least 21 flights cancelled at Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam airports on Tuesday. The cancellations affected services to Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam and Kadapa. An official said 15 flights scheduled to operate from Vijayawada airport on Wednesday had also been cancelled.

The Andhra Pradesh government had arranged 2,131 cyclone shelters across 20 districts and placed 1,087 medical teams on standby in areas likely to be affected. Officials said 8,281 emergency beds and 1,274 ambulances had also been made available.
Deep Dive
Authorities had moved people out of vulnerable areas and shifted 1,351 pregnant women to hospitals. The government had stocked two months' worth of essential commodities at 14,686 ration shops, while cyclone alerts had been sent to the mobile phones of 2.70 crore people.
Railways monitored 600 km of tracks, cancelled services
The South Coast Railway had cancelled 24 trains scheduled for Wednesday, while the East Coast Railway had cancelled 22. The South Eastern Railway had also cancelled four trains, officials said.
IMD director general Mrunjay Mohapatra had warned of potentially damaging winds along the coast.
Odisha had moved over 30,000 people to cyclone shelters
Odisha had intensified its preparations, with heavy rain already reported in parts of the state. Entry to sea beaches had been prohibited.
Special Relief Commissioner (SRC) Rajesh P Patil said 135 permanent cyclone shelters and around 1,600 temporary shelters had been prepared to accommodate people from vulnerable areas.
Jharkhand had shut schools, issued yellow alert
In neighbouring Jharkhand, the Ranchi district administration had ordered schools to remain closed on October 28 and 29 as authorities prepared for adverse weather.
A yellow alert for heavy rain had been issued for Ranchi, Khunti, Simdega, Gumla, Lohardaga, Saraikela-Kharsawan, East Singhbhum and West Singhbhum for 24 hours from 8.30 am on October 28.

You don’t hear the defenders of so-called western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.
Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.
Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”
A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, King of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.
“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”
Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialogue, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: the Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”
But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.
So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”
The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”
In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “The Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”
Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

Flight operations at Mumbai International Airport faced disruption on Tuesday evening after a network glitch forced airport staff to switch to manual check-in procedures, delaying passengers travelling with IndiGo and Air India.
The outage began at around 7.05 pm and lasted approximately 50 minutes, slowing check-in processes and boarding scanner operations, according to reports by PTI and Hindustan Times.
Airport sources cited by Gulf News said gate changes and crew delays added to the confusion in departure halls.
Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL), the private operator of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA), confirmed the temporary network disruption. It said teams had introduced manual processing measures to minimise passenger inconvenience and ensure essential airport services continued.
In a statement cited by PTI, MIAL said the airport had “experienced a temporary network disruption on Tuesday evening” and that its teams had implemented manual procedures to maintain continuity of essential operations.
The operator maintained that the disruption had not affected airport or flight operations, although reports indicated delays in passenger processing and boarding.
Data from live flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed that departures from Mumbai airport were delayed by an average of 50 minutes. As of around 9.30 pm, 327 flights had been delayed, while 13% of flights had been cancelled.
It remained unclear how many of the reported delays and cancellations were directly linked to the network outage.
Airport teams worked to resolve the technical issue and continued essential services through manual processing.
Although the disruption did not bring airport operations to a complete halt, the slowdown in check-in and boarding procedures affected passengers during the evening rush.

N.S. woman refused to comply with phone scammer, so would-be fraudster swatted her house
'There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong,' says Lynn Clark Colpitts
A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.
The original call seemed like a routine phone scam. A woman claiming to be from the CIBC fraud department called Lynn Clark Colpitts and said someone had applied for a credit card in her name. In order to block it, she advised Clark Colpitts to download an app called CIBC Guard.
Colpitts said she didn’t feel comfortable doing that or sharing any information over the phone. While she was on the call she conferenced her IT expert from work into the call who told her to do nothing until she contacted her branch.
"I told her politely, I said I'm sorry I have to go by what my IT guy told me to do. And then she used some profanity toward me,” Clark Colpitts said.
“She called me a f-----g b---h, twice, and then hung up on me.”
Clark Colpitts figured she’d dodged a scam but 20 minutes later things escalated.
'She was threatening me the whole time'
“She calls me back and says, ‘I've got a surprise for you. Go to your front door. There's a surprise waiting for you there.’ And I'm like, ‘What are you talking about?’"
Sure enough, as she stepped onto her porch she saw heavily armed officers from the Colchester District RCMP and Truro Police in her yard and on the street.
“They holler at me and ask me who I am,” Clark Colpitts said. “And I tell them who I am and they tell me to get down to the end of the driveway.”
Several officers entered her home while Clark Colpitts tried to explain there was no such threat. While police checked on the property the fraudster kept up the phone calls to Clark Colpitts. She held it up so police could hear it.
“She was threatening me the whole time saying that she wasn't done with me and that this was gonna keep going on.”
RCMP explained to Clark Colpitts that they’d gotten a call about a hostage taking — and shooting — at her address.
Calls, emails and death threats
“It appears to be a level of retribution by the fraudsters in this case,” said Staff Sgt. Mark Rose, commander of the Colchester District RCMP.
“[It appears] they did this to cause her harm and pain and distress by having the police respond to her residence all because she didn’t follow the original instructions on the phone."
The calls from the female fraudster continued on Friday and into Saturday.
Staff Sgt. Mark Rose is the commander of the Colchester District RCMP. (Galen McRae/CBC)
“She just kept going on and on and on. It was relentless," Clark Colpitts said.
And there were emails too. Death threats.
Clark Colpitts is a realtor. She got a phone call from a coworker who said someone had hacked into their agency’s website, took down Clark Colpitts's photograph and replaced it with what Clark Colpitts says was a “deformed animal.” All of it has left her scared to be in her own home.
Swatting attack
David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security, which is based in Fredericton, says Canadians have lost tens of millions of dollars to phone scams, but this is the first time he’s aware of it escalating into a “swatting” attack. That’s when a person calls police to someone’s property to report a crime or emergency that is entirely fiction.
“This seems like a criminal who was definitely not having a good day and decided to dramatically escalate the dangerousness and seriousness of this situation,” Shipley said.
“I would argue that this is a form of terrorism,” he said. “Canadians aren't used to having the SWAT team from the police department show up with assault rifles and body armour and riot shields to their front door. That's incredibly, incredibly traumatic.”
Rose said police have to take these calls at face value and deliver the appropriate response.
“We've offered victim support services to [Clark Colpitts] and we are working with our law enforcement partners in other countries — and in Canada — to determine if this connects to other offences and try to determine who's responsible for this.”
CIBC told CBC News in a statement that there is no app called "CIBC Guard" and that it would never contact customers requesting personal or financial information, or request you download an app. It urged people to be extremely cautious when dealing with unsolicited emails, texts or phone calls, and not to rely on caller ID.
The bank said it's actively working to educate clients about impersonation and other scams, and it urges people to contact 911 if there is an urgent threat to their safety or the safety of others.
Meanwhile Clark Colpitts says she's traumatized.
“There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong.”

LANCASTER, Pa. — They saved Petunia first. She was the second cow. Her brother Louie had died within hours of his birth. But over two harrowing, sleepless nights, the three researchers kept Petunia alive to wheel her from the barn to the veterinary hospital and inject her with a virus carrying new genes.
Petunia had a bovine form of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), a life-threatening condition that is also unusually prevalent within the Mennonite community here. The goal wasn’t to save the 79-pound calf. That would be a bonus. The goal, for Kevin Strauss, was to prove that an MSUD gene therapy could work — that after two decades he could finally offer the desperate families who entered his medical clinic here a simple, one-time fix.
It worked. Today, Petunia is a feisty, 5-year-old, hay-munching, 1,500 pound heifer. Yet not a single one of Strauss’s patients has received the treatment that saved her life, not even in a clinical trial.

As one of the leads on CBS mainstay Blue Bloods, which ended its 14-season run in 2024, Bridget Moynahan enjoyed a run of rare stability in a rapidly evolving TV industry.
The actor reflected on the environment of change and disruption during the latest installment of the Deadline Dinners series, which was held October 21 at the North Fork Television Festival. Along with streaming’s rise to dominance, more recently the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger (forming Skydance) and a big shakeup at Netflix have added to uncertainty about the industry’s future.
Don’t count Moynahan among the skeptics, however. “I still feel optimistic about great stories and creativity being able to break through,” Moynahan said. “Despite all of the changes, people will always gravitate toward stories, so I do feel hopeful. You have to have hope.”
The conversation, moderated by Deadline New York Business Editor Dade Hayes, touched on various points in Moynahan’s career. Her signature roles have been on shows like Sex and the City (and followup And Just Like That) as well as the John Wick films.
Watch on Deadline
American Beech Hotel in Greenport, NY, hosted the dinner, an intimate gathering of two dozen people in the boutique hotel’s ground-floor boite. Attendees included fellow actors Kate Walsh (Grey’s Anatomy) and Michael Nathanson (The Knick) as well as festival stakeholders from the legal, industry and sponsorship realms.
Now in its 11th year, the festival has leaned into its setting on Long Island’s East End, about 90 miles from New York City. The region is notably more tranquil than its glitzier sibling to the south, the Hamptons. While it may be quieter on the North Fork, some major figures in finance, media and technology have homes there, and Greenport has evolved from its roots as a remote fishing village into a significant cultural hub.
A separate festival-curated conversation on October 21 featured actor Kelly AuCoin from Billions. On the following night, Walsh, Anthony Anderson and Kelsey Grammer received awards at a gala dinner. The festival also screened independent pilots and convened a panel about how artificial intelligence is reshaping the TV business.
Moynahan, who produced an indie pilot that premiered at the 2025 North Fork fest, said she has enjoyed her chances to get behind the camera. She directed three episodes of Blue Bloods and another of spinoff Boston Blue. Asked about genres or areas she hopes to explore next, Moynahan said, “There are a lot of shows I am watching now” with that in mind. One example is Youth, the HBO series created by Sharon Horgan, which Moynahan considers an ideal blend of entertainment and serious purpose.
When Moynahan asked the table if they had watched Youth, several guests loudly chimed in, adding their own favorites and comparing notes. As the free-flowing conversation continued, it wound up illustrating Moynahan’s point about the eternal hunger for stories well told.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has reportedly left the country for the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, with questions mounting over his whereabouts after he failed to meet a Supreme Court deadline to surrender his passports, Reuters reported citing two sources.
However, a senior Brazilian Federal Police official as per the new outlet said Bolsonaro had not exited the country through any regular migration point, leaving the circumstances surrounding his reported departure unclear.
The US Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Bolsonaro's lawyer declined to comment, Reuters stated.
Quick answers to key questions
Reuters reported, citing two sources, that Bolsonaro had left for the United States. However, a senior Federal Police official said he had not exited through a regular migration point, so the circumstances remain unclear.
His precise location has not been confirmed. The available information does not establish where he is or how he reportedly travelled to the United States.
The order was part of a money-laundering investigation. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing in the case.
The 24-hour deadline expired, and sources cited by Reuters said his travel documents had been cancelled. The article says the potential legal consequences of missing the deadline remain unanswered.
No. He had not formally conceded and said he would seek to have the result annulled, citing alleged voting irregularities. His Liberal Party acknowledged Lula’s victory.
The reported departure came after Brazil's Supreme Court gave Flavio 24 hours on Monday to surrender his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing in the case.
The deadline subsequently expired, and two other sources as per the news outlet said his travel documents had been cancelled.
The development raises questions about his whereabouts and how he may have travelled to the United States despite the order. The available information does not establish his precise route or current location.

As footage of ICE raids, deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.
At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.
“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”
After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco histor, to the Iran war, migrant workers, racism, and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.
“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa. That's reality.”
Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”
Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera, living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa–a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.
“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”
Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.
“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.
The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.
Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.
It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “amigo inteligente” that eventually became Coyotec.
LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.
Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.
Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.
Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”
Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.
“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”
“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”
While Coyotec may be the first Latino AI radio host, it is far from the first amigo inteligente on the airwaves.
In June 2023, Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT. AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.
In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori, depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).
The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters. Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”
AI personalities are also popping up in televised news. Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.
Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human.”
But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.
Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.
Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.
Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.
A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.
"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."
Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative—a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."
While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”
She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities.
In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”
While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."
Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.
"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”
Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana. Make noise that matters.”
