Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

In Summary
- Earclip-style earbuds are getting very popular these days, with the likes of Sennheiser and Samsung also launching buds in this style.
- While they are more stable than conventional earbuds and are designed to let ambient sound in, earclip-style buds have their own pros and cons.
- If you are thinking of grabbing a pair of earclip-style buds for yourself, here are some important points to keep in mind about these buds, which make them very different from traditional, ‘normal’ earbuds.
Sony has released its first. Sennheiser has released its first one too. And so has Samsung. And many others – including Apple and Google – are believed to be readying theirs. We are talking about the clip-style or clip-on earbuds that are now becoming increasingly popular in the personal audio market. As their name indicates, these earbuds are shaped like clips and are attached to your outer ear, rather than inserted into your ear canal. They generally comprise two tiny cylinders, one of which is a speaker and the other of which is a battery, connected with a band, and they are designed to clip onto your ear.
Although they were first seen on the market a couple of years ago, most notably from Huawei and Bose, and were released by many budget-friendly brands, clip-style earbuds are now taking their place in the audio tech spotlight. But what makes these relatively new totally wireless earbuds different from other TWS earbuds, and should you be thinking of getting one for yourself?
Well, here are thirteen points we think you need to know about clip-style earbuds before you clip a pair to your own ears:
Table of Contents
They are on-ear and “open” and generally more comfortable
Clip-style earbuds are on-ear buds, and clip on to the outer ear like an ear cuff. This means that they lie on top of or near the ear canal, and do not go inside it, like many other earbuds. This makes them more comfortable to wear for most users – you do not feel something is inside your ear or just dangling near your earlobe.
They are light
In terms of weight, clip-style earbuds are about the same weight as general buds – about 5-7 grams, based on the design and materials used. For instance, the Sony LinkBuds Clip are about 6.4 grams each, while the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are 7 grams each, and the AirPods are about 5 grams.
They are incredibly stable and almost NEVER fall off
Clip-style earbuds are among the most stable wireless earbuds. This is because they actually “clip” on to the user’s ear, gently pressing it between a speaker and battery cylinder or sphere. As a result, they are actually attached to your ear on both ends. You can shake your head violently, and they still won’t fall off. In our book, they are as stable as earbuds with hooks that go around your ears.
No ear tip options – one size fits all
As clip-style earbuds do not go into the ear canal, there are almost always no earbud options to let you adjust for a better fit. It is pretty much a one-size-for-everyone rule out there. This can cause a few problems, as the next point will show.
The size of your ear could affect your experience
The fact that there are no size adjustment options available at all in most clip-style earbuds and that they are basically clipped onto your ear means that your experience of them could depend on the size of your ear. Those with relatively large ears might find the speaker end of the buds lying farther away from their ear canal, while those with small ears might find the speaker end coming right on top of their ear canal. There is unfortunately no cure for this, other than making the connecting band on these earbuds adjustable or flexible, which no brand is doing so far.
They come with bigger drivers…
Most clip-style earbuds come with slightly larger drivers than those seen on most TWS. While most TWS have drivers of the size of 5 mm to 8 mm, most clip-style earbuds have drivers that are 10 mm or larger. For instance, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless have 7 mm drivers, and the AirPods are believed to have 7.5 mm drivers, while the Sony LinkBuds Clip have 10 mm drivers, and the Moto Buds Loop have 12 mm drivers.
…but are not the loudest
The interesting part, however, is that even though they have larger drivers, most clip-style earbuds are not as loud as other TWS. This is because the larger drivers push sound towards the ear, often going past pockets of air that lie between the buds and the ear canal. Some of the sound inevitably gets lost in this, resulting in lower volume levels.
Love bass? These are not great options
We are going to be up front about it – clip-style earbuds, and in fact most ‘open’ earbuds are not for those who love audio with plenty of bass. The open fit of these buds is not ideal for bass, which sounds best in a packed setup, allowing for reverberations and rumble. Many brands attempt to tune their buds to accent the bass and even use larger drivers, but the result is seldom close to what we get from in-ear earbuds.
External noise comes in…too much external noise sometimes
One of the biggest attractions of clip-style earbuds is that they allow external or ambient sounds to come in too, and do not seal you away from the outside world. However, this is a bit of a mixed blessing, as too much external noise, combined with the lower volumes of these ear clips, can drown out audio. We would not recommend using them in very noisy conditions like traffic jams, or even in gyms with loud noises – those sounds will come right in.
And there is no ANC either, but ENC exists
As they are “open” in design terms, and are actually made in a manner to allow external sounds to come in, clip-style earbuds do not have any active noise cancellation. The microphones on them – for phone calls – do come with some environmental noise cancellation, so call quality on many of these buds can actually be quite good.
Controls can be…challenging
Thanks to their design, which makes them very small, clip-style earbuds almost always have touch controls – there is hardly any room for buttons on them. And as the buds themselves tend to be small, these can be difficult to use and get used to. One inevitably figures out a way to get them working, but they are never quite as comfortable as those on other TWS and earbuds, especially those with stems. These are best controlled from the connected device.
Perfect for those times when you need to listen to your surroundings too (offices, large families, outdoor runs, etc.)
The fact that they are light, stay securely attached to your ear, and allow some ambient noise to come in makes the clip-style earbuds perfect for those places where you need to be aware of sounds around you. They are great for offices in which you need to keep your ears open for queries and remarks from colleagues or even for ringing phones, and even for those who stay in large families and need to keep their ears open, even while listening to music. And of course, we think they are perfect for those who love to go on outdoor runs and rides, as they stay in place and give one access to one’s phone and audio (when allowed) and also keep one aware of traffic and people around one.
Not for audiophiles, gamers, or for intense listening sessions
No matter what the brands tell you, clip-style earbuds are not for those who are very serious about their audio. They seldom deliver the kind of detail and audio quality that one gets from other TWS at their price points. At the most, one can hope for a reasonable level of clarity and a relatively balanced audio signature. While equalizers can make a difference to different frequencies, clip-on style earbuds are not really for audio purists or for those who like to listen very intensely to their music. Their relative lack of volume and limited bass also mean they are not the best option for gaming or even watching films, even though some of them do come with spatial audio. They are, however, excellent for podcasts and live streaming audio, absolutely super for audiobooks, and more than adequate for casual listening.
And one more thing…
They have a special ring carrying mode
One of the biggest problems with most TWS is putting them back in their cases. You need to find the case, open it, take them out of your ears, put them back in the case, and snap it shut. All of which can take some time, especially when you are in a hurry (say, when you want to talk to someone, or get on or off the Metro). Well, that can be avoided with clip-style earbuds. Thanks to their shape, you can simply wrap a clip-style earbud around one of your fingers. Just like a ring. Don’t worry, it won’t fall off easily. No need to fiddle around trying to find their case immediately.

A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections
TEL AVIV, Israel — Israel is holding pivotal elections on Tuesday in what many Israelis call the most consequential vote in their country's history after the last few years of war.
Polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu trailing in the race behind his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. But it may take weeks or months before it's clear who will be designated the winner.
That's because voters will not directly choose between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Instead, they will vote for one of a dozen main parties running for office in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
The real contest will begin after election day, when party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.
Here is a guide to the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.
Who are the leading candidates?
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking another term in office.
Netanyahu has led the most right-wing government in Israel's history. His coalition has included Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, leaders of far-right, religious nationalist parties that are also running in this election, as well as two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
Netanyahu has led Israel through more than three years of war and regional conflict, from the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza to fighting involving Lebanon, Iran, Syria and Yemen. He is campaigning on Israel's military achievements and his close relationship with President Trump, who recently endorsed him. Netanyahu has also made confronting Iran, and ultimately seeking the fall of its regime, a central part of his campaign.
His principal challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israeli military who is running for prime minister for the first time as the leader of a new center-right party called Yashar, Hebrew for "Straight" or "Upright."
Eisenkot's son, Gal, an Israeli soldier, was killed in Gaza during the war. Recent polls have shown Eisenkot has the strongest chance of replacing Netanyahu, although no party or political bloc appears assured of winning a parliamentary majority.
Eisenkot's Yashar includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.
How could Arab parties play a role in the results?
Two predominantly Arab parties are also running, including the United Arab List, also known as Ra'am, which made history in 2021 as the first Arab Islamist party to join an Israeli governing coalition. The party says it is willing to work with predominantly Jewish parties in exchange for policies fighting crime and promoting housing, infrastructure and other problems facing Israel's Arab minority community, which makes up about 20 percent of the country's population.
But nearly all the main predominantly Jewish political parties, including Eisenkot's, remain reluctant to rely on Arab parties to form a coalition. That reluctance could leave the anti-Netanyahu camp without the 61 seats it needs for a governing majority.
What is the election about?
Accountability for Oct. 7: The Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage, looms over the election. Netanyahu has resisted calls to establish a state commission of inquiry into the political and security failures that preceded the attack. Eisenkot and other opposition leaders say they would establish such a commission soon after taking office.
Who should serve in the military: Nearly three years of fighting across several fronts have placed a heavy burden on Israel's standing army and military reservists. The military says it needs additional personnel, intensifying a decades-old dispute over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. Netanyahu, reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties for political support, has resisted enlisting them, while Eisenkot is campaigning to expand military service to more ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israel's judiciary: Before the Oct. 7 attack, Netanyahu's government pursued a judicial overhaul that would have weakened the supreme court and given the governing coalition greater influence over the appointment of judges. The plan triggered some of the largest protests in Israel's history. Netanyahu's far-right partners are campaigning on renewed efforts to limit the power of the courts, while Eisenkot advocates for an independent and powerful judiciary. Netanyahu remains on trial for corruption, and says the charges are politically motivated.
Israel's international isolation
The wars in Gaza and the region, and Israel's policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many governments overseas, and public support for Israel in the U.S. has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters. Netanyahu emphasizes his relationship with Trump and argues that military strength has improved Israel's strategic position. Eisenkot and his allies say continued international isolation threatens Israel's economy, diplomatic relationships and security.
What could happen after the election?
A party does not need to finish first in the race for the party leader to be Israel's next prime minister. What matters is whether he can assemble a coalition with majority support in parliament.
Most recent polls suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to a majority. That leaves several possible outcomes:
- Eisenkot's allies could break their campaign promises and form a coalition relying on support from one or more Arab parties, either as formal coalition members or from outside the coalition, and the opposition would rule with a minority government
- Netanyahu and Eisenkot could form a broad unity government, although Eisenkot has publicly ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
- Netanyahu could agree to a plea deal that would dismiss his criminal charges in court, in exchange for stepping down as prime minister and serving under Eisenkot as a senior minister.
- A deadlock, where neither side may be able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.
Even if Eisenkot cannot immediately form a coalition, a parliamentary majority opposed to Netanyahu could try to elect a new Knesset speaker, establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks, and advance legislation on ultra-Orthodox military service.
Netanyahu would try to do everything he can to prevent such an outcome. His Likud party's billboards are already promoting a scenario in which the party could claim that the election was stolen, a move that could lead to chaos in the days after the vote.
What direction would Israel take depending on who wins the election?
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently supports the establishment of a Palestinian state in the foreseeable future. Their most significant differences concern democratic institutions, the occupied West Bank and Israel's relationship with the world.
Netanyahu has governed with ultra-Orthodox and far right parties that support settlement expansion in the West Bank and a weaker supreme court. His far-right partners have pushed for annexation of the West Bank and expulsion of Palestinians, drawing sanctions from the U.K. and Europe.
Eisenkot presents himself as a more institutional and pragmatic alternative. He has also taken a tougher position against violence by Israeli settlers and says he would act against settlement outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.
Eisenkot has opposed settlement construction in E1, a strategically sensitive area just east of Jerusalem. Critics of the settlement plan say Israeli construction there would further divide the West Bank and make the creation of a territorially contiguous Palestinian state much more difficult.
The choice facing Israeli voters is therefore not a straightforward contest between left and right. It is also a contest over Netanyahu's leadership, accountability for Oct. 7, the role of religion in the state, the independence of Israel's institutions and what kind of alliances the country will pursue at home and abroad.
NPR's Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

GTA 6 looks set to feature the most diverse NPCs in the series yet, with everything from body types and heights to unique physical animations adding more life to its world. But that raises an interesting question: will NPCs also carry their own weapons? Rockstar is clearly putting a lot of effort into making GTA 6’s Leonida map feel as alive and unpredictable as possible, and armed NPCs could make the world feel more dangerous. So, here’s everything we know about this feature.
Will NPCs Carry Weapons in GTA 6?
Yes, NPCs will carry weapons in GTA 6, and they will not hesitate to use them on Jason and Lucia if the situation calls for it. However, not every NPC will carry a weapon, and most will likely flee the scene if our protagonists cause a ruckus with their own set of weapons in GTA 6.
NPC interaction has evolved from Red Dead Redemption 2, meaning you’ll still have the option to “Greet” or “Taunt” them in GTA 6, which will lead to a confrontation if you pick the latter. But Rockstar has confirmed that NPCs may choose to attack Jason or Lucia with their weapons even if they don’t provoke or taunt them, because Leonida is just that unpredictable.
Furthermore, if you eavesdrop on or follow a stranger in GTA 6, they will react to your actions and confront you, which may or may not escalate into a full-blown shootout. We’ve also seen multiple store owners shoot at Jason and Lucia with shotguns and other weapons in the GTA 6 Extended Look on Netflix, so some robberies won’t be simple.
One of the first signs of NPCs carrying weapons appeared in GTA 6’s debut trailer, which showed a grandma in a pink outfit wielding a hammer. She later appeared in the Extended Look, where Jason and Lucia confronted her.
Furthermore, Rockstar’s multiple GTA 6 screenshots show different locations with various NPCs carrying weapons, from rednecks to drug dealers. So, be careful when doing certain activities in GTA 6 in Leonida, as one wrong move could spook an NPC and turn a peaceful outing into a messy situation.
Can NPCs Perform Robberies in GTA 6?
Rockstar has confirmed via early GTA 6 previews that NPCs can actually perform unscripted robberies with weapons in the open world. Jason and Lucia can also encounter other criminals carrying out robberies while exploring Leonida.
In one instance, a woman tried to rob a convenience store just as Jason was about to do the same, prompting the store owner to react organically to the unfolding chaos. So, you can either stop their crimes to maintain your Criminal Profile in GTA 6 or take all the loot for yourself.
NPCs will react to Jason and Lucia carrying concealed weapons, with most fleeing in fear while others may try to disarm them, as seen in the GTA 6 Extended Look. Furthermore, Jason and Lucia can store weapons inside car trunks in GTA 6 for more convenient robberies, which could also mean that other NPCs might do the same.
Rockstar has gone to extreme lengths to make sure every player has a unique experience while exploring the State of Leonida. What you experience with NPCs will vary from, let’s say, your friend’s GTA 6 playthrough. That said, how do you plan to deal with NPCs carrying guns in GTA 6? United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby loves gambling, and now he's using AI as an ace up his sleeve.
Speaking on the "Cheeky Pint" podcast, Kirby said that over the past eight months, he's had an "AI epiphany" about the tech's best uses, which was triggered by one of his favorite pastimes — sports betting.
"Summarizing documents and all that crap, I think it's ridiculous," Kirby said. "I can read my calendar. I don't need to summarize my day."
Instead, he has found vibe coding far more valuable.
Kirby told "Cheeky Pint" host and Stripe cofounder John Collison that he hired a tutor for three hourlong sessions, then used AI to make a webpage for sports gambling.
"I've always been into gambling. For better or worse," Kirby said.
Between sets in a two-and-a-half-hour gym session, he typed prompts on his iPad to vibe-code a page with "four or five" drop-down menus for different sports, dates, and bets. Kirby said it links to four sportsbooks and pulls up the best odds; then he can enter a dollar amount, and it places the bet for him.
"I could do it with three hours of tutoring on my own, could write a program to do that, was an epiphany for me," Kirby said. "I think I called them on that Saturday, our team, and like, 'We're all in on this.'"
His appetite for risk has helped Kirby make bets on airline strategy that have paid off. For example, when carriers around the world retired their airplanes during the pandemic, United instead ordered hundreds of new jets — buoying the airline when travel demand boomed after lockdowns ended.
The United CEO previously spoke about his love for gambling in an April interview with The Wall Street Journal, where he described being kicked out of casinos for counting cards before he started in the airline industry.
He told "Cheeky Pint" that he went back to Las Vegas when the Super Bowl was held there in 2024.
After setting up a credit line to play poker, he had to hand over his ID.
"It was like 15 years ago that I got barred at the Bellagio last time," he said. "The manager comes over, and he's like, 'Mr. Kirby, you're welcome to play any game in the casino, but just so you know, still no blackjack.'"

Attacks kill at least 60 Orthodox Christians in Ethiopia, church says
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reports that two attacks in Oromia have killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Two attacks in Ethiopia’s Oromia region killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians, the country’s Orthodox Church said, urging authorities to protect civilians and bring those responsible to justice.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s Holy Synod said Monday that 14 people were killed in Merti district on Oct. 20 and a further 46 in Shirka district on Oct. 24. Both districts are in Oromia’s Arsi Zone.
More than 20 people were seriously wounded and 20 homes were burned down, the church said, describing the killings as “brutal and merciless massacres.”
Oromia regional government spokesperson Hailu Adugna blamed the Oromo Liberation Army, or OLA, for the attacks. He accused the rebels and their allies of trying to provoke ethnic and religious conflict to divert attention from military losses in northern Ethiopia. He presented no evidence supporting the accusations in the statement.
Adugna expressed sorrow over the deaths and destruction and said that regional authorities had begun taking action against those responsible. He pledged assistance to people wounded or displaced.
The OLA couldn't be reached for comment. Its leader, Kumsa Diriba, also known as Jaal Marroo, denied that his fighters target civilians in an interview with The Associated Press published in February.
“Our war is not against the people,” he said at the time.
The OLA is one of seven groups in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, formed in September with the aim of removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. Other members include the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and the Amhara Fano National Movement.
The church said that the attacks violated constitutional protections for religious freedom and the right to life. It called on authorities to publicly condemn the killings and prevent further violence.
Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest region and home to roughly 40 million people, has endured a conflict between government forces and the OLA since 2018. Other armed groups and criminal gangs also operate there, with civilians facing killings, extortion and kidnapping.
U.N. investigators have accused the OLA of killings, rapes and kidnappings. Human rights monitors have also documented abuses by government forces, including indiscriminate drone strikes, extrajudicial killings and disappearances.
Sarah Kimani, Amnesty International’s media manager, told the AP in a January interview that the organization’s research documents summary executions, torture, abductions and rape by both government forces and the OLA.
She said that internet blackouts and restrictions on independent media and civil society concealed the extent of civilian suffering.
“What we have been able to document now is just the tip of the iceberg,” Kimani said.

Women plan street demonstrations in more than 20 Polish cities and towns on Thursday (October 22, 2026) to protest the lack of access to free and legal abortion.
They're accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to fulfil its promise to relax Poland's strict abortion laws, and are protesting even though the Parliament passed two bills on Tuesday (October 20) aimed at easing abortion rules. The measures are likely to be vetoed by the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki.
Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.
She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stood no chance of withstanding Nawrocki's veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women's support to win elections next year.
Most abortions are performed secretly
Since 1993, legal abortions have been allowed in Catholic Poland only in cases of severe fetal abnormality, risk to the mother's life and health, or the pregnancy being a result of rape or incest.
Also Read | Doctors decide: On legal abortion
Polish women have been pushing for the legalisation of abortion ever since, including in a nationwide wave of demonstrations of women wearing black called “Black Protest,” which began in 2016.
Rather than being liberalised, Poland's abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of fetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, an overwhelming majority of which are carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
And abortion remains a taboo subject in Poland, which now has one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws, with only Malta imposing stricter limits.
Activists accuse Polish government of disinformation
PM Tusk's pro-European coalition won the 2023 election in part on a promise to liberalise Poland's abortion laws. But in 2024, Mr. Tusk said his government wouldn't be able to overcome the likely veto of a conservative president. Instead, measures were introduced to prevent hospitals from refusing to perform legal abortions on religious grounds.
"The state will increasingly effectively stand on the side of the woman when she is making dramatic decisions in her life,” Mr. Tusk said in 2024 when he announced the measures.
Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared to 452 in all of 2022, before Mr. Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.
Activists organising Thursday's (October 20) protests are claiming the Mr. Tusk government has betrayed Polish women — and that PM Tusk's claims that women's access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.
“The government's promises act as a type of disinformation,” Ms. Marcinek told the AP. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is ok, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it's very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”
Meanwhile, international donors are less interested in supporting Polish women's rights because they mistakenly believe things have improved, Ms. Marcinek said.
Activists dispense abortion pills outside Parliament
In 2025, the Abortion Dream Team opened an “ abortion clinic ” across from the parliament building in Warsaw where women can get information about their options, or even take their abortion pills in the company of supporting activists.
This September, the activists also launched a parcel locker dispensing abortion pills at the same location, nicknamed “Abortomat."
The dispenser is operated by the international feminist non-profit Women Help Women. It enables women needing abortions to get the pills the next day, rather than wait for up to two weeks for home delivery, Ms. Marcinek said.
“There are also people who cannot safely order such pills at their own address, for example because of an unsupportive family or abusive partner," she said. “These women can get a pin number and pick up the pills in the machine the next day.”
“In Poland, assisting with an abortion is a criminal offence. Even passing the pills from hand to hand can be considered a crime,” the Abortion Dream Team wrote in a statement. "That's why we're hacking the Criminal Code and bringing abortion into the 21st century.”

A stolen 11th-Century Chola bronze idol of Kannappa Nayanar, looted from a temple in Tamil Nadu and later spotted at a prestigious European art fair, has returned to India from the Netherlands following an international investigation that combined archival police records, photographic evidence and artificial intelligence.
The bronze was repatriated last week along with a collection of 11th-Century Chola-era royal charter plates voluntarily relinquished by Leiden University Library. The recovery followed coordinated efforts by the Tamil Nadu Idol Wing CID, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), Dutch authorities, India Pride Project (IPP), and the Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA).
The case posed a particular challenge because the idol was stolen before the encrustations on it could be removed after its discovery in a buried hoard during renovation work at Arulmigu Agneeswarar Temple in Tiruppugazhur, Nagapattinam district. It resurfaced years later in a clean condition at The European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) in Maastricht, the Netherlands.
The breakthrough came in March 2025, when ARCA experts Stefano Alessandrini and Ibrahim Bulut photographed the bronze displayed at the stand of Marcel Nies Oriental Art. They shared the images with their colleague, who alerted S. Vijay Kumar, co-founder of IPP, an organisation that traces stolen Indian cultural objects and campaigns for their repatriation.
They alerted the Idol Wing CID through IPP’s network. Additional Superintendent of Police Balamurugan located the original First Information Report (FIR) documenting the theft from the temple, establishing a crucial link between the sculpture displayed in Europe and the missing idol.
The next challenge was to establish that both photographs depicted the same object. The original discovery images showed the bronze covered in encrustations, whereas the sculpture at TEFAF had been cleaned.
Mr. Kumar used IPP’s proprietary AI tool, Ekalavya, to digitally remove the encrustations from the discovery photographs. This enabled the team to compare the sculpture’s contours, proportions, and other physical features with the images taken at the art fair. Image and histogram comparisons revealed strong correspondences, providing evidence to support the identification.
The findings, along with the original FIR and supporting documentation, were shared with the Idol Wing CID and Dutch authorities. Idol Wing CID, subsequently coordinated with the ASI in New Delhi to initiate proceedings with the Dutch authorities. On March 23, 2025, Dutch police seized the bronze following a request from Indian authorities.
The ensuing investigation led to the dealer voluntarily relinquishing the sculpture, clearing the way for its return. The repatriation was not accompanied by a formal public announcement from the Dutch authorities.
The 11th-Century bronze depicts Thinnan, revered as Kannappa Nayanar, one of the 63 saints of Saivism. According to the 12th-Century Periya Puranam, Kannappa demonstrated his devotion to Lord Shiva by offering his own eyes. The idol was among 27 bronze images unearthed during excavation for an Appar Mandapa at the temple. The circumstances in which the hoard was buried remain uncertain.

Quick Answer
Windows 11 Home is ideal for everyday tasks like browsing, gaming, and office work. Windows 11 Pro adds BitLocker encryption, Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and advanced management tools. Pro suits professionals and businesses, while Home is enough for most users. You can upgrade from Home to Pro without reinstalling Windows.
Unlike macOS, Windows comes in different versions. Windows 11 Home is the most common version designed for everyday use, while Windows 11 Pro is for professionals and business users who want maximum security and useful remote features.
Most PCs and laptops mostly come with Windows 11 Home out of the box. It is enough for most users. However, if you need specific features for enhanced device security and remote access, Windows 11 Pro is a strong option, especially for professionals who handle sensitive information and for businesses that need to access devices remotely when staff are away from home.
If you are a beginner, choosing between Windows 11 Home and Pro can be confusing, especially since they look almost identical and it’s hard to tell them apart at first. In this guide, you will learn the differences between Home and Pro and which one you should choose.
What do Windows 11 Home and Pro have in common?
Windows 11 Pro is basically an extension of Windows 11 Home. Compared to Windows 11 Home, it adds a few extra features designed for business and professionals. However, both versions share most basic, everyday features.
Starting with the interface, both look and feel similar and support the same core Windows features, everyday apps, and software. Both also support Windows Hello, Secure Boot, Find My Device, and receive frequent Windows security updates.
For security, both Windows 11 Home and Windows 11 Pro include a firewall and network protection, support Windows Hello sign-in options, and support Secure Boot on compatible hardware.
Microsoft also offers basic device encryption in Windows 11 Home on supported PCs. However, full BitLocker management is only available on Windows 11 Pro, which you can learn about in the next section.
Since every major core feature of Windows is the same, and every app runs without any issues, and both versions have support for everyday apps and software, you won’t find much difference between them if your main activities include: accessing Windows core features, browsing, video calls, editing videos, documents, streaming, browsing, and gaming. However, keep in mind that while Windows 11 Home and Pro offer the basics for everyday users, performance depends on your PC hardware, including the processor, memory, and graphics card.
Even if you initially choose Windows 11 Home, you can upgrade to Windows 11 Pro without extra hardware.
The Pro features that can change your decision
Windows 11 Pro is designed for people who care about security and want to control their PC when they are away from home. The biggest difference is BitLocker encryption: Windows 11 Home offers only basic device encryption on supported PCs, while Windows 11 Pro offers full BitLocker management, so if you lose your PC and someone accesses your encrypted storage without authorization, they can’t easily retrieve your data.
This is especially useful for businesses with confidential information, so Windows 11 Pro makes more sense. Windows 11 Pro offers BitLocker encryption and supports Remote Desktop hosting, which isn’t available in Windows 11 Home. A Windows 11 Pro-supported PC can act as a Remote Desktop host, so you can connect to it from another device when you are away from home. This is especially useful when you are away from home and want to access an important file or use an important application that’s installed on your device.
Another Windows 11 Pro-exclusive feature is Windows Sandbox, which lets you run a temporary, isolated Windows environment on your computer, especially useful for running risky applications that may contain malware and could damage or access sensitive files on your device.
Windows 11 Pro also supports Hyper-V virtual machines, where you can install another version of Windows on your laptop and test your software.
This is especially useful for developers testing your app on various Windows versions. Another major difference is the Group Policy Editor, which lets Windows 11 Pro users access admin controls and advanced Windows settings.
It is not just software; Windows 11 Pro also extends your hardware capabilities. For instance, Windows 11 Home supports up to 128 GB of memory, while Pro supports up to 2 TB. Another big difference is price; Pro costs more because of these extra features.
Checking your edition before you set up or upgrade
The best part of Windows 11 Pro is that you can upgrade from Windows 11 Home. Even if you are currently using Windows 11 Home or chose Windows 11 when buying a new laptop or computer, you can easily upgrade to Windows 11 Pro later.
To check which version of Windows you are using, go to Settings > System > About and look under Windows specifications. Then open System > Activation to check its activation status. If you are on Windows 11, you can compare the features. Nerdused carries Windows 11 product keys, and this Windows 11 Home vs Pro guide can help you review the differences as you decide.
Upgrading from Home to Pro without a clean reinstall
As I said before, you can also upgrade from Windows 11 Home to Pro without losing your files or reinstalling Windows. First, make sure Windows 11 Home is activated.
For safety, I highly recommend backing up your important files and installing all available Windows updates.
Once done, open Settings, go to System, then Activation. From there, click Change next to Change product key. Enter a valid Windows 11 product key, then follow the on-screen instructions to upgrade.
If you don’t have the key, select Upgrade your Windows, open the Store, purchase one from the Microsoft Store, then restart and follow the on-screen instructions, restarting the PC if prompted. Then return to Settings > System > Activation and confirm your device is running Windows 11 Pro.
To summarise, choose Windows 11 Home if you mainly use your device for browsing, gaming, video editing, office work, and other everyday tasks.
However, choose Windows 11 Pro if you are a professional or want advanced security features such as BitLocker encryption and remote control of your device while you are away from home. You can test different Windows versions and install one inside your current Windows. Support for features such as Remote Desktop hosting, Hyper-V, and business management tools.

Paris Marx’s new book couldn’t have landed at a better time. The longtime critic of Big Tech and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast has been thinking about data centers for years, and Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires comes out right as opposition hits a fever pitch.
“I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh.
While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand.
I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers?
PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there.
The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community.
ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon.
I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs.
Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.”
In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid.
The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system.
The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers.
[Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now.
When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated.
What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that?
I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI?
We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned.
But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns.
Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down.
You ended the book with a specific example in New Zealand of a community-led effort to create a more accurate speech-recognition model of the Māori language, using local cloud providers to host the data. I really liked this alternative vision of a non-extractive way to harness the powers of AI. Have you thought about what we could do to make some changes and how this build-out is going?
I would like to see governments go really hard on actually putting firmer regulations on the development of data centers. But those should also be paired with regulations on the AI products themselves. We had a lot of promises about what generative AI was going to deliver that haven't been realized. There has also been a long list of harms that have arisen from these technologies that we were not told would come along with them. Our governments do not seem to be so willing to actually take that on. They're buying the narrative that generative AI is still what Sam Altman sold it to be in early 2023 rather than what it has become today.
I think that we do need to be thinking of how we do technology differently, especially in this moment where we're dedicating so many resources to the infrastructure to enable generative AI. We should be asking, how much computation do we really need? How many resources are actually justifiable to put into this project? What are we actually getting out of it, right? Does what we're getting from what Silicon Valley is creating really justify the resources that we are collectively sacrificing in order to realize it? If we actually did the assessment, I think that we would very clearly find that there's no way to justify what we are doing right now—from a financial perspective, but also from a social and environmental one.
What We’re Writing
Speaking of those climate targets, it’s not just the Irish government that’s thinking about them. My colleague Joel Khalil covers how the European Union’s thirst for AI is running into European countries’ climate goals. Joel tells me he wouldn’t be surprised if data centers become a political flash point in Europe, like they are in the US, as countries go to the polls next year. “The fascinating thing about the European data center build-out is the collision of competing interests: national-level policy butts up against local priorities, ambitions for economic growth stand in conflict with climate objectives, and planning bureaucracy foils attempts by AI companies to rapidly expand their fleets,” he says. “It’s hard to see how Europe could possibly have it all.”
What We’re Reading
- The New York Times covers how the AI and data center boom is boosting a surprising commodity: gray paint.
- The massive build-out of data centers in Texas threatens years of progress in the state cutting air pollution. The Texas Tribune has more.
- Google has apologized for clearing more than 800 acres of forest in Finland without getting the necessary environmental permits to build part of a €13 million data center project. The Guardian reports that the tech giant is facing backlash in the country that could bleed into elections next spring.

At the annual European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, a new report brought forward yet another monumental moment in cancer science: A Phase 3 study showed that the “cancer vaccine” intismeran autogene reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42% compared with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) alone. This is the first neoantigen and mRNA therapy to have met its Phase 3 endpoint in oncology and is part of a collection of well-conducted studies showing promise for cancer therapeutic vaccines.
The question is no longer whether personalized cancer vaccines can work. The question now becomes how to accelerate development and increase access for the patients who could benefit.
The evolution of cancer genetics provides valuable insights as we consider cancer vaccine access. In 1990, a University of California, Berkeley, team led by Mary-Claire King identified the location of the BRCA1 gene, the first gene linked to hereditary breast cancer. BRCA2 was discovered five years later, and by 1996, the first commercial test for these two mutations hit the market. For the first time, people could learn whether they carried an inherited cancer risk before the disease appeared, and take potentially lifesaving action with earlier and more frequent screening, preventative surgery or prophylactic medication.
But patents and price kept testing expensive for years. Guidelines required a family history before testing. And no one in the care system clearly owned the whole process. The science arrived in the 1990s, but the delivery system never caught up. Thirty years later, the test now costs a few hundred dollars, but it’s still not reaching most patients whose cancers could have been caught earlier or prevented altogether.
If we want the coming wave of cancer vaccines to reach patients faster than BRCA testing did, there are several challenges to address now.
A regulatory framework that wasn’t built for n-of-1 therapeutics
Today’s regulatory pathways were designed for drugs that are identical and for devices and tests that perform the same function for every patient. Forcing personalized vaccines into a traditional drug pathway has consequences. Regulatory requirements and market pressure together push drug manufacturers toward narrow indications, one tumor type and one disease stage at a time. Each narrow program carries its own trial costs, and those costs eventually show up in the therapy’s retail price.
There are early signs of movement. A forthcoming $200 million public-private partnership from the National Cancer Institute and Foundation for the NIH, called the Therapeutic Cancer Vaccines Initiative, aims to build clinical trial networks, data standards, and infrastructure to accelerate evidence development for personalized cancer vaccines and bring them to patients within the decade.
A framework that validates the neoantigen-selection pipeline and manufacturing platform, then allows faster extension to new cancers with rigorous post-market evidence, could lower costs and widen access without lowering the bar for safety.
Artificial intelligence can also cut cost and time at nearly every step in between, from tissue analysis to manufacturing quality control.
A fragmented delivery model breeds middlemen
Personalized cancer vaccines are not a conventional pill or drug that can be manufactured in bulk and shipped — each vaccine is made for a specific patient’s cancer. Consider what it takes to get one patient their vaccine: A tumor sample must be collected and preserved properly at surgery. The tumor and a blood sample are then sequenced, and scientists use complex data pipelines to identify neoantigens and design the vaccine. The vaccine must then be manufactured, shipped, and administered on schedule, followed by years of monitoring.
Today, each of those steps would belong to a different organization, with its own contract, incentives, and economics, with no one accountable for the full delivery chain on something that is n-of-1 to that patient.
If we think of cancer vaccines as a drug, the cost and inconvenience of the cancer vaccine experience will drastically dilute their potential. We need to define the “product” not as what is in the vial but as an integrated end-to-end model of care that delivers a full patient experience and ensures optimal health outcomes.
Value to patients doesn’t align with payers
For an individual patient, preventing a cancer recurrence is priceless. But to a payer, cancer vaccines will look like a very expensive form of prevention, not a required therapy to face a current disease. A health plan that expects members to churn within one to two years has little financial incentive to pay for an expensive “benefit” that another plan will collect.
Similar to cancer screenings, access becomes forced only through patient advocacy and eventual legislation. Coverage that is forced through legislation means that the friction to access the specific therapy or tool is not proactively addressed, let alone removed.
Yet the economics favor prevention of cancer recurrences. A recurrence that becomes metastatic disease can mean years of costly immunotherapy, imaging, and hospital care. Multiyear or outcomes-based contracts could let payers share in those savings, and Medicare, which covers many patients for life, doesn’t face the same churn problem. Employers and direct-to-patient programs may open further paths, though each raises equity concerns.
Guidelines can accelerate access or stall it
In practice, clinical guidelines determine what gets ordered, covered, and reimbursed. They are also slow. Many professional guidelines still have not caught up with the technological innovations that have come to market over the last 10-15 years, such as genetic and minimal residual disease testing. Personalized therapies will make guidelines even more challenging, as guideline bodies were built to evaluate a fixed product in a defined population. But if guidelines treat each new indication with a multiyear review, the new therapies will keep outrunning the recommendations.
Guideline organizations, professional societies, and payers should agree now on how they will evaluate platform therapies: what evidence is sufficient to extend a recommendation to a related setting, and how real-world data will be used to update it quickly.
At the recent STAT Summit in Boston, Gary Keblish, a New York City public school teacher, described what he called his path to a successful outcome after a high-risk melanoma diagnosis in 2019. After surgery, he enrolled in an earlier trial of intismeran autogene, and today, he is still teaching. The results presented at ESMO are not an abstraction for patients like Gary — they are the difference between planning around the next scan and planning for next year’s curriculum.
There is still much to learn about how to optimize these vaccines, which cancers they will work in, and which technologies work best. As that research continues, we must create a system within which these vaccines can reach patients as quickly as possible.
Karen E. Knudsen, Ph.D., MBA, is a scientist, health care leader, and business executive who currently serves as CEO of the Parker Institute. She is the former CEO of American Cancer Society and its advocacy affiliate the ACS CAN, and previously served as enterprise director of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center. Othman Laraki is a technology entrepreneur, an investor, and the co-founder and CEO of Color Health. He is a longtime investor and adviser to leading companies such as Pinterest, AngelList, Slack, Instacart, Gitlab, and others.

Rockstar workers in the UK will hold a union vote just as GTA 6 is released
A legal case alleging union-busting at the game developer will also wrap next month.
Most gamers may be focused on the countdown to the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19, but there will also be a fair bit of drama unfolding behind the scenes at developer Rockstar Games over the coming weeks. According to a social media post from Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, workers at Rockstar's UK offices are reportedly scheduled to vote on recognizing their branch of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWUGB) from November 12 to November 26. If the employee vote is a success, the Rockstar Game Workers Union would become the largest recognized union in the UK's game industry.
Adding another layer to the combined cultural and corporate hype around late November, an employment tribunal between Rockstar and the IWUGB that was scheduled to end earlier in October has also been extended. That case is now expected to have closing arguments delivered on November 17 or 18, just before the GTA 6 launch. The IWUGB brought a complaint against Rockstar after the game developer laid off more than 30 employees in October 2025, most of whom were either union members or engaged in organizing efforts. The move raised alarms that the studio was engaged in union-busting, although the company claimed the employees were let go due to misconduct related to sharing confidential information. The Rockstar Game Workers Union, covering people at all of the company's offices across the UK, was announced in May 2026.
In a feature piece earlier this month that interviewed several people from Rockstar, Schreier reported that the unionizing workers who remained have been in ongoing discussion with the company's management in the intervening months. "We go where the team goes," Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar, told Schreier. "So if they want a union, they will have a union."

Britain’s medicines regulator on Friday approved Johnson & Johnson’s daily pill for adults and teenagers with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, a skin condition causing red, scaly and often itchy or painful patches.
The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved the oral drug Icotyde for people aged 12 and older who weigh at least 40 kg. The approval was based on four late-stage trials in 2,500 people with the disease, including 72 teenagers aged 12 to under 18. In all four studies, patients who took the drug saw better results after 16 weeks than those given a placebo, the regulator said.
Icotyde was approved in the U.S. earlier this year for the same condition — its first approved indication. The drug is made in collaboration with Protagonist Therapeutics. J&J is also studying the drug, chemically known as icotrokinra, for ulcerative colitis, psoriatic arthritis and Crohn’s disease.
The company expects the treatment to bring in $5 billion in peak sales across multiple indications. The drug competes with established psoriasis treatments such as Bristol Myers Squibb’s Sotyktu and AbbVie’s blockbuster Skyrizi.

Andrews died of tear in artery around heart - autopsy
- Published
Hyron Andrews - the former Sale second row found dead at his new team's hotel base before a Champions Cup match in France on Saturday - died of natural causes, an autopsy has found.
The 31-year-old, who joined the Johannesburg-based Lions this summer, suffered a tear in the aorta, an artery which carries blood from the heart to the rest of the body.
The rupture led to blood filling the muscle sac surrounding his heart.
Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle, with investigators working on the theory that he had either suffered a fall, a heart attack or, as transpired, an aneurysm, where a bulging blood vessel breaks.
A tear in the aorta is a rare and dangerous medical condition, which can be caused by undetected high blood pressure or a birth defect.
His body is yet to be returned to his native South Africa.
Andrews' wife Maighlin, with whom he had two young sons, has asked for "respect, privacy and patience during this difficult time as the repatriation process begins", according to a statement from the Lions., external
His team-mates went ahead with their game against La Rochelle on Saturday in his honour.
The visitors were applauded into the Stade Marcel-Deflandre by home fans,, external while several of the Lions players were in tears during a minute's silence before kick-off.
Sale, with whom Andrews spent two and half seasons, also paid tribute, with director of rugby Alex Sanderson saying that his team "to a man, loved playing with Hyron and being around him".

For nearly a month, Indians across the country have courted the ire and might of the state over a question no citizen in a democratic nation should have to ask. Their anger stems from the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise which has removed more than 13 crore names from the rolls since June 2025. Over a quarter were claimed dead or duplicated, while most were marked as absent or shifted. At one booth in Delhi’s Bela Estate, officials cut 728 out of 729 voters, citing address proof discrepancies. Who decided that so many names should come off the rolls and on what basis?
While the political answer is being debated on the streets and in Parliament, it is clear that the SIR has changed how a voter’s place on the roll is decided. In 1995, the Supreme Court held that a name already on the roll should be presumed to be there legally. The SIR replaced that presumption with a data-matching exercise. The Election Commission of India (ECI) has relied heavily on software for a public task where a single error costs a citizen their vote.
Rolls from the last intensive revision (mostly in 2002) were hastily digitised from Bengali, Kannada, and other regional languages, auto-transliterated by the machine into English, and matched against new enumeration forms. Then a second layer of “logical discrepancies,” such as a parent-child age gap of less than 15 years, was applied. Among those who failed the test were twins (age gap less than nine months), voters of the Oraon tribal group whose surname Xalxo was auto-translated to Khalkho, and those whose father’s name was ‘Md.’ in one list and ‘Mohammed’ in the other. To reconcile the record, little logic or reasoning was applied. According to the Internet Freedom Foundation, these rules flagged 17% of West Bengal’s electors and 41% of Madhya Pradesh’s. A system that suspects four in 10 voters in a State needs to come under scrutiny.
Such sweeping pattern-matching guarantees false positives. In West Bengal, 91% of exclusion appeals decided by the tribunals were reversed; a reversal rate that high should worry whoever designed the process. And by the time their eligibility was restored, these people had already lost the opportunity to vote in the 2026 Assembly election.
Drawing the line
This is why it matters where the line is drawn for who is “suspicious”. How many eligible voters are risked to remove one ineligible voter? Legally, Election Registration Officers (EROs) determine where the limit lies. Yet in the SIR, the ECI has never revealed what the acceptable margin of error is or the data itself. Two of the three Election Commissioners are on record objecting to the centralisation of the database and the restrictions imposed on local officers’ authority. In Goa, officers heard 97 flagged voters and found all eligible, but couldn’t restore them because the software had no option to reverse the earlier action. An audit of ECINet’s publicly served code by the civic-tech group Charchagram found that access for State officials can be switched off centrally, and that a separate setting can bar registration officers in West Bengal alone from viewing voters’ forms and hearing records. Whether these features have been used is not known.
The ECI claims that automation is only meant to assist human decisions. This would be true if officers actually had the chance to evaluate every flagged entry. In Delhi, each booth-level officer received about 200 notices to verify within a very tight deadline. When the queue becomes practically unmanageable, the machine’s verdict on an individual case inevitably becomes the State’s verdict.
The citizen then pays to undo this through hearings and lost wages, or is forced to remain disenfranchised if unable to appeal. In West Bengal, the damage went beyond voting when a June State order marked the ration cards of SIR-removed voters as inactive. The SC has since restored access to food. India has sold its digital public infrastructure to the rest of the world on the premise of inclusion at scale. Built on faulty data, the same architecture excludes at scale, and an error in one register follows a person into the next.
This doesn’t mean that the rolls shouldn’t be cleaned. What must change is where the risk tolerance lies. A dead voter left on the roll is a clerical error. A living voter who is struck off loses their constitutional right. The ECI should disclose the matching rules and error rates and open itself to an independent audit. No name should be struck off until an officer with actual time and authority verifies the real person behind the data.
The model is already travelling. In January, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar offered the ECINet platform to help other countries build their own versions. In August, U.S. President Donald Trumpcited India’s photo ID rules to push for stricter U.S. voter laws. Whatever standard the world’s largest democracy accepts for electoral error, other nations will follow.
Nishtha Gupta is a technology policy researcher based in New Delhi.

Maharashtra deploys ₹1.2-crore machines to check quality of medicines in government hospitals
Maharashtra health minister, Prakash Abitkar, stated that this device will play a key role in efforts to combat spurious and counterfeit medicines.
The Maharashtra government purchased eight counterfeit-drug detection machines to verify the quality of medications distributed through its health system across the state and prevent substandard or counterfeit medicines from reaching patients.
Worth ₹1.2 crore each, these handheld devices can detect spurious tablets, syrups, and even injections within minutes. Using the reference drug constituents already set in the system, it will compare and match the ingredients of the sample drug to be tested.
“While Maharashtra became the first state to introduce this technology with eight devices, other states like Rajasthan are in the process of ordering 116 devices following spurious Oxytocin injections that claimed the lives of pregnant women earlier in July this year. Madhya Pradesh is expected to take 10 devices, while Jammu and Kashmir is set to get four devices. Globally, this technology is used by about 50 countries for monitoring the quality of drugs,” Vaibhav Dhasal, managing director of Dawall Life Science Pvt Ltd, integrator and channel partner.
Maharashtra health minister, Prakash Abitkar, stated that this device will play a key role in efforts to combat spurious and counterfeit medicines within the state health system.
The device will be used only for preliminary testing; action will be taken against drug manufacturers or even government officials only after the spurious drug samples are verified at the 12 NABL-recognised testing laboratories.
Flying squads set up
Maharashtra has already set up eight flying squads, each equipped with one such device, to monitor the quality of medicines dispensed at government hospitals and clinics across the state.
These flying squads - each team consisting of one qualified pharmacist and a trained government official - will conduct monthly, random testing at various government health facilities in the state, including district hospitals, women’s hospitals, and other healthcare facilities. This also includes medicines procured through the Haffkine Bio-Pharmaceutical Corporation (Medical Goods Procurement Authority), district-level procurement systems and local-level purchases.
Abitkar stated that while the actual regulatory enforcement regarding pharmaceuticals falls under the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the health department would identify spurious and counterfeit drugs from its system and forward them to the relevant authority for action.
Health minister Abitkar said the initiative will be instrumental in fostering greater transparency, accountability, and regular monitoring within the medicine procurement and supply process.
“Quality control of medicines is just as critical as the availability of doctors, infrastructure, and the supply of drugs for quality healthcare for citizens,” Abitkar emphasised.
