Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
- Published
For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.
But that may end soon.
Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.
New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.
The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.
Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.
A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.
A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.
"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.
Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".
While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.
Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.
But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.
Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).
Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.
Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.
Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.
"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.
Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.
"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.
Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

Ghaziabad: 25-year-old arrested for murdering commuter over road rage
The officials identified the victim as Jalalpur resident Himanshu Chaudhary, 32, who was on a scooty and was headed home from his factory.
The police on Tuesday arrested a 25-year-old man who, on October 8, allegedly stabbed to death a 31-year-old commuter following a fight over a road rage incident in Muradnagar, police officials said.
The officials identified the victim as Jalalpur resident Himanshu Chaudhary, 32, who was on a scooty and was headed home from his factory. The arrested suspect was identified as a 25-year-old man from nearby Noorganj Mohalla.
What happened?
The two areas are close to each other, and the incident happened on the main Jalalabad Road around 7:30 pm on October 8.
“Chaudhary was returning home on his scooty while the suspect man was on a bike coming from the opposite direction. Midway, the handles of their two-wheelers touched each other, and they got disbalanced. There was a verbal altercation, and the victim headed home. After going ahead about 50 metres, the victim returned, and a fight started with the suspect. During the fight, the suspect pulled out a knife and stabbed him brutally and fled,” Sunil Kumar, ACP of Muradnagar/Masuri circle, told HT.
The police said the injured man took help from men on a bike, and they dropped him home nearby.

Several police teams scanned over 100 CCTVs in order to get clues to the incident. Luckily for police, the suspect left behind a small bag near the incident site. This bag contained some documents, which finally led police to trace him. His identity was also established with the help of CCTV footage of the incident site,” ACP added.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): Chief Minister Mohan Yadav will inaugurate the Urban Conclave at the Brilliant Convention Centre in the city on Wednesday. The event aims to accelerate urban development in Madhya Pradesh, attract infrastructure investment and promote technology-driven, sustainable cities.
The Chief Minister will also hold one-on-one meetings with investors to discuss investment opportunities, project implementation and potential partnerships.
The conclave will focus on developing Tier-II cities through improved housing, redevelopment, master planning, Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) and development corridors. Discussions will also cover Transferable Development Rights (TDR), Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) approvals, Floor Area Ratio (FAR) and measures to simplify regulatory procedures and improve ease of doing business.
Digital governance sessions will examine automated building plan approvals, online No Objection Certificates (NOCs) and development permissions, Geographic Information System (GIS)-based urban planning, colony regulations and project management information systems.
Climate-resilient and sustainable cities
Experts will deliberate on climate-resilient urban development, water security and the circular economy.
Key subjects will include urban water reuse, Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) 2.0, city forests, central parks, air quality improvement, electric vehicles and solid waste management.
Waste-to-energy projects, Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs), solar power and the Compressed Biogas (CBG) ecosystem will also feature in discussions.
Urban financing and investment opportunities
The conclave will explore funding models for urban infrastructure, including public-private partnerships (PPPs), municipal bonds, green bonds, temple bonds, joint ventures and financing through multilateral development banks.
Grants, financial modelling and viability gap funding will also be discussed to encourage private investment and support project implementation.
Urban development and housing minister Kailash Vijayvargiya, additional chief secretary Sanjay Dubey and commissioner of urban development and housing Sanket Bhondve will attend the event, along with senior officials, industry representatives and subject experts.

Logistics company LEAP India reported a net profit of ₹17.8 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 62% from nearly ₹11 Cr in the year-ago period. Sequentially, the company’s profit dipped 28% from ₹24.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company's EBITDA rose 25% YoY to ₹109.7 Cr, with the EBITDA margin expanding 91 basis points to 50.8%. The company's profit was impacted by a one-time charge of ₹6.8 Cr for prepayment of long-term borrowings. Meanwhile, operating revenue jumped 18.2% to ₹211.2 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹178.7 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a QoQ basis, the company’s top line remained largely flat and rose 3.8% from ₹203.4 Cr in Q1 FY27. Including other income of ₹4.7 Cr, total income for the period stood at ₹215.9 Cr in the quarter under review. Meanwhile, expenses rose 14.7% to ₹185.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹161.5 Cr in the quarter ended September 2025. LEAP India also incurred an additional ₹6 Cr in tax expenses during the quarter. The company also announced two strategic acquisitions. Through its wholly owned subsidiaries, LEAP signed agreements to acquire the businesses of Vimprotech and Total International Packaging Solutions (TIPS) for a combined consideration of ₹142 Cr. The businesses generated ₹65 Cr in revenue in FY26 and serve more than 200 customers across sectors including electronics, white goods, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, automotive and food and beverages. Vimprotech brings in-house plastics design, mould-making and manufacturing capabilities across facilities in Puducherry and Tamil Nadu. TIPS adds an automotive container-pooling business with four warehouses across Bengaluru, Nashik and Tirunelveli. The acquisitions are expected to strengthen backward integration, reduce reliance on external suppliers and create cross-selling opportunities for pallets, crates, containers and MHE. Founded in 2013 by Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions spanning equipment pooling, inventory management, transportation, and repair and maintenance. It serves customers across sectors such as FMCG, beverages, ecommerce, automotive and retail. Asset pooling remained the core growth driver. Income from asset pooling increased 19% YoY in Q2 FY27, while material handling equipment (MHE) income rose 52%. LEAP operates a pool of 15.5 Mn assets valued at over ₹1,820 Cr, serving more than 1,100 customers across 11,000-plus touchpoints and 27 fulfilment centres. Customer churn remained below 0.5%. Asset utilisation stood at 89.3% for pallets and 82.3% for MHE as of September 2026, while container utilisation improved to 73.7%. LEAP estimates that it commands around 90% of India's organised pallet-pooling market, which it expects to expand as organised warehousing, supply-chain automation and modern retail drive demand. LEAP's balance sheet also strengthened. Net debt nearly halved to ₹433.7 Cr from ₹801 Cr a year earlier, while the debt-to-equity ratio improved to 0.48x from 0.96x. Net debt-to-EBITDA declined to around 1.9x from 4.4x. "Strong growth, continued improvements in cost efficiency and rising profitability position us well to sustain this momentum. With a scalable business model, disciplined execution and a clear focus on operational excellence, we remain confident in our ability to deliver long-term value and strengthen the trust our shareholders have placed in us," Mathew said. Shares of LEAP India ended today's trading session 3.06% higher at ₹126.35 apiece on the BSE.

AI-native cybersecurity startup Protectt.ai plans to acquire a controlling stake in AIShield, an AI security platform incubated within Bosch Global Software Technologies (BGSW). Bosch will retain a minority stake in AIShield following the transaction. Backed by Bessemer Venture Partners, Protectt.ai will acquire the stake through a deal comprising primary and secondary components. The companies have not disclosed the transaction value or timeline. “There will be cash, a secondary component and future investments as required. The current structure is a combination of cash and ESOPs. Future investments will depend on the requirements of the business,” Protectt.ai cofounder Manish Mimani told Inc42. Founded in 2022 by Shiv Kumar and Amit Phadke, AIShield was incubated within BGSW. It develops security solutions for machine learning models, generative AI applications and AI supply chains, helping enterprises defend against attacks designed to manipulate AI systems and address compliance risks. The partnership will combine AIShield’s AI security capabilities with Protectt.ai’s mobile security platform, allowing the latter to expand into enterprise AI security. AIShield will continue to operate as an independent entity under Protectt.ai once the deal is completed, with its own professional management team and a focus on AI security research and product development. It will also be able to raise external funding in the future. Protectt.ai plans to work with private companies and government organisations through AIShield to build an India-developed AI security platform, Mimani said. From Mobile Security To Enterprise AI Founded in 2020 by Manish Mimani and Mohanraj Selvaraj, Protectt.ai provides mobile threat defence solutions that help businesses protect applications against cyber threats and fraud. Its platform also serves as a compliance hub for app owners, helping them adhere to regulations issued by entities such as the RBI, SEBI and NPCI. The startup also offers a full-stack AI security platform with tools to test AI agents for vulnerabilities, secure connections between AI applications and external tools, and monitor AI agents while they operate. Protectt.ai’s security technology runs on more than 1 Bn mobile devices and processes 15 Bn mobile application sessions every month, Mimani said. He expects mobile applications to increasingly rely on AI agents to perform tasks, potentially reducing the need for users to navigate conventional app interfaces over the next one to two years. Protectt.ai had already been researching AI model scanning and AI agent security as part of its product roadmap. Through the AIShield acquisition, the startup aims to extend these capabilities beyond mobile applications to enterprise use cases across sectors. Some members of Protectt.ai’s AI security team will move to AIShield, although the number has yet to be finalised. AIShield currently has around 12–15 employees and plans to expand its team to 50–60 people by March 2027. It plans to hire PhD researchers, master’s graduates and other technical talent from leading institutions to strengthen its research and engineering capabilities. The team will focus on developing products, conducting research and filing patents, Mimani said. Protectt.ai Eyes Further Acquisitions The AIShield deal is Protectt.ai’s first such acquisition. The startup set up an M&A team earlier in 2026 to evaluate potential acquisitions and partnerships, with a focus on building capabilities and addressing gaps in its existing offerings. Protectt.ai is exploring opportunities in areas such as API security and cloud security that could complement its current capabilities, Mimani said. The startup secured around $16 Mn in a Series A funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners and Bajaj Finance in 2025. Mimani added that Protectt.ai is evaluating opportunities and expects to consider raising fresh funds in 2027. India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

On 22 October 2026, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur acknowledged that face-offs with Chinese forces had occurred at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. On 23 October 2026, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the situation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) becomes “disturbed” when Chinese troops deviate from established patrolling patterns.
Amid these developments, several videos are being circulated on social media (here, here, and here), purportedly showing clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border, including claims of an Indian soldier’s capture and alleged attempts by Chinese troops to cross the border. Let’s verify the claims made in these posts in this article.
Claim: The videos show clashes between Indian and Chinese troops along the Arunachal Pradesh border in October 2026.
Fact: None of the viral videos shows the reported India–China border face-offs in October 2026. The first and third videos were circulating on social media by December 2025, while the second features footage filmed on 28 September 2021, as reported by CNN. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts allege that an Indian soldier suffering from diabetes and altitude-related health complications fainted while on duty near the Line of Actual Control (LAC). Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) personnel provided him with first aid and medical assistance before safely handing him over to his own unit. The posts portray the incident as a humanitarian gesture amid India–China border tensions.
A News18 Hindi report published on 16 December 2025, featuring a screenshot of the viral video, claimed that Chinese soldiers had assisted an unconscious Indian soldier. While highlighting the humanitarian aspect, the report also noted scepticism over the video, particularly why the soldier’s legs appeared to be tied, raising questions about whether the incident was a genuine humanitarian gesture or an attempt by China to improve its image.
However, we could not independently verify the video’s origin or the context in which it was recorded. The available evidence indicates that the video predates the October 2026 border face-offs. At the time of writing, the Indian Army had issued no statement confirming the capture of any Indian soldier during these incidents.
Video 2
During our investigation, we found that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. The video has been online at least since December 2022.
A CNN report published on 15 December 2022 featuring the same visuals stated that the footage was filmed on 28 September 2021. According to CNN, a serving Indian military officer familiar with clashes along the India–China border confirmed that the video was recorded in Arunachal Pradesh, near the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border between the two countries.
Video 3
During our investigation, we found several social media posts (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals dating back to December 2025. This confirms that the viral video predates the reported India–China border tensions in October 2026 and is unrelated to the recent developments. These posts claimed that the video shows Indian soldiers beating Chinese troops allegedly attempting to infiltrate Arunachal Pradesh, describing it as an old border clash.
An X post by the Indian Army’s Fact Check Unit debunking the viral video stated that the footage was unauthenticated and was falsely presented as a recent October 2026 confrontation, creating rumours and confusion about the situation along the LAC. It also warned that old videos are often circulated as recent incidents and urged citizens to avoid sharing unverified footage and rely on official sources for updates.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the India–China border face-offs in October 2026.

Pope will meet with survivors of clergy abuse during upcoming trip to Latin America, Vatican says
The Vatican says Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin America
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin America, which will take the American pope to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, the Vatican said Tuesday.
The Vatican statement didn’t say when the encounters would take place or where, but said “several meetings are planned,” suggesting more than one encounter. The Nov. 6-17 trip is going ahead as planned despite Leo's Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery which had put the trip in question.
Continuing the practice of his two recent predecessors, Leo met with abuse survivors in June in Spain and most recently in France. Ahead of the French trip, the Vatican confirmed the meeting ahead of time rather than after it took place, as had been the previous practice.
“These meetings reflect the pope’s desire to express his solidarity with those who have suffered and continue to suffer as a result of this violence, to work with them to build paths to healing that are accessible to anyone in need, and to ensure that the church is a safe and spiritually healthy place that lives out and communicates the Gospel,” according to a Vatican statement Tuesday.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru, and he saw first-hand the effects of abuse on victims. He was the designated bishop in the Peruvian bishops conference to hear from victims of an influential but abusive movement, the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
The former Cardinal Robert Prevost then was instrumental in Pope Francis’ decision in 2025 to suppress the movement.
Francis’ native Argentina, for its part, has had a wretched reckoning with abuse and victims there have been demanding action from the Vatican, including to address cases in which Francis was personally involved.

Australia fight back to keep Cummins out of unwanted club... for now
- Published
Third Test, Cape Town (day one of five)
South Africa 329: Ackerman 95, Markram 78; Starc 6-72
Australia: Yet to bat
It is the club every cricket captain desperately tries to avoid.
Nasser Hussain is a fully paid-up member.
Ricky Ponting won it all in charge of Australia, yet people still talk about his decision to bowl at Edgbaston when Glenn McGrath was on his way to hospital in 2005.
The 27th October, the 2026 Cape Town decider, could yet be an occasion for which Pat Cummins is always remembered – a Test which means he joins that unfortunate group of skippers who chose to bowl when they should have opted to bat.
It is down to his bowlers that that is not already all but a certainty.
South Africa v Australia
Third Test, Cape Town
27-31 October, 08:00 GMT
Follow live text updates on the BBC Sport website and app.
After a shocking start, a bad call at the toss compounded by a wayward bowling performance across the first two hours, Australia roared back into the Test in the afternoon.
They were helped by some careless South African batting as their happy hookers allowed a position of 203-1 to become 232-6.
Aiden Markram, David Bedingham and Wiaan Mulder were all out attempting to take on the short balls – for 78, 50 and nought respectively.
On 95, opener Marques Ackerman ran past one from Nathan Lyon with the glory of a first Protea century in his second Test in his sights and captain Temba Bavuma was undone by a straight ball from Lyon.
Either side of a knock of 179 last week, Bavuma has got out to off-spin three times in three innings – all for single-figure scores.
And while Australia stuck to their task in the afternoon, fielding well and drying up the scoring after 140 runs were leaked at more than four runs per over in the first session, most impressive was the way Mitchell Starc thundered in the day's final moments.
At 327-6, South Africa could yet have finished this enthralling day - one fitting of a series decider from which the winner will finish the series on top of the rankings – in the ascendancy.
Instead, Starc took four wickets in six deliveries with the new ball, first prising out Ryan Rickelton for 42 and Marco Jansen 52.
He targeted pads and stumps, bowled Gerald Coetzee and pinned Kagiso Rabada lbw for ducks. South Africa were 329 all out.
Somehow, after everything, if either side is happy, it is Australia.
Such is the time difference, many back home missed this fightback, having rolled over when Scott Boland was left out again, Cummins chose to bowl under blue skies and South Africa plundered the bowling through the opening session.
When Starc was being slapped and steered for four consecutive fours by Ackerman, few anticipated this finale. Not since Ponting's insertion of England 21 years ago had a 100-run opening partnership been made for a side put into bat by Australia.
But Cummins' Australia held firm again where other sides have folded.
As a side they remain imperfect. They could yet lose this Test - a result that could have wider repercussions going forward to next year's Ashes.
Their batting line-up, with opener Nic Maddinson sent on a flight home after two Tests, Marnus Labuschagne retained despite a run of innings without a century longer than most careers and, crucially, with Steve Smith out injured is flawed.
But Australia find a way, often when teetering somewhere near the brink.
It is 11 months since knives were sharpening after four sessions of last winter's Ashes series.
Batter Usman Khawaja was injured playing golf, the batting line-up weak and the back-ups to an ageing pace attack not up to the mark. They won that Test in two days and took the series 4-1.
This could prove an even more impressive reversal at the bottom of Africa.
The end result does not prove Cummins was right with his morning decision, however.
"It feels like there's a bit of moisture in the wicket so we will have first use of it," he said after putting South Africa into bat.
Eleven overs later, Lyon was bowling his spin. Not since Shane Warne in 2000 had an Australian spinner been in the attack so early after their captain chose to bowl.
Instead, the obvious explanation appears that he made his call to protect a struggling batting line-up.
Matt Renshaw will be pushed back up to open, having impressed in the first Test at number five, and Labuschagne given another, possibly final, chance.
Batter Josh Inglis, one of the four to come into this Australian XI, has not faced a red ball in a competitive match since March - nor Cameron Green since August.
Will a day's play help ease those batters back into this Test, or simply delay the inevitable?
Cummins' entry into that unwanted club has been delayed by his bowlers' streetwise nature and ability to sense a moment.
Now his batters must ensure he never steps foot inside at all.

A Liberal-National MP has called for a rethink of pre-poll voting at federal elections, including potentially shortening the amount of time booths are open, amid concerns of threats to voters and volunteers.
Security risks to politicians and their staff have been front and centre this week, as parliament returned after the alleged attack on Helen Haines, which left the independent MP in a serious but stable condition after both her legs were amputated.
The member for the Queensland electorate of Groom, Garth Hamilton, said the risk of having members of the public and volunteers lined up at booths near car parks or roads needed to be assessed.
“I’ve had three elections and I’ve witnessed three interactions between cars and people at pre-poll, two accidental, one wasn’t,” Hamilton said on Tuesday.
“The threat is already there, the potential is already there in a heightened environment.”
Pre-polling booths usually open one to two weeks before an election. The Toowoomba-based politician said the length of the pre-polling period, the allocation of resources at centres and the role of postal voting were all measures that could be considered to lower the risk to voters and staff.
“What we obviously want is not in any way to restrict anybody’s access to democracy, but we also want to make sure that it’s done in a safe way,” Hamilton said. “There’s a reasonable conversation to be had on the shape of pre-poll in Australia, if these threats are increasing, and that’s what we’re hearing from the AFP.”
Australians are increasingly choosing to vote early ahead of polling day. More than 9m votes, or 56%, were cast at early voting centres, according to the Australian Electoral Commission’s 2025 election report.
It is understood Jerome Laxale, a Labor MP who chairs the parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 election, raised safety and his committee’s interim report on the issue at a caucus meeting on Tuesday.
The report recommends the electoral commission reviews the resourcing requirements and duration of pre-poll voting to ensure adequate arrangements are in place, noting the rising number of people opting to cast their ballot early.
The AEC advised the committee that shortening the pre-poll period would not decrease early voting, but would instead “compress the growing demand into a shorter period and increase operational risks, such as queues and shortages of appropriate venues”.
Laxale, who has represented the NSW seat of Bennelong since 2022, said it was incumbent on the parliament to provide a safe and welcoming atmosphere at a polling booth.
“Democracy doesn’t collapse, it just crumbles,” he said.
“If people go, ‘you know what? I don’t want to deal with that. I’m not going to vote,’ then that has a snowball effect, which will undermine and erode our democratic process. Voting has to be safe and secure.”
Submissions to the inquiry detailed neo-Nazis turning up to booths with speakers, volunteers being bullied and harassed and voters leaving polling centres in tears.
The independent MP Monique Ryan said candidates, volunteers, and campaign workers facing threats of violence should be given clear guidance for how they might engage with federal and state police.
“We need to go back to democracy sausages and bake sales, not voters feeling intimidated and harassed as they approach polling booths,” she said.

Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”

BRO's Project Arunank strengthens India's border connectivity along China frontier
The BRO's Project Arunank marked its 19th Raising Day in Arunachal Pradesh, highlighting its role in strengthening strategic roads, military mobility and last-mile connectivity along the China border. From all-weather routes and resilient engineering to community welfare, the project supports India's border preparedness and development in challenging Himalayan terrain.
As the Border Roads Organisation’s (BRO) Project Arunank marked its 19th Raising Day in Arunachal Pradesh on October 24, the occasion highlighted a critical element of India’s border strategy: strengthening military mobility, logistics and last-mile connectivity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China.
Established in October 2008, Project Arunank has been developing and maintaining strategic infrastructure across Arunachal Pradesh, where steep mountains, dense forests, heavy rainfall and difficult climatic conditions pose persistent challenges to road construction and maintenance. Its work contributes to India’s efforts to improve connectivity along the eastern frontier, where reliable roads are essential for moving troops, equipment and supplies to forward areas.
INFRASTRUCTURE AS A STRATEGIC NECESSITY ALONG LAC
China’s infrastructure development across the Tibetan plateau and in areas close to the disputed boundary has underscored the importance of strengthening India’s own border connectivity. For New Delhi, the challenge extends beyond building roads to ensuring that strategically important routes remain usable in difficult terrain and adverse weather.
Roads and bridges directly affect the Armed Forces’ ability to mobilise personnel, transport equipment and sustain deployments in remote areas. Better connectivity can help ease logistical constraints and improve access to forward locations, although operational preparedness also depends on supporting infrastructure, equipment, manpower and maintenance.
The scale of India’s infrastructure effort in Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in a Ministry of Defence update from 2022, which reported that the BRO had undertaken work on 64 roads spanning 3,097.15 km in the state over the preceding five years. The figures illustrate the scale of road development in a strategically significant region, although they reflect an earlier reporting period rather than the current total.
LAST-MILE CONNECTIVITY AND OPERATIONAL READINESS
For India, the strategic value of border infrastructure lies not only in constructing major routes but also in improving last-mile connectivity to remote settlements and strategically important areas. Roads linking forward locations, supported by bridges and reliable maintenance, can improve the movement of personnel and supplies while reducing the isolation of communities in difficult-to-access regions.
A key example of Project Arunank’s work is the 278-km Hapoli–Sarli–Huri Road, which the BRO reported in 2025 had been blacktopped for the first time since Independence. The project illustrates how improved road surfaces can strengthen all-weather connectivity and link remote parts of Arunachal Pradesh with wider transport networks.
The development of such routes is particularly relevant in a region where geographical constraints can increase the time, cost and complexity of transporting essential supplies. Reliable connectivity is therefore an important component of both military logistics and civilian access.
ENGINEERING FOR THE HIMALAYAN TERRAIN
Project Arunank continues to focus on engineering solutions designed to improve the durability and resilience of infrastructure in challenging conditions. These include alternative construction materials, geocells and slope-protection measures.
Such techniques are important in Arunachal Pradesh, where landslides, erosion, heavy rainfall and seasonal disruptions can damage roads and interrupt movement. In this terrain, maintaining existing infrastructure is as important as constructing new roads. Regular upkeep, resilient engineering and the timely restoration of damaged stretches are essential to keeping routes functional.
The effectiveness of border infrastructure depends not simply on the length of roads built but also on their reliability, accessibility and ability to withstand local environmental conditions.
BORDER DEVELOPMENT BEYOND MILITARY REQUIREMENTS
The strategic importance of infrastructure also extends to the civilian population. Improved road connectivity can help residents of remote border settlements access healthcare, education, markets and government services while creating opportunities for local economic activity.
Project Arunank has also undertaken welfare measures for Casual Paid Labourers (CPLs), including improved shelters, protective clothing, sanitation facilities and regular medical camps. Its community and environmental initiatives include cleanliness drives, cyber-awareness programmes, cycling and yoga events, and the planting of 25,815 trees under the ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ campaign, according to information released for its Raising Day.
Development in border areas is an important complement to infrastructure expansion. Better connectivity can support local livelihoods and improve the delivery of essential services while helping communities remain connected to the wider state and country.
THE ROAD AHEAD
As Project Arunank enters its 19th year, its work underscores a central requirement of India’s eastern border strategy: infrastructure must combine strategic utility, resilience in difficult terrain and benefits for local communities.
Along the LAC, dependable roads and bridges are essential for military mobility and sustained logistics. At the same time, connectivity to remote settlements remains a key development priority. The challenge ahead is to continue expanding access, strengthen the durability of existing routes and ensure that infrastructure remains functional under demanding conditions.
For India, strengthening border infrastructure in Arunachal Pradesh is therefore not merely a construction exercise. It is a long-term investment in operational preparedness, reliable connectivity and the development of communities living along the country’s sensitive eastern frontier.

The final ice patch has vanished from Slovenia’s Triglav glacier, the latest Alpine casualty of Europe’s scorching summer.
The once mighty ice mass lost 93% of its surface area between 1983 and 2003, shrinking to cover less than a hectare of overheated rock, but went on to surprise researchers who feared its imminent demise, clinging on to the mountain for two more decades.
In the last five years, which includes Europe’s three hottest years on record, the remaining ice has melted to a handful of isolated pockets, with the final remnant of the main body measuring just a few metres by the end of summer. New photos of the mountainside – taken either side of snowfall this month – confirm that no ice remains.
Matija Zorn, director of the Anton Melik Geographical Institute, said Mount Triglav “holds a central place in Slovenian national identity” and the demise of the glacier represents the loss of an important data source and indicator of climate change.
“Every year I knew that the ice was going to be less and less,” he said. “But I was shocked every year [by] how much less ice was up there.”
Fierce heatwaves made hotter by carbon pollution have ravaged the Alps and reduced big white glaciers to what scientists have called “moonlike” rock deserts. Last month, Swiss glaciologists found that nearly a fifth of the country’s ice had disappeared in the last five years, with a 5.5% drop in volume in 2026.
In Slovenia, home to the south-eastern tip of the Alps, the Triglav glacier suffered most of its decline in the last century. Historical photographs and documents suggest the glacier covered about 40 hectares in the mid-1800s. By 1946, when scientists conducted the first formal measurements, its area had shrunk to just 14 hectares.
Zorn, who first took measurements at the glacier in 2001, said the rate of change was surprising even in the decades in which the glacier defied expectations. The spot at which he had to put on crampons to prevent slipping jumped back year after year as the glacier receded.
“The melting is incredible,” he said. “In 2002 … we took a core of ice out for some geochemical analysis and it was like 5 metres [deep]. The next year, I was standing on the same spot … not on ice, but on rock.”
Triglav is Slovenia’s highest peak, a cultural touchpoint that every person in the country of skiers and climbers is expected to climb at least once. Although the glacier has vanished, scientists have found ice in the caves beneath Triglav as its retreat has exposed new shafts. A second glacier on the Skuta mountain has also shrunk and thinned, but the remaining patch of ice is better shaded than Triglav and is expected to hold out for a few more years.
Western Europe suffered through its hottest summer on record this year, causing at least 50,000 estimated heat deaths and costly secondary effects that ranged from failed harvests to power plants being forced to shut down. Scientists are still assessing the damage done to ecosystems.
Miha Pavšek, a glaciologist and mountain guide, said “nature is changing in front of our eyes” but people were not yet taking it seriously.
“With the melting of the glacier, a part of me is also going away,” said Pavšek, who has a photograph of his parents there in 1957. “There are some things that humans thought were eternal. Glaciers are obviously not.”

Anthropic filed its hotly anticipated IPO prospectus on Monday, spelling out parts of the company’s business, strategy, and risk profile ahead of its public debut. Though the filing, known as an S-1, is several hundred pages long, it has some notable omissions—namely, certain financial figures.
“Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $_____ for the three months ended September 30, 2026,” reads the first of dozens of such examples.
It’s relatively common for companies to redact certain information in their S-1 filings, and Securities and Exchange Commission rules allow for a certain degree of leniency around the practice, particularly when it comes to information considered “confidential.”
Still, it’s helpful to know what, exactly, these companies decide to leave out. In Anthropic’s case, the missing details largely revolve around financials for its most recent quarter, which concluded at the end of September, and lease agreements tied to its compute investments. While experts expect many details to be disclosed before Anthropic goes public, their current absence may hint at the uncertainties of investing in artificial intelligence, as companies work to secure sufficient compute.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.
Michael Dambra, accounting and law professor at University at Buffalo School of Management, tells WIRED that there are “practical reasons” for its third quarter numbers to be absent: September 30 was only a few weeks ago, and “closing the books for a company of this size takes time.”
Companies can also be liable for misstatements in their registration statements, “so there is a strong incentive not to publish numbers before they have been fully vetted,” Dambra says. SEC rules require that “Anthropic would need to update the filing with third-quarter financials” if the company goes public any later than about mid-November, he says.
As for data center lease agreements, Erica Neuman, an accounting professor at Youngstown State University, says it’s “not unusual” for companies to redact confidential details from “contract exhibits,” which could include lease terms.
However, Neuman adds that it’s worth scrutinizing whether Anthropic’s redactions would prevent, or make it more difficult, for investors to analyze Anthropic’s financial obligations and whether they may impact the company’s cash flow.
Many of Anthropic’s financial obligations relate to compute, which is the “most significant operating cost in our business,” according to the S-1. It’s also a business risk for the company, and it’s laid out both in terms of undersupply and overinvestment. (Parts of the AI industry have been warning that chip constraints could slow the progress of AI.)
Anthropic’s prospectus puts more emphasis on the risks of overinvestment, stating that the company needs to make forward investments in compute resources that will seem “irresponsibly large” at first glance.
Chips, Anthropic explains, are approached as a “single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners,” including Amazon, Google, Nvidia, and AMD. The company notes that it has entered into contracts “with an aggregate committed spend of more than $____, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.” Some of these contracts are set to be completed before December of 2030, while others may extend through 2045.
Though the prospectus touches on Anthropic’s compute uncertainties due to factors like limited land and power resources, Patrick Moorhead, CEO and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy believes investors are owed more detail.
“It’s about characterizing the odds and impact individually across each of the areas. Anthropic owes investors more information, such as a probability of these individual issues, characterizing the percentage chance and the degree of the impact,” he tells WIRED. “Not ‘could materially impact.’”
Anthropic does provide some eye-catching estimates in footnotes. Since December 31, 2025, it has started or amended “compute and infrastructure” leases with “future minimum payment obligations” worth approximately $417 billion in aggregate. Since June 30, it’s added another $245 billion to its future payment obligations, all related to infrastructure agreements. It also expanded “certain existing commercial agreements” that it caveats “have not yet been finalized,” for an additional $125 billion to $150 billion.
Include “short term” agreements with “minimum non-cancelable payments,” Anthropic says, and that’s another $21 billion. In total, it will owe, at minimum, an estimated $808 billion if it follows through on all of this.
Ben Bajarin, chief executive and a principal analyst at Creative Strategies who tracks the chip industry, says that this is likely just the first draft of Anthropic’s prospectus, and that he expects a lot of gaps to be filled in an updated version.
Despite how common S-1 redactions are, Dambra describes them as “controversial.” While companies may argue that they’re “protecting proprietary information,” Dambra says that skeptics accuse them of using redactions “opportunistically” in order to “avoid disclosing politically or socially sensitive information.”
However, Dambra argues that redacting information may come at a cost. He notes that companies with redactions in their S-1s were also more likely to “underprice” their shares at the initial public offering.
When companies redact information in their S-1, Dambra says they typically understand that they’ve created an “information gap” between them and outside investors. Understanding that investors will treat this gap with “suspicion,” companies may feel inclined to “entice” them to participate in the IPO by setting a lower starting price.
It’s unclear what Anthropic’s opening price may end up being, or how investors may be interpreting the redactions in the company’s S-1. But according to Bajarin, the whole AI industry is one form of “blank” or another when it comes to crunching the numbers based on access to chips and infrastructure right now. So, yes, it’s all a risk.
“All of this,” he says, “just shows how absurdly early we are in enterprise adoption of an AI market that will be more than $3 trillion yearly and likely growing.”

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Local ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine
MYKOLAIV, Ukraine — A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.
The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.
According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.
The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.
Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.
The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, though deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.
Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.
Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.
Oleshky is in the partially occupied Kherson region, about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces.
It was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the town due to a dam collapse.
Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region's administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 invasion but retreated across the river several months later.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
- Published
The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.
Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.
With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.
The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.
"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."
The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.
The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.
Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.
In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.
There is also another possible business angle behind this push.
Kugelman says Rubio had two reasons to meet the Ambani family. First, to secure greater refining of Venezuelan oil and second to seek assurances that Reliance remained interested in backing a proposed Texas refinery.
In March, Trump announced a proposed refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas on his Truth Social platform. He said that it would be the first major new refinery in the US in 50 years.
Reliance has not publicly commented on it and there are no details on the project or when the work is expected to begin.
"The Texas facility may not be as immediately important to US interests as the arrangement tied to Venezuelan oil, but I still think it's part of the story," he says.
However, analysts point out that closer cooperation with Reliance and progress on energy security do not necessarily mean a trade deal is imminent.
"I don't think anyone really expected a trade deal to be announced at this point, but this trip seems to have helped get the relationship back on track, to the extent that it can, given the significant points of tension that remain," Kugelman said.
Rajani Sinha, the chief economist at credit rating agency CareEdge, told the BBC that greater cooperation could allay energy security concerns in both countries, help push the stalled trade negotiations forward and "boost trade and sentiment" in India.
Meera Shankar says that India is possibly "waiting for the US to formalise its tariff positions so that we know whether Delhi has a preferential trade deal".
She adds that, although ties between the two countries have been strained in recent times, their bilateral trade continues to grow.
India's merchandise exports to the US was $50.81bn between April and September, up 11.1% from the previous year, according to India's ministry of commerce. Its imports rose to $32.33bn from $25.66bn in the same period. India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to $18.48bn from $20.07bn a year earlier.
"The economic relationship remains strong, but a long period of uncertainty could eventually affect it," Shankar said.
So, for now, the visit may have possibly helped get the relationship back on track, but whether that translates into a trade agreement or a lasting shift in energy ties remains to be seen.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.
