Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

UP teen alleges abduction with bike, police expose story made to dodge scolding
A Kaushambi teenager allegedly fabricated his kidnapping after taking a motorcycle without permission. Police questioning revealed he invented the story to avoid his family's anger.
A Class 10 student in Uttar Pradesh’s Kaushambi allegedly fabricated a kidnapping story after leaving home on a motorcycle without permission, police said. The teenager reportedly made up the account to avoid being scolded by his family for taking the bike.
The incident came to light after the boy’s father, Ashish Kumar, initially approached police to report that his 15-year-old son, Prashant, had gone missing with the motorcycle. A subsequent call reporting the teenager’s alleged kidnapping triggered a police response in the district.
Prashant, a resident of Bhaddurpur village under the jurisdiction of Manjhanpur police station, had claimed that he went outside to use the toilet in the morning and found two unidentified men inside the house when he returned. He alleged that the men abducted him along with a motorcycle parked at the house, tied his hands and covered his mouth before taking him towards the Kokhraj area.
According to his initial account, he managed to escape near the Rohi Overbridge by jumping off the motorcycle as the alleged kidnappers travelled along the route.
POLICE QUESTIONING EXPOSES ALLEGED HOAX
Deputy Superintendent of Police Saurabh Sawant said the boy’s father first visited the Teva police outpost and reported that Prashant had left home on a motorcycle. Police began searching for the teenager.
At around 11.30 am, another call was received through the UP-112 emergency service, this time reporting the alleged kidnapping in the Kokhraj police station area. A police response vehicle reached the spot near Rohi Overbridge, where the caller was present with the boy and the motorcycle.
The family initially claimed that two unidentified men had kidnapped Prashant before abandoning him at the location and fleeing.
However, during questioning, the teenager allegedly admitted that he had taken the motorcycle because he was not allowed to ride it at home. He reportedly invented the kidnapping story to avoid facing his family’s anger over leaving with the vehicle without permission.

The Osmania General Hospital (OGH) in Hyderabad has established a dedicated gender-affirming surgery service in the government healthcare sector in Telangana, marking a step towards improving access to specialised healthcare for transgender persons.
The Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery has introduced the service through a multidisciplinary team of specialists from plastic surgery, anaesthesiology, endocrinology, urology, gynaecology and psychiatry, along with nursing staff and other healthcare professionals. The initiative has been developed over the past eight months, said doctors.
The team has successfully performed several procedures for transgender people, including frontal bossing reduction, autologous fat grafting for breast augmentation, breast augmentation using implants, penile inversion vaginoplasty and bilateral nipple-areola complex-sparing mastectomy. Breast implants have also been facilitated through letters of credit under the Chief Minister’s Relief Fund (CMRF).
The initiative aims to provide safe, accessible and affordable gender-affirming surgical care within the public healthcare system, particularly for individuals who face financial and logistical barriers to accessing specialised procedures.
The service follows a multidisciplinary approach, with emphasis on patient evaluation, individualised surgical planning, perioperative care and post-operative follow-up. The hospital has also received support from the Queer Badhu Parents Association, whose president, Mukunda Mala, helped facilitate the renovation of a three-bed ward for transgender patients recovering from surgery, said Dr P. Lakshmi, Professor and Head of Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.
The hospital plans to expand the range of gender-affirming procedures offered and further strengthen the multidisciplinary programme. The initiative is expected to help more transgender people access specialised surgical care through the government healthcare system while promoting inclusive, dignified and comprehensive healthcare.

The first batch of Apple’s first folding phone may already have some screen issues.
The iPhone Duo is a strong first foldable from the company, but multiple Reddit reports say the phone's inner screen cracks when customers open the device. Some apparently happen very soon, like during device setup. (Others might be from influencers trying to break the thing, like YouTuber JerryRigEverything.) People are already calling this “crackgate.”
It's unclear how widespread the problem is or whether it only affects a small number of units. (WIRED's review unit hasn't had any issues after more than two weeks of daily use.) Apple did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
This is familiar territory for foldable phones. A hinge means strain on the screen and the components inside. It's also a place for dust to seep in and break the phone, as with Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold in 2019, forcing the company to pause sales and fix the issue. Some devices handle it better than others, and as the product category has grown, those issues have largely diminished. But fewer problems don't mean easier fixes.
On Sunday, repair company iFixit released its teardown of the iPhone Duo, including a video detailing the specific parts inside and what to look out for if people need to fix their $1,999 phone one day—maybe sooner than they think.
The phone got a provisional repairability rating of 5/10, though that score may be updated to factor in how Apple supplies replacement parts. A 5/10 doesn’t sound great, but it’s actually the highest repair rating iFixit has given any foldable phone.
“The state of foldables today is one of the hardest engineering challenges across a number of disciplines out there in the market today,” iFixit CEO Kyle Wiens said at an event the day before Apple announced its folding phone in September. “It is the pinnacle of material engineering and materials science. It is ludicrously difficult to accomplish this.”
The iPhone Duo earned good marks on some repair fronts. The battery and back panels are straightforward to remove and replace. The outer trim comes off in one piece. The 5.4-inch front screen comes off easily enough. Disassembling the pieces and putting everything back together is doable too, since almost everything is secured with brackets and screws you can remove and reuse.
The tricky part, according to iFixit, is the inner display. A thin matte nano-texture finish sits on top of the OLED screen, and if you’re not careful, you could easily peel the layer off. (Apple strictly tells users not to remove this finish on a support page.)
Removing the full inner screen requires melting the adhesive with a heat gun and some real elbow grease to pull the screen away. Users have reported breaking this part of the screen, and it seems it is the most fragile component and the hardest to replace. (Apple has an inner screen repair service, but it costs $999.) The Duo also collects dust in typical places like the USB-C port, outer edges, and speaker, but it accumulates along the inner hinge, causing it to sound "crunchy" like other folding devices when dust gets inside.
Apple long resisted letting users repair their own devices. When it finally started offering real repair options in 2021, its programs got off to a rough start and were less helpful than they could have been. Slowly but surely, thanks to various legislation in the US and the European Union, Apple has been introducing efforts to let people fix their own things. The iPhone Duo had a widely accessible repair manual on launch day, which hasn't always been the case for how the company shares that kind of information.
The iPhone Duo may not be perfectly repairable—folding phones might never get there. But when a device starts having problems like cracked screens, it’ll be nice to know how to fix the thing.

Girija (name changed) spent years working as a domestic worker before her failing knees made it difficult for her to continue. Hoping to find a more manageable way to earn a living, the 60-year-old borrowed money from acquaintances and set up a roadside vegetable stall. But another health problem emerged, making it difficult to keep the business running.
“She learnt that she was suffering from urinary incontinence. Taking frequent loo breaks while managing the stall was not practical, and she eventually decided to shut shop, losing her source of income in the process,” says Gurajada Sobha Pernidevi, founder-president of Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, a voluntary organisation working for the welfare of women.
For older people with limited financial means, a health problem can do more than cause physical discomfort; it can take away their livelihood, independence and opportunities to socialise. Conditions that are difficult to discuss, such as urinary incontinence, are often endured in silence because of embarrassment and the cost of managing them.
Unlike ailments that call for joint replacement surgery or a cardiac stent, these less visible difficulties of ageing often receive scant attention, despite their potential to disrupt daily life. However, as Telangana’s share of elderly population grows, addressing such overlooked needs will become increasingly important.
Telangana’s population aged 60 and above is projected to rise from 12.5% in 2026 to 17.1% in 2036, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s report, ‘State Finances — A Study of Budgets of 2025-26: Demographic Transition in India — Implications for State Finances’.
The State is expected to join the category of ageing ones, where senior citizens account for at least 15% of the population. The projected demographic shift raises questions about how healthcare, caregiving and community support can keep pace with the needs of older people, particularly those who live alone or cannot afford private services.
Associations working with senior citizens say the challenges range from obtaining medicines and reaching hospitals to finding dependable caregivers and accessing mental health support.
P. Shyam Kumar, State project coordinator at HelpAge India, says doorstep medical services, including palliative care, could make healthcare more accessible. Nutritional supplements and the delivery of medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists could also help older people manage their health.
“Without adequate support, their condition may deteriorate, leading to more hospital visits, additional expenses and greater dependence on family members. So, supplying medicines through Accredited Social Health Activists may work in this direction,” he adds.
The pace mismatch
Access to healthcare is not simply a matter of getting an appointment or obtaining medicines. Older people who depend on younger family members for hospital visits may have to wait until someone can take time off work and accompany them.
Members of several associations say a family member’s availability often influences whether and when an older person seeks medical attention. Those with limited mobility may need transport, a wheelchair or stretcher. In a multi-storey building without a suitable lift, even getting someone downstairs can require additional assistance and planning. Hospital visits can involve long walks between departments, diagnostic tests and consultations, making them particularly difficult for those without someone to accompany them.
The problem does not end at the hospital gate. For older people who cannot leave home, finding a doctor willing to make a home visit can be equally difficult. “This is a crucial requirement of those who are unable to step out of their house,” says Sobha.
For older couples whose children have moved away for work, one partner falling ill can leave the other struggling to coordinate treatment, travel and follow-up visits. The absence of accessible transport and medical services at home can turn routine healthcare into an exhausting exercise.
Shanti, trustee and volunteer at Roshni Trust, which has organised mental health camps in bastis, says Hyderabad’s urban spaces do little to encourage inclusion and social interaction among older people. “The city is designed for isolation and does not promote inclusiveness,” she says.
Shanti calls for government centres at the basti level, on the lines of Anganwadis, where older people can access basic facilities, attend health camps and receive nutritious food. Such centres could also offer a place to meet others, reducing isolation among those who spend much of their time at home.
The search for dependable care
For older people who need help with daily activities, finding a caregiver presents its own difficulties. Volunteers point to the need for people who understand the physical and emotional needs of senior citizens, as well as concerns about safety when elderly couples live alone and their children live elsewhere. Sobha recalls the case of an elderly woman who sleeps during the day and stays awake at night to keep an eye on her caregiver, fearing for her safety.
“This fear weighs on many older people who live with hired help,” she adds.
Through Telangana Stree Seva Samstha, she along with 80-plus volunteers, distributes adult diapers, commode converter seats, walking sticks, books and other resources to those who need them.
S. Bhooma Reddy (78), editor of Voice of Senior Citizens magazine, says the demand for caregivers is substantial, with some families hiring them even when their children live in the same building. “The caregivers are paid a monthly salary of around ₹25,000, apart from being provided food and accommodation,” he adds.
Such arrangements, however, remain beyond the reach of many households. Families from financially disadvantaged backgrounds often live in cramped homes and juggle work, household responsibilities and the care of parents or in-laws with limited resources.
V. Manjula, president of Gruha Karmikula Union-Telangana, says opening community halls where older people are provided regular meals and medicines would be a significant source of support for those from poor backgrounds.
The consequences of inadequate family support can be more severe than the absence of daily assistance. Associations report cases of older people being abandoned at hospitals, railway stations and bus stops. They also cite instances of elderly parents being neglected after transferring property to their children. Physical ailments are not the only problems that can go unnoticed as people grow older. Depression and dementia, too, may remain undiagnosed because their early signs are mistaken for normal aspects of ageing.
K. Chandra Sekhar, 70, founder-director of ASHA Hospitals, says families often seek specialist help only after symptoms have worsened. Forgetfulness, which can be an early sign of dementia, is frequently dismissed as a natural consequence of growing old. Such assumptions can delay diagnosis and prevent older people and their families from accessing appropriate support.
“Early diagnosis can improve quality of life and help caregivers prepare for the support that may be required as a condition progresses,” he says.
A loss of interest in activities once enjoyed, reduced appetite and weight loss, less social interaction and multiple physical complaints can be signs of depression, Dr. Chandra Sekhar points out. Older people experiencing forgetfulness can consult neurologists or psychiatrists.
While health camps often screen for physical illnesses, camps focused on identifying mental health problems are rarely organised, he says.
Aarathi Bellary, consultant physician and co-founder of Aayu Geriatrics, says some older people overlook age-related health problems even when symptoms become apparent.
“While physiological issues get attention, mental health issues in old age are barely discussed. One should not dismiss every problem as an inevitable part of ageing. It is important to consult the relevant medical specialists,” she says.
Dr. Bellary also encourages older people to pursue hobbies, maintain an active social life and take part in activities that allow them to share their knowledge and experience. Such engagement can help them remain socially connected rather than being defined solely by their health needs.
Planning for assisted living
For those who need more sustained support, assisted living and other residential care options could fill a gap between hospital treatment and independent living. Hyderabad, however, has only a few such facilities.
Ambati Rampapa Rao, chairman of PACCS Healthcare Pvt Ltd, which has a subsidiary, Ucchvas Transitional Care Centres, says longer life expectancy has made it necessary to plan for the changing needs of older people, particularly when their children move out of their hometown.
Ageing can bring a range of difficulties, including reduced physical strength, tremors, weight loss, malnutrition and emotional or psychological problems, affecting one’s ability to carry out everyday activities.
Dr. Rao outlines three broad categories of elderly care. Transitional care provides support immediately after hospital discharge, ranging from a few weeks to several years, with some degree of medical supervision; assisted living caters to those whose age and medical history call for monitoring and preventive care; and elderly living facilities serve people who remain mobile but have minor health problems.
“Social and aspirational security has to be factored in while designing spaces for the elderly, to meet their emotional and intellectual aspirations. This has to be planned for people of all financial segments,” he says.
With corporates exploring investments in the sector, the number of facilities could increase. But affordability remains central to whether these services can reach those who need them the most.
Care beyond the family
The Telangana government has sanctioned 37 multi-service daycare centres for senior citizens, of which 32 are operational. Run by non-governmental organisations with full financial support and monitoring from the government, the centres encourage social interaction and provide nutritious food, indoor games and basic medical check-ups once a week.
For older people who depend on regular meals or monitoring of health conditions, however, the reliability of these services matters as much as their availability. One elderly woman says she worries that health problems could jeopardise her access to the centre.
“My sugar levels shoot up if I don’t have food on time. Someone else may develop other health problems. If we fall ill at the centre, our children may consider taking us there a hassle and ask us to stop going,” she says.
Her concern points to a larger dilemma: services intended to support older people may not be enough if families view the time and effort involved in accessing them as a burden.
As Telangana’s elderly population grows, the challenge will be to make care accessible not only to those who can afford paid assistance, but also to people whose health problems, limited mobility or financial circumstances threaten their independence.

Antimatter is not known for being easy to get ahold of. That’s part of why these particles remain so cryptic. But recently, a team of physicists at Northwestern University managed to trap a single antimatter particle for months. Cooling it to temperatures near absolute zero, they could control its quantum states with great precision without even touching it. The experiment, published in Physical Review Letters, represents a breakthrough in our understanding of one of the great mysteries of physics.
In theory, antimatter should be everywhere. Mathematics predicts that every particle of matter has an equivalent antiparticle, a fact that scientists have verified experimentally. The universe should therefore contain similar amounts of both, but almost everything we observe is made up of ordinary matter, and we still don’t know why.
It is possible to produce antimatter particles in laboratories, but studying them is still incredibly difficult. When an antiparticle comes into contact with ordinary matter, the two annihilate each other and release energy. To prevent research facilities from exploding, scientists use vacuum chambers and electromagnetic fields that suspend the antiparticles in isolation. But this only partially solves the problem. Studying these particles, especially experimenting with their behavior on a quantum scale, remains challenging.
For this experiment, researchers at Northwestern trapped a positron, the antimatter counterpart of electrons. The team, led by Gerald Gabrielse, developed a device known as a single-positron quantum cyclotron, which used electric and magnetic fields to hold the positron in a vacuum at a temperature close to absolute zero. This means the antimatter particle was at its lowest energy state, allowing the researchers to induce controlled changes in its quantum behavior. Unlike other methods in particle physics, this approach didn’t destroy the particle. The researchers were therefore able to keep the single antiparticle trapped for months, allowing them to repeat measurements.
So what can taming antimatter particles actually teach us? Scientists know that matter and antimatter have very similar properties. For example, an electron and a positron have exactly the same mass, although their electric charges are opposite. However, questions still remain about exactly how similar these two forms of matter are and whether there are small differences that have gone unnoticed in experiments conducted to date.
To this end, researchers want to compare the magnetic properties of both particles. Physicists have already made very precise measurements with electrons, but achieving the same level of precision with positrons has proven more difficult. According to the American Physical Society, the new device could enable measurements of antimatter particles about 30 times more precise than scientists were capable of before.
So far, the experiment has not revealed any unexpected differences between the two particles. What the researchers have achieved is an improvement in their ability to detect these differences in antimatter particles. If future measurements find that a positron responds to magnetic fields differently than an electron, scientists would have to revise some of the laws they use to explain the behavior of matter and antimatter.

Remember the charm of walking into a Crossword store, picking up a book and spending hours reading it without anyone expecting you to buy it? With cosy reading corners, a café on the side and occasional author interactions, it gave book lovers a place to unwind, explore and lose themselves in stories. Or Hamleys, where little eyes light up and young hearts skip a beat at the sight of colourful toys and a magical world that feels straight out of a storybook. Brands such as Pepperfry have also made shopping more personal by letting customers experience how furniture and décor would look and feel in fully furnished living rooms, bedrooms and dining spaces. Chumbak, meanwhile, brings its playful personality to life through colourful interiors and distinctive designs that make its stores as vibrant as the products on display. Of course, how can one forget Decathlon? Long before experiential retail became a buzzword, these stores gave customers several reasons to visit beyond simply making a purchase. Now, a new wave of fashion and lifestyle brands is borrowing this playbook to take experiential retail a step further. Rather than simply creating attractive spaces or encouraging product discovery, brands such as Gully Labs, Comet, Nothing, Almost Gods and Broadway are experimenting with store design and riffing on traditional retail motifs to bring their brand identity to life. Take Comet's flagship store in Bengaluru's Indiranagar, for instance. With shattered walls, suspended rock formations and sneakers seemingly emerging from concrete, the space resembles the aftermath of a comet crashing to the ground rather than a conventional footwear showroom. Yet, the experience isn't just about aesthetics. Instead of crowding shelves with inventory, Comet displays a curated selection of sneakers, with additional sizes stored in concealed drawers. Its dedicated section, The Vault, showcases sold-out sneakers like museum exhibits, even though they are no longer available for purchase. The D2C sneaker brand spent around seven to eight months designing and building the store, working with an architecture firm to bring its unusual concept to life. While store design has increasingly become a way to communicate brand identity, build communities and create unique experiences, how are brands balancing creative ambition with the unit economics realities? And can their distinctive retail experiences become a lasting competitive advantage? Reinventing The Storefront For years, the conventional retail store followed a familiar pattern. Products occupied shelves, promotional displays highlighted the latest collections, and layouts were designed to move shoppers towards the billing counter. That formula works, but does not really motivate customers, who can buy almost anything from their phones, to make the effort to visit a store. The reason is simple. They are looking for more than a transaction. The influence of this thinking is visible at Broadway, a multi-brand fashion and lifestyle retailer housing more than 200 brands. Rather than relying entirely on merchandise displays, it has integrated services and activities that encourage customers to explore products in different ways. For example, its stores feature salon experiences for beauty product trials and sampling, alongside dedicated stages where brands can organise events and interact with their communities. It also offers AI-assisted analysis to help shoppers identify shades and products that suit their skin tones and complexion, with stylists able to recommend products accordingly. However, the process involves continuous experimentation. “A service that appears attractive during planning may not necessarily appeal to customers once introduced. These decisions are refined based on customer behaviour rather than treated as permanent elements of the original design,” said a sectoral expert. But the push towards experiential retail is not being driven by changing consumer expectations alone. For digital-first brands, it is also becoming a question of customer acquisition. Ujwal Sutaria, founding partner at VC firm TDV Partners believes the rising cost of digital advertising is making physical stores an increasingly interesting brand-building channel. "Digital acquisition costs in India have become brutal, and a store on a 100 ft road can work as a better ad than any Instagram budget,” Sutaria said. This is particularly relevant for brands selling premium products. For a shopper considering a pair of sneakers north of ₹5K, the opportunity to examine the product, understand its craftsmanship and experience the brand firsthand could help overcome hesitation that digital advertising alone may struggle to address. Are There Execution Challenges? According to Mitali Juneja, creative director at architectural design planning and studio, Studio Ordonnance, the architecture firm behind Comet and Almost Gods' stores, most established retailers still prefer conventional formats. The hesitation may not be financial. In larger organisations, proposals have to go through multiple levels of approval. Also, many decision-makers could be wary of committing to unfamiliar or unconventional ideas. On the flip side, founder-led brands have greater flexibility to experiment, offering the reason why some of the more visible experiments are emerging from younger brands rather than established retail chains. Next, even after a concept is approved, a transition to a physical space can be difficult. Unconventional installations often require techniques that local fabricators have little experience with. For Comet’s suspended rock structures, for instance, Mitali's team had to repeatedly guide workers accustomed to making traditional sculptures. To minimise errors, detailed working drawings and inspections at different construction stages are needed. Architects must also adapt designs to the property’s structural limitations, including ceiling heights and building specifications. However, she believes the bigger challenge is balancing creativity with functionality. Product visibility, customer comfort and the ease of trying or purchasing merchandise cannot be compromised simply to create an unusual-looking store. The goal, therefore, is not just to deliver an impressive space, but one that works equally well for the brand and its customers. Can The Experience Pay For Itself? For fashion and lifestyle brands already grappling with high rentals and operating costs, the question is whether a distinctive store can generate enough value to justify the additional investment. Sutaria believes that looking at store-level sales alone misses the wider contribution of experiential retail. A customer may discover a sneaker brand offline, try its products and eventually purchase online. Similarly, a store event could generate interest well beyond its immediate neighbourhood. "Store P&L alone is the wrong lens. I'd look at the halo effect: Is online traffic and conversion rising in nearby pincodes? What's the blended CAC for customers who discover the brand in-store? Do they repeat more often?" Sutaria explained. However, the challenge is establishing whether these interactions generate additional business or simply create visibility. For multi-brand retailers such as Broadway, this becomes even harder, as product trials, sampling and engagement with individual brands may not immediately translate into sales. Yet, the investment can pay off. According to Comet cofounder Utkarsh Gupta, its Indiranagar flagship achieved a seven-month capex payback despite costing 20–50% more than a conventional store. He also claims it records the highest conversion rate among footwear stores on that high street. However, Sutaria cautions that the economics must ultimately justify the experience. “If the store lowers blended CAC and improves repeat rates enough to lift brand-level LTV, the capex is justified. Otherwise, it's just an expensive billboard." Can Every Store Be A Flagship? Even if an experiential store delivers strong returns, replicating the same concept across dozens of locations can be expensive and time-consuming. Comet is addressing this by standardising most of its design elements while experimenting at select locations. According to Gupta, nearly 90% of the brand’s design elements are scalable, allowing it to retain a consistent identity without repeating the seven-to-eight-month development process required for its first flagship. However, Sutaria also believes that most single-brand D2C companies will follow a different approach. “The scalable version is a hub-and-spoke model: one or two flagships build culture, while smaller formats and shared-shelf platforms drive reach. That's why Broadway is interesting. Its 40,000 sq ft Bandra flagship houses 200+ brands, spreading the cost of the experience across multiple businesses." Such shared formats could offer emerging fashion and lifestyle brands access to product discovery, sampling and community engagement without requiring each to build an expensive standalone store. Still, expansion is not the only challenge. An elaborate store can lose its novelty, while excessive investment in physical retail can divert resources from product development and distribution. Juneja of Studio Ordonnance believes some experimental design elements will eventually disappear because they are impractical. However, she expects the broader shift towards stores that express a brand's identity to continue. The real test, therefore, will be creating spaces that remain distinctive without compromising the shopping experience or the economics of running a retail business. THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW KOBSOOK IS BRINGING NEURODIVERGENT ARTISTS TO SNEAKER DESIGN KobSook turns original artwork by neurodivergent artists into limited-edition canvas sneakers. The brand works with AEMP (Inclusive Accessible TechEd) as a training partner to help artists develop skills in design and other business operations. Its portfolio spans high-tops, low-top sneakers, loafers and slip-ons for men and women, with designs featuring doodles, abstract patterns, colourful checks and other original artwork. Products listed on its website span roughly ₹1,700 to ₹2,500 at sale prices. KobSook produces limited quantities of each design rather than relying on mass production, and also accepts requests for customised designs. The brand sells through its own website and ecommerce marketplaces including Myntra, Amazon, AJIO and Flipkart. The Deep Dive Ecommerce Buzz L Catterton Bets On Glance: The consumer-focused investment firm has invested in InMobi-backed Glance to support the latter’s US expansion. Currently, Glance uses agentic AI to drive product discovery and purchases across smartphones and connected TVs, including through partnerships with Samsung, Motorola and DIRECTV in the US. Myntra Swings To Loss: Flipkart-owned Myntra reported a net loss of ₹581.8 Cr in FY26, reversing a ₹546.3 Cr profit a year earlier. This came on the back of its operating revenue falling 13.5% to ₹5,242.5 Cr. The move comes as Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27 PharmEasy Veterans Raise ₹63 Cr: Founded by five former PharmEasy executives, Chapter Homes raised ₹63 Cr at a valuation of nearly ₹1,000 Cr. The startup plans to expand beyond its HOKIPO home furnishings brand into cookware, home décor and small kitchen appliances, using AI and a shared supply chain to scale its portfolio. The Operator Question How can pop-up shops at festive carnivals (Durga Puja/Diwali/Christmas melas) help unconventional new-age lifestyle brands? What is the cost involved? Is it worth the investment? How should brands measure the ROI? Speaking to Inc42, Cure By Design founder Daanish Matheen spoke about the pop-up shop aspect of D2C retail. The startup offers hemp-based CBD oils, balms and pain-relief solutions, alongside personal care and nutrition products such as shampoos, face washes, serums and food items. For unconventional lifestyle brands like Cure By Design, festive pop-ups offer an opportunity to reach new audiences, build trust, and increase brand awareness. Since cannabidiol (CBD) is still an emerging category in India, these events allow the brand to educate consumers, address misconceptions, and encourage first-time purchases. Costs vary depending on the event, location, and footfall, with expenses including stall rentals, staffing, logistics, and branding. We've participated in pop-ups occasionally but have reduced them significantly since opening our retail stores in Bengaluru and Chennai. Permanent stores provide better customer engagement, stronger credibility, and more consistent conversions. For us, ROI goes beyond immediate sales. We evaluate customer acquisition costs, leads generated, repeat purchases, and long-term customer value. Ultimately, pop-ups are worthwhile when they attract the right audience and build lasting customer relationships rather than simply generating footfall.

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressives councillors.
The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13 percentage point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared to Bradford’s 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.
Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. Her win also signals voters see that progressive urban politics can resist cost-of-living backlash that has toppled over governments.
On Monday night, Chow thanked her supporters and Bradford.
“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”
Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023.
Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.
While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.
Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.
In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers other vulnerable institutions.
In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”
Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.
Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes.
Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on city council.

- The claim that illegal votes cast on behalf of dead people still listed on voter rolls have swayed U.S. elections is historically false.
- U.S. President Donald Trump helped popularize the claim as part of his "Stop the Steal" rhetoric before and after he lost the 2020 presidential election.
- Multiple studies, including one Trump reportedly paid a research group to conduct, found that though instances have occurred, the number of votes actually cast in the names of dead people and counted is too small to sway election results.
- Not all instances of dead people voting involve intentional fraud, either, though fraud is a factor in a fraction of cases. Sometimes, votes attributed to dead people have been counted due to clerical errors or simply because of a timing issue; e.g., a voter submits a mail-in ballot, maybe early, and then dies before Election Day (although several states deem such votes legitimate).
The long-standing claim that U.S. election results have been swayed by votes illegally cast on behalf of dead people resurfaced during the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections.
The rumor is recirculated every election cycle but gained new momentum before and after the 2020 presidential election thanks to President Donald Trump's "Stop the Steal" rhetoric, which also played a role in sparking the insurrection at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
In recent months, Trump again floated the idea that dead people were voting in droves.
"Hundreds of thousands of noncitizens and dead people are listed and active on the voter rolls, and yet we still have elections with no voter ID, no proof of citizenship and tens of millions of ballots floating aimlessly through the mail," he said during a July news conference (at 35:45).
We found this claim to be false.
This fact check builds on and updates reporting Snopes initially conducted ahead of the 2024 presidential election. Below, we break down how we determined that the claim widespread election fraud has taken place in the form of dead people voting is false:
How often are dead peoples' ballots cast?
The short answer: Though it can sometimes happen, studies show the rate of dead people voting is insignificant and is not enough to sway election results.
As mail-in voting has become increasingly accessible — particularly spurred by the COVID-19 pandemic — the public's trust in the electoral system has declined, according to a 2020 study by the Pew Research Center.
Every U.S. state offers some form of absentee or mail-in voting, meaning that voters have the option to mail in their vote instead of voting in person. Some states require voters to initiate the mail-in process by ordering a ballot, and some require voters to provide a reason they're unable to vote in person, such as illness or disability, in order to receive a mail-in ballot. Eight states — California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington — have an automatic mail-in ballot system.
(ballotpedia.org)
Despite assertions that mail-in voting makes it easier for nefarious actors to vote on behalf of dead people, a 2020 study by Stanford University based on data from Washington state — one of the most prominent mail-in states in recent decades — found that between 2011 and 2018, there were only 14 dead people whose ballots were cast "suspiciously long" after their deaths. That represents 0.0003% of Washington voters for that time period. They identified these 14 people by matching birthdates and their full names to ballots, including middle names.
The study said:
Even these few cases may reflect two individuals with the same name and birth date, or clerical errors, rather than fraud. If we relax requirements for matching middle names to accommodate people who may not have middle names, we estimate that there are an additional 43 cases of potential fraud, but these are more likely to be false positives. On the whole, the results suggest that it is extremely rare for dead people's ballots to be counted as votes in Washington's universal vote-by-mail system.
The study noted that because Washington has had years to perfect its mail-in process, other states could potentially have a higher rate of dead people voting.
Following Trump's loss in 2020, he contested the outcome of six battleground states in particular: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In 2021, The Associated Press conducted a review of every potential case of voter fraud in those states, including cases where ballots were cast in the names of dead people.
The AP found fewer than 475 cases of fraud in those six states — a number that would not have had a significant effect on the 2020 presidential election results.
In 2023, The Washington Post reported that Trump's campaign had paid researchers $600,000 to investigate potential fraud in that same election. According to the Post, there was "no reason to believe the final vote totals in five key states were fraudulent." (The Trump-commissioned report has not been made public, as of this writing, and only reportedly surfaced after the Justice Department obtained it through a subpoena.)
Why might a state count a dead person's vote?
Not all instances of dead people voting are the result of intentional fraud, though that does make up a fraction of cases. Sometimes, dead people's votes are counted simply because of a timing issue; e.g., a voter submits a mail-in ballot, maybe early, and then dies before Election Day (although several states permit this).
Clerical errors, though rare, can either result in dead peoples' votes being mistakenly counted or votes cast by people who are alive being mistakenly marked as cast by a dead person.
Intentional fraud
There have been recorded cases in which someone intentionally committed voter fraud by submitting a ballot in the name of a dead person. In some cases, the ballot for a deceased family member showed up in the mail and a member of the household submitted it on their behalf.
Russel Hobbs, a 56-year-old man from Washington state, illegally signed and submitted a ballot in his wife's name in the 2020 election. She had died about three months earlier. "I think [Hobbs] just tried to honor his deceased loved one," his attorney said to the Tacoma News Tribune. He was sentenced to 80 hours of community service.
In another 2020 case, a man from Pennsylvania cast a vote on behalf of his dead mother, but the state caught the illegal ballot and sentenced him to five years of probation. "I was isolated last year in lockdown," Bruce Bartman told the court by way of explanation. "I listened to too much propaganda and made a stupid mistake."
But despite the existence of such recorded cases of fraud — whether it was grief, propaganda or something else that motivated the acts — the number of those cases is so low so as to not have an effect on national elections.
Clerical and data errors
People who verify ballots aren't immune to mistakes, and in some cases clerical errors have resulted in a living person being mistakenly marked as deceased.
Jason Roberts, a political science professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, reportedly told the AP in 2022 that "election integrity groups scouring voter files often mistake a living voter for a deceased voter if they have similar names, birthdays or hometowns, resulting in false fraud claims."
For example, according to The Brennan Center for Justice — an independent, nonpartisan law and policy organization at the New York University School of Law — "a 2007 investigation of about 100 'dead voters' in Missouri revealed that every single purported case was properly attributed either to a matching error, a problem in the underlying data, or a clerical error by elections officials or voters."
What if someone mails in their vote then dies before Election Day?
As of this writing, 10 states specifically allow the votes of deceased persons who filled in ballots before they died to be count. Twelve states explicitly prohibit such votes from being counted, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures,a bipartisan policy research organization. The report reads:
- Ten states—Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, North Dakota, Tennessee and Virginia—have statutes that explicitly permit counting absentee ballots cast by voters who die before Election Day. California permits counting these ballots through administrative regulation rather than statute. One state—Connecticut—only counts these ballots if the deceased voter is a member of the armed services.
- Twelve states—Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, South Dakota and Wisconsin—have statutes that explicitly prohibit counting absentee ballots cast by voters who die before Election Day. Missouri law states that such ballots be rejected only if sufficient evidence is shown to an election authority that the voter has died before the opening of the polls on Election Day, and the deceased voter's ballot is still sealed in the ballot envelope. Michigan requires that a clerk make their "best effort to remove the absent voter ballot" and spoil that voter's ballot.
- At least two states—Kentucky and Mississippi—also prohibit counting deceased voters' ballots, but through attorneys general opinions, rather than statute.
Other states either don't have explicit guidance or stipulate that absentee ballots can be challenged on the grounds that a voter died before the day of the election.
What countermeasures exist?
With a combination of punishments for illegal voting and efforts to monitor the legitimacy of ballots, states work to combat votes "cast" by dead people, whether intentionally or accidentally.
Legal penalties for intentionally casting a vote on behalf of a dead person may include probation, a fine or even prison time, depending on the specific charges and the state.
Also, election offices take steps to keep voter lists accurate, such as regularly checking death records, obituaries and driver's-license cancellation records. The Help America Vote Act of 2002 requires states to work with the state agency in charge of recording deaths (most often a bureau of vital statistics or the health department) to keep registration records up to date.
Other acceptable methods for voter verification vary by state, such as notification by a funeral director or the military, family reports, obituaries and other forms of record.

Publishing house Kodansha announced Tuesday that manga artist Tetsuya Chiba, best known for co-creating the popular boxing series “Ashita no Joe,” died at 87 last Thursday at a hospital in Tokyo.
With a career spanning seven decades, Chiba was a key figure in establishing sports manga as a major genre. In 2024, he became the first manga artist to receive the Order of Culture, one of the country’s highest cultural honors.
“Tetsuya Chiba created numerous masterpieces throughout his 70-year career, driven by a strong love for and faith in the medium of manga,” Kodansha’s statement read, going on to highlight the Chiba Tetsuya Award, which was established 46 years ago to nurture new talent. “Many aspiring manga artists took their first steps toward professional careers with his words in their hearts — and they continue to be active in the industry today. His immense contributions to the manga world are irreplaceable.”

Congress gets permission for rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, but with conditions
The conditions laid down by Delhi Police require the organisers to ensure adequate security arrangements, install high-definition CCTV cameras, provide drinking water and toilets, deploy volunteers and ensure that the gathering remains peaceful. The rally's scheduled duration cannot be extended under any circumstances.
The Delhi Police has cleared the Congress rally scheduled at Ramlila Maidan on November 1, 2026, imposing a series of conditions on the organisers, including a strict 5 pm deadline to conclude the event, CCTV surveillance and a ban on marches outside the venue. The no-objection certificate (NOC), issued on October 17, remains valid and has not been revoked, according to a copy of the permission letter.
The development comes amid a row over the Congress and INDIA bloc's proposed programme against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The opposition parties had planned a “public impeachment” event on October 30 as a curtain-raiser for the November 1 rally, but Congress general secretary (organisation) K C Venugopal alleged that permission for the initially planned venue, Ashok Hotel, was withdrawn following police intervention.
Venugopal had said the Congress booked Ramlila Maidan from October 25 to November 3 and decided to shift the programme there after facing difficulties securing a venue. He also alleged that police had stopped workers from setting up infrastructure at the ground.
The November 1 rally is part of the opposition's campaign over alleged electoral irregularities and its ‘vote chori’ allegations against the BJP. The Congress and its INDIA bloc allies have also raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded accountability from the Election Commission.
RALLY MUST END BY 5 PM, NO OVERNIGHT STAY
Under the conditions laid down by the Delhi Police, the rally must conclude by 5 pm on November 1, with no extension of the programme permitted under any circumstances. The process of dispersing participants must begin immediately after the event ends.
The organisers have also been barred from allowing participants to stay at Ramlila Maidan overnight, either before or after the rally. Any march from the venue to another location during the event is prohibited.

CCTV SURVEILLANCE, CONTROL ROOM MANDATORY
The permission requires the organisers to install high-definition CCTV cameras at the venue's entry and exit gates, stage, seating areas and surrounding locations. A control room equipped with at least five monitors must be set up, with arrangements to record the footage.
Organisers must also provide adequate drinking water through tankers and ensure sufficient toilet facilities for participants, including separate toilet blocks for women.
A sufficient number of volunteers must be deployed to manage the crowd and ensure the smooth conduct of the rally. All volunteers must be identifiable through a uniform dress code or badges.
NO INFLAMMATORY SPEECHES, VIOLENCE
The Delhi Police has made the organisers responsible for ensuring that the rally remains peaceful and does not lead to violence, disorder or any disruption of law and order.
Speeches from the stage must not create tensions or disturb social harmony on the basis of caste, religion or colour. If a speaker delivers an inflammatory or threatening speech, the organisers must immediately switch off the microphone and remove the speaker from the stage.
The organisers are also required to cooperate fully with the police and comply with all applicable laws and regulations. They must make adequate arrangements to manage participants and maintain public order throughout the event.
ORGANISERS MUST SUBMIT DETAILS TO POLICE
The organisers are required to cooperate fully with the Delhi Police and comply with all applicable laws and regulations. They must make the necessary arrangements to manage participants and maintain public order throughout the gathering.
The police have also directed them to submit a list of invitees and volunteers, a minute-by-minute schedule of the programme, the number of buses expected and their registration numbers. Any violation of the conditions may invite legal action against the organisers, police have said.

Australia to tighten sunscreen testing after popular products fail protection claims
Tests found that 16 of 20 popular products failed to deliver the protection promised on their labels

Australia is proposing tougher rules for sunscreen manufacturers after tests found that 16 of 20 popular products failed to deliver the sun protection factor (SPF) advertised on their labels.
The findings came to light in 2025, when consumer group Choice tested popular sunscreens and found that some products offered nowhere near the protection promised on their packaging.
Ultra Violette’s Lean Screen SPF 50+ Mattifying Zinc Skinscreen, for instance, returned an SPF rating of just four. The product was later withdrawn, along with other sunscreens made using the same base formula.
The company’s co-founders, Ava Chandler-Matthews and Bec Jefferd, apologised to customers last year, offered them refunds, and asked them to stop using the product, according to reports.
Now, Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) wants manufacturers to test the finished products they sell, rather than relying on results from tests of their base formulas alone. Brands would have to submit their results to the regulator before putting products on sale and repeat testing throughout their shelf life.
The proposed changes state that the results would remain confidential, and the TGA would not routinely check the data before products reached shop shelves, according to ABC News.
Until now, manufacturers have not had to provide SPF test results unless the regulator specifically requested them.
Andy Kelly, Choice’s director of consumer impact, welcomed the proposals but said the regulator needed to go further. In a statement on Tuesday, the consumer group called for test results to be made public and for the TGA to carry out its own compliance testing.
“In the interest of transparency and public safety, we believe these results should be made available to everyone and that the TGA should routinely monitor test results, as well as conduct its own compliance testing program,” Choice said in a statement.
The TGA considered publishing the results but decided against it, citing concerns about commercial confidentiality, intellectual property and the risk that consumers might misinterpret technical data.
Robyn Langham, the TGA’s chief medical adviser, said: “This is about making SPF claims more reliable, reinforcing suppliers’ responsibility for their products, and giving the TGA faster access to evidence when concerns arise.”
Some foundations and other cosmetics sold in Australia can advertise SPF 50+ even though sun protection is not their primary purpose.
The TGA wants to limit the SPF claims these products can make, making it easier for consumers to distinguish them from sunscreens designed primarily to protect against ultraviolet radiation.
The reforms are not yet in force.
The TGA received 119 submissions during a consultation held between March and May 2026, and says some changes could be introduced in the short term, while others will require further consultation or legislative amendments.
Australia has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world, with two in three Australians expected to be diagnosed during their lifetime. Around 2,000 people die from the disease each year, according to Cancer Council Australia.

World champion Jepchirchir fails drugs test
- Published
Olympic and World Championships marathon gold medallist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO.
Kenyan Jepchirchir provided the sample prior to winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026.
The 33-year-old clocked a time of two hours, 18 minutes and 31 seconds to win in Sydney.
EPO, or erythropoietin, is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it is only detectable in the urine or blood for a short window of time, and increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream.
Jepchirchir became the Olympic women's marathon champion at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and returned to the Japanese capital to win the World Championships in September 2025.
She broke the women's half-marathon world record in 2017 and on three occasions in 2020.
In addition to Sydney, her other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
Jepchirchir won the Sydney race, which became the seventh world major in 2025, by more than three minutes from compatriot Irene Chepet Cheptai.
She provided the sample which tested positive for EPO while in Kenya prior to the race.
